Mr. THOMSON. What are we doing in relation to buying in Korea? 

Are we buying steel in Japan?

Mr. POATS. No; we are not. There has been some confusion in the public description of our policy. We are undertaking a pilot procurement procedure a 90to 120-day trial-permitting Vietnamese importers to buy either directly from the United States or from those less developed Asian countries which agree to accept in payment an AID letter of credit tied to purchases from the United States of steel products, tools with a high iron and steel content, and a stipulated quantity of scrap.

These Asian producers such as the Koreans or Taiwanese-two countries which have accepted this letter-of-credit arrangement-may buy the semifinished materials which go into galvanized sheet or pipe, from any free world source. The Koreans or Chinese receive payment in a letter of credit tied to procurement of the U.S. products that I mentioned.

The consequence of this, we believe, will be that Taiwan and Korea will increase their purchases of iron and steel products from the United States in amounts greater than the amount they expend in Japan-if they buy from Japan-on semifinished steel. 

Mr. THOMSON. Are we really trying to help our fighting ally Korea economically by the military and economic purchases there?"

ewart afeg

Mr. POATS. In a sense, yes. This policy resulted from our inability adequately to enforce the componentry rules which apply on most commodities.

In a homogeneous commodity like a sheet of steel, it is difficult to determine where the components came from. We found the componentry rule hard to enforce. The Koreans argued they were complying because they were buying in the United States scrap valued at more than the value of the scrap that went into the semifinished black plate purchased in Japan.

We disagreed with that interpretation and suspended procurement of steel products from Korea. This happened shortly after the 

Koreans sent troops to Vietnam.

The Koreans at that time were seeking to expand their sales to Vietham. They resented this denial of a market to them which they thought they held legitimately. I was also concerned that to suspend procurement of this important item in the commercial import program would have a damaging effect on prices in Vietnam and would cause further inflationary pressures.

We worked out a scheme which we felt certain would assure continued rapid supply of low-cost galvanized sheet to Vietnam, would offer Korea a chance for exports, and, at the same time, would not damage the U.S. steel industry or the U.S. balance of payments. 

I presented this scheme to representatives of the steel industry in this country, and they endorsed it. 

Subsequently, after there was some controversy about it, I had a meeting with representatives of the Iron & Steel Institute. They expressed no opposition to the plan. There has been opposition to it by some salesmen of American steel products who I think, frankly, simply don't understand that the ultimate consequence will be that these dollars will flow back to the U.S. iron and steel industry. 

Mr. THOMSON. I asked Mr. Bell the other day if his appeals for civilians to go into the program to stabilize the villages had produced any response other than from members of the U.S. Congress. Could you give us your view on how people are volunteering to assist?

Mr. POATS. We are getting many volunteers. We have conducted several recruiting campaigns in major cities. One is going on now in New Orleans. We are attempting to insure that we get good people, people who can learn the Vietnamese language, people who can adapt to a village situation and work well with the military forces and the local government.

We are expanding our staff. The staff in the provinces will be nearly doubled by this coming June over last June. We are putting many recruits into training. This causes temporary shortages of people in the field. This is a hard decision to make but we think it is the right one.

We have set up a training program at the University of Hawaii to concentrate our training of these village level workers for Vietnam, Thailand, and Laos.

On trade they have made it pretty clear that they would not trade with us. For us to take any public initiative in this area would be construed wrongly by them and to some extent by other nations in the area and would lead nowhere.

INFORMATION ON TITLE VIII 

The new title underscores the special significance of the expanded southeast Asia development program which the President proposed in his speech delivered at Johns Hopkins University on April 7, 1965.

Section 271, whch relates to general provisions, is the first section of the new title. Congressional approval of the title will reaffirm the importance the United 

States places on economic and social progress in achieving foreign policy objectives of peace and stability in southeast Asia, placing special emphasis upon cooperative efforts to solve social and economic problems in the region.

Section 271 authorizes the President to furnish assistance to southeast Asia through multilateral institutions and through multilateral and/or bilateral programs or projects which serve regional development purposes. The furnishing of assistance under this title would, of course, be subject to appropriation requests to the Congress, based on specific programs. 

While it is not possible at this time to indicate specific magnitudes of funds for which appropriations will be sought under the proposed authority, the executive branch considers favorable action by the Congress to be of particularly timely importance.

We feel that the establishment of a separate title and special authority for assistance to southeast Asia has the unique advantage of demonstrating this emphasis as a new departure thereby drawing the interest of other countries and encouraging their contributions to multilaterally administered funds for development in southeast Asia. Increased involvement on the part of developed nations in the future of southeast Asia is an important objective of the President's new approach to the problems of the region. 

The criteria set forth under section 272 of the new title are designed to encourage Asian initiatives in development and to stimulate cooperative efforts in solving common problems. Thus, funds used for the purposes of this title could be made available to the International Bank for Reconstruction and 

Development and the Asian Development Bank under their supervision, employing their criteria and procedures instead of those of AID. This would insure that these two Banks could operate as truly independent international institutions and administer effectively multilateral funds made up of contributions from more than one country.

Section 273 of the new title authorizes appropriations to the President for each of the fiscal years 1967 through 1971 of such funds as may be necessary to carry out the purposes of this title. However, no appropriation under this title is being requested at this time for fiscal year 1967. The executive branch will seek funds under this authorization as additional programs are developed. In fiscal year 1967 the initial portions of the expanded southeast Asia development program will continue to be carried out on a limited basis with technical cooperation and supporting assistance funds, to the extent those funds are available for such activities.

The executive branch would, of course, be available for further examination of the program by the committee. This would permit the committee to make informed recommendations regarding the course of AID programs under title

At the top of page 12 of your statement you say that U.S. AID personnel are working in the rural areas of Laos. Can you tell the committee if any Lao Government personnel are working with AID and IVS personnel in these villages and what do they do? This you can supply for the record if you would. 

Thank you. 

 LAO GOVERNMENT PERSONNEL INVOLVEMENT IN VILLAGE CLUSTER PROGRAM 

AID community development advisers and IVS personnel work closely at provincial levels with provincial Governors and district officials in the development of rural programs. Tassangs, the equivalent of our elected township supervisors, and Naibans (village chiefs) are often the center of planning activity. Agents of several Royal Lao Government ministries provide services in the villages. 

Among these are the Agricultural Extension Service, the Lao Veterinary Service, the Forestry and Water Service, and the Public Works Department. In addition to the provision of teachers for the school system, the Education Ministry provides trained "basic educators" who work with villagers in the areas of adult education, sanitation, simple construction, and home economics. Public Health 

Ministry medics provide basic medical services. The Lao Army also runs some civic action programs in rural areas which are similar to those of the basic educators. 40 One of the main objectives of the rural development program in Laos is to maintain and increase popular support for the Royal Lao Government. Lao officials are intimately involved in the direction of the program at all levels. An indication of the interest in this area is that the Prime Minister also holds the rural affairs portfolio.

The Royal Lao Government is working rapidly to strengthen its extension programs in rural areas. Due to a lack of skilled manpower, many of these programs are currently on a pilot basis and do not yet cover all of Laos. In fact, Lao Government participation in development is actually more intensive in areas where a formal program such as the AID-assisted village cluster program operates.

STATEMENT OF VICE ADM. L. C. HEINZ, U.S. NAVY, DIRECTOR OF MILITARY ASSISTANCE, OFFICE OF THE ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF DEFENSE FOR INTERNATIONAL SECURITY AFFAIRS 

Admiral HEINZ. Mr. Chairman, I would like first to give you a brief presentation on the congressional presentation document of this year and talk to my statement.

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, since succeeding 

General Wood as Director of Military Assistance last September, I 

have looked forward to testifying in support of the program. I hope to make the most of this opportunity by giving you a report on the status of our fiscal year 1966 military assistance assets and by presenting the proposed fiscal year 1967 military assistance program. 

First, your attention is invited to the changes which have taken place in fiscal year 1966 since our proposals were submitted to the Congress last spring. The originally proposed fiscal year 1966 military assistance program was based on new obligational authority in the amount of $1,170 billion-a $1 billion "baseline" program and an additional $170 million earmarked to provide for the special combat needs in Vietnam and Laos. (Total obligational authority, including recoupments and reappropriations, amounted to $1.258 billion.) The

Secretary of Defense cautioned that the total of $170 million for southeast Asia, "may represent a conservative estimate, since it is based 229

upon our current analysis of possible developments over which we do not have full control.”

Recent events underscore the significance of the Secretary's statement. They account for the fact that we have had to make full use of the $300 million drawdown authority provided in section 510 of the authorizing legislation-a recourse used only when interests vital to the security of the United States are at stake. Adding the $300 million drawdown and an increase of $33.3 million over our original estimate of recoupments and reappropriations to the initial fiscal year 1966 figure of $1.258 billion in total obligational authority, we arrive at a revised figure of $1.591.3 billion in total obligational authority for fiscal year 1966 (as of January 1966). 

Also as a result of the conflict in Asia, new arrangements have been made to fund the rapidly rising requirements for support of South Vietnamese and other free world military assistance forces currently engaged in combat operations against the Vietcong and North Vietnamese infiltrators. În accordance with the southeast Asia supplemental appropriations bill for fiscal year 1966, responsibility for funding such support and related costs is being assumed by the military departments. All unexpended balances of current and prior year programs for Vietnam originally funded under the military assistance program are being "transferred to and merged with the accounts of the military departments." 

Under this same appropriation, there is being allocated to the Department of Defense the $375 million specifically appropriated to the President in the supplemental "for liquidation of obligations incurred pursuant to the authority in section 510 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended." The supplemental appropriation for military assistance has been requested "to replenish Department of Defense stocks of equipment and materiel which were used" (in fiscal years 1965 and 1966) because of "increased military assistance requirements in Vietnam." It permits compliance with the provision of section 510 of the Foreign Assistance Act, which makes drawdown of defense stocks and services "subject to subsequent reimbursement therefor from subsequent appropriations for military assistance."

In addition to the changes resulting from the war, certain other changes have been made in fiscal year 1966 country programs. The suspension of deliveries to India and Pakistan last September is the most obvious case in point [security deletion].

The Republic of Korea units are giving an excellent account of themselves in combat operations [security deletion]. 

An increase in the worldwide and regional costs reflects the need for emergency support requirements of the inter-American peacekeeping forces in the Dominican Republic, and for replacement of stocks to accommodate increased demands placed on the Logistics Center [security deletion] because of Vietnam. There has also been an addition to worldwide and regional costs for research and development associated with modification, test, evaluation, and development of technical data for the intsallation of iet engines on C-119 aircraft.

Now, let us turn to the proposed fiscal year 1967 military assistance program. I shall summarize that program and some of the basic reasoning underlying it.

The geographical distribution of the proposed program is perhaps most meaningful when the regional dollar totals are translated into terms of percentage of the $1.027 billion in total obligational authority on which the program is based. These percentages are as follows: Europe. 

Near East and south Asia [security deletion].

Africa_

This distribution prompts me to digress for a moment and explain the arrangement of this year's presentation document. Two years ago we departed from the traditional geographical pattern and divided the proposed program into "objective categories" rather than regional sections. Our purpose was to emphasize the relationship between the allocation of assets and the specific purposes military assistance was intended to serve. It became apparent, however, during the course of two successive congressional presentation cycles that the advantages we anticipated were clearly outweighed by the disadvantages. We have, therefore, returned this year to the more conventional regional arrangement. This arrangement parallels the regional organization of the State Department bureaus and their Defense Department counterparts, as well as your subcommittee structure. For this reason, I believe you will welcome its return.

Now, in accordance with the expressed desires of the committee, I shall run through the presentation document so that you will be familiar with both its contents and arrangement. My introductory remarks have already covered the general and historical data contained in the introductory summary, including the section 634(d) report, which is made in accordance with the statutory requirement that the Congress be informed of changes in the current fiscal year program.

I shall, therefore, move forward to a survey of the fiscal year 1967 program presentation for the European region. 

Military assistance is reaching the end of its job in Western Europe. 

Since the inception of the program in 1950, the number of European countries receiving grant materiel aid has dropped from a total of 14 to the 4 still included in the program for fiscal year 1967. Whereas programs for the remaining four countries-Denmark, Norway, Portugal, and Spain-now account for only 3.5 percent of the worldwide total, some 79 percent of the total program went to Western Europe in 1950, when the major purpose of military assistance was to build up allied strength against the threat of Communist aggression directed toward that area. Programs for 10 countries have already been phased out or consist of the final deliveries of equipment programed in previous years.

This trend will continue. We expect to terminate grant materiel assistance for Denmark and Norway in the near future. The proposed 

Danish program completes our commitments [security deletion]. In 

Norway, military assistance has played a major role in facilitating effective Norwegian participation in NATO. In 1962, we made an agreement with Norway to assist the buildup of her air forces, as we

had done with its naval forces in 1960. The 1967 program is the last large program for this country. 

There is a small program for Portugal [security deletion]. 

Grant aid for Portugal consists primarily of training assistance; also payments which were prior funded on the cost-shared destroyer program dating back to a 1960 commitment. Other deliveries include 

T-37 trainer aircraft, spares for the NATO committed maritime patrol squadron, and training aids, documents, and publications [security deletion].

Since 1963, the United States has continued to station forces and operate in the Azores on a de facto basis pursuant to assurances from the Portuguese Foreign Minister, pending negotiations. These negotiations continue in the form of occasional discussions between our Ambassador and the Portuguese Foreign Minister and by the Portuguese Ambassador with the State Department in Washington, but no progress has been made recently. [Security deletion.] 

Military assistance programed for Spain is also keyed to insuring our continuing access to strategically important bases and installations which are vital to optimum deployment of U.S. forces. [Security deletion.]

Military assistance to Spain has both provided the quid pro quo for valuable and essential base rights and has generated substantial Spanish military procurement in the United States. 

While Western Europe is approaching military self-sufficiency, many of the countries in the next section, the Near East, still require substantial U.S. assistance. [Security deletion.] 

We are requesting a total of $240 million in grant aid during fiscal year 1967 for the 11 other countries in this area. This represents 

23.4 percent of the anticipated total obligational authority for the coming year.

A major emphasis of our total military assistance effort throughout the Near East and south Asia is on developing programs which will encourage and elicit maximum self-help on the part of recipient countries.

A case in point is Greece, which is taking on more of the burden of supporting her own forces. We no longer provide any commercial consumables. Greece has also set up maintenance, assembly, and overhaul lines for vehicles which we provide in "where is-as is" condition. 

This arrangement enables us to furnish, within the resources available, a greater amount of other kinds of assistance. 

The goal of our program for Greece is toward modernization of the army and the air force. We recently had talks with the Greeks concerning the composition of their forces, encouraging more realistic planning over a 5-year period, taking into account total resources available. We expect that discussions with Greece will continue, and hope they will result in increased efficiency in the application of both Greek and United States funds to the strengthening of the country's defense posture.

Turkey is another country wherein application of the principle of self-help is producing results. [Security deletion.] Turkey is also producing increasing amounts and more types of ammunition, and augmenting her maintenance and repair capabilities for all types of

equipment. She is now capable of assembling small naval craft. this capability develops, we are substituting small-craft kits inste of completed craft. Through such measures, we are able to accor plish much more toward maintaining Turkish defenses. [Securi deletion.]

I shall now turn to Latin America. Here, the specific objectives of military assistance are the development of Latin American forces capable of maintaining internal security against threats of violence and subversion, whether Communist-inspired and supported or "home grown;" encouraging the armed forces to support and strengthen democratic institutions and to undertake civic action projects which both

contribute to the social and economic development of the country and bring the armed forces and civilian populace closer together; and, finally, to develop selected units for possible use in carrying out peacekeeping assignments under the aegis of the Organization of American 

States or the United Nations.

We are also seizing every opportunity to urge upon Latin American nations the need for a realistic correlation between both force levels and defense budgets and the actual requirements which must be met to insure their countries' security.

Let me expand a bit on the first objective, that of strengthening internal security. The Communist Tri-Continent Conference, held in 

Havana in January 1966, called for the continued active support of armed insurgency in Latin America, with Venezuela, British Guiana, Peru, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Paraguay, Nicaragua, and Guatemala mentioned as specific targets. We can expect the subversive struggle to go on, and to continue to call for a planned, organized effort by the countries concerned to overcome it. This effort will require not only well-trained and equipped armed forces, but also coordination of their operations with those of improved police units in the target countries. There are gratifying evidences of progress in this direction. 

We are also encouraged by the increasing participation of Latin American forces in civic action projects which include such diverse and useful projects as port visits in the upper reaches of the rivers by small naval units and flying hospitals and clinics which utilize air force aircraft.

The program we propose for Latin America in fiscal year 1967 is specifically designed to support the efforts and encourage the trends I have been discussing. It will provide assistance to 19 countries in the total amount of $71.9 million in full compliance with the legislative provisions which apply to our effort in Latin America. STATEMENT OF ADMIRAL U. S. G. SHARP, U.S. NAVY, COMMANDER IN CHIEF, PACIFIC 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I appreciate the opportunity to appear again before this distinguished committee. 

Last year in discussing the PACOM military assistance program, my comments encompassed the strategic situation in the Far East, particularly in southeast Asia. My comments this year will follow the same pattern, with emphasis on military assistance programs as they relate to the strategic situation. 

I will address my comments to three main aspects which, taken together, form the backdrop of the military assistance program. 

First, there is the Communist threat, second the strength of friendly and allied forces assisted by the United States, and third, the war in southeast Asia. I shall take up each of these subjects separately. 

First, the threat. The aggressive militant threat of Communist power in Asia continues and that is our basic problem. The primary military threat is, of course, Communist China and their number one asset is their manpower-approximately 2,500,000 in their armed. forces.

During the past year, China's threat has focused increasingly on Vietnam. The Chinese Communists are obviously testing the effectiveness of so-called wars of national liberation as an instrument for the achievement of Communist control over other nations. The war in southeast Asia will provide a critical test of the future success or failure of that concept. They must already be having some second thoughts about the ultimate success of these tactics. Further, I believe that the Chinese Communists probably now realize that they cannot force the United States to abandon the free countries of the Far East.

Meanwhile, the heaviest concentration of Chinese scarce resources has been allocated to the development of nuclear weapons. This has been done even though living standards, while slowly recovering from the debacle of the great leap forward, remains extremely low. Within the next few years it is possible that they will have a very limited medium range ballistic missile capability which will expand during the next decade.

This threat could be used in the Far East as a form of regional blackmail and to enhance Peiping's prestige. [Security deletion.] 

As you well know, our forces in Vietnam have been rapidly increased this last year. Korea and Australia have also made significant contributions to free world military strength there. [Security deletion.]

While most of these increased forces are positioned with respect to the war in Vietnam, we still must support our allies around the whole perimeter of the west Pacific and maintain adequate reserves capable of rapid deployment when and where needed. [Security deletion. 

South Korea, although under an armistice, still faces the threat of 

[security deletion] North Korean line_divisions [security deletion] 

in position for rapid movement south. It can be assumed the Chinese 

Communists can substantially reinforce the North Koreans in a relatively short time with [security deletion]. We must maintain effec-

tive Republic of Korea and United States forces in Korea to face this threat. [Security deletion.] 

As you know, about 21,000 troops of the Republic of Korea are on duty in Vietnam. The Tiger Division, which arrived in South Vietnam last October, has performed very well. It is a well equipped, well trained, and a most capable unit. [Security deletion.] These forces testify to the effectiveness of our military assistance program. 

Japan has made progress, with our assistance [security deletion] in building its self-defense forces which are almost wholly selfsupported. The Japanese maintain their own internal security, provide security for United States and Japanese military facilities and, in coordination with the United States, contribute to defense against external aggression. The Japanese air self-defense force has assumed responsibility for the air defense of Japan. [Security deletion.] We are continuing to advise the Japanese, to provide training, and to assist in their purchase of U.S. military equipment. 

[Security deletion.] 

The Republic of China armed forces, with a strength of approximately 600,000, are not only effective in preventing Chinese Communist invasion of Taiwan and the Pescadores, but also tie down a substantial number of divisions on mainland China. Nationalist 

China is a major link in our defense strategy. Its bases, airfields, and early warning capabilities are valuable in supporting free world defensive requirements [security deletion]. Also, the Nationalist 

Chinese have provided nonmilitary assistance to the Republic of Viet nam. [Security deletion.] 

Our national policy toward grant-aid recipient countries has emphasized the need to develop self-sufficiency programs. Under this policy, the Republic of China has increased her production capabilities at the Combined Service Forces arsenals and factories. They are manufacturing parts for rebuilding of World War II vehicles which constitute the majority of all vehicles in their armed forces. [Security deletion.]

Our military assistance program has been and will continue to be a key factor in the efforts of the countries I have mentioned to resist Communist domination, and this leads me to southeast Asia. [Security deletion.]

Our ally, Thailand, has been threatened by the Chinese Communists that it will be the next target of the "war of national liberation." [Security deletion.] Thailand does not intend to become the victim of aggression. [Security deletion.] 

Our military assistance program in Thailand is concentrated on equipping and training units that are required for counterinsurgency. [Security deletion.] Within our materiel program we are also attempting to modernize their armed forces in accord with their capability to use and maintain the equipment. We have confidence that Thailand can and will put forth the effort to justify the military assistance we will offer. [Security deletion.]

At this point, I want to speak briefly about the war in Vietnam. 

As you know, the funding for Vietnamese forces is no longer contained in the military assistance program. However, the countries of southeast Asia are so interrelated that a review of the Vietnam situation is pertinent to these hearings.

In 1965, the size of the enemy forces in South Vietnam and the pattern of infiltration changed significantly. Infiltration had been used primarily to encadre the Vietcong, [security deletion] but in 1965, units of the regular North Vietnamese Army were introduced as tactical fighting units. We have identified several North Vietnamese units of regimental strength in South Vietnam [security deletion].

A new element recently appeared with reports of the infiltration of an antiaircraft battalion. [Security deletion.] To our knowledge, this would be the first unit introduced solely to provide protection against aircraft.

It is estimated that the trails through Laos and the southern part of North Vietnam have the capacity to move over 4,500 men per month and may have actually achieved that level toward the end of 

1965. Of course, the routes must also carry ammunition, supplies, and equipment. [Security deletion.] 

What is Hanoi's strategy? They probably believed that the introduction of their regular army units last year would provide the extra combat power needed to achieve complete victory some time in 1965. This did not happen because we committed U.S. and other free world forces to combat. The enemy's strategy now seems to be based on the conviction that we will tire before he does. Hanoi has stated that the enormous costs of our long supply lines, coupled with the casualties they intend to inflict on U.S. forces will cause us to negotiate on their terms. The Communists bank on their willingness to expend lives at a rate we would consider unacceptable. 

Now as to the forces on our side. Vietnamese regulars total about 

300,000, of which 267,000 are army. [Security deletion.] The paramilitary forces which now number about 250,000 are steadily increasing their strength. South Korean, Australian, and New Zealand forces total about 23,000 and United States forces now exceed 220,000. 

Now to turn to our air operations against the enemy. What has been the result of this campaign? We have concluded that it has a considerable impact on North Vietnam. [Security deletion.] 

What is the military outlook in South Vietnam? In the long run, the war must be won in the south. There are some signs of declining morale among the Vietcong. The enemy's established base areas in 

South Vietnam are no longer secure because of our ground operations and B-52 raids. The South Vietnamese Army is slowly increasing in size and effectiveness. Our great advantages of firepower and superior mobility will become increasingly effective as our units gain experience.

On the other hand, we face a long and grim struggle, but with the prospect of the pendulum swinging slowly to the side of South Vietnam. How fast and how decisively this swing occurs depends on many factors. However, the most important step toward achieving our objectives in South Vietnam will have been taken when we convince Hanoi that we are going to keep on fighting until our objectives are achieved. We are engaged in a difficult war in southeast Asia which is demanding a large part of our military resources in the Pacific. Our prospects of achieving our objectives are good. At the same time, we

are strengthening the free countries on the periphery of communism in Asia.

Our overall military position in the Far East is favorable because of the progress made through the military assistance program. The forces developed by this program, backed by U.S. strength, are maintaining a strong bulwark against Communist subversion. The military assistance program has, in addition, given our allies the confidence of their own strength and encouraged their confidence in the United States. It was the Communist threat which brought this program into existence and it is the same threat which requires its continuation. I urge your continued support.

 INFILTRATION FROM NORTH VIETNAM 

The 4,500 figure consistently used as the estimated monthly capability of North Vietnamese to infiltrate combat troops into South Vietnam is neither a fixed nor a magic number. It is rather the result of careful evaluation of pertinent factors. For example, we now have persuasive evidence, in part from extensive interrogations of North Vietnamese soldiers captured in South Vietnam, that during the winter of 1963 and spring of 1964, Hanoi embarked on a major program to increase infiltration, including infiltration of regular units of the North Vietnamese Army into South Vietnam through the Laos infiltration trails that had been used as early as 1960. 

We know from a study of our aerial photography that, concurrently, North Vietnam was completing the construction of a string of infiltration staging and supply points within its own territory and in Laos. Throughout 1965, we observed the extension of motorable routes southward. Most recently, for example, our reconnaissance has documented the systematic expansion of motorable routes deep into southern Laos. Segments observed have been constructed to within 15 miles of the tri-border area of Cambodia-Laos-South Vietnam, and clearing operations for this new road extend to within 5 miles of the border. 

In short, what emerges from thousands of photographs is a picture of an enormous effort by North Vietnam, beginning more than a year before American combat troops were in South Vietnam, to develop supply lines and to transport supplies through Laos to South Vietnam.

It is from analysis of information such as this that we have developed our estimate that North Vietnam has the capability to generate and infiltrate up to 

4,500 combat troops monthly.

COMPARISON OF CENTURION AND PATTON TANKS 

A number of observers and commentators on the Indo-Pak border war last September have examined and reflected upon the outcome of its fierce armored engagements, and several British analysts have contended that the Centurion

tanks employed by the Indians proved superior to the U.S.-built Patton tanks with which the Paks were equipped. Although the record is by no means clear in this area, postbattle evaluation strongly suggests this was not in fact the case. 

The ultimate advantage in armored engagements depends to a large degree on variables which are always difficult to assess. Of these, the most important are the effective technical employment of armor, the degree of training of tank crews, and the terrain.

No tank is designed to withstand completely penetration by all antitank weapons because the factors of weight versus vulnerability have such a profound effect upon mobility (i.e., as armor thickness increases, weight increases, and mobility decreases). The heavier the tank, the greater the problems of track ground pressure, bridging limitations, and logistics support. 

Further, penetration of a tank hull is also a function of range and type of projectile; i.e., a high-velocity kinetic energy round of armor-piercing ammunition when fired at close range will penetrate a greater thickness of armor plate than the same round fired at a greater range.

STATEMENT OF ROBERT S. MONAMARA, SECRETARY OF DEFENSE, BEFORE THE HOUSE FOREIGN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE IN SUPPORT OF THE FISCAL YEAR 1967 MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, today, for the seventh time in 6 years, it is my privilege to testify before the Foreign Affairs Committee in support of the military assistance program. As I have stated on each previous occasion, I remain convinced that military assistance is an important instrument of U.S. foreign policy and a significant extension of our own national defense posture.

Since I last appeared before this committee in support of the military assistance program, we have been forced by the infiltration of increasing numbers of regular North Vietnamese troops into South Vietnam to employ U.S. combat forces there. And the need to achieve greater efficiency in the joint United 

States-South Vietnamese military effort has made it necessary to separate military assistance to South Vietnam from the remainder of the military assistance program. By shifting the cost of supporting South Vietnam's forces to the Department of Defense budget we have relieved the military assistance program of some of the pressures which in recent years have threatened to distort seriously the remainder of the country programs. I believe the military assistance pro- 265

gram can now be maintained on a more rational basis, and that we will be able to avoid some of the political and economic costs of reprograming to meet the rising costs of active hostilities in Vietnam. Moreover, we should be able to plan ahead more effectively and to relate the development of free world forces more effectively to the development of our own forces. 

During the last year I reviewed the military assistance program for the next 5 years, based on a detailed reappraisal of selected country programs. This reappraisal examined the threat, the proposed strategy of defense, the strength and missions of local forces, and the strength and missions of U.S. forces likely to be available, with respect to major recipients of military assistance. The analysis also endeavored to evaluate, in each case, the extent to which political considerations are important determinants of the size and character of the military assistance program. Accordingly, it was not confined solely to examining the military rationale for MAP.

I want to assure you that this reappraisal has confirmed the fundamental validity of our military assistance program and demonstrated anew its vital contributions to the attainment of our military, political, and economic objectives. 

Moreover, I am convinced as a result of the reappraisal that we can make significant progress within a $1 billion program toward meeting the most critical needs for modernizing free world forces. Our studies indicate, however, that a heavy burden of modernization costs will be with us through the 5-year planning period. 

Further, they indicate the need for continuing attention to the interrelationships between U.S. and MAP-supported forces if we are to achieve balance in free world military capabilities and to get the most for our MAP dollars. 

Now, with these points in mind, let us turn to a consideration of the proposed fiscal year 1967 military assistance and sales program. It is entirely consistent with the provisions of the new Military Assistance and Sales Act of 1966 which has been submitted to the Congress as separate legislation and introduced by your distinguished chairman. I am sure you are fully conversant with the general tenor of the bill. In addition to requesting a 5-year authorization, it calls for:

Effective coordination between economic and military programs. There will be no change in existing policy with respect to coordinating military assistance with economic assistance and foreign policy. 

Greater emphasis on self-help by those we aid. 

Greater emphasis on civic action programs for nation building. 

Emphasis on training and education of foreign military personnel. 

Continued shift from grant aid to military sales wherever possible.

THE FISCAL YEAR 1967 REQUEST 

You may recall that when I appeared before this committee almost 3 years ago, on April 8, 1963, shortly after the issuance of the Clay Committee report recommending progressive reduction of military assistance programs, I stated that, "barring any large scale unforeseen emergency, we hope to reduce the new obligational authority budget to a level of $1 billion no later than fiscal year 1968." 

The program we are presenting today is based on $917 million in new obligational authority. The total obligational authority in the amount of $1,027 million results from the addition of an estimated $110 million in recoupments and reappropriations to the $917 million budget request. 

This program-which excludes Vietnam-would be somewhat less than $900 million but for the abnormal requirements elsewhere in southeast Asia. Put another way, it is the equivalent of a $950 million program, including provision for the normal needs of Laos and of Vietnam calculated at roughly double the 

1960 level.

This is the first time since the inception of the program in 1950 that we have been able to ask for less than $1 billion. We have succeeded in reducing the program to the $1 billion level by reducing the number of recipient countries to those which are in demonstrable need of continuing grant military support and which are making maximum use of their own resources, and by concentrating our grant support on those forces whose potential contribution to free world security is the greatest. But I must add a word of caution here. Developments in southeast Asia, particularly in relation to the security of Laos and Thailand, could impose additional requirements for MAP support beyond those provided for in the $917 million request. 

The difficulties inherent in such a reduced program are large. The proposed fiscal year 1967 miiltary assistance program is the product of many hard choices.

The proposed program will meet only the minimum essential needs of allied and friendly forces whose defense capabilities enhance the security of the entire free world. It will provide a modest amount to meet credit assistance needs principally in those countries shifting from grant to sales programs. 

DISTRIBUTION OF THE PROGRAM 

We have once again allocated almost three-fourths of the total program to the 10 countries adjacent to the borders of Soviet Russia and Communist China where our forward strategy draws the front lines of free world common defense. 

Because the armed forces of countries such as Greece, Turkey, Iran, and the Republics of China and Korea are essential elements of the total free world deterrent, it is in our national interest to see that they do not lack the means to match their will to resist aggression. 

In newly independent and developing nations less directly threatened by Communist neighors, the military assistance program is primarily designed to strenghen internal security. Our assistance to such countries will continue to emphasize civic action programs through which indigenous military forces can contribute to nation building. We shall also continue to emphasize the training component of military assistance which has long proved to be one of the most valuable aspects of the program.

We are taking steps to insure that military assistance training complements other United States efforts, referred to in the President's state of the Union message, to encourage a broader and deeper distribution throughout the world of the priceless benefits of education. In this regard, we have just concluded a conference designed to foster greater understanding of the benefits accruing from attendance by foreign military personnel at military and civilian schools in the United States under the military assistance program. Our training program provides unique opportunities to expose potential leaders of the developing nations to our institutions, goals, and ideals and thereby to develop valuable understanding and friendship.

The 55 recipient countries included in the proposed program fall into 5 regional groupings which parallel the organization of your subcommittees and set the pattern for this year's presentation.

FAR EAST 

I shall begin with the Far East, to which area we propose to allocate $387 million or 37.7 percent of our anticipated total obligational authority in fiscal year 1967.

The power situation in the Far East is characterized basically by the great disparity between the inherent economic and military strength of allied and friendly countries and that of Communist China. The small countries located on the fringes of the Chinese land mass-South Vietnam, Laos, Thailand, the Philippines, and the Republic of China and Korea-are inherently at a power disadvantage with respect to their powerful neighbor. The strength of the 

United States, our presence, our will, our commitments to defend them are, therefore, essential ingredients of stability in the Far East. Military assistance is important both for what it contributes directly to the strengh of these nations and as a manifestation of U.S. will and commitment. 

Military assistance to free countries in the Far East area greatly enhances their will and ability to resist external aggression. It enables these small countries to maintain sizable military forces well in excess of their own economic capacities. It strengthens their capabilities to maintain internal security and resist conventional attack, fosters a sense of military and political self-confidence in the face of Communist China's threats and permits them to contribute toward the maintenance of a favorable balance of military power in the Far East. Military assistance thus exerts a favorable impact on the balance of power in Asia and on the maintenance of stability around the rim of mainland China. 

A few brief comments on individual country problems and programs will, I believe, support these general conclusions. Thailand

Thailand is a nation of major importance to the United States in southeast Asia because of its size and strategic position on the mainland, its political stability, and its encouraging economic growth. Thailand faces an immediate and growing threat of subversion and insurgency, sponsored by Hanoi and

Peking. By virtue of its geographical position, it is also exposed to the danger of attack from conventional military forces, and the threat of seizure by enemy forces of strategic areas in Laos along the Thai border. 

In the last year Red China has blatantly advertised its preparations for subversive insurgency designed to overthrow the Thai Government; and, in fact, armed bands have become increasingly active in the northeastern provinces bordering Laos. In consideration of the growing internal security problem and the possibility that hostilities in Laos and Vietnam could spread to Thailand, it is clearly in the U.S. interest to strengthen the capabilities of the Thai military forces for counterinsurgency. The proposed Thai MAP program will focus our support on this objective. 

The Philippines 

Our military assistance program for the Philippines provides the means for urgently needed improvements in the training and equipment of Philippine Armed Forces. The Philippines maintains modest forces in order to insure its internal security and to be prepared to fulfill its obligations as a member of SEATO. 

South Korea

The Republic of Korea provides a striking example of the benefits we and our allies continue to derive from the military assistance program. More than 20,000 

ROK forces, trained and equipped with military assistance funds, are now deployed and actively engaged in the struggle in Vietnam. These Korean troops are proving again their well-known fighting mettle. Their presence in South Vietnam was made possible by the confidence in U.S. commitments and support which our assistance program has helped to instill. 

The proposed MAP program provides for the modernization of certain critical categories of equipment and for essential operating costs of the substantial Korean forces which stand guard, together with two U.S. divisions, along the demilitarized zone in Korea. I believe the continuing threat in the Far East requires that we continue major military assistance to the Korean Armed Forces. This military assistance will enable the Republic of Korea to maintain these forces without excessive limitations on its promising economic and social progress. 

The Republic of China 

Red China's leaders have clearly stated their intention to use every means open to them to eliminate the Government of China and seize control of Taiwan. Our bilateral security commitment to the defense of Taiwan and the Pescadores remains vital to the survival of the Government of the Republic of China. Although it has been increasingly successful in improving the military supply system, maintaining equipment and bearing an increasing share of its own defense costs, we shall have to continue to supply certain types of military equipment which cannot be produced locally. Military assistance is essential if the burden of defense is not to reach a level endangering the social and economic progress on Taiwan-those advances which serve as a reminder to the mainland of the benefits of freedom. We are now considering a modest military assistance sales program, denoting our confidence in the future economic growth of the Republic of China.

NEAR EAST-SOUTH ASIA 

Because of their importance to the United States, the countries of this area have received almost $5 billion worth of military assistance through fiscal year 1966. We are proposing that they receive another $240 million in military grant aid in fiscal year 1967, representing 23 percent of anticipated total obligational authority. 

Greece and Turkey

In the Near East and south Asia, Greece and Turkey form important elements in our collective security arrangements by protecting the southeast flank of NATO. Their forces, together with those of the United States and other 

NATO allies, constitute a strong deterrent to the Communist military threat. 

The record of our military assistance to Greece and Turkey since 1947 is noteworthy. It has measurably aided in defeating aggression and in preventing its recurrence. It has built effective military capabilities from forces that once were ill-equipped and poorly organized. Furthermore, it is aimed not only at building and maintaining forces to meet the external threat, but also at enabling this to be done without diverting resources critical to their social and economic

development. Both countries still face serious difficulties in maintaining modern forces with their own resources, even when supplemented by military assistance at the proposed levels.

We have recently begun discussions with both Governments, as a part of an overall NATO effort, to reexamine their present force goals and structures with a view to bringing them into closer alinement with the best estimates of total available resources. To this end, we are encouraging the Governments of 

Greece and Turkey to adopt 5-year force planning. While this proposal does not involve any commitment of U.S. funds, we believe it will nevertheless lead to an improved allocation of those resources (Greek, Turkish, and United States) that can be made available for military purposes. 

I believe it has been demonstrated that achievement of our objectives in Greece and Turkey-containment of the military threat, improvement of force structures, adequate modernization, and economic stability and growth-calls for a continuation of substantial U.S. military assistance. For the next fiscal year it will require, at a minimum, the application of MAP funds at the levels requested. Iran

Iran occupies a strategic location between the Soviet Union and the warmwater ports of the Persian Gulf and the important petroleum resources of the Arabian Peninsula. Its military forces, strengthened by our military assistance, constitute a significant deterrent to Communist aggression and help to assure Iran's continued internal stability. U.S. military assistance, in the form of both grants and sales, thus continues to be important in helping to provide the environment necessary for political, social, and economic development. 

Through military assistance, we contribute to the significant economic progress taking place in Iran, which is already enabling Iran to pay for a greater share of its own security costs. 

South Asia

I now turn to south Asia which has become, through a combination of circumstances and geography, a vital strategic area in the present contest between the expansionist and nonexpansionist power centers. In friendly hands or as nonalined States, south Asia can be a bridge between Europe and the Far East and a major physical barrier to the southward expansion of Red China and the U.S.S.R.; in hostile hands, it would seal the long term hope of building a free 

Asian coalition able to provide adequate counterweight to an expansionist China. 

It is, therefore, an area of great importance and consequence to the United States.

The United States needs national independence and stability in south Asia, and current U.S. strategy assumes this. If India and Pakistan were to be lost to communism or chaos, the struggle in South Vietnam would lose much of its strategic validity. We must recognize, however, that achievement of these aims, which are also those of both India and Pakistan, is dependent on the outcome of complex internal struggles and external conflicts. 

Success in the struggle to develop modern states in both India and Pakistan means coping with the problems of sustaining vast populations while at the same time advancing toward modernization. This central task demands the full energies of the peoples concerned. Its successful accomplishment must not be frustrated by either the divisive effects of territorial disputes or the designs of expansionist powers bent on dominance in Asia. 

With respect to the outbreak of armed conflict between India and Pakistan, as you know, we suspended military aid and commercial sales deliveries on September 8, 1965. We have strongly supported the United Nations Security 

Council resolution of September 20, calling for a cease-fire, for a withdrawal of armed personnel to the positions held before August 5, 1965, and for further consideration of steps that can be taken toward a settlement of the political problem underlying the present conflict. It is encouraging that the Soviets have adopted a similar position as evidenced by their role at the Tashkent 

Conference in January of this year.

In light of India's and Pakistan's compliance with the withdrawal provisions of the Security Council resolutions and with the Tashkent Declaration, and in view of other encouraging steps taken by both to restore peace in the subcontinent, we have modified the ban on military shipments to South Asia to the extent of permitting selected and limited [security delection] sales of nonlethal military equipment on a case-by-case basis. Our ban on grant military

assistance continues. Any further relaxation of our policy will be contingent on the further course of events in south Asia and on a further assessment of the U.S. interest in supporting the military forces of India and Pakistan. 

With respect to Pakistan, we desire improved and cordial relations. We recognize that Pakistan as a sovereign power is going to maintain a respectable level of military forces [security deletion]. With respect to India, an important fact is that we share with that country the basic aim of containing Chinese expansion. It is also true that India's strength and stability are of decisive importance to the question whether Asia is going to develop along democratic or totalitarian lines.

LATIN AMERICA 

Our major objective in Latin America is economic and social development, toward which the entire Alliance for Progress effort is directed. But we cannot hope to attain that objective unless governments throughout the area have efficient and adequate security forces to thwart elements interested in blocking that progress for their own ends. Unfortunately, such elements are at work in almost every Latin American country. There are groups which oppose change simply because they wish to preserve the benefits they derive from maintenance of the status quo. There are also those groups which see a chance to seize power in the atmosphere of dissatisfaction and unrest which results from unsatisfactory social and economic progress. These latter groups are usually, but not always aided and abetted from abroad. 

It is for this reason that our military assistance program for Latin America continues to be oriented toward internal security and civic action. This assistance is not directed at eliminating protest or enforcing conformity, but rather at helping provide an environment in which economic and social tasks can be effectively pursued. Governments must be able to eliminate violence if peaceful change through democratic processes is to be achieved. 

Accordingly, the specific objectives of the military assistance program for Latin America are to encourage and support the development of indigenous forces capable of maintaining internal security against threats of violence and subversion, dealing effectively with guerrilla warfare and the clandestine movement of men and armaments across land, sea, and air borders for subversive purposes. We also seek to augment and facilitate the participation of appropriate Latin American military units in civic action projects. These projects contribute both to the nation building and to the establishment of greater rapport between the populace and the Armed Forces, which frequently represent the authority of the Government in the eyes of the people. The military assistance program also enables us to help those nations that wish to develop selected units for possible use in carrying out peacekeeping missions under the aegis of the OAS and the U.N. Finally, we count upon military assistance programs for Latin America as a channel through which to communicate our continuing interest in fostering a constructive and democratic approach by the military to their professional responsibilities and to the solution of national problems.

The proposed fiscal year 1967 military assistance program for Latin America amounts to $74.9 million. This will provide for 19 individual country programs amounting to [security deletion] million, or [security deletion] of our anticipated total obligational authority, and another [security deletion] million for Latin American regional programs and multilateral military activities which have been given impetus by the "Fulbright amendment" to the Foreign 

Assistance Act. [Security deletion.] 

In accordance with the general and specific objectives I have outlined, the major portion of the proposed program for Latin America [security deletion] will be devoted to strengthening internal security capabilities of indigenous forces, with emphasis on communications, mobility, and counterinsurgency training. Another [security deletion] of the total program is allocated to the provision of equipment and training associated with civic action. Programs for all 19 countries include training for Latin American military personnel at U.S. schools in the Canal Zone and in the United States. Such training not only contributes to the improvement of military skills and professional attitudes, but it also promotes the broader objectives of U.S. policy by exposing Latin 

American military personnel to American concepts and enhancing the mutual understanding and respect which must characterize our relationships with them if our cooperation is to be fully productive.

AFRICA 

For Africa, we propose a military assistance program of $31.8 million for fiscal year 1967 (of which $22.2 million is for equipment and $9.6 million for training and related purposes). This amount, about 3 percent of anticipated total obligational authority, will mainly go to a few countries where the United States has important interests and installations. The balance will be distributed among 10 other countries, chiefly in the form of training programs, communications, and transportation equipment. Programs for six of these countries amount to less than $1 million each. 

U.S. foreign policy in Africa south of the Sahara is directed toward helping these countries to preserve their independence and to achieve the balanced economic, social, and political development essential to freedom and stability. 

Military assistance can play a subordinate but significant role in support of that policy by assisting, where necessary, in the development of forces capable of providing the internal security necessary for progress in national development. 

While the former metropoles are expected to provide continued security assistance, there are certain cases in which U.S. military assistance is the only realistic alternative to unstable internal security situations. In such cases, however, our assistance is carefully designed to prevent its contributing to an arms race. 

The African areas of most immediate strategic concern to the free world are those bordering on the Mediterranean and in the horn. The former guards the southern flank of NATO, and the latter stands at the approaches to the Red Sea. 

Our military assistance helps these countries to maintain internal security and stability essential to their economic and social development. It also helps to lessen the tensions resulting from the inflow into the area of large quantities of Soviet materiel and training. 

Africa will continue to face many difficult problems in the immediate future, as indicated by the recent flurry of coups. While these coups have been triggered for a variety of reasons, the frail political structure of the new African governments is clearly demonstrated. At the same time, the Communists are vigorously pursuing programs designed to enhance their influence. 

Until the African nations have had an opportunity to develop their economies and strengthen their political institutions, there will be a wide variety of opportunities for both Sino-Soviet and local Communist activities. We should therefore continue, within the resources available for this purpose, to join other free world nations in assisting certain African nations to improve their stability in order that they may effectively combine economic aid and their own resources to move more rapidly toward their own chosen political and economic goals. Withholding such assistance at the present time would greatly handicap the countries concerned in their efforts to build stable and viable nations.

EUROPE 

Today, Western Europe presents a picture of unprecedented prosperity and stability, thanks in no small measure to the great efforts which the American people have made to rehabilitate the war-ravaged economies of that area and to bolster its defense against the Soviet threat. NATO, in its 17th year of existence, continues, despite what one reads in the press, to fulfill the purposes for which it was created by its members and "to unite their efforts for collective defense and for the preservation of peace and security."

Our own basic objectives in Western Europe are simply to insure the security of that area against Communist aggression and to further its economic growth and political stability. We are neither unaware of, nor dismayed by the problems confronting us in or about NATO. Despite the disruptive actions of a present member, France, our support of the most successful defensive alliance in history will continue unabated. While we regret French actions, we know that our allies share in our determination to maintain the strength and cohesiveness of NATO. We are, and will remain, committed to the North Atlantic Alliance because it continues to provide an indispensable means of maintaining the collective security of the West.

I believe that the accomplishments of NATO over the past year have demonstrated that the alliance is fully responsive to changing circumstances. As long as the Soviet Union represents a major potential military threat in Europe, there will be no substitute more effective than the collective and integrated defense of the West. The changes which have taken place in the nature of the Soviet

threat to Western Europe in recent years have not affected the basic realities that made the alliance a political and military necessity some 17 years ago. 

Those same 17 years have, however, brought a tremendous change in Western European requirements for military assistance. Although more than half of our total investment since the inception of the program in 1950 has gone into the NATO buildup, the signal success of that common defense effort, together with the rapid economic recovery of Western Europe, have made possible a corresponding reduction in the proportionate amount of military assistance allocated to the area. This reduction is clearly reflected in the drop from a high of 79 percent to a low of 3.5 percent which represents the $36 million earmarked for grant aid to Western Europe in fiscal year 1967. 

Today, all NATO nations except Greece and Turkey, which I have already discussed, are capable of providing for their own self- and common-defense needs. 

Of the original 14 Western European recipients of grant aid, including both NATO and non-NATO countries, only 4 will continue to receive grant aid in fiscal year 1967. Two of these-Norway and Denmark-will also be phased out as soon as prior-year commitments are completed in the near future. 

Grant aid programs for the other two-Spain and Portugal-will be continued in consonance with our continuing need for the important bases and installations which they make available to the United States.

First, the $90 million listed for NATO infrastructure is the amount required in fiscal year 1967 to fund the agreed cost of the U.S. share in the development of joint use facilities essential to effective deployment of U.S. and other national forces committed to NATO. I want to make special mention of the $56.7 million credit sales item listed among worldwide and regional programs. This amount represents only the new obligational authority which we need to augment credit funds already available in our MAP revolving account for sales. It will enable us to provide a total of $244 million in credit sales, mainly for developing countries, many of whom are shifting from grant to sales. This credit, supplemented by credit available through private and Eximbank sources for the industrially developed countries, and combined with cash sales, should make it possible to achieve military export sales orders of at least $1.5 billion in fiscal year 1967. 

The use of military assistance funds to facilitate military export sales in cases where the purchasing nation cannot afford to buy for cash is clearly consistent with both the national interest and the intent and spirit of the pending

Military Assistance and Sales Act of 1966. The director of the sales program will testify later in support of the sales portion of the proposed new legislation. 

He will elaborate on our efforts to encourage appropriate purchase of military equipment from the United States by allied and friendly countries economically capable of making such purchases. These efforts are directed toward the dual objective of shifting from grant aid to military sales wherever possible and of exerting a favorable influence on the U.S. balance of payments. Our growing sales program is closely coordinated within the Government to insure its compatibility with our economic assistance program and with foreign policy. 

SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE 

Although supporting assistance is a responsibility of the Agency for International Development rather than the Department of Defense, it is an integral part of our total effort to promote free world peace and progress. Once again this year, I consider it appropriate to advocate favorable legislative action on the administration's $747.2 million fiscal year 1967 request therefor. The $550 million earmarked for Vietnam is the largest single item in the proposed economic aid budget, and it is vital to an eventually favorable outcome of the struggle in the hard-pressed country. Another $197 million will be used for aid to countries whose security is directly threatened. It is concentrated in programs for Laos, Korea, and Thailand, which are directly threatened. 

CONCLUSION 

It is my firm and final conclusion, afer taking into careful consideration all pertinent factors and possible alternatives, that the authorization and the appropriations requested by the administration are clearly consistent with the national interest and represent the most economical means for attaining the specific security and foreign policy objectives which military assistance is designed to promote. I know of no other means by which we can make equivalent contributions to our own and to free world security at comparable cost. I sincerely hope that your own evaluation of the proposed program will lead you to the same conclusions. 

[Security deletion.] STATEMENT BY GEN. EARLE G. WHEELER, U.S. ARMY, CHAIRMAN OF THE JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF, BEFORE THE HOUSE FOREIGN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE ON MILI- TARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I welcome this opportunity to appear before you in support of the military assistance program for the fiscal year 1967. The Joint Chiefs of Staff consider an adequate military aid program to be an essential and integral part of the military strategy of the United States, a required complement to our own national military programs. 

Cooperative effort and joint commitment by allied and friendly nations have created a free world military posture which represents a total strength far greater than the strength of any single nation. The concept of military assistance to free world countries is a response to a spectrum of threat to the United States and to U.S. worldwide security interests as well as to these free world countries. This response is set forth in the joint strategic objectives plan which translates national objectives and policies into military objectives, prescribes strategic concepts for the employment of forces, and defines basic undertakings to achieve these objectives and concepts. The MAP is not a simple extension of U.S. forces and military power but is a reflection of the mutual security interests of the United States and MAP recipients involving political as well as military factors. Thus, U.S. forces supplement and complement; they can substitute and offset only in a limited sense. Furthermore, our U.S. capability, even considering projected increases in mobility, power, and versatility, is not without limit. Equivalent dollars applied to U.S. force levels will not provide an equivalent free world posture [security deletion]. A direct and consistent correlation of enemy threat, MAP funding levels, and U.S. objectives in the strategic context is difficult to establish arithmetically. The many political and diplomatic variables which affect MAP appropriations; international political, economic, and military instability which impact on specific U.S. objectives; and the existence of open hostilities in Vietnam, have required reasoned judgments where quantitative computations could not be made. 60-929-66-pt. 24

In the end, the military assistance we recommend is pared down to those countries that are of particular importance to our security and to those military forces within those countries that bear a particular complementary relation to our own. Thus, we in the Joint Chiefs of Staff are constantly reminded of the interlocking relationships existing between our national military programs and those of military assistance. I trust the committee will also keep in mind this important relationship.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff have viewed the level of the military assistance programs of the last 3 years with concern. Annual appropriations at the current level will barely provide the required day-to-day operating costs of ships, aircraft, and equipment necessary to prevent backsliding in current capabilities. 

Since fiscal year 1964 many well-planned force improvements have had to be deferred indefinitely. This deferment is the more significant because the quality of the equipment of the armed forces of the Soviet Union, Communist China, and the other Communist-controlled nations is improving steadily. While we are not unmindful of the fact that there are considerations other than military, such as our ultimate political and economic objectives for the several areas, which must be evaluated in determining the level of the annual military assistance program, we are of the opinion that further reductions below the current level are not justified by the military situation confronting the United States and its free world allies today and in the near term. 

Almost three-fourths of this year's program will go to support forces in countries on the periphery of the great Communist land mass. These funds will enable Korea, the Philippines, Republic of China, Thailand, Laos, Iran, Turkey, and

Greece to maintain almost 2 million men under arms in collective defense of mutual security interests, i.e., those which we share with them. It would be far more expensive if we had to replace any part of this 2 million men with men from our own Armed Forces. None of these peripheral countries has the capacity to assume full support of its forces which are essential to our mutual security interests. It is appropriate for them to maintain their forces in the interest of common defense, and it is appropriate for us to assist in support of these forces. 

To reduce our assistance is to weaken forward defense forces and is an invitation to Communist effort to occupy the power vacuums that could result. In my opinion, reduction of the funds allocated to such country programs would be the poorest kind of economy for the United States, and one for which we might ultimately have to pay many times over. 

Of the small remainder of the annual program, the assistance to our Latin American neighbors is extremely important. Our country programs for this area are oriented primarily toward internal security. Not to recognize the era of social, economic, and political change that our Latin American neighbors are facing would be to ignore a key trend of our time. Change is a traditional feature of Latin American politics, and in recent years it has been the military establishment which in many instances has provided the greatest stabilizing factor for orderly change and continuity of constitutional government. There are other nations, of course, who would gladly offer military assistance to our Latin American friends in order to gain opportunities for political infiltration. 

In short, this is no time for the United States to reduce this part of the military assistance program below a level that will further these ends. 

Those remaining funds programed for other areas and purposes, while relatively small in dollars, are significant since they are tied to our own special interests and specific obligations. The military assistance program as a whole is a very tightly constructed package. 

To conclude, in the words of the President, this MAP budget "is the bare minimum required if we are to keep our commitments to our allies and friendly armed forces to provide the equipment and training essential to free world defense." I assure you that the program submission before you, which is minimal, has the full support of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Vietnam today is the continuing expansion of the Vietcong forces (a) by the infiltration from the north of approximately 4,500 men a month, and (b) by further recruitment, in part by terror tactics, of some 3,000, 4,000, or 5,000 men a month in the south.
