The area for which I am responsible is shown on each of these charts. 

It includes all of Africa excepting Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria, and Libya. It includes the Malagasy Republic; the countries of the Middle 

East except Turkey, a member of NATO, and the countries of southern Asia to the Burma border. The island of Ceylon is also included. 

Water areas included in this area of responsibility are the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.

The total area is inhabited by 28 percent of the world's population and encompasses 30 percent of the world's land mass. These two facts alone render the area strategically important. 

The MEAFSA area is an area of contrasts. 

MEAFSA is a world of diversity and adversity-of superlatives and historical firsts. The Biblical cradle of man, it also produced the first great civilizations and empires which have endured for more years before Christ than the modern empires have lasted after Christ. 

Eight of the world's eleven major religions were born here. 

Here we find the highest mountain, Everest-the lowest elevation, the Dead Sea-the longest single river, the Nile-the loftiest mountain ranges, steaming jungles, and scorching deserts.

We have here the most diamonds and gold-and more importantly, the most oil. Uranium is found here and precious stones. Money was invented here-but some people have never seen any. 

Knowledge was born here illiteracy lives here. 

Distinctions are sharp between race and religion, class and caste, tribe and clan.

Here we have the world's oldest nation, Egypt-and 35 of the world's new nations all struggling to build nationhood. 

And here we have the longest continuous land frontier between the free world and the Communist world. All of these facts point up the strategic importance of this area. 

For a military commander, the magnitude of the time-space factor is unique.

Africa is three times as large as the United States; distances within it are great. Add to that 4,300 miles from my headquarters at Mac- 

Dill Air Force Base, Fla., to the nearest point, Dakar, Senegal-or consider the 8,700 miles to Calcutta, India-then the military problems come into better focus.

Lack of good bases, scarcity of usable in-country resources, inadequate communications, paucity of adequate support facilities-all point to vastly different military problems than found in the more highly developed regions.

Military assistance programs are the major instruments by which 

I carry out my responsibilities.

During fiscal year 1967, the United States will have active military assistance programs in 19 countries in the MEAFSA area.

We have three military assistance advisory groups-or MAAG'slocated in Iran, Ethiopia, and Pakistan. These countries are shown in red on the chart. We have military missions in the six countries colored green. Beginning in west Africa, these countries are Mali, Liberia, Guinea, the Republic of the Congo (Léopoldville), Saudi Arabia, and India. Small military assistance programs are administered under my direction by the U.S. defense attachés in Senegal, Nigeria, Sudan, Yemen, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq, Afghanistan, and Nepal. These countries are shown in blue on the chart. 

The goal of our military assistance programs is to assist recipient nations in developing forces tailored to their specific needs and capabilities rather than to build replicas of U.S. forces. [Security deletion.] We work steadily toward the replacement of grant aid funds by military sales, self-help, and third-country assistance wherever possible. Substantial progress is being made in this re spect [security deletion]. 

Formal, modest research and development programs are supplementing the military assistance program in Iran and Ethiopia in 1966. 

This is a form of self-help which can be a very valuable means for ultimately reducing grant aid.

For example, the Ethiopians were encouraged to develop their own field ration as a substitute for the expensive and not particularly useful grant-aid-furnished U.S. field rations, which they wanted. In a few months they developed a good field ration based on local diets and issued it to their troops in the field. 

In another case, it was found that heavy U.S. tentage with store fittings was not best suited for the Ethiopian soldiers especially in the sweltering heat of some lower altitudes. Instead of accepting a request for additional grant aid for tentage, the Ethiopians were urged to develop a lightweight tent more suited to their needs. This action is presently underway and, which when standardized for local troop use, will have the added economic bonus of using locally grown cotton.

In Iran, two U.S. research and development advisers are being added to the MAAG staff this year. The purpose is to assist the Iranian armed forces in developing a solid, in-country R. & D. effort. 

As a matter of priority, our MAAG's and missions continue to encourage self-development of country capabilities for production of their own military materiel to fill their own specific needs. Three key principles I insist be emphasized are simplicity, practicability—and utility.

We also influence the armed forces of recipient nations to undertake civic actions within their capabilities. This involves a variety of contributions to civic improvement such as building roads, schools, improving sanitation, and providing good sources of water. The Iranian forces have done a remarkable job, and have thereby changed to a large extent the attitude of the people toward the armed forces from one of fear and distrust to an attitude of friendliness and dependence. 

In Ethiopia, the work has not been so widespread, but it is spreading. In our training efforts in Ethiopia we hope to attain a standard of training that will permit each battalion to spend 1 month a year on

substantial civic projects such as building roads, which are sorely needed.

Another important facet of our activities is in the field of humane actions. Often these activities are less dramatic than others but they are equally effective. Within this field we have provided: 

Medicines and drugs to Iran in the summer of 1965. 

A medical team to Somalia in mid-1965 to help overcome a health crisis.

An engineer team to Mali to teach simple road and bridge building, and another one to Guinea.

On a larger scale, we furnished aircraft to haul food, medicines, and other essential civilian supplies to the northeast Congo during the crisis period last year.

The Middle East Force, a small naval element under my operational command that operates in the Persian Gulf, Red Sea, and Indian 

Ocean area also engaged in civic actions.

In December 1965, the Commander, Middle East Force, gave sorely needed medicines to a hospital in Hodeida, Yemen. His men helped paint a building of the World Health Center organization and a maternity and child feeding center. 

In another case, just last month, the men of the Middle East Force painted the interior of two buildings of a large tuberculosis hospital in Mogadiscio, Somalia. This voluntary act created a very favorable local impression because the Somalis were afraid to enter the building for fear of contracting the disease.

All our activities are designed to support U.S. national objectives in the area. We strive to achieve these objectives: 

By encouraging self-help as a contribution to sound economic growth.

By producing an atmosphere of security which permits the internal life of a country to develop if not yet flourish. 

By increasing the understanding between Americans and people of MEAFSA area countries, thus sustaining friendly relations with those people.

By strengthening the integrity, unity, and collective security of the friendly MEAFSA countries. 

And through these and other actions we seek to encourage countries which wish to maintain freedom.

While on this subject, five of the seven Government takeovers in the 

African portion of my area since last November-the Congo, Central

African Republic, Dahomey, Nigeria, and Ghana-[security deletion], stabilized internal situations in the countries. [Security deletion.] 

While Mobutu has faced the real problems of the Congo, the problems are large and complex. We have yet to see concrete results emerging.

In Dahomey, a political stalemate developed last year between the country's dual executives. The resulting governmental inaction toward solving the country's chronically weak economic and fiscal situation created growing national instability. Army Commander General 

Soglo initially took matters into his own hands [security deletion] and installed a caretaker civilian government. When the interim government also proved ineffective, Soglo assumed full executive powers for himself last December.

President Dacko of the Central African Republic was deposed on 

January 1 of this year by the Army Chief of Staff, Colonel Bokassa 

On January 4, the Upper Volta Army Chief of Staff, Lieutenant 

Colonel Lamizana acceded to popular pressure and assumed control of the Government from the President [security deletion]. 

At the turn of this year, regionalism and tribal frictions in Nigeria were threatening the very existence of the country. [Security deletion.] Faced with this chaotic situation, a group of young, Britishtrained officers [security deletion] seized control. General Ironsi, the army commander, was installed as head of state. 

In the beginning of 1966, Ghana was on the brink of economic collapse due to Nkrumah's profligate spending. Seizing upon his absence from the country on a visit to China, Lieutenant General Ankrah and other moderate army officers took control of the country on February 24, forming a National Liberation Council. They have threatened to try Nkrumah for all manner of crimes against the state should he re turn to Ghana. [Security deletion.] 

On February 23 Prime Minister Obote took over all executive powers of the Government, ordered the arrest of the five members of his Cabinet, and suspended parts of the Constitution. [Security deletion.]

In summarizing these remarks on Africa, I wish to point out that since the numerous African countries are the result of colonialism, political boundaries are arbitrary, frequently dividing tribal and ethnic groups. In addition, few of the countries alone have substantial economic resources, but together in various groupings, the resources are sizable. These two considerations cause me to believe [security deletion] economic life of Africa will stew for many years to come, that eventually some regroupings may occur which will result in viable national entities. We, of course, hope this can be accomplished peacefully and to this end one would hope that the African leaders would stress developments at home [security deletion].

In discussing our 1967 programs I will break my discussion into: 

First, countries with MAAG's where we have substantial and well rounded programs.

Second, countries with large missions. Incidentally, while MAAG's and missions function alike, missions generally do not cover as broad a scope of activities as do MAAG's. For example, our mission to 

Saudi Arabia is a training mission, the one in India is a supply mission, and so on, each being tailored to the specific needs as expressed in the several country-to-country agreements or aides memoire that apply. 

Third, countries with small missions or with MAP administered through Defense attachés.

As an exception, I will discuss the mission to India and MAAG- Pakistan together due to the interrelation of our activities in these two countries.

The Indo-Pak conflict, you will recall, began on August 5, 1965, when armed personnel [security deletion] began crossing the Kashmir cease-fire line, which had been established by the U.N. in 1949, 

[security deletion]. 

Fortunately, this ill-fated military venture was brought to a rapid close through a cease-fire arranged by the United Nations. [Security deletion.]

Subsequently, the Tashkent agreement laid the foundation for peaceful negotiations which are progressing about as rapidly as one could reasonably expect. Despite this deplorable sequence of events, both sides have given an earnest indication of their willingness to act responsibly in cooperation with the international community. 

The suspension on further deliveries of military equipment was made to preclude any further intensification of the conflict. This suspension remains in effect for grant aid material. However, a slight relaxation has been authorized for [security deletion] sales of nonlethal material. These are reviewed on a case-by-case basis. [Security deletion.]

While on the subject of training, one of the most rewarding results throughout military assistance is found in the carryover attitudes of

the foreign personnel trained in our U.S. military educational system. 

While the dollar amounts for such training have been relatively small, there has been a total of about 2,250 foreign personnel from the MEAFSA area trained in the United States since 1950. To me, a significant fact is that 90 percent of the students did complete their programed training. By this individual training in the United States, the students can also learn and absorb a great deal about our way of life by just being here observing and talking to Americans. The individual training has the advantage of being a long-range investment [security deletion] far beyond the time that a MAP-furnished piece of military hardware may last. A continuing effort is made to insure that the individuals selected for this training are of the best available quality.

To summarize, while each country program is directed toward the integration of maximum self-help and military sales with our longrange objective of continually reducing grant aid, I must emphasize that the program outlined for the MEAFSA area of responsibility contains only what we consider to be the barest essentials required to support overall U.S. objectives. This is because we do not have money to do more. I believe this program will provide the military strength required to maintain internal security and deter overt Communist aggressions.

I also consider it will provide a solid basis for the genuine freedom which these countries are striving to achieve in their own way. 

I appreciate this opportunity to discuss the MEAFSA military assistance program with you. MAP has had a significant impact on our alliances, base rights, efforts to build a world in which there is a genuine freedom of choice and universal respect for the rule of law. 

Therefore, I urge that the full program submission be authorized and appropriated.

SUMMARY OF MAP-SUPPORTED CIVIC ACTION PROGRAMS IN THE MEAFSA AREA 

The U.S. military assistance program has supported and encouraged civic action programs in MEAFSA area countries over the past 4 years. MAP is providing equipment from bulldozers to medical kits, as well as technical training, to improve foreign military talents to assist in social and economic development.

MEAFSA area MAAG and mission chiefs are required to emphasize the development of civic action programs in their respective countries. This requirement is established and promulgated in the following official directives, letters, inspections, and conferences: 

1. The Department of Defense Military Assistance Manual. 

2. U.S. Strike Command Manual 795-1, entitled "Military Assistance Objec tives and Force Basis." 

3. U.S. Strike Command Manual 795–3, entitled "Support Activities Guidance." 

4. The country planning book for each MEAFSA area country where an active military assistance program exists. 

5. Personal letters from time to time by General Adams to each MAAG/mission chief. 

6. Annual CINCSTRIKE/USCINCMEAFSA MAAG Chiefs' Conference. 

7. Annual command inspections of MEAFSA area MAAGs/missions by headquarters, U.S. Strike Command. 

The following are specific examples of civic actions within the MEAFSA area: 

Iran The MAP-sponsored civic action program in Iran is an excellent example of interdepartmental and international cooperation: 

1. Iranian Army units are very active in working with the rural people for the construction of roads essential to marketing crops, transportation of supplies to presently inaccessible rural villages and delivery of fodder to farmers. In villages, irrigation ditches have been constructed and wells drilled. During severe winter months, military units spend long hours on snow-removal projects, clearing roadways that would otherwise remain impassable until spring.

2. Joint military and civilian teams of doctors visit the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman areas to administer medical treatment to thousands of villagers. 

3. The gendarmerie performs tuberculosis detection and control in provincial centers, as well as operating a mobile dental clinic to treat villagers in remote areas. 

4. During severe winter weather, the Iranian Air Force conducts massive airlifts to drop food, clothing, medical supplies, corn and bran to starving people and livestock in isolated villages of the Azerbaijan and Gorgan areas. The air force provided flood relief to villages in the Dezful area a year ago, including medical supplies, food, clothing, and transportation. 

5. The Iranian Navy has a continuing program to deliver drinking water and provide medical assistance to the islands and remote areas along the Persian Gulf. 

6. The armed forces are fighting illiteracy by teaching recruits to read and write. The army's vocational training centers have been established with U.S. assistance and teach the recruit a basic skill before he returns to his village. 

From this has grown the countrywide programs of the literacy corps, health and sanitation corps, and the rural development program that have brought into action on a cooperative basis the Ministries of War, Health, Agriculture, Education, and Economy. Pakistan

Pest control in a West Pakistan river valley; disaster relief, epidemic and flood relief; oceanographic survey to establish erosion control; technical education (electrical and mechanical engineering schools); civil aviation improvement-support to Pakistan International Airways; agricultural development (military farms to supply dairy products to civilians). Africa

MAP encourages and supports civic action in several countries of Africa, for example: 

1. Ethiopia.-A major civic action project is the construction by an Ethiopian engineer battalion of farm-to-market roads urgently needed to improve the economy. Projects at the local level are helping to improve education, sanitation, and health. MAP has furnished construction equipment and is providing supplies for outpatient medical treatment. 

2. Guinea. The United States is providing equipment, materials, and training through MAP to help Guinean Army engineers build and repair feeder roads. 

3. Mali.-The United States is providing equipment, materials, and training through MAP to help Malian Army engineers built and repair feeder roads. 

4. Liberia.-A Liberian engineer battalion, supported and equipped by MAP, has rehabilitated schools and constructed feeder roads connecting villages to main roads. The battalion has also introduced modern sanitation methods to parts of the back country. These projects have enhanced the Government's program of rural and tribal integration into national life. 

5. Senegal.-A Senegalese Army engineer battalion works on civic action projects using MAP equipment. The battalion has engaged in construction of allweather, farm-to-market roads and is planning to build or improve airstrips for all-weather operations. 

Basic principles

From past and current experience, certain basic principles underlying successful civic action have emerged: 

1. Civic action should essentally be a host country program. The United 

States gives assistance, but the major effort has and should come from the country itself. 

2. In putting professional and military skills to use in helping people better their living conditions, the armed forces should work with the people, not just for them. 

3. By working side by side on civic action projects, the civilian and soldier develop a better understanding of each other's needs and proper roles, as well as each learning how he can contribute to economic and social development.

TUESDAY, APRIL 19, 1966 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, in executive session, at 10:25 a.m., in room  

The committee meets this morning in a continuation of the hearings on H.R. 12449 and H.R. 12450, the two foreign aid bills.

Our witness this morning is the Honorable Henry J. Kuss, Jr., Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense (ISA) for International Lo gistics Negotiations. 

Mr. Kuss, I understand you have a prepared statement. You may proceed, sir.

STATEMENT OF HON. HENRY J. KUSS, JR., DEPUTY ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF DEFENSE (ISA) FOR INTERNATIONAL LOGISTICS NEGOTIATIONS 

Mr. Kuss. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

I am indeed grateful for the opportunity to appear today before this committee on the foreign military sales program. This marks the third time I have appeared before this committee to review the foreign military sales program and it also marks the 10th year since I worked with this committee to establish the embryo of the revolving credit fund which is an important element of the total sales program. 

Over these years and more particularly in the last few years legislation on foreign military sales has resulted in the development of a sales tool that we have found to be quite capable in facilitating the kinds of arrangements for individual and collective security required to promote the peace of the world and the foreign policy, security, and general welfare of the United States. 

The general theme or setting for today's presentation is contained in the President's message to Congress on February 1, 1966, wherein he spoke of the more and more extensive use of this new tool to assist peoples of the world in their efforts toward internal and external security. The President said we will shift our military aid programs from grant to sales whenever possible-and without jeopardizing our security interests or programs of economic development. He noted that military sales now exceed the dollar volume of the normal grant aid program. He commented that this not only means a substantial 477

favorable impact on the balance of payments but it also demonstrates the willingness of our allies to carry an increasing share of their own defense costs.

Thus, the sales tool has become increasingly a major tool of Government diplomacy in the area of international security. It is a tool that results in about $12 billion of sales activity annually as part of much broader efforts between our Government and other governments to promote our mutual security.

There have been some who view the word "sales" solely in commercial terms and therefore I thought I might comment a bit on this aspect of the program. It is certainly true that over $9 billion of orders and commitments will result in dividends for stockholders and over 1 million man-years of employment for labor. These are important aspects of the program but not the most significant. The more significant aspect is the relationship which these sales have had to our foreign affairs. They constitute a very small percent, perhaps less than 5 percent, of total military production and development in the United States on the other hand, they constitute 15 to 25 percent on the average and sometimes 50 to 75 percent of defense expenditures of some of the friendly countries with whom our Government is associated in the world. This means that while the foreign military sale may be very peripheral to our commercial interests it is decidedly anything but peripheral in the eyes of the purchasing country and is treated in the administration of our foreign affairs with this perspective in mind. 

Military sales are equally small in terms of our total annual defense spending, accounting for less than 4 percent of the total. However, at the same time, receipts from military sales account for about one-half of the deployment costs of our forces, measured in balance-of-payments terms. The ability of this country to follow a forward strategy is heavily influenced by the balance-of-payment costs attributable to such a strategy. Thus, foreign military sales are of major interest to the Nation because they facilitate arrangements from our security throughout the world.

Working largely on a government-to-government basis in the foreign military sales field under the authority of the Foreign Assistance Act, well over 90 percent of the effort has been concentrated in 10 countries over the last 4 years. What this really means is that our major sales are to those countries who are principally involved in carrying out the purpose of promoting peace and security. 

This includes German forces who have bought over $3 billion from us in the last 4 years and who will in time of war actually make up, together with our five divisions in Europe, one of the major field armies defending NATO. 

The United Kingdom, who, with the signing of the recent F-111 program, is expected to spend over $2 billion in the United States for military arms in future years and who constitutes the principal European nation maintaining with the United States worldwide responsibility for the maintenance of peace-from Germany to the 

Atlantic Ocean to the Indian Ocean to Malaysia.

Australia, a nation alive to the problem of preparedness in southeast Asia and the need to provide for its defense has made arrangements for the purchase of almost $800 million of military products from the United States.

Italy, Canada, Belgium, and other NATO missions who constitute a major link in our worldwide forward strategy, purchased almost another billion dollars of products to strengthen their defense. 

Japan, conscious of its self-defense responsibilities, in that context of a growing national product, is expected to purchase several hundred million dollars of defense products.

As you see, the significance of these sales is great to the United States in terms of military cooperation. They represent a relationship military-to-military, a relationship that manifests itself in cooperation and logistics through the entire defense establishment of the free world.

This point should really be understood in more specific terms to understand the relationship of foreign military sales to the foreign policy, security, and general welfare of the United States. 

As I have already mentioned with respect to Germany, our program is part of a very carefully worked out set of international activities between the German armed forces and the American armed forces. 

These activities are of benefit to the equipment, logistics, and training readiness of the German armed forces, as well as being of benefit to both nations in making it economically feasible for the United States to deploy a large force in the forward area. It is a program that manifests itself in carefully planned meetings of military and civilian staffs at all levels of Government-integrated lines of logistics communication-integrated lines of voice and digital communications throughout our entire depot supply system-cooperation in research and development-joint use of training facilities and depots wherever possible-the joint development of weapons like the main battle tank of 1970 and even the undertaking of problems like the metric-versus-inch system way ahead of its time, as part of that tank program. 

In the United Kingdom the foreign military sales program was a program worked out in direct response to the United Kingdom's needs to put forth a defense establishment within an economic belttightening program. The three recent aircraft programs were part of an action to save well over $1 billion in the British defense budget. 

Without this action the British armed forces would have been considerably more restricted in manifesting a British defense responsibility throughout the world. This was a program that represented our national interest in world affairs, as well. Its solution in the context of international politics required the most astute exercise of diplomacy under the objectives and authority of the Foreign Assistance Act.

In Australia our military export program was first a manifestation of close United States-Australian military-to-military interests. Secondly, it was a result of the growing Australian recognition of the severity of the southeast Asian problem and, thirdly, a cooperation in broadest field of international finance utilizing the foreign military sales program tool.

Our program in Canada was and is a demonstration of the reciprocity required between two nations whose economies are so closely linked. Without such recognition the Canadian armed forces could not gain the benefits of the Canadian-American defense common market.

In Iran, sales agreements were negotiated in such a way that they were as much a recognition of the need for military strength against the Communist threat as they were a recognition of the need to maintain the expenditure of resources on military activity within certain. reasonable financial levels-levels that did not interfere with the economic and social progress of each country's program. I would like to note particularly the arrangement with Iran is conditional to the improving financial condition of the country. As part of our undertaking with them the Government of Iran has assured us that the program of military purchases will not cause undue strain on their foreign exchange reserves nor jeopardize their plans for economic and social development. 

It was further agreed that representatives of both countries would meet not less frequently than once a year to assess the general progress and the balance of payments and budget impacts. 

Similarly, our examination of the future military sales in Latin America involves as much a question of the relationship to the entire success of the Alliance for Progress as it does individual military sales. As Mr. McNamara noted the other day, we spend more of our time in places like this not selling than selling. 

In the Middle East our actions are directed toward maintaining a reasonable stability through the provision of limited arms designed to promote internal security and legitimate self-defense. It should. be noted that the introduction of nearly $2 billion in Soviet bloc arms poured into the area has contributed toward altering its arms balance and stability.

The United States wants to avoid contributing to an arms race in the Middle East and becoming a major supplier in the area. Accordingly, the United States reserves the right to consider limited sales of defensive equipment to friendly states in the Middle East,. but the "case-by-case" principle must be maintained. Every effort will be exerted to prevent both nuclear proliferation and the introduction of other sophisticated weapons systems into the area that may jeopardize the delicate balance of power. 

Thus you see the many ways and means by which foreign military sales program activity-carried out under the authority of Congressadministered in close coordination between the Departments of State and Defense becomes an instrument of international affairs to accomplish the objectives of mutual security. 

No major change in these authorities is requested this year. These authorities are, however, placed in a separate chapter 3 of the bill which clearly indicates the task of sales as that of advancing the overall objectives of the act by facilitating the acquisition on a reimbursable basis of Defense articles and Defense services by friendly countries having sufficient wealth to maintain, utilize effectively, and equip their own military forces wholly or in part without grant assistance. 

In addition there has been introduced in the Senate a proposal to add to the objectives of the chapter two statements. The first concerns arms control and states that "the chapter should be administered so as to encourage regional arms control and disarmament agreements and so as to discourage arms races especially among less welldeveloped countries." The second statement concerns financial ability. 

It states that in the administration of this chapter with respect to less well-developed countries, special account should be taken of the coun- 

---

try's ability to pay and the record of the armed forces of such country with respect to civilian constitutional government. 

I should like to assure this committee that this is precisely the way in which we have tried to utilize the foreign military sales tool and the way in which we intend to administer the act in the future. 

I have with me today Mr. Forman, who is Assistant General Counsel for International Affairs, and who has worked with me for this full 10 years in developing the foreign military sales program tool. 

In addition, Mr. Forman and his too few assistants spend a great deal of their time with my key assistants in negotiating specific international agreements on sales. I suppose that between Mr. Forman's staff and my own that well over 1,000 days were spent overseas last year in negotiating and consummating the kind of government-togovernment agreements that I spoke of earlier. Mr. Forman and I would be glad to provide any additional information on the foreign military sales program that you wish. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Kuss.

Mr. Kuss, there is substantial volume of sales of military equipment to foreign governments by U.S. manufacturers and dealers which are subject to the munitions control legislation, section 414, of the Mutual Security Act of 1954 but which are entirely outside the authority of the Foreign Assistance Act. What is the total volume per year on these commercial sales?

Mr. Kuss. They vary, of course, year by year. I would estimate in fiscal 1965, for example, the total of military exports we estimate was $1.8 billion. The amount going through government was $1.5 billion; of that, $300 million was the balance. They vary from $300 million to about $500 million a year in this commercial area.

Chapter 3 of the bill appearing on pages 24 to 33 of the bill deals vith military sales and related matters. Mr. FORMAN. There are three amendments in the bill. Section 

3(b), which is on page 20 of the bill, contains two changes to the evolving fund for financing sales. One change provides for the ransfer to the fund of existing unliquidated balances of new obligaional authority, which has been appropriated in the past, to the evolving fund. At the present time those balances are still carried fter obligation in the parent military assistance account. They do not show up in the revolving fund.

The second change is to authorize the President to take the money which is allocated for financing sales in the military assistance program ppropriation which has not been obligated and put that directly into he act. The purpose of both of these changes which were recommended by he Bureau of the Budget is to enable the President's budget document to show a more complete picture of the program of foreign miliary sales and the status of the accounts, since these items do not now how up. You don't now see in the account itself the amount which as already been financed out of military assistance program new obligational authority. 

Have I made that explanation clear?

Mr. HAYS. I understand that. What else have you done?

Mr. FORMAN. Section 44 is not a new authority. It is a limitation on an authority we now have. Under the act as it now stands, we are authorized to sell foreign currencies and use those foreign currencies either for grant aid purposes or convert the foreign currencies into dollars which then are used by the revolving fund. 

The new section 44 limits the extent to which we may sell foreign currencies by providing that we may do so only to the extent the Treasury determines that an excess of U.S. Government holdings of that currency will not result. This amendment is in line with other statutes which have been enacted by the Congress, such as amendments to the Foreign Assistance Act and also section 6 of the Interest Equali zation Tax Extension Act of last year. 

The third amendment is in section 51, concerning barter. Under the existing law, if we use MAP funds to finance the transaction we can take the material we receive in exchange and either use that for grant aid program, for resale to a third country, or for resale to one of the Armed Forces.

The Armed Forces by this means-for example, should one of our Armed Forces want something that is being produced by another country-can obtain it through an indirect barter transaction as long as MAP funds are used to finance the transaction. This ties up MAP funds for the duration of the time it takes to complete the transaction.

Section 51 will eliminate the MAP intermediate use of MAP funds for that purpose and enable the military departments to engage in direct barter transaction without the use of MAP funds. 

Those are the three amendments which affect that chapter.

SALE OF SURPLUS 750-POUND BOMBS TO GERMAN COMPANY 

To free needed storage space and reduce maintenance costs, the Air Force n 1963 authorized the disposal of surplus munitions, including 750-pound bombs, n Europe. This was done in accordance with existing Defense Department directives.

In early 1964, the Air Force sold 7,562 bombs of the 750-pound class to Kaus and Steinhausen, a German company interested in reducing the explosive concent of the bombs to basic chemicals for resale as fertilizer, and in selling the casing as scrap metal. The total price to the buyer was $12,736. 

The appearance of a buyer was welcomed, since at that time there was little market for surplus bombs, and disposal action would have consisted of scrapping by the Air Force which, due to the nature of the material, was costly. In 1965, as the accelerated military activities in SEA indicated an unprecelented usage of munitions, including bombs, production of 750-pound bombs was initiated. As a means of supplementing stocks and holding dollar expenlitures for new bombs to a minimum, it was also deemed prudent to acquire Dombs from any other available source. 

It was learned in the fall of 1965 that 5,570 of the 7,562 bombs sold to Kaus and Steinhausen had not yet been demilitarized. The contractor was approached

and he agreed to sell the bombs back to the U.S. Government. Negotiations for repurchase were begun and a price of $125,000 was agreed upon, taking into account the considerable costs incurred by the contractor, plus his loss of expected profits. For example, he had already invested time and money in development of the reduction process, he had leased remote real estate for storage, and had acquired equipment. It should be noted that his asking price was roughly $210,000, as compared with the final negotiated figure of $125,000. 

Considering the present cost of $440 for new bombs, or $2.5 million for 5,570 bombs, this transaction was very favorable to the U.S. Government.

Mr. Kuss. So we take tanks which are in storage, which are surplus to our needs, and we sell those tanks. However, where a country insists on a new tank, then the U.S. Army places a contract for a new tank.

INTERNATIONAL LOGISTICS NEGOTIATIONS RELATIONSHIP WITH U.S. AND FOREIGN GOVERNMENT AGENCIES 

My office serves as a DOD central control and clearance house in the management of defense sales activities. In this capacity my staff and I assist the Secretary in the establishment of overall sales policies and procedures in coordination with the State Department, the Agency for International Development, the Treasury Department and other Government agencies as necessary. Important 60-929-66-pt. 3-

defense sales are usually negotiated by my office under a government-to-government agreement umbrella. As a matter of policy, my office does not promote the sale of any specific military equipment, but provides the country with technical information on all eligible and releasable military hardware available for current and/or future procurement. I usually insist that the final decision on the selection of military equipment remain the sole responsibility of the foreign government, subject to any overriding political-military-economic considerations. 

Under these conditions, U.S. industry remains in the background during government-to-government consultation, providing technical inputs to International Logistics Negotiations and/or the foreign government as required and authorized.

There is another media through which my office exchanges ideas with industry and that is through the Committee on Military Exports of the Defense Industry Advisory Council. This committee, about 25 in number, is composed of representatives from the management level of U.S. defense industries who have responsibilities for the export of military products, as well as private financing and banking institutions which are active in the military export field. The committee provides a forum for the exchange of views between Government and U.S. industry in promoting, negotiating, and supporting the export of U.S. military products. It is restricted by its charter to act in an advisory capacity only to the Secretary of Defense. (DOD directive No. 5030.31, October 2, 1964, subject: 

Committee on Military Exports of the Defense Industry Advisory Council.) 

In our dealings with U.S. and foreign industry and foreign government agencies, International Logistics Negotiations is governed by the provisions of 

DOD directive No. 5500.7, May 17, 1963, subject: "Standards of Conduct," as revised March 22, 1966, and OSD administrative instruction No. 52, December 15, 1964, subject: "Standards of Conduct." Paragraph II, A, B, and C of OSD 

instruction No. 52 reads as follows: 

"A. No person shall allow himself to be placed in a position in which a conflict of interests might arise or might justifiably be suspected. Such a conflict of interests may arise or appear to arise by reason of the acceptance of favors, gratuities, or entertainment of any kind or by any other action which could influence or be reasonably interpreted as influencing the strict impartiality that must prevail in all business relationships in which the public interest is involved. 

Favors, gratuities, or entertainment bestowed upon the families of military or civilian personnel shall be considered in the same light as those bestowed upon such personnel. "B. Where there is a reasonable doubt as to the propriety of accepting favors, gratuities, or entertainment or of attending functions or accepting other invitations of a hospitable nature, all personnel shall refrain therefrom. "C. Special treatment shall not be accorded to particular individuals or firms unless equivalent treatment is also accorded to other individuals or firms justifiably entitled thereto."

My office, in its association with the representatives of foreign countries, extends official entertainment courtesies in keeping with propriety as dictated by the occasion and conducted on a modest basis. All requests for International 

Logistics Negotiations official representation funds must be approved by the 

Assistant Secretary of Defense (International Security Affairs) and Assistant Secretary of Defense (Administration) and the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

WEDNESDAY, APRIL 20, 1966 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, pursuant to adjournment, at 10:15 a.m. in room 

The committee meets this morning in executive session on a continuation of the hearings on foreign aid bills H.R. 12449 and H.R. 12450.

Our witness this morning is Hon. Donald W. Hoagland, Assistant 

Administrator for Development Finance and Private Enterprise, Agency for International Development. 

Mr. Hoagland, you have a prepared statement and you may proceed, sir. 

(The prepared statement of Mr. Hoagland follows:) STATEMENT OF HON. DONALD W. HOAGLAND, ASSISTANT ADMIN- ISTRATOR FOR DEVELOPMENT FINANCE AND PRIVATE ENTER- PRISE, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a pleasure for me to appear once more before this committee to report to you on the private enterprise activities of AID. The purpose of these activities is to strengthen free enterprise in less developed countries and to increase the role of U.S. private enterprise in our assistance effort.

Today I want to review briefly the significant developments in our private enterprise activities since my last appearance before you; the changes in our authorizing statute we are requesting this year; and the Agency's response to the report of the Advisory Committee on Private Enterprise in Foreign Aid.

We administer a range of information services, risk-sharing programs, and financial programs designed to encourage greater participation by U.S. investors, with the technical and managerial skills which they typically contribute, in projects in the less developed countries. 

Our information activities are closely coordinated with the valuable activities of the Department of Commerce. Our principal publication is "Aids to Business (Overseas Investment)." To date we have distributed over 80,000 copies of this booklet which summarizes the assistance to investors offered by our Agency. 

Our Businessmen's Information Center here in Washington advises interested firms and individuals on AID's programs, and puts businessmen in quick contact with the appropriate action officers. The center is now averaging approximately 400 inquiries per month from visitors, through correspondence and by telephone. 

Our "Catalog of Investment Information and Opportunities" is a unique collection of economic and technical feasibility studies dealing with the less developed countries. The contents of the catalog are continuously reviewed and refreshed. In May 1964 when the first index was distributed, the catalog contained some 1,200 studies. The fourth edition of the index, released in January of 507

this year, lists over 1,600 titles. We have distributed the index widely and the catalog is being heavily used. Requests for copies of the studies (or abstracts of the studies) are running at the rate of 400 per month. 

In response to the President's call for increased emphasis on economic development in southeast Asia, a special southeast Asia supplement to the catalog will be released next month. It will include, in addition to the studies already in the system, some 150 new studies which have recently been collected for this purpose. 

It will also include a current analysis of investment laws and conditions for each country.

Under the investment survey program we are able to underwrite 50 percent of the cost to a businessman of examining a new investment opportunity. We authorized 63 of these surveys in 1965, compared with 46 in 1964. In the case of positive decisions the investor bears the entire cost of the survey. If the decision is negative, we stand ready to reimburse 50 percent of approved costs against receipt of a professionally acceptable study, which we can then make available to other investors through the catalog. Between the origin of the program in 

1962 and December 31, 1965, 172 surveys were authorized. Of these, 83 are in varying stages of completion. There have been 70 negative decisions or grant withdrawals. To date investors have decided to invest in 19 projects, such as a hybrid corn seed and feed plant in Brazil, a dairy products plant in Pakistan, and a cement plant in Greece. 

The ratio of positive decisions to total decisions is about 1 to 4. The positive decisions represent planned investment of just under $50 million while the negative decisions to date represent a potential cost to the U.S. Government of $461,000. Thus for each dollar of this potential cost we can point to $108 in planned investment.

We are making a particular effort to reach firms of modest size with this program. An encouraging number of applications are from this size firm. We are requesting authority for such funds as may be necessary for this program for the next 5 years.

The specific risk guarantee program by which we guarantee new investments against the three political risks of inconvertibility, expropriation and damage from war, revolution or insurrection, has grown dramatically in recent years: [In millions] 1961. 1962. 1963. 1964. 1965. 

Calendar year 

Number of coverages 50 144 186 486 645 Value $71.0 440.0 426.0 707.8 954.0 

The net amount of specific risk investment guarantees outstanding at the end of 1965 stood at $2.5 billion. This is more than twice the amount outstanding at the end of 1963. Last year Congress authorized an increase in the issuing authority available for this program from $2.5 billion to $5 billion. Applications continue to increase. We now have on hand over $13 billion in applications for insurance coverage. Many of these applications do not materialize as contracts because they are filed in the early stages of project planning. However, we estimate that we will need, and have requested, an increase in this guarantee authority from $5 billion to a ceiling of $10 billion to cover the next 5 years. The list of countries that have agreed to institute this program has continued to grow-73 less developed countries have now entered into the necessary agreements. Since the beginning of 1965 agreements have been signed with Brazil, Dahomey, Chad, Uganda, British Guiana, Upper Volta, Rwanda, Singapore, British Honduras, and Ceylon. During that same period our agreements with India, Thailand. Korea, Malaysia, and Costa Rica were amended to provide additional coverages. The agreement with Brazil was aunounced at this time last year. The program is now in operation. Several contracts have been issued and we have on hand applications for over $200 million in guarantee coverage. 

Section 620 (1) of the Foreign Assistance Act requires that assistance be terminated by December 31, 1966, to those countries that have not signed bilateral

agreements covering inconvertibility and expropriation. There are relatively few countries in which the agreements necessary to escape the application of section 620 (1) are now lacking. It may be in the national interest to continue assistance to these countries, even in the absence of investment guarantee agreements. Therefore we propose that Congress replace the present mandatory termination provision with one providing for presidential flexibility.

Certain operational changes in the program are significant. 

We have compiled a statement of the policies and procedures of the program in a new handbook and have made certain changes in our fee structure. On March 15, 1966, the fee for convertibility insurance was reduced from one-half of 1 percent per annum to one-fourth of 1 percent per annum. At the same time we began to offer optional coverage against the risks of expropriation and war damage in a combined contract. The combined coverage is available at a single rate of seven-eights of 1 percent per annum instead of the rate of one-half of 1 percent per annum which applies to each of the separate coverages. In addition, the fee for standby coverage has been reduced from one-half of 1 percent to one-tenth of 1 percent. We expect these changes to improve the capacity of the program to attract additional investment to the developing countries. 

Claims against the program continue to be light, although they are larger than last year.

Three new claims have been filed in the past 12 months. reserves are more than ample to cover these claims. Our

The extended risk guarantee authority for nonhousing projects under section 221 (b) (2) authorizes us to guarantee investors against loss of up to 75 percent of the investment. This applies to all risks except the fraud or misconduct of the investor. The statutory ceiling on this authority is currently $175 million. 

Progress under this program has continued to be slow. We have authorized guarantees totaling $14.1 million for four projects. Three of these were issued in 1965 for a carbon black plant in Colombia, a fish cannery in Somalia, and a fertilizer plant in Korea. A guarantee for a second fertilizer plant in Korea was authorized last year, but canceled by the investor who decided to go ahead without it. Two major industrial projects are in the final stages of negotiation. 

There is a strong possibility that another $20 million in guarantees for these projects will be authorized before the end of this fiscal year. An additional $40 million in projects have been shown to us as formal applications or serious inquiries.

We have recently worked out with the investment community a change in the structure of the guarantee contract, which is more likely to meet the investor's needs than any form we have offered so far. The institutional investors who need full protection will have it, and the commercial lenders in the project will hold the early maturities without an extended risk guarantee. 

Last year Congress provided $175 million in authority for this program to cover a 2-year period. We now request $300 million in authority to extend to 

June 30, 1973.

Under the Latin American housing guarantee program there were 14 housing projects completed or under construction as of February 28, 1966. These projects involve a total investment of $82.2 million, covering the construction of 

16,000 dwelling units. Another 36 projects, involving $157.2 million in investment and 28,000 dwelling units, are in various stages of processing. As you know, the Agency recently announced new criteria for the expanded Latin American housing guarantee program authorized in last year's act. 

Outside of Latin America, one guarantee has been authorized for a housing project in the Republic of China; other applications are being processed for projects in Thailand and several African countries. 

From the proceeds of title I, Public Law 480 sales we made 38 local currency Cooley loans to U.S. firms or their affiliates in 13 countries amounting to the dollar equivalent of $35.4 million in 1965. These loans were for such varied activities as the production of cement in Bolivia, wire rope in Colombia, chemicals and tractors in India, paperboard in Israel, food products in Pakistan; and for the establishment of a small business investment in Tunisia. The proposed food-for-freedom legislation provides for a continuation of this kind of lending. 

In addition to these programs, specifically designed to encourage and assist U.S. private investors, I also wish to report on programs which provide financial assistance to private enterprise, whether locally owned, U.S. owned, or joint venture.

We have lent substantial amounts of local currency generated by AID program loans to local credit institutions for relending to the private sector. One

such institution, the private investment fund in Colombia, has relent pesos to over 100 subborrowers in amounts totaling over $45 million equivalent. Funds will be established in Brazil and Chile which will relend counterpart currencies to help finance imports of U.S. spare parts and equipment. 

We continue to support intermediate credit institutions as a major means of spurring private enterprise development. During calendar year 1965, eight dollar loans amounting to $46.5 million were authorized to eight institutions. 

We make dollar and local currency loans to industrial development banks, housing institutions, agricultural credit banks, and banks for cooperatives. 

The ownership of these institutions may be private, Government, or mixed but in each case they make their subloans to private borrowers. 

With regard to direct dollar loans to private borrowers, AID authorized nine loans amounting to $100.2 million during 1965. This is about the level of our lending to private borrowers in 1964, reflecting availability of funds from alternative free world sources, such as local intermediate credit institutions, private lenders, the Export-Import Bank, the IFC, and the IDB. Loans were authorized in 1965 for such projects as a cement plant and a hardboard factory in Brazil, two chemical fertilizer plants and a cement factory in Korea, and a gas transmission system in Pakistan.

Program loans continue to play a key role in private enterprise development. 

During calendar year 1965 we authorized 10 nonproject loans amounting to $371.5 million. By providing foreign exchange for the purchase of U.S. capital goods, spare parts and industrial raw materials, these loans are a strong stimulus to the productivity of the private sector. In addition, they contribute significantly to our ability to influence aid-receiving governments to establish realistic exchange rates, liberalize import restrictions, enact important tax measures, and combat inflation.

Our programs to encourage private U.S. investment in developing countries strengthen our Nation's businesses and in addition do much more. These businesses carry essential technology and know-how to places where they are most needed. Their impact expands and multiplies through suppliers, employees, customers, partners, stockholders, and competitors. As a result, AID's interest in private enterprise goes far beyond its interest in facilitating and encouraging U.S. private investment. The dollar loans, program loans, and local currency loans I have described furnish significant financial support for a strengthened local economy. However, to improve the local conditions for local and foreign private investment a comprehensive approach must be taken, and a broad effort undertaken to identify and deal with obstacles to private economic activity in countries where significant AID programs are underway. In addition to financial assistance, this brings into play a wide range of technical assistance in such fields as investment promotion, management and vocational training, and improvement of legal and financial institutions. It also points to a wide area of exchange of ideas between aid-receiving and aid-giving countries looking toward the elimination of restrictive, ineffective, or inefficient policies and procedures.

We are already doing many things of this kind in our major country programs. 

In Turkey, for example, a new Government has been elected on a platform which included a statement of intention to place strong reliance on the capacity of Turkish private industry to grow to meet the country's needs. In response, we are engaged in projects to assist and strengthen the Turkish Management Association, the Management Consulting Center, and the National Productivity Center. We are strengthening the capacity of the banking system to extend credit on longer terms to small and medium-sized businesses outside of the major metropolitan areas. We are supporting technical and vocational education, inplant training, and labor relations training. 

In other countries different components may be present. In Latin America, for example, the use of cooperative mechanisms has proven particularly effective and continues to expand. 

In recognition of the breadth of these possibilities, an amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1963 called for the establishment of a nine-member group to "carry out studies and make recommendations for achieving the most effective utilization of the private enterprise provisions of this act. ***"

The Advisory Committee on Private Enterprise in Foreign Aid, chaired by 

Arthur K. Watson of the IBM World Trade Corp., presented its report to the 

President on August 25, 1965.

The report's 33 recommendations are directed to many aspects of private involvement in the development process: Private foreign investment; stimulation of private economic activity within the developing countries; the role of business, the universities, the voluntary agencies, professional associations and foundations; the overriding importance of the development of economic resources.

Many of the recommendations are quite specific. For example: that AID expand the use of its extended risk guarantee authority; that it offer combined specific risk guaranty coverage and lower the fees; that the United States sign and ratify the World Bank-sponsored Convention for the Settlement of Investment Disputes; that Congress enact tax legislation offering incentives for U.S. business to invest in LDC's.

Other recommendations are broad, designed to influence the tone and emphasis of AID's total program. 

Action has been completed on a number of specific recommendations. The 

Secretary of the Treasury has signed the Convention for the Settlement of Investment Disputes which is now before the Congress for ratification. As mentioned above. AID now offers combined war and expropriation coverage and has reduced premium rates for its specific risk guarantees. The U.S.

Government is broadening its collaborative efforts with other governments in the antitrust field as recommended by the Committee. Action has been com. pleted permitting the IFC to borrow up to $400 million from the World Bank for investment in private enterprise in the member countries. The emphasis on the importance of education in development strategy recommended by the Committee is fully reflected in the fiscal year 1967 foreign aid proposals. AID and the Export-Import Bank have reviewed their guaranty policies covering exports of technical and professional services as recommended by the Committee. 

The President has endorsed the concept of binational foundations utilizing excess local currencies. Plans for the establishment of the first such foundation in India were announced in March 1966. 

Among the broader recommendations, the Committee's first recommendation, that AID make an intensive study, in selected countries, of the factors affecting the climate for investment, both domestic and foreign, is particularly important. 

Studies are underway in Thailand, Korea, Turkey, Brazil, Chile, and Tunisia.

They will provide the analytical background against which our existing programs can be tested in the light of the Committee's recommendations dealing with: investment project identification, analysis and promotion; capital loans and credit availability; legal and administrative structures and procedures; vocational and management skills. The objective is not a study but rather a longrange strategy to develop flourishing local economies. 

The report has been well received throughout AID as a thoughtful and useful analysis of the role private resources can and must play in economic and social development. It has given a useful stimulus to AID's efforts and will have a continuing influence in shaping and guiding future programs. 

In an effort to involve a major non-Federal resource in development assistance, and to improve the business management of local industrial and commercial enterprises in the less developed countries we have assisted in the launching of the International Executive Service Corps. This is a private organization, managing the activities of volunteers from the ranks of senior American business executives. During 1965 the program grew steadily and at the yearend had over 100 projects underway in 18 countries. It has a distinguished board of directors, and an able, energetic chief executive officer in the person of Frank Pace, Jr. Typical of the assignments undertaken by these executives are: assistance to the management of a dairy firm in Iran; improvement of merchandising procedures of a department store in Panama; improving production procedures of a manufacturer of general electrical products in Taiwan. This is a young program, but the early results are promising. 

During 1965 the Development Assistance Committee of the OECD decided to include private investment matters in its activities. Representatives of member countries have held several meetings resulting in a work program to exchange information on their experience in using investment incentives, to coordinate public and private development efforts, to improve statistics on the private flows of capital from all capital exporting countries to developing countries and to study the overall economic effects of foreign private investment.

The Business and Industry Advisory Committee of the OECD is expected to play a leading role in this work. 

In his foreign aid message this year, the President made it clear that most of the work of economic development must be done by the people of the developing countries themselves. He outlined major calls to action for the people of the developing countries-he identified actions which are necessary to real progress, emphasizing that they are difficult but necessary, and that "we will not continue any partnership in which only we recognize that fact." One was a challenge to "create the climate which will attract foreign investment, and keep local money at home." In a real sense, the entire assistance program supports that effort. Major capital improvements supply power, transportation, and communications essential to business growth. Nonproject and local currency lending, and many forms of technical assistance support private economic activity.

But the job cannot be done by Government alone. In carrying out strengthened programs in the fields of agriculture, health, and education, we will turn increasingly to the private resources of this country to participate. The President stated the essentials of this approach, in which we think our greatest opportunity for increased effectiveness lies, in his foreign aid message: "The U.S. Government can do only a small part of the job of helping and encouraging businessmen abroad. We must rely more and more on the great reservoirs of knowledge and experience in our business and professional communities. These groups have already provided invaluable service and advice. We in Government must find ways to make even greater use of these priceless assets."

Mr. HOAGLAND. Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure for me to appear once more before this committee to report to you on the private enterprise activities of AID. The purpose of these activities is to strengthen free enterprise in less developed countries and to increase the role of U.S. private enterprise in our assistance effort. 

Today I want to review briefly the significant developments in our private enterprise activities since my last appearance before you; the changes in our authorizing statute we are requesting this year; and the 

Agency's response to the report of the Advisory Committee on Private 

Enterprise in Foreign Aid. 

We administer a range of information services, risk-sharing programs and financial programs designed to encourage greater participation by U.S. investors, with the technical and managerial skills which they typically contribute, in projects in the less developed countries.

The program representing the largest volume of activity with which we deal is the specific risk investment guarantee program. This program has been in operation since 1949 and it has been growing at a very strong rate. In calendar year 1961 we issued 50 coverages with a dollar value of $71 million. In 1963 these figures had grown to 186 coverages at $426 million. In 1964 it was 486 coverages at $707 million.

During calendar year 1965, we issued 645 coverages valued at $954 million. This means, for example, that the 1965 rate of issuance was more than double the 1963 rate of issuance. I am particularly happy to report that since in previous years there has been concern about the growth of that program, I feel confident at the present time it is meeting the needs of investors. It is improving both substantively and mechanically, as it is continuing to find new and effective ways to be responsive to the general concern of investors over the particular risks

it covers, the risks of incontrovertibility, expropriation, and damage from war, revolution or insurrection. 

This year we are asking for an increase in the authority of that program from the current ceiling of $5 billion to a ceiling for an additional 5-year period of $10 billion. This anticipates a rate of issuance of approximately a billion dollars a year and builds into the authority approximately-although this is necessarily an estimate the rate of growth that we are presently experiencing. The $10 billion figure is what we anticipate would be needed to carry us through the period of authorization requested by the administration bill. 

During 1965 we again made progress on the execution of bilateral agreements with additional countries considering the institution of this program. Ten additional countries have signed these agreements since the beginning of 1965. The most significant of them is Brazil. 

I reported on the signing of the Brazil agreement to you last year, but I can now report that the program has been ratified by the Brazilian Congress, that guarantees have been issued and that the program is operative in Brazil. 

Mr. ADAIR. Does that cover all three of the specific risks?

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes, sir, it does, as well as the extended risk guarantee, the one which guarantees against all risks not just political risks, with the exception of the risk of the investor's own fraud and misconduct.

Under this authority during 1965 we issued three contracts using slightly over $14 million in authority. This authority is one that has not yet been used on a broad scale. 

The ingredients to me seem to be there for a financial device which can meet the needs of investors seeking dollar credits in situations of importance to our general purpose to facilitate an increase in the participation of private enterprise in economic development. The mechanism is a complex one. It has not yet been refined to the point where it can be used in large quantity. 

At the present time we are in the final stages of negotiation of transactions using the form of guarantee that we discussed last year on which we anticipate the greatest immediate use of this authority. 

This is the kind of guarantee which would split the authority so that a commercial bank would take the risk on the early maturities and an institutional lender would take the risk on the late maturities. 

Taking this approach, 75 percent of the debt involved in an investment plan could be held by an institutional lender and receive the full benefits of the guarantee.

This would be a guarantee of 75 percent of the debt involved, but it would give the guarantee benefits to the long-term lender and it would put the shorter term investor at risk. The commercial bank, I believe, would find it in its interest to take a risk of 2, 3, or perhaps 4 years in the developing country situations but I doubt very much that institutional lenders would take any risk at all on long-term investments in developing countries under the present conditions. We have worked very closely with the investment community in trying to refine this style of guarantee to meet their needs and in the past few weeks we have worked out arrangements that would make it possible for the

guarantee to run directly to the institutional lender rather than to run to him by participation through the interest of the commercial bank, which is at risk on the early years.

This difference was in response to the reactions we had to the style of guarantee that we described to you last year and is the form of transaction on which as I say we are very close to concluding arrangements in three transactions currently before us. This does not represent a high rate of use of the available authority. 

Nevertheless, I think that the potential of this kind of authority and the importance of working patiently and ingeniously toward methods of bringing commercial banks and institutional lenders into the process of financing developing country investments justifies the request we make that for the 5-year period contemplated by the administration bill, plus the necessary period to maintain the availability of the authority after the last year of the legislation, there be established a level of $300 million of authority for this program. 

This is an annual level somewhat below the annual level that is available under the existing authority, but it maintains this program at a level which would give institutions the confidence that the program has the support of Congress, will continue to be in existence and is something that they can use in their investment plans for the long term.

The other point I wish to refer to in terms of specific activities during the last year relates to the Advisory Committee on Private 

Enterprise in Foreign Aid. This is the Committee chaired by Arthur 

Watson of IBM, which reported in August of 1965. This Committee made a wide range of recommendations, 33, directed to many aspects of private involvement in the development process. 

They dealt with private foreign investment, with the stimulation of private economic activity within developing countries, and the role of business, labor, universities, voluntary agencies, cooperative associations in the development process. 

A number of their recommendations were concrete and specific and have been adopted. Some of them were involved in the aid legislation adopted by the Congress last year-changes in the specific risk guarantee authority in particular. The action already taken in connection with the convention for the settlement of investment disputes which is now before the Congress for ratification, is in conformity with the recommendation of that Committee.

We have gone ahead with reductions in the fees for specific risk guarantees, again in response to one of their recommendations, and have made arrangements to offer a combined coverage on expropriation and war risk which pursues one of their recommendations, although it does not adopt it precisely.

Action has been completed permitting the IFC to borrow up to $400 million from the World Bank for investment in private enterprise in its member countries.

The emphasis that they placed on the importance of education in development has been fully responded to by the administration in its fiscal year 1967 proposals to the Congress.

The President has generally endorsed the concept of bi-national foundations using excess local currencies and plans for the establishment of such a foundation in India were announced in March of this year.
