There is a broader set of recommendations made by the Committee which can't be responded to quite as concretely and specifically_as that. They have in general urged us to pursue tax incentives. We accept that idea and are examining several alternatives. 

They have in their first recommendation urged us to make intensive studies in selected countries of all of the factors affecting the climate for investment for local and foreign investment. We are now engaged in doing that in Thailand, Korea, Turkey, Brazil, Chile, and

Tunisia. This approach is reflected as well in several other recommendations that encourage us to undertake a broader program of feasibility studies, to improve the legal and financial institutions that support private investment, and to undertake additional programs for management education, and to transfer technical training and technology to the developing countries through the use of the skills in our own private sector.

We agree with the general principle of those recommendations. We feel we have been doing a considerable amount of work of this kind, but we accept the spur this gives us to do a better job and to analyze more carefully, evaluate more thoroughly the programs of this kind that we are carrying on. Tra

The general content of the AID foreign enterprise activity should 

I propose, be viewed not solely as support for U.S. private enterprise going abroad, but as support for the strengthening of the concept of private enterprise and the strengthening of the private sectors in the countries in which we work, and as one of the major facets of a comprehensive and promising aid program. 

The President has made it clear in his foreign aid message that he considers that the efforts of a country to improve the climate for foreign investment and to take those steps necessary to keep its own capital at home and effectively employed are to be considered as explicit and significant parts of the self-help performance of a country that we should examine in order to determine whether it make sense for us to have significant aid programs in the country. 

Finally, he made it clear that in all of the aspects of our foreign assistance work the U.S. Government can do only a small part of the job. We must rely more and more on the reservoirs of knowledge and experience in our own business and professional communities. 

These groups have already provided invaluable service and advice. 

We in Government must find ways to make even greater use of these priceless assets. This is a theme that we pursue with all of the energy we can.

I think there are many aspects of the aid program that can be made more effective by an improvement in our contacts with and use of American private resources. We look to a greater emphasis on that effort in coming years.

I would be glad to deal at this point with any questions you may have, Mr. Chairman. #metob n 60-929-66-pt. 3—7

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Hoagland. 

Mr. Hoagland, I understand that a situation has arisen which tends to discourage the use of the investment guarantee program by U.S. investors where part of the financing for the oversea projects might be financed by the Export-Import Bank. It is my impression that the 

Export-Import Bank wants a U.S. investor to assign some of its protection under the investment guarantee program to the bank. 

It is not my understanding that the investment guarantee program was intended to guarantee investments of U.S. Government agencies. 

I thought it was to apply strictly to private investments by U.S. investors. Will you discuss this problem for the record? Are you aware of it?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I am aware of this problem, Mr. Chairman. This is a complicated issue and one in which in effect it is necessary to consider what the intention of Congress may have been in situations of this kind. The situation involved would be one in which the Eximbank is making a loan to a proposed project sponsored by a private 

American firm.

That firm would be a stockholder-let's assume it might be the only stockholder in the company receiving the loan. The investor would come to AID for guarantee protection against losses from risks such as expropriation and if there had been no Export-Import Bank loan in the picture, we would have proceeded to offer this coverage in an amount equal to the amount invested, plus earnings of the operation abroad if they are kept in the project up to an amount equal to the original amount of the investment.

This is to encourage reinvestment and Congress made a specific amendment in the statute to permit us to issue the guarantees to cover not only the original investment but also earnings that are kept in the project.

The Eximbank approaches this subject naturally from the point of view of its own responsibilities and is concerned that it is inappropriate for a situation to arise in which an investor might be compensated and come away from a project which has collapsed as a result of some such calamity of this kind, not just with his investment, but with substantial profits represented by these earnings while the U.S. 

Government suffers a loss because the Export-Import Bank had a loan in the project which is not paid off. 

The thing we have to remember here is that our guarantee insurance goes to a stockholder, an investor, but not to the company in which the investment is made. So that when we pay off on an expropriation guarantee, our money goes to the investor and it isn't therefore in the hands of somebody who owed it to the Export-Import Bank. The investor might go away with his investment, while the Export-Import 

Bank suffers a loss.

As we see our responsibilities, we were supposed to be guaranteeing investors against expropriation and our authority should be used the same way whether there is an Export-Import Bank loan or not. 

The Eximbank feels it is inappropriate for this to happen and that the United States should not suffer a loss through the Export- Import Bank loan default when the investor makes a profit. We are

discussing this matter at the present time and it is a matter on which an expression of the intention of Congress would be helpful to us. 

You might want to request a statement for the record from the Export- 

Import Bank on this matter.

 ARTHUR D. LITTLE, INC., CONTRACT-NIGERIA 

Expansion of investment in Nigerian industry is an important part of the nation's 6-year plan. During the period 1963 through 1965 over $300 million worth of new industrial investment has been made in Nigeria. Counting projects which are presently planned and likely to go ahead this figure may be increased by another $100 million.

Since Arthur D. Little, Inc. (ADL), has been under contract with AID to promote investment in Nigeria, progress may be reported as follows: new investment in manufacturing in 1963 totaled $76 million, creating 39 functioning plants. In 1964 new investment totaled $52 million in 27 plants. Additionally in 1963, $68 million was invested in 14 new plants still under construction at yearend, and $118 million invested for expansion of 22 existing facilities as well as $33 million in planned investment still in the blueprint stage.  LOANS ADMINISTERED BY AID IN DELINQUENT STATUS

SPECIFIC RISK GUARANTEES 

Reconciliation.-Chart: Investment guarantees total amount in force, 196165 (p. 31, presentation book) and dollar value of contracts written, 1961-65 (p. 4, Donald W. Hoagland statement).

The increases in the amounts of specific risk investment guarantees outstanding at the end of each calendar year, shown in the chart, are less than the amounts of new guarantee coverage written for each of the years as indicated on page 4 of the statement. The principal reason for the variance is the fact that the yearend amounts reflect reductions and terminations of existing contracts which had taken place during the year while the amounts of new guarantee coverage written do not. Other factors which contribute to the difference, although to a lesser degree, stem from the internal reporting mechanism. For example, postdated contracts (i.e., contracts taking effect up to 6 months after execution) are issued under the guarantee program. The yearend may intervene between the execution date and the effective date of coverage. In other cases, contracts executed late in one calendar year may not be picked up by the Controller in time to be included in the amount outstanding at the end of the year.

 INTERNATIONAL EXECUTIVE SERVICE CORPS AND OTHER NONPROFIT ORGANIZATIONS PROVIDING TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE TO INDUSTRY IN THE LESS DEVELOPED COUNTRIES 

As of December 31, 1965, there were 54 technical service contract or grant agreements entered into by AID with nonprofit firms and associations, exclusive of universities. There appears to be only one organization, the Council for International Progress in Management, some of whose activities are in the same general area as IESC. Some other nonprofit organizations, the Brookings Institution and the Stanford Research Institute, have made studies in the past year under AID contracts to broadly assist private enterprise in some of the less developed countries. There is no standard overhead rate used in these technical service contracts. Charges for administrative services are negotiated case by case and generally definitions of direct and indirect costs reimbursable at different rates are established.

The Council for International Progress in Management has a number of contracts with AID for services to be performed in less developed countries. The 

Council plans and conducts seminars for industrial managers from private businesses in foreign countries, assists local management by providing management specialists and technical advisers. It provides investment counsel and production assistance as well as development planning and training programs. In 1965, its AID contracts totaled $1.022 million for which it was reimbursed a little over $100,000 for home office staff services.

The International Executive Service Corps, a new organization which completed its first full year of project activity in January 1966, received from AID for the calendar year 1965 the sum of $690,476.69 to carry on its program of direct assistance to private enterprise in developing countries. Of this amount, $188,575 was for salaries. Home office administrative charges totaled $76,774.18. 

Under the terms of the grant agreement with IESC, AID reimburses the Corps for specific percentages of approved project and nonproject costs. Through calendar year 1965, AID reimbursed 80 percent of IESC direct project costs and 75 percent of its indirect project costs. For the year beginning January 15, 1966, the percentages were reduced to 75 percent and 65 percent, respectively. Further reductions are anticipated as IESC receives increasing support from the American business community and reduces the starting up level of its operating costs. 

The IESC is a new approach to improving the management practices of private enterprises in the less developed countries. The idea of sending an experienced

man. 

American businessman as an unpaid volunteer to assist a business in his line was first advanced by two members of Congress and a prominent American business- After a review by several departments of the Government and with congressional approval, AID made a grant to the newly formed IESC providing financial assistance for its early development. To speed the organization of 

IESC and make its program available on a worldwide basis the initial funding was substantial. There are some other nonprofit organizations, but not in the field of business, which also receive substantial financial assistance from AID. 

The Executive Corps program has been well received in 20 of the less developed countries and by the American business community. Its project level is continuing to accelerate and the direct business to business assistance which it provides appears to be serving a need in the less developed countries. 

Mr. HOAGLAND. There are many organizations, cooperatives, savings and loan organizations, who have contracts with us to furnish technical assistance. CIPM is a very valuable source of this kind of help whose contract has been extended for another year and which is carrying on some interesting work in connection with placing foreign students in American industry for a year following their graduate work in this country. 

I don't have in mind a fixed number of organizations of this kind but I would be glad to furnish you with additional material of this kind.

Mr. ADAIR. In the proposed legislation you have suggested that the specific risk guarantees, or the risk guarantees be extended to 1973. Is that the proposal you are making?

Mr. HOAGLAND. There is no date with respect to the political risk guarantees. On those there is simply a ceiling amount. With respect to the extended risk guarantees, there is the date of 1973.

Mr. ADAIR. If your housing guarantees are proposed to be extended to 1971, why do you select different dates as to other terminations?

As people have already indicated, I have most serious doubts that you will get the 5-year authority requested, but I am interested in why you select different dates for this.

Mr. HOAGLAND. The section 211(b) (2) that deals with extended risk guarantees is also an authority that covers housing guarantees. To the extent that housing guarantees are authorized under 221(b)(2), the extension to 1973 would apply to them as well. As for the housing guarantees for Latin America, if the date is 1971, then this is simply a difference in practice that has carried on because of the way these two sections have been dealt with in the past and for no other reason. 

Mr. ADAIR. You must confess it is a little confusing to have two dates for two similar programs. In the little time I have left, I have some very specific questions, and these have been touched upon before. 

You are giving a combined war risk and expropriation coverage now at seven-eighths of 1 percent; is that correct? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes, sir. 

Mr. ADAIR. What do you charge for the three specific risk coverages?

Mr. HOAGLAND. Before those changes were made, there was a charge of one-half of 1 percent for each coverage. People took out varying amounts and the net cost of the insurance wasn't 12 percent. 

It was somewhere down around 14 percent. 

Under the present proposal, under the new fee schedule there is an option to take the war and expropriation coverages as a package for seven-eighths of 1 percent, and convertibility insurance is available whether you take the other package or not at one-fourth of 1 percent instead of one-half. 

Mr. ADAIR. But you don't give them a three-way deal at 1 percent, say? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. That is right. 

Mr. ADAIR. Can you now?

Mr. HOAGLAND. It is not offered as a three-way deal. Convertibility insurance cost a quarter of a percent if you take it all by itself or in any other way. 

Mr. ADAIR. That would make 11% percent. This perhaps isn't an important matter, but it just crossed my mind, that you might want to make a package arrangement for those three coverages.

Mr. HOAGLAND. This has been suggested and we have considered it. 

The difference, and the reason we didn't go all the way was that convertibility comes up every year as dividends and interest are paid and you still have the whole investment in place.

If you are looking at expropriation or war, it is the investment in place that gets damaged. If your coverage dwindles away because of

Mr. Hoagland, to what do you attribute the fact that the Latin 

American housing program is practically bogged down? Bureaucracy? Hospitality in the AID or what? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. They participate very heavily.

Mr. HAYS. Why? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think the difficulties in getting projects finished off have to do with the difficulty, the complications of handling housing projects in areas where institutions don't exist for doing these things in the effective routine way that they are done in this country and other countries that are used to handling projects. 

We also have the problem of relating the use of our authority to the maximum development of institutions in those countries that will let them do more housing and create a multiplier effect. Working this out adds complications, I must admit. 

Mr. HAYS. You use the FHA to process these, is that right?

Mr. HOAGLAND. Because we think they start off knowing more about it and have a group of people experienced in the field that would be able to do it better than our own staff do.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Whalley. 

Mr. WHALLEY.  

Mr. Hoagland, after completing an investment survey you say you guarantee new investments against risks of convertibility, war damage, revolution and insurrection. On the basis of these guarantees what has been the experience of the investors? First, what is the average return on the investment? Second, is the return greater than if the investment was made in the United States in the same type business? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. We haven't kept figures showing the investment experience of the group of investors who have our investment guarantee coverages as a separate group. Looking generally at the history of investment there has been this kind of history. The Department of Commerce figures show that the average rate of return on U.S. domestic manufacturing has risen in recent years to a level of about 13 percent. 

The rate of return on direct investment in Europe used to be very much higher than that. In 1959 it was up around 18 percent. It has come back down as our rates of return have gone up and they are fairly close to each other. In the developing countries the rates of return are presently running a small fraction, I would say 2 or 3 percent, below the average rates of return on direct investments in the United States or in Europe.

Mr. WHALLEY. In your opinion why wouldn't the investor invest his money in the United States if the return is less in other places? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think it is because, first of all, those are average figures and none of them think they are going to be the average. 

Beyond that Americans firms are looking to the future. They see the presence of 2 billion people in the rest of the world who are going to grow in their capacity to consume and use products manufactured someplace and they are actively going out to find those markets and to be sure as they develop the American producers are the ones who have them and not somebody else.

Mr. WHALLEY. In other words, they are making an investment both in the United States and these other countries.

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes, sir.

Mr. WHALLEY. Thank you. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Farbstein. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. 

Mr. Hoagland, what is the reaction of the various countries where we have excess currencies when it comes to making loans to foreign investors of that local currency?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think they have been cooperative with the Cooley loan program, which is the one we principally use to make loans to firms that are affiliated with American companies. The general use of these currencies is consistent with their desire to build up business activity. I think they can see the payrolls and general economic benefits of continuing business activity. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Does that apply to housing also?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think there have been a few cases in which this kind of currency has been used to finance housing investment; yes. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Have you had any complaints from any individual who sought to go into some of these countries where excess currency rests and has met resistance by the country as far as housing projects are concerned?

Mr. HOAGLAND. They haven't come to my attention. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Whose attention would they come to if they were made?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think they would come to the attention of our operating offices. My office does not operate the housing programs. 

If they are seeking Cooley funds or local currency funds the direct contact would be either with our mission in the field or with the Regional Bureau Office in Washington to whom the mission reports. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Would you say that it is necessary to get cooperation of the government of a particular country in order to proceed with a project? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes, sir. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Have you found instances, or would you have the opportunity of learning whether there were instances of resistance on the part of these governments to any projects proposed by American corporations or companies? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. I certainly would have that opportunity. If you would like me to undertake some kind of search of this kind I would be glad to.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Do you know of any proposed projects that have been resisted by these foreign countries wherein we have excess local currency?

Mr. HOAGLAND. Do you mean housing projects 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Housing is one of them. 

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. I think there was quite a to-do about some company here that wanted to build a fertilizer plant in India.

Mr. HOAGLAND. I was going to refer to fertilizer investment in India. 

Particularly in fertilizer production, the problem is a live, current problem. It isn't so much Indian resistance to the construction of fertilizer plants. It is the problem of working out all the parts of the transaction. There is not complete satisfaction with the positions the Indian Government has taken on these things although they have made some very positive moves forward in the last 6 months. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. I also understand there was resistance by the Indian Government to proposed housing projects where local labor was going to be used, where local products would be used in building and the American company wanted to go down there with the building blocks. I would like for you to check if it is possible to learn how many applications for loans have been turned down by our Government for local excess currency where American firms have sought to engage in some industry within a foreign country. Also if you have any knowledge how many different projects have been resisted by any foreign governments where applications have been sought for consent; and if there has been resistance why has there been resistance by the foreign government, and if we have turned down any companies that sought to use excess currencies in foreign countries why have we done that? I would like to get a picture of whether or not the statements contained in your memorandum here that we have made $40 to $50 million or $90 million worth of local currency loans are actually so. Also I would like to get the names of the companies to whom these various loans were made and for what purposes they were made. And whether or not these are profitmaking companies or whether these are solely non-profit-making companies. I would like to know what is happening to all this Cooley money that has been building up and why it has been building up to the degree it has. 

You have a billion dollars around, probably a billion dollars in India and Pakistan and the United Arab Republic, hundreds of millions of dollars and nothing is being done, when I know there are American companies that want to go into these various countries and use some of those funds and they meet with resistance all the way down the line.

Mr. HOAGLAND. I would be glad to furnish the information that you have asked for but I would like to comment, if I may, Mr. Chairman, that of the funds that we have accumulated in the excess currency countries, by no means all of it, a small portion of it is available for financing of business ventures under the Cooley program. Even in that small proportion I believe we have more than enough funds available in these excess countries to handle the demand. 

I am not aware that any significant cutback has occurred in excess currency countries, because companies with good projects have not been able to go forward because of our lack of currency. We have done nearly $200 million of lending of this kind. I wish we had funds of this kind in countries other than these excess countries. The demand,

I believe, is being met except clearly for cases in which countries would be resisting the project, whether it is local currency financing or dollar financing. T 

​TAIM) 

02 In India, for example, and in other countries the country is concerned about whether the industry that is coming in is going to contribute to the solution of its own balance-of-payments problem. If the industry is one which is going to sell its products locally and not help the country export this creates a special problem for countries who have a severe balance-of-payments problem. I think we would be sympathetic with that since we are working with them trying to solve it. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. In what category would you put housing?

Mr. HOAGLAND. Housing is an activity that would not cause an inflow to the country of foreign exchange. The question the country has to resolve in connection with housing is what priorities it wants to apply in the allocation of its own resources. The currency is a claim on its resources and it has to decide whether its people need housing more than they need fertilizer, whether its people need housing more than they need something that will contribute to other improvements in their agriculture. This is a matter of great policy importance in any country and where the countries are severely underdeveloped it is a hard choice.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. In other words, every country has a veto as to whether or not any of that local currency can be used. We could keep on piling up zillions of it and it still could not be used, is that not à fact?

Mr. HOAGLAND. That is technically correct. It assumes that we have no voice or influence with the country as a result of our relations with them and the presence of an AID program and I think that restores the balance to an important extent. COOLEY LOAN PROGRAM 

1. From January 1, 1962, through December 31, 1965, AID has authorized 

180 Cooley loans in the amount of $196 million (U.S. dollar equivalent). A tabulation of these loans, showing country, borrower, amount, industry, purpose, and authorization date, is set forth in table A. 

2. In the period January 1, 1962, to February 18, 1966, AID received a total of 135 applications that did not result in Cooley loans being made. A tabulation of these applications, showing country, industry and purpose, amount requested, and the reason the loan was not made, is set forth in table B. In preparing this tabulation AID has defined an application as a submission containing the following information: A specific request for a Cooley loan in a specific amount; identification of the putative borrower; a description of the project to be financed; where eligibility depends on U.S. affiliation, the identification of a presumably eligible U.S. business firm; where it does not, a description of how the export of U.S. agricultural products would be increased; and identification in reasonable detail, by amounts and sources, of the other capital to be invested in the project.

3. No Cooley loan applications have been fully formally disapproved by the 

Indian Government. When a loan proposal includes features that may be contrary to that Government's policy with regard to Cooley loans, it is the practice of AID to discuss (or request the prospective applicant to discuss) the proposal informally with the Indian Government in order to get its concur. rence before an application is prepared. Normally the Indian Government would question the use of Cooley funds for working capital, loans to U.S. companies for purchase of equity stock, projects involving a debt-equity ratio of more than 2 to 1, projects in industries not considered by that Government to be of a developmental nature, and projects for which local financing is available on comparable or appropriate terms. 

4. With regard to housing, it is our understanding that the Government of 

India has not generally favored housing projects with United States or other foreign participation because it has not been persuaded that the services provided by the foreign interests generally know-how, since labor and material are provided locally-have been worth the foreign exchange cost of royalties and dividends, etc., payable to the foreign interests. Rather it believes (or has believed in relation to the proposals presented to it) that adequate knowhow in the construction of housing can be procured from Indian sources and paid for in local currency, without any drain on its foreign exchange resources. 

Because of this view, no housing project proposals in India have matured into applications for Cooley or other U.S. loans. We do not know how many housing proposals by U.S. interests have been presented to, and received unfavorable consideration by, the Government of India. 332

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Gross. 

Mr. Hoagland, in connection with Mr. Zablocki's questions concerning the employment of so-called nonprofit organizations, do you employ consultants? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. The Agency does employ consultants; yes, sir. 

Mr. GROSS. Would you be good enough to provide for the record a list of these consultants for the past 3 years and the amounts paid to them?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think that would be a substantial list, Mr. Congressman. Do you mean to include contract services as well as consultants as such? Consultants generally are individuals, is that what you had in mind?

Mr. GROSS. You have already been asked for the information concerning the employment of so-called nonprofit organizations. 

Yes, I would like to know who you are employing as consultants in addition to the staffs that are permanently employed, yours and others, in connection with your operation. Is this too much to ask? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. No, sir; I don't believe it is.

Mr. GROSS. Let's find out how far beyond the permanent staff you go. (The information requested is as follows:)

Mr. GROSS. You are encouraging U.S. private investment abroad. 

What effect does this have on the balance-of-payments situation? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. The present policy we are pursuing is that the encouragement of private U.S. investment in developing countries is something we would continue to do even if we attempt to restrict private investment in the industrialized countries for the sake of our balance of payments. The direct capital flows to the developing countries as a result of private investment were $803 million in 1965 and $578 million in 1964, not counting reinvested earnings which would add a couple of hundred million. Mr. GROSS. Mr. Hoagland, since I have other questions to ask, and 

I would like to ask them, can you say whether this has an adverse effect upon the balance-of-payments situation?

Mr. HOAGLAND. It has a short-run bookkeeping adverse effect, and a longrun plus effect.

Mr. GROSS. I would like to go into that further, because I don't agree with you on that. The Watson Committee urged the United States to give full support to the principle of an investment code under international sponsorship. AID commented that no significant support for the OECD draft convention—that is, for the protection of foreign property has yet appeared among the developing countries. Why has there been no support among the developing countries for this code? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think it is because they are very concerned about their power to advance their affairs and handle investment without the participation of outside judges of their internal law. In most of these situations what they are concerned about is that they anticipate the way they adopt laws and reach judgments in their courts are going to be questioned internationally, and they think that as long as they are offering nondiscriminatory treatment for foreign investment with their local investment that that is all that ought to be asked of them. 

Mr. GROSS. They are perfectly willing to take American dollars, are they not, without joining in establishing a code or assuring-giving us any reasonable assurance of safety of investment?

Mr. HOAGLAND. They have entered into other kinds of agreements with us such as the bilateral guarantee agreement, which is cooperative. 

Mr. GROSS. This leads to the question. We have dished out $130 billion or more in foreign aid around the world, and this we were told through the years was for the purpose of creating a favorable climate for American investment; to make American investments safe abroad.

How much longer are you going to continue this program, or is it to go on indefinitely and forever?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think this program is for more than to make 

American investment safe abroad, as you appreciate, Mr. Congressman. It is to make a contribution to the peace and security of the world, and to build nations that will be partners and neighbors that we can get along with and be both secure and prosperous with in the long run. The program is designed and planned to work itself out of business. I cannot tell you how long that is going to take, but that is the purpose of it.

Mr. GROSS. Do you have any more situations like that in London where there was a guarantee to protect the Knott Hotels Corp.?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I don't know that situation, Mr. Congressman. 

Mr. GROSS. This was some years ago. I have never been able to understand why there was any necessity for any guarantee program in England.

Mr. HOAGLAND. This refers, I assume, to the period immediately after World War II when we had convertibility insurance and we were at that time responsive to the dollar gap in Europe and trying to reconstruct that area and encourage American industry and investment to go there, in much the same spirit as is involved in these programs. 

Mr. GROSS. Are the multilateral organizations, such as the U.N. and 

OAS to assist the development and improvement of local financial institutions and support of private enterprise in the less developed countries? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. Specialized agencies of the U.N. carry on technical assistance programs that would contribute particularly to industrial techniques, and the improvement of development banks and institutions of this kind that would service the private sector. 

The World Bank is particularly strong in this respect in financing and improving intermediate credit institutions that would service private borrowers. 

Mr. GROSS. Are you saying that is true as to both the U.N. and the OAS?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think it would be less true of them than the 

World Bank.

Mr. GROSS. I would think so. Do our food-for-peace agreements with all countries include I believe that has been brought up under the Cooley programs by Mr. Farbstein-do they include all the Cooley loan provisions and, if not, why not?

Mr. HOAGLAND. It is part of the negotiation in every situation. 

During the past year out of, I would say, 10 food-for-peace agreements, about 5 were with small African countries in which very little allocation for Cooley was possible simply because there was no demand, but an allocation was made. The only ones in which there were none made was in the Congo, in Vietnam, and in Afghanistan where there was no demand for the funds. Unless there is no demand, there is some percentage set aside. 

Mr. GROSS. Are the British still charging the going rate of interest in England on their loans to foreign countries?

Mr. HOAGLAND. They have this past year made a change in policy which has resulted in loans which in some cases are longer in term and lower in interest rates than ours. They have some no-interest loans now to developing countries from England. 

Mr. GROSS. I cannot help but ask a question, perhaps you can't answer it, but where do the British get the money to make no-interest loans, since we are propping up the pound sterling. 

Mr. Chairman, that is all.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Roybal. 

Mr. ROYBAL. Mr. Hoagland, I am fast coming to the conclusion that your program in Latin America looks a lot better on paper than it does on the scene. In a recent visit to Latin America I noticed that AID people lived in the best districts in whatever country they happen to be assigned to. It appears to me that they don't seem to care

too much about the slum dweller and that their programs do not really include the people who live in the slum community. This I saw in 

Peru, for example, and even some in Chile. 

What specifically is being done to provide housing for the people in the lowest income brackets-not only in Peru and Chile, but throughout Latin America?

Mr. HOAGLAND. The housing program in the form enacted by the 

Congress last year shifts as you know from a pilot demonstration type of program to a program authorized to go into four particular kinds of projects. One of them is the type of project which will finance housing for low-income families for a maximum sales price of $2,500. The hope is that we can get those units down to as low as $1,500. At the same time, in terms of what the general interests of the slum dweller is, and of the most severely impoverished portion of the population, one of the most difficult choices you have to make is, given the fact that we cannot and would not want to simply support a country's economy, we want to use our resources in the way that makes a maximum contribution and moves them to make the maximum contribution, and there is a hard choice to where to put it. If we spread the money around in dollar bills to the poorest people, we wouldn't accomplish anything. We have to tackle the problems comprehensively, and that is the way it is being done where our interest is strong enough. 

Mr. ROYBAL. What I was referring to specifically was a program that I saw in its inception in which the people in the slum areas were forming cooperatives. They started making their own homes, using indigenous materials, and their own labor. The house would definitely not cost $2,500 because these people couldn't afford to pay $2,500 in their lifetime. This to me is the type of program that we should be advancing in certain Latin American countries. 

What is being done insofar as AID is concerned in regard to a program of this kind where they, themselves, participate in building their own houses, in providing their own sewage and good sanitary conditions?

As I say, I have seen a pilot project of a private group that is doing this, and I would want to know what AID is doing in this regard. 

Mr. HOAGLAND. I agree self-help housing is an excellent mechanism. 

This is the kind of thing that has to be generated from within, from the energy and the initiative of the people concerned. But the Inter- 

American Development Bank in particular is actively assisting in loans and other activities to encourage this kind of housing. The forms of housing guarantees that we have been discussing are by definition to guarantee the cost of construction. Other programs to encourage credit unions and savings and loans and to encourage housing that might be put together by cooperatives are handled largely through technical assistance where we sent advisers to help groups of this kind who have this kind of energy.

Mr. ROYBAL. This again makes this thing very complicated to that individual. He is not interested in the finances of a credit union. Nor does he understand the finances of a savings and loan. He is interested in his immediate problem. What is AID doing to motivate these people to form their own cooperatives so at a very minimum they can get away from their atmosphere of poverty and squalor?

Mr. HOAGLAND. We have arrangements with cooperative organizations in this country to support the activities of the respresentatives of the cooperative movements in the cities of Latin America, who are teaching this concept as you describe it. We place a high value on it. 

Mr. ROYBAL. Do you have such a person in Peru; Lima, for example?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I am confident there is such a person. 

Mr. ROYBAL. I didn't have the pleasure of meeting this gentleman, if he was there. It could be that he just happened not to be in town. 

I saw no evidence, however, of any activity in this direction. 

Mr. HOAGLAND. It is more likely that he might have been in the back country.

Mr. ROYBAL. That is where I visited. I visited the back country. I visited I think all of the slum areas of Peru and I saw no evidence of AID doing this. In fact, the Peace Corps was instrumental in making funds available so that the people in these slum areas were providing their own sewage system. They were doing it on a voluntary basis. each man was devoting so much time a week to this project. From what little funds were available the campesino provided his share and was matched by funds from the Peace Corps. 

What type of program have you developed that will put this concept into effect throughout Latin America? I think this is the only way you can reach the people who cannot possibly afford to pay $2,500 in their lifetime?

Mr. HOAGLAND. As I say, it is through the activities of representatives of American cooperative organizations and through community development programs, the financing of rural community water systems, and the rural educational systems where the people of the areas have to combine and work together to support the activity that is involved.

Peru is a good example of where an extensive community development program is being undertaken, particularly in the rural areas. 

Mr. ROYBAL. You are talking about something that I am sure they don't understand. They are not knowledgeable nor are they really interested in high financing procedures. They are interested in someone from your Agency going in with them, motivating them to help themselves, organizing them on a so-called grassroots level so that together they can accomplish what they have not been able to do throughout the generations; that is, get out of their slum conditions. They are not asking for a five-bedroom home; they are, however, asking for something better than they have had before. I think this can be done if the AID program goes into this type of program development in various areas throughout Latin America. 

I sincerely recommend that you look into this type of community development program very seriously, and see if something can be done to apply this concept. 

Mr. HOAGLAND. Thank you.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Thomson. 

Mr. THOMSON. 

Mr. Hoagland, on page 4 of your statement you discuss the increase in the specific risk guarantee investment program. Can you tell us whether there is any relationship between the amount of guarantee

investment in these countries, and the amount of other forms of aid that are provided? In other words, does aid decrease in a country in proportion to the specific risk guarantee investment increase?

Mr. HOAGLAND. It does not, Mr. Congressman. This figure does not represent assets going into the country. It represents contingent liability in the event of certain particular kinds of loss. It is important to point out that the figure on value of coverage is very much larger than the amount of investment, because if a single dollar of investment is covered against three risks that shows up as $3 of coverage. The amount of investment covered is anywhere from 30 to 50 percent in various years of the amount of coverage issued. 

The answer to your question is "No."

Mr. THOMSON. The coverage does represent some investment and some activity in that country? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes, sir.

Mr. THOMSON. There is no relationship between an increase in investment activity and the amount of aid that this country might continue to supply?

Mr. HOAGLAND. The examination of the country's needs includes a consideration of the amount of private investment from all sources that can be expected in the country. This is part of the analysis of how it is progressing, and what its needs might be, and what the chances are of doing something constructive with aid financing. 

These figures do not represent investment all in a single year; therefore, it is not a figure that can be used in examining the various sources of capital that might be coming to a country in any particular year. 

Mr. THOMSON. Then this investment program doesn't provide any hope that there can be a decrease in the amount of aid that might be needed in that country?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I would not want it to be construed that way because as investment increases, and as it becomes apparent, as it did in Taiwan and Greece, that a country can attract private investment, this is the very kind of progression that will cause us to conclude that aid can be phased out as it has been in those countries. This figure represents a contribution to the process of encouraging private investment, and as private investment responds and as more of it flows, this has a direct part in the conclusion that we hope to come to with every country, that private or other sources of capital are moving for natural causes and it would not be necessary to continue an aid program. 

Mr. THOMSON. Then you are saying that it does contribute but it is very remote?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I would say that it does contribute, and that it is intangible, but it is not remote. It is direct. It just isn't arithmetically applied except in the analysis of the country's total economy every year.

Mr. THOMSON. In the analysis that you have made on page 2 you say you have an analysis of investment conditions in certain countries. 

Do you have such an analysis for India, for example? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. The bottom of page 2, did you say? 

Mr. THOMSON. Yes; where you say you have just completed a new series of studies and they have been collected for the purpose of dissemination. I thought if you had one for India I would like to receive it.

Mr. HOAGLAND. The material that is referred to there is the work done to develop a special collection of data for southeast Asia, and India is not included in that work. This reference to the current analysis of investment laws and conditions does not include India. This included the countries in the region of particularly the Vietnam region and the surrounding countries that are the subject of the southeast 

Asia development effort. 

Mr. THOMSON. Refer to your preceding paragraph and you say you have a catalog containing some 1,200 studies. Then you say the fourth edition, the index released in January of this year, lists over 

1,600 titles. Do you have any on India in that group? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes, sir. I am sure there are studies outstanding of investment laws and conditions in India. There are several good works written by Mr. Kust and Mr. Surrey that go over this ground, and I would be glad to send you either a reference to some of them or what we think are the best ones.

Mr. THOMSON. I would like to have some of the best ones. 

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes, sir. 

Mr. THOMSON. Are you requesting a 5-year authorization in your part of the foreign aid program? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes, sir.

Mr. THOMSON. I notice that among all of the outstanding countries that you list in your remarks you mention Korea and you mention 

Brazil and others, but you don't happen to mention India. Is that because we are having difficulties in that country? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. The list of countries, the places where I have listed countries naturally were for various purposes- 

Mr. THOMSON. On page- 

Mr. HOAGLAND. On page 5-excuse me.

Mr. THOMSON. On page 3 you mention Brazil, the hybrid seed plant in Brazil.

Mr. HOAGLAND. Yes. That is an interesting case because the company that investigated the hybrid seed business in Brazil under our investment survey program decided to make the investment in Brazil and then went ahead and undertook another survey in India. 

Mr. THOMSON. They didn't like India, did they?

Mr. HOAGLAND. I don't know what their answer has been. This is the Cargill Co. I understand the survey is underway at this time. 

It is certainly true that the conditions of entry for companies considering investment in India are troublesome at the present time. 

Mr. THOMSON. On page 6 you mention a fertilizer plant is going into Korea. But recent press stories by the administration indicate that is one of the primary concerns in India. You don't mention India in that category either.

Mr. HOAGLAND. There are some very active negotiations now. And of the extended risk guarantees that I referred to, things that may be coming up in the next few months, two of them have to do with possible fertilizer plants, one in Brazil and one in India. 

There are I would say five or six fertilizer investments under discussion with India and this is a field in which it seems to me the Indian Government has been facing its problem and making some changes that give us some reason to think that they will encourage private investment. After all, some time ago they wouldn't permit

fertilizer production to be undertaken in the private sector at all. 

They now will.

Mr. THOMSON. Does your index or your analysis point up these problems? When you analyze a country do you list the problems that exist or do you just list the possible benefits?

Mr. HOAGLAND. This is intended to be reliable information. When a study of a country is done we try to be sure it is a good one before it goes in the index. At the same time what you are describing and the feel for the situation that you are reflecting depends on current information. Studies that go into indexes do have the problem of talking about something that happened, inevitably, 6 months ago at least. 

This kind of information, the feel for current conditions in a country is something that has to be acquired from other sources. 

Mr. THOMSON. Thank you very much.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. McVicker. 

Mr. McVICKER. 

Mr. Hoagland, on page 8 you mentioned that substantial amounts of local currency have been re-lent to the private sector, to local credit institutions.

Would it be too much of a job to take the area of Latin America, Central and South America, and get a rundown on the amount of money that has gone into either host country institutions or to regional institutions, of either U.S. money or local currency? 

Mr. HOAGLAND. We can furnish that, yes. (The information appears on p. 570.) 

Mr. McVICKER. The question has come up this morning again on this housing problem in Latin America. This is the subject of a great deal of interest in this committee. I am sure you are aware of that. 

We have been told here by other witnesses that there have been some projects approved since the bill was passed last year and we have been told equally there has been none. There is certainly something wrong here.

Many of us had the opportunity to see one or more of these projects. 

We are impressed by what we see. But now we see a terrible foot dragging or some kind of breakdown in the utilization of our energies toward these projects, both low income and middle income. 

My own impression, Mr. Hoagland, is not the question that has been raised this morning of individuals, but I have a feeling somehow there is a process here in which there is so much redtape, so much checking, not only by AID but by other agencies of the Government to make sure that when the money is finally let loose or the guarantee is finally given that the project will not end up an embarrassment knowing that this committee and the press of this country would take one such project and castigate anybody that was involved in it. 

I think the real problem is how do we arrange so that individuals like yourself-I personally think the Government is fortunate to have you and people like you-how could we give you the kind of leeway that you should have if you were in the private sector and not the government sector.

I don't think this is a personal thing against an individual. I think it goes back to the McCarthy era and other similar experiences. I think what is needed is somehow to find a system in relationship here with the Congress, especially to this committee in particular, to release the kind of energies that you would have released if you were a pri-

vate individual and would take the kind of chances on investment that you are responsible for trying to get the private sector to do. 

I have made a statement, Mr. Hoagland, more than asked a question. 

You might respond to it if you will, if you wish to. 

Mr. HOAGLAND. You have certainly put your finger on the heart of the problem. We are dealing here with an authority that puts the 

American taxpayer 100 percent at risk on any dollar that is lost in these projects, and we are creating projects which symbolize the presence and participation in Latin America of the Alliance for Progress and the United States and its private sector in the development of an area. These have to be good projects. 

Part of what we are trying to do is not simply to build the structure that people are going to live in but to start something moving that is going to repeat itself so that the general problem of housing in the country will be responsibly launched in some constructive direction that will repeat itself well. 

Mr. McVICKER. Yet, Mr. Hoagland, in a country in Central America I saw a project that was a success. I saw an application for a similar project that probably will not go through. It is almost as if people were afraid of success.

Yet if you talk to them they weren't sure the first one was going to be. There was a great sigh of relief that it is working. The American Government people ask: Why go through that strain a second time? I think that is the heart of the problem I saw there. 

What I am really asking is this: I would think this committee would be extremely interested in some kind of suggestion as to how we could give you some support for sticking your neck out, cutting redtape.

I am convinced one major reason why you haven't used any of the $150 million additional for housing guarantees that we gave you last year is because of the balance-of-payments problem. 

Has the balance of payments, as it goes sifting through all the sectors of government, put such a roadblock that you hold up? We should be told. This is the impression I get. I had to sift a long time to get that as a solid impression. If that is the case, let's say so and then let's decide where we go and how we go. 

Mr. HOAGLAND. I was earlier attempting to respond to a different kind of criticism, which was to the handling of the guaranteed projects on which there was no question but what AID intended under the balance-of-payments guidelines to go forward.

As to the level of the program in the future, it is quite true that the pace at which the authority is going to be used is being worked out with reference to the country's general problem arising out of its balance of payments. It shouldn't be left obscure that the rate of action in the program is currently being established by reference to our balance of payments.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Fulton. 

Mr. FULTON. Off the record. (Discussion off the record.) 

Mr. FULTON. I am glad to see there is increasing use of the specific risk guarantee program, because that was originated on this House 

Foreign Affairs Committee and pushed.

I would like to have you put in the record the time of processing over the past several years of the applications for insurance coverage. 

I note that you have on hand over $13 billion in applications, which sounds a lot for a bank. 

 PROCESSING TIME-SPECIFIC RISK GUARANTEE APPLICATIONS 

A recent study of all contracts signed during calendar year 1965 and the first quarter of calendar year 1966 revealed the following information concerning the lapse of time between the date the FGA was received and the date that the contract was executed.¹ [In days] 

Median time..

First quarter, 1966 188 228 Complete studies have not been made on contracts issued in prior years although samples have been taken periodically because of the realization that the time involved in negotiating and processing is of major importance to investors. A sample of roughly 22 percent of the contracts written in 1963 indicated a lapse of 271 days between the receipt of FGA and execution of the contract. Another sample taken in 1964 which took into consideration 14 percent of the contracts written in that year showed a lapse of 292 days between receipt of FGA and execution of the contract. 

Even though these figures reflect a reduction in processing time over the past few years, it is still difficult to conclude on the basis of statistics alone whether the delays encountered are caused by the investor or AID. Studies indicate the responsibility for delay varies from case to case and at present the matter is under close examination in order to isolate areas within the agency where "snags" tend to occur. Efforts are also being made to enable investors to provide required information promptly and accurately. These efforts include a recently revised edition of the Investment Guarantees handbook which supplies detailed information on the program and a carefully designed application form which seeks to extract from the investor all of the lements pertinent to the granting of investment guarantees.

1 The period between the receipt of the FGA (foreign government approval) and the execution of the contract is the most significant in the entire process of issuing investment guarantees and hence, the focal point of studies. Several steps, including the filing of an application for a waiver letter, usually take place before the FGA is received but earnest negotiations normally do not begin until this key requirement is met.

PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO SECTION 620 (1) 

The effectiveness of section 620(1) as a persuasive element in inducing countries to enter into an agreement to institute the investment guarantee program for inconvertibility and expropriation lies in its potential use. Once the termination date is reached, the effectiveness is lost. Extension of the termination date for relatively short period tends to diminish effectiveness. 

The proposed amendment directs the President to consider termination of aid if any country fails to have such an agreement by December 31, 1966. Consideration will have to be given to termination of AID assistance after careful assessment of all of the U.S. policy objectives surrounding such assistance-but bearing in mind the strong policy objective of making such agreements to facilitate U.S. private investment in the country involved. 

The proposed amendment is designed to put the United States in a position which would allow aid to flow to those countries which had not instituted the guarantee program before December 31, 1966, where and when it would be in the national interest to do so.

AID PROGRAM LOANS AND EXIMBANK LOANS 

The lending resources of the Export-Import Bank (Eximbank) and AID are used in a complementary fashion. Export-Import Bank long-term loans are normally related to a specific project. They are repayable in dollars and finance only U.S. dollar costs. Repayment terms on Eximbank loans are those appropriate to the project. AID program loans assist in meeting the overall foreign exchange requirements of the borrowing country. They are also repayable in dollars and are used predominantly for the procurement of U.S. goods and services. Repayment terms are geared to the debt servicing capacity of the borrowing country.

Before making program loans, AID is required by the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 to take into account the availability of financing from other sources. This includes financing available from the Eximbank, as well as other national and international lending agencies.

The lending activities of the Eximbank and AID are closely coordinated. The 

President and Chairman of the Board of the Eximbank is a member of the interagency Development Loan Committee, which is chaired by the Administrator of AID. Both aid and the Eximbank are represented on the National Advisory 

Council on International Monetary and Financial Policies. In addition, an 

AID staff member attends, on behalf of the Department of State and AID, the regular meetings of the Eximbank's Board of Directors.

Mr. Hoagland, I would like to ask you whether your responsibilities would be affected in any way if there were a 5-year authorization for this program instead of the present year-by-year basis, and if so in what way would your responsibilities be affected?

Mr. HOAGLAND. In connection with the investment guarantee authorities I think there is some modest improvement in the probabilities that investors will go ahead with plans if they know the program is going to be in existence for a significant number of years. 

In the past, this has been covered by making the authority stretch somewhat in amount beyond what is immediately required, and I would say that the 5-year program would have a tendency in this direction but not be critical. The aspect in which I think there would be a real gain has to do with the effort we make to make performance in terms of strengthening the private sector a part of our evaluation of a country's self-help performance.

When we are trying to work out the terms of aid and work with a country on an examination of the things it does to justify our going forward with assistance, we want to be able to show that we are ready to respond if they are ready to take the actions we think are necessary. 

Among the things we are in a position to work on are the conditions for private investment. Our effectiveness in improving the conditions for private investment will relate to the credibility with

which we come before the country saying we are going to undertake some aid activities if it seems promising in this country and in our interest. And among the things we are concerned with is how you handle private investment in your own private sector. 

When the aid program is on a 1-year authorization basis and we are trying to influence their policies in connection with private investment, we have a weaker weapon than if it is a 5-year authorization. 

In that respect

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. In what sense? Why are you not in a position to be persuasive in showing that you want to help if they can meet the conditions?

Mr. HOAGLAND. Because what we are talking to them about is fundamental changes in conditions and in policy that are to last for a considerable period of time.

If it is unclear whether we are going to be in a position to respond with AID assistance, and this would not be in the form of a commitment, if it is unclear how long we are going to be there, during the time that some kind of improvement is needed, we are not as persuasive as if we are in a position to work with them on a development plan over some period of time. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Why is it unclear? In any event the money is not going to be available. I could understand your argument if the money was going to be available over a long period of time. Mr. HOAGLAND. Unless there is an authorization there is no basis for appropriation.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Of course not. I am not arguing that. I understand that. This has nothing to do with their appreciation of whether we are going to help them once they make these changes in their own economy.

Mr. HOAGLAND. I think it has to do with their evaluation of whether the intentions of the U.S. Government to continue this kind of assistance are clearly enough set forth so that it is in their interest to cooperate with us

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. The intention is basically whether we are going to provide the money. That is not clearer because the programs are authorized. Another problem would be that if they are trained here they are trained at a level of sophistication for a type of industry which really is not what they have to go back to if they do go home, and that the kind of business training we have here has to be adapted and altered to really be suitable for people who are going to be handling business responsibilities in developing countries. Mr. HOAGLAND. No. The Watson recommendations were just last summer, and I would say in terms of new projects since then no new school of business administration has been launched since that. It takes more time than that to organize a project.

It is a fraction of what a U.S. salary for the man would be but the purpose is to be sure that the business pays something for what it gets.

There is also financing by contributions from the business community. We are looking forward to a greater participation by the business community, and we expect there will be fundraising efforts made sometime during the fall of 1966. Following that we will have a better reading on the extent to which the business community will be prepared to assume the full burden of financing this activity. 

This is our target. We do not yet know whether we are going to reach it.
