Washington, D.C.

The committee met in executive session at 10:05 a.m., in room  

The committee meets this morning in executive session for a continuation of the hearings on the foreign aid bills, H.R. 12449 and 

H.R. 12450.

Our witness this morning is the Honorable Joseph J. Sisco, Assistant Secretary for International Organization Affairs, Department of State.

Mr. Sisco, you have a prepared statement and you may proceed, sir. 

STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH J. SISCO, ASSISTANT SECRETARY FOR INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATION AFFAIRS, DEPARTMENT OF STATE 

Mr. Sisco. I thought what I would do was make a brief oral statement and with your permission submit a longer statement for the record. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered. 

(The prepared statement of Mr. Sisco is as follows:) STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH J. SISCO, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATion Affairs, BEFORE THE HOUSE FOREIGN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I appreciate the opportunity of appearing before you today in support of the President's recommendations for voluntary contributions to international organizations and programs. The President has proposed authorization of the appropriation of such amounts as may be necessary for such contributions over the next 5 years. For fiscal year 1967, he has recommended new obligational authority in the amount of $140.5 million which, together with a carryover of $4.1 million, will make $144.6 million available for commitment. 

As Assistant Secretary of State for International Organization Affairs, I am responsibile for U.S. contributions to virtually all the international bodies to which the United States belongs. Those contributions to international organizations which are in the nature of dues are presented annually as part of the State Department's regular budget. The voluntary contributions, which are authorized by the Foreign Assistance Act, are also administered by my bureau by delegation from the Administrator of the Agency for International Development. 

In a recent memorandum to the Secretary of State, President Johnson has directed that we apply to international agencies the same rigorous standards of program performance and budget review as we do to our Federal programs. 571

"Our purpose," he stated, "must be to see that— "Future expansion of the activities of the international organizations is governed by the tests of feasibility and reasonableness. "The programs of the organizations are vigorously scrutinized so that funds are allocated only to high priority projects which we are convinced are in the interests of the international community and of our own country; and "Each international agency operates with a maximum of effectiveness and economy."

The President also called upon the heads of the various Federal departments and agencies involved in participation in international programs to give their full cooperation to the Department of State in carrying out his instructions. 

In accordance with the President's directive, we are intensifying efforts to insure that the multilateral activities in which we join are carried out efficiently and economically.

Of the $144.6 million proposed for commitment in fiscal year 1967, about 85 percent will be used in multilateral programs which will help give the people of the less-developed world the knowledge and skills, the food and the strength, to move toward self-sufficiency. With a few exceptions, we are asking about the same amount of money as last year.

By action of the U.N. General Assembly last fall the expanded program of technical assistance, which was initiated in 1950, and the Special Fund, which got underway in 1959, were combined into the U.N. development program with a single top management and a single governing council. The United States was in the forefront in initiating this merger, which will produce greater efficiency in the planning and execution of this major U.N. development assistance activity. Under the technical assistance arm of the U.N. development program, know-how is transferred to the less-developed countries through the provision of experts and the granting of fellowships for training abroad. The Special Fund sector concentrates on surveys of natural resources, economic feasibility studies, establishment of training institutions, and the creation of research institutes. 

The Special Fund is serving an important function through its preinvestment activities. According to data released by Mr. Paul Hoffman, formerly executive head of the Special Fund and now Administrator of the combined program, 22 completed Special Fund projects in the preinvestment field developed the necessary plans and data to attract capital totaling more than $1 billion. The cost to the U.N. for these projects was about $28 million. 

In 1960, the U.N. General Assembly set an annual target of $150 million in contributions to the U.N. development program. This target was exceeded for the first time in 1965 and last fall the General Assembly increased the annual target to $200 million. For 1966, a total of $105.4 million has already been pledged by 

110 countries other than the United States while the United States pledged $65 million. In light of the demonstrated willingness of other countries to increase their support of the program and on the condition that our contribution will not exceed 40 percent of total governmental contributions, it is proposed that the U.S. contribution in 1967 be raised to $70 million. For every $4 that we contribute, the other governments will put up $6. 

Widely known throughout the less developed world for its many activities benefiting children and mothers, the U.N. Children's Fund received additional recognition last year when it was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. The United 

States should take pride in the fact that Mr. Henry Labouisse was chosen to suc- 

Iceed Mr. Maurice Pate, another American who had served as the Executive 

Director of UNICEF since its inception at the end of World War II. 

In cooperation with other agencies in the U.N. family, UNICEF continues to carry out useful work in the field of disease control, health services, and nutrition. In recent years it has given increased emphasis to education and vocational training. The United States continues to be prepared to match other governmental contributions at the 40-percent ratio. We propose a contribution of $12 million to UNICEF's program in 1967-the same amount as last year. 

Following an experimental 3-year period, the world food program, which is jointly supervised by the United Nations and the Food and Agriculture Organization, is now embarked on a broader continuing program for the utilization of foodstuffs on a multilateral basis to promote economic and social development. 

At a pledging session held in January this year, Secretary Freeman pledged up to $92 million in agricultural commodities, shipping services to move the com-

modities to their destinations, and up to $6 million in cash; the pledge was made subject to congressional action. The commodity pledge includes a 50-percent matching provision and the cash pledge a limitation of 40 percent. We are requesting $2 million in this bill as our fiscal year 1967 cash contribution, the same as last year. Cash contributions are used primarily for administrative costs. 

Through the international recruitment and placement of personnel with the necessary skills and language competence, the U.N. technical and operational assistance program for the Congo (Leopoldville) helps meet that country's continuing need for technical advisers and operational experts. In fiscal year 1967 it is proposed to contribute $5 million to the U.N., the same amount as last year, for financing of positions which we consider of key importance in the fields of public finance, economic analysis and coordination, civil aviation and meteorology, puble works, telecommunications, police training, and natural resources planning. We hope it will be possible to phase out of this modest program over the next several years as the Congolese develop their own capacities to take over these functions.

The major purpose of the operational program of the International Atomic Energy Agency is to help the less-developed countries share in the peaceful uses of the broad spectrum of benefits afforded by atomic science. 

The program operates through provision of fellowships for study abroad and of experts and equipment for training in atomic science in the developing countries themselves. 

Through this program the Agency also builds experience which will be useful when, as we hope, it will play a larger role in assuring proper safeguards of atomic energy installations throughout the world.

The executive branch proposes to pledge up to $600,000, with a limitation of 37.5 percent of total cash contributions, to the Agency's program for 1967-a reduction from previous years' shares. In addition, it is proposed to make available fellowships for training in the United States the services of U.S. experts, and small equipment grants with maximum value of $400,000. Thus, a total of $1 million, the same as previous years, is proposed for fiscal year 1967. 

Through the exchange of information and the provision of technical assistance, the International Secretariat for Volunteer Service encourages the establishment of volunteer service programs comparable to the U.S. Peace Corps for service abroad and to VISTA for domestic service. Since 1963 ISVS has helped 

24 countries to set up such programs. Last year about 7,000 volunteers were enrolled in these programs. A further contribution to the ISVS budget for 

1967 is proposed at a level of $65,000, subject to the conditions that the U.S. share does not exceed 28 percent and that our contribution will be used only to finance the costs of informational clearinghouse functions. 

The World Bank's present estimate of the fiscal year 1967 installment due on our commitment to the Indus Basin Development Fund is $33 million. In spite of temporary delays resulting from the outbreak of hostilities between India and Pakistan last September, construction is generally on schedule and was 65 percent complete as of the end of 1965. Mr. Richard Palmer, officer-incharge, Pakistan Affairs, AID, is here to provide additional information on the 

Indus Basin project.

In his message to the Congress on foreign aid, the President identified "the incessant cycle of hunger, ignorance, and disease" as "the common blight of the developing world" and said that this vicious pattern can be broken and must be broken if democracy is to survive. The voluntary contributions to international programs which are appropriated as part of our foreign aid serve in important ways to attack the central problems of the developing countries. 

During the present year we estimate that $23.6 million of our voluntary contributions to such programs as the U.N. Children's Fund, the U.N. development program, and UNRWA are being used for health improvement activities. 

Through the U.N. development program and the world food program about $24 million of our contributions are being utilized for improvement of the agricultural output of the less-developed countries, and approximately $21 million is being devoted to the improvement of educational systems through the U.N. development program. II

The second major category of programs proposed for U.S. support in fiscal year 

1967 are those designed to maintain peace and promote stability in the eastern 

Mediterranean area.

The U.N. Relief and Works Agency provides basic health and education services for the more than a million Palestine refugees on its rolls. It also provides a minimum food ration for 873,000 of the refugees. While some of the refugees, utilizing skills obtained through the UNRWA educational program, are able to find employment and become at least partially self-supporting, the basic problem remains unsolved because the parties concerned have been unable to agree on a program to implement the U.N. resolution of 1948 which states the refugees have a right to repatriation or compensation for lost properties. With a view to making the most efficient use of available resources the U.N. 

General Assembly in the fall of 1965 directed UNRWA to "take such measures, including the rectification of the relief rolls * *to assure ** *the most equitable distribution of relief based on need * * *" The Commissioner-General is now seeking ways to implement this directive through cooperation with the Arab host governments. Although much remains to be done in rectification, the 

Commissioner-General made limited progress on this problem last year. Moreover, he has been urgently requested by the United States to assure that members of the Palestine Liberation Army are removed from UNRWA's rolls. 

The U.S. contribution to UNRWA for fiscal year 1965 was $24.7 million. For fiscal year 1966 the executive branch proposed a reduction of $1 million in agricultural commodities. In addition, Congress reduced the cash portion by $800,000. Our total pledge for fiscal year 1966 therefore was $22.9 million. 

During the past winter, UNRWA indicated that it could utilize additional agricultural commodities, and the United States agreed to furnish them on the understanding that there would be a commensurate reduction in our cash contribution. Our contribution for fiscal year 1966 is therefore composed of $14 million in cash and $8.9 million in foodstuffs. 

In view of the continuing natural increase of the refugee population and of the rising prices of goods and services purchased by UNRWA, the executive branch recommends a contribution for fiscal year 1967 at the same level as in fiscal year 1966. The Commissioner General is actively seeking additional contributions from other governments, and several European countries have indicated a willingness to increase their contributions over previous years' levels. 

The United States has supported the Commissioner General's efforts, and it is expected that the U.S. share of total governmental contributions will gradually diminish.

The United States also helps to maintain order in the Middle East through contributions to the costs of the U.N. Emergency Force, which since 1956 has been stationed on the armistice line and international frontier between Israel and the United Arab Republic. As the result of a U.S. initiative the size and costs of the force were restudied in late 1965, and on the basis of that report, the U.N. 

General Assembly reduced the 1966 appropriation by almost $4 million to a level of $15 million.

The UNEF financing resolution adopted by the General Assembly for both 1965 and 1966 apportioned 5 percent of the total cost to the developing countries on the basis of the U.N. regular scale of assessments; the balance was apportioned to 26 developed countries on the basis of the regular U.N. scale of assessments adjusted to take into account reductions accorded to the developing countries. Thus, as in past years, proportionately higher amounts are allocated to the richer countries than the poorer countries. The resolution apportions an additional amount to the 26 developed member states equal to 25 percent of its base apportionment "in order to meet reserve requirements." It is understood that this 25 percent will be used to cover the shortfall expected to result from the failure of certain members to pay their UNEF apportionments. 

The U.S. share of the costs of UNEF for calendar year 1966, as apportioned by the General Assembly, is $6,838,000. This amount is requested as part of the fiscal year 1967 estimate for voluntary contributions to international organizations. III

Funds available for voluntary contributions are being used this year to meet the U.S. share of the costs of the U.N. force in Cyprus (UNFICYP). The financing of UNFICYP has been on a purely voluntary basis, with 41 countries pledging support. Since the force was inaugurated in March 1964, the United 

States has pledged approximately 40 percent of the total costs. When the Pres-

ident's fiscal year 1967 budget was prepared some months ago, our hope was that by the beginning of fiscal year 1967 progress would have been made on a political solution and the force might be phased out. Regrettably, we cannot report such progress. If the force is continued into fiscal year 1967, as now appears likely, funds available from the voluntary contributions appropriation or from the contingency fund will be used. 

Finally, we are proposing further contributions to two relatively new members of the U.N. family; $150,000 is proposed as a second contribution to the 

International Agency for Research on Cancer, which is being established at Lyon, France, under the auspices of the World Health Organization. In addition to the 

United States, six other nations are supporting an international attack on cancer, at this point primarily through research on the epidemiology of the disease. 

Each of the members have agreed to contribute $150,000 annually for 5 years. 

A second contribution is also proposed to the U.N. Institute for Training and 

Research, a new organ of the U.N. designed to train international civil servants as well as diplomats of the developing countries, and to conduct research on important problems of peace and progress; $400,000 is requested for contribution to the regular budget of the Institute, with a limitation of 40 percent on our contribution. In addition, $100,000 is requested to finance Adlai E. Stevenson fellowships administered by the Institute. areas.

I urge you to approve the recommendations on voluntary contributions to international organizations and programs which are before you. 

Mr. Sisco. Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity to appear in support of the President's recommendations for voluntary contributions to international organizations. I would like to note at the outset that while I have appeared before this committee on previous accasions, this is the first time that I will have appeared before the full committee as Assistant Secretary of State.

I just want to make one comment regarding my basic approach to my job and to the question of U.S. policy in the U.N. This is an organization that I have dealt with personally in the last 15 years. It is one which in my judgment was oversold in 1945 at the time of the 

San Francisco Conference.

We as Americans have tended to view this organization pretty much as a panacea and as a cure-all. I think in the last 20 years we have learned that this is an organization with both capacities and limitations, and that the basic yardstick that has to be applied by any policymaker is, How does this organization serve the national interests of the United States? That is basically my approach to the whole question of the U.N. and U.S. policy toward it. 

We are recommending, as indicated on page 57 of the presentation book, new obligational authority for $140.5 million with a carryover of $4.1 million from last year, bringing the total to $144 million plus. 

I would like to make a few comments regarding the principal pro grams within the framework of chapter III. 

First, we have the United Nations Development Program. For 1967 

we are requesting authorization for $70 million, which represents an

increase of $5 million from last year. As the committee is aware, last fall the General Assembly merged two very important programs, namely, the expanded Program of Technical Assistance and the Special Fund into one program, which is now called the U.N. Development Program.

It is under single management, under a single governing council and it is headed by an American, Mr. Paul Hoffman. The reason we were in the forefront in merging these two organizations is that we felt it would result in an organization of greater efficiency, better both in planning and in execution.

I might also explain that another reason why we supported this merger is that more and more we want the various specialized agencies of the United Nations to go to the central fund; namely the U.N. 

Development Program, for the costs of a number of the programs of assistance to the developing countries. 

[Security deletion.] The principal development regarding the U.N. Development Pro gram over the past year is that the General Assembly this last fall established a new target of $200 million. The original target of $150 million was established by the General Assembly in 1960. 

The interesting thing is that this is a real success story in terms of the number of countries that have this year decided to make specific contributions in support of the U.N. Development Program. Already this year $105 million has been pledged by over 110 countries other than the United States. 

Our pledge, as you know, does not exceed 40 percent. Recently Mr.

Hoffman put out an overall review of the program. I think the most significant point in this overall review is that 22 completed projects in the preinvestment field have helped to develop plans that attracted something like $1 billion worth of capital investment. The cost of these projects to the U.N. itself was only $28 million. 

We support this program because we feel that, like a number of the other U.N. programs in the economic and social field, it is really trying to attack the root causes of war, it is trying to help create conditions of stability and by providing skills and know-how, helping a number of these developing countries to stand on their own two feet. 

It serves our interest in that we want these countries to be able to stand on their own feet, free of interference by others.

Another program that I would like to say a word about is UNICEF. 

We are requesting the same amount of money as in the previous year, $12 million. I would only say that this program has been so universally recognized as a successful one that it was awarded the Nobel 

Peace Prize last year. 

There are a number of other programs that are listed, about which I will make no comment, Mr. Chairman. I am submitting a fuller statement for the record.

I do want to say just a word regarding the second major category which is dealt with; namely, the question of peacekeeping and the maintenance of peace. We are asking this year for the same amount as last year for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency. As this committee knows, this is an agency that has been in existence for a good

many years. It is providing health and educational services for over a million refugees, as well as providing rations for something like 875,000.

We have sought during the past year, very much in the spirit of the views expressed in this committee in previous years, to see whether we could make some progress on the problem of rectification; namely, the elimination of ineligible persons on the relief rolls. Progress in the past has been very modest indeed. Since 1950, there were 320,818 net deletions from the ration rolls, offset by additions of 237,484 children for a net reduction in the total number of refugees on the ration rolls of 83,334. In the past two and a half years the net reduction of the ration rolls was 8,951.

As is indicated on page 57, Mr. Chairman, we are asking this year for authorization of $6.8 million to pay for the costs of the United 

Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East. This $6.8 million request is based on a resolution that was adopted by the General Assembly last fall which is designed to apportion the expenses of the United Nations Emergency Force among the maximum number of members of the United Nations.

The formula that was adopted was simply this: About 5 percent of the total cost of the budget is apportioned to the developing countries and the rest of it is apportioned among 26 developed countries, including the United States, on the basis of the regular United Nations scale adjusted to take into account the reductions accorded to developing countries.

This resolution also apportions an additional amount, 25 percent of the base apportionment, in order to meet reserve requirements and take care of any shortfall that might occur in payment for the force. This $6.8 million which is being requested for 1967 is the same amount which the United States will have paid for 1966. 

I would draw the attention of the committee to the fact that no money is requested to pay for the costs of the United Nations Force in Cyprus. Actually the reason for this is that when these figures were put together some months ago, it was our hope that the United Nations Force could have been phased out beginning this coming fiscal year. 

Unfortunately there hasn't been any appreciable progress on a polit ical solution [security deletion]. 

I want to say a brief word regarding the state of affairs on peacekeeping at the United Nations at the present time. First of all as the committee is aware, there have been very fundamental differences regarding how future peacekeeping operations should be financed, and how they should be authorized. Basically the differences between ourselves and the Soviet Union are political and they reflect a difference of view as to what kind of a role the U.N. should play in the peacekeeping field.

The objective of the Soviet Union continues to be to reduce the U.N. to a debating society, whereas our whole approach has been, and continues to be, that we want a U.N. with an executive capacity to act, one that can help maintain the peace, because in the last 20 years this organization, particularly in the peacekeeping field, has served in the first instance the national interest of the United States.

There has been no fundamental agreement regarding either the financing or the authorizing of future peacekeeping operations. Even though two committees have been dealing with this matter in the U.N. over the past weeks, and will be doing so over the coming months, there remain the same differences which resulted in the article 19 issue in which neither the French nor the Soviets have been willing to pay for their part of the expenses for the United Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East and for the United Nations operation in the Congo. These basic differences continue and what it amounts to is that we are unwilling to agree with the Soviet contention that all future peacekeeping operations, both as to authorization as well as financing, should be subjected to the Soviet veto. 

We feel that the residual power of the General Assembly should be maintained and we cannot agree with the view that the Soviets continue to press, namely that no peacekeeping operation can be undertaken by the U.N. unless it has the full concurrence of the Soviet Union. 

We will continue, Mr. Chairman, to press for the broadest possible sharing of the burden as far as future peacekeeping operations are concerned, but it is clear as a result of the regrettable unwillingness of the General Assembly to apply the loss of vote sanction to either the French or Russians a year ago, that it is pretty generally recognized now at the U.N. that when a major power has a fundamental political objection to a peacekeeping operation, there is no way in which the General Assembly can enforce the loss of vote sanction. 

This means that it is not enforceable against the Soviet Union, nor would it, of course, be enforceable against us. Insofar as the future is concerned, as one looks ahead regarding the U.N. peacekeeping role, the situation is serious, but not fatal. What it really means is that those like-minded states who support a peacekeeping operation politically will in the future have to band together informally and support politically desirable peacekeeping operations with the kind of resources that are needed.

I don't think it would serve the national interest of the United States to permit a few of the recalcitrant states to prevent the United Nations from taking any peacekeeping action in the future. We cannot therefore agree to the Soviet contention that all peacekeeping operations come within the exclusive purview of the Security Council itself. 

That is about all I wanted to say, Mr. Chairman. I am ready to answer any questions that I can.

 INDIAN SELF-HELP MEASURES 

India's economic achievements since independence have been substantial as a result of India's efforts to help herself. For example, the country is generally recognized as a pioneer of economic planning. It established a comprehensive planning organization and, despite its enormous development needs, determined to generate economic and social growth without resort to authoritarian methods. 

India's determination is reflected in its efforts to mobilize its own resources. 

During the past 15 years, savings have been raised from 5 percent to 10 percent of national income, and investment from 5 percent to almost 14 percent. The 

Government has been courageous in raising taxes, and inflation has been largely contained, except for the most recent period. Furthermore, though U.S. and other free world assistance has provided the critical margin of capital needed by India for her overall economic growth, India now finances about 80 percent of the cost of development activities from its own domestic resources. 

In the critical area of food, the Indian Government has taken several steps to combat the distribution problem, such as developing plans for better transportation facilities, making spot checks on grain storage facilities to uncover hoarded supplies and encouraging farmers and merchants to cooperate in bringing grain to the market. However, the main solution lies in the ability of the 

Indian Government to help themselves, which they are doing with increasing effectiveness.

The Indian Government also realizes that increased agricultural production will little help India's economic progress unless it is able to reduce its birth rate. Prime Minister Gandhi made clear at a National Press Club meeting during her recent visit to the United States that India is undertaking positive action in population control when she said, "We have launched a vast family planning program. The magnitude of our effort will be evident from just two statistics. Eighteen thousand family planning centers are actually operating in the country today. We have also increased the budget for family planning twentyfold." 60-929-66-pt. 4- -2

rs. BOLTON. Do Russia and France contribute to the Secretariat? r. Sisco. The Secretariat? I am not aware that they do. You alking about the International Secretariat for Volunteer Servrs. BOLTON. Yes, and whatever-is there no other voluntary- 

T. SISCO. In terms of the ISVS fund they are not contributors. rs. BOLTON. They wouldn't be. r. Sisco. The only contributors as indicated earlier rs. BOLTON. Is Sweden the only one that has paid in on that?

T. SISCO. No, there are those that have been named. rs. BOLTON. Did France have some suggestions last year; budget rms? What has happened to them? 

r. SISCO. Yes. Last year at the General Assembly the French that it was very important for the U.N. to take a very hard look only at the question of solvency in the United Nations itself, but vise at programs and budgets in the entire system of specialized cies. s a result of this French initiative, with the very strong support. e United States, the General Assembly established a Committee of rteen experts to look into the question of U.N. solvency as well as e budgets and specialized agency programs. The Committee of teen has completed the first half of its work. What it did was to at the long-range situation as it results from the fact that the sians and the French continue to be unwilling to pay for their debts both on UNEF and the United Nations force in the Congo. at it came up with was a set of figures that had been submitted by Secretary General which really clearly indicates that these arages are still very much on the books, that what is needed in r to bring the U.N. to solvency in the fullest sense is for these recalcitrant members in particular to pay what they owe. t the same time the Committee of Fourteen looked at this problem he short range. By the short range, I mean it addressed itself he question of what is needed over the next year in the form oluntary contributions, so as to assure that the United Nations continue to operate with reasonable effectiveness. concluded that what would be needed in voluntary contributions roughly something between $52 and $73 million during the next -. When I say it concluded this, I mean the majority of the memincluding ourselves, concluded this, because the French and the sians did not agree this is what was needed. 

That happened at this committee meeting was that you had a reflecof the fundamental differences between ourselves and the Soviet, ch have existed over the past 3 or 4 years. The strategy of the et Union and the French members was to try to get this committee rive at a judgment that the smallest amount of money would be ed over the next year in order to bring the U.N. to solvency. r strategy was simply this: that if it could get this committee y "Well, you don't really need a working capital fund, the U.N. y doesn't owe $55 million to the members that have provided ices for peacekeeping operations in the past, the U.N. need not back credits to the members who have provided services, these

operations in the past were illegal." If you took that line as the 

Russians and the French pressed, then you could come out with a conclusion that all that would be needed to restore the U.N. solvency in the next year would be $25 million, and Russia and France could make symbolic contributions.

The net effect would be that the Committee of Fourteen would write off the debts of the Russians and the French. We didn't fall into that trap. What we said was, and what the majority view of this committee was, that these arrearages are on the books, we are still going to press for collection, but it did not mean that the committee in any way wrote off these debts. In the long range the only way the U.N. is really going to become solvent is for these debts to be paid and for the money to come in on the regular budget. 

So the differences which have been in existence over the last 3 or 4 years were reflected in this committee. What implication is there for the U.N. in terms of future peacekeeping? I think the implication is very clear. The majority of the General Assembly is not going to apply the loss of vote sanction against a major power that has a fundamental political objection to a future peacekeeping operation. 

They are no more going to apply it against us than they would against the Soviet Union.

If this is a reality and a fact of life in the U.N. it is very regrettable that the principle of collective financial responsibility has been undermined, but for those countries such as ourselves who have seen how United Nations peacekeeping operations in the past have served the national interest of the United States, it means that the only effective peacekeeping operations that can be undertaken in the future will be those which have the political support of those who feel that a peacekeeping operation is important and those who support these peacekeeping operations politically will have to support them with substantial resources.

There are all kinds of ways in which future peacekeeping operations can be paid for. As far as we are concerned, we don't want to rest on any one option. Wherever there is a parallelism of interest between ourselves and the Soviet Union, we are going to try to get a future peacekeeping operation paid on the basis of the principle of collective financial responsibility. 

Let me give you an example. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Would you mind. He is pretty bad on us. He doesn't let us have time. I wonder if perhaps you would be good enough to brief it for me for the record. 

Mr. SISCO. Yes. (The information appears on p. 591.) 

Mrs. BOLTON. I would like to ask you what efforts are being made to keep us from contributing to Cuba?

Mr. Sisco. If I understand your question, Mrs. Bolton, at least that aspect with which I deal, there have been some questions raised with respect to two projects which have been approved by the United Na tions Development Program for Cuba. 

I would like to respond to that very briefly in this way. At this past board meeting in January there was a project that was approved for

the University of Havana, faculty of engineering, to the tune of about $2 million. There were 82 projects approved in January 1966, including a project, for example, for the expanding engineering training at the National Technical Center in South Vietnam for about $1.5 million.

The United Nations Development Program has normally used the ground rule that projects are not approved or rejected for political reasons alone. If you look at the record of the U.N. Special Fund since 1959, you find that a total of 604 projects have been approved in 92 nations. Of this total of 604 projects, only 2 projects have been approved for Cuba, whereas 591 have been approved for free world countries.

We opposed the projects for Cuba, the one approved in 1961 as well as the one that was approved at this recent board meeting. When it came up before the Council in January, Mr. Roosevelt argued that Cuba's shortage of technicians and engineers is due mainly to Cuba's own policies which have caused large numbers of qualified people to leave the country. He said we did not believe that an international agency should be called upon to remedy this shortage. 

The Governing Council does not, as a matter of practice, take votes on individual projects. As a result the project went through and even if there had been a vote, of course we would have been outvoted on this simply because of the rule that projects are neither approved nor rejected on the basis of political reasons. 

Mrs. BOLTON. What would you reply to your constituents on this whole business when they write you in fury that we are doing things for Cuba?

Mr. Sisco. I think there is a very good reply, Mrs. Bolton, that is as you really look at this overall program and you look at 600 projects- 

Mrs. BOLTON. You have to look at the world.

Mr. Sisco. You have to look at the world. Frankly, we did all we could to prevent its adoption as it related to Cuba. If you address it only to Cuba, I think the answer is much more difficult. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Yes, and that is the problem we have. 

Mr. SISCO. The U.N. Development Program has issued a paper which states that no U.S. dollars that we contribute will be used on these projects.

The question is asked, are not all contributions to the UNDP merged? 

If so, how can we be sure that no U.S. contributions are being used for Cuban projects?

The answer is this: It is true that 40 percent of the total financial resources of the Special Fund are supplied by the United States. But over 100 other countries also contribute to the Fund. Most of these contributions, making up the remaining 60 percent, are in currencies other than dollars. These contributions are held in separate accounts outside of the United States; they are not integrated with U.S. dollar contributions and their end uses are clearly identifiable. It is these non-dollar currencies which will be used for the Cuban projects. 

Mrs. BOLTON. That is just a manipulation of books, of course. 

Thank you very much.

Mr. ADAIR. Mr. Chairman and Mr. Sisco, I would like to go back, if you could turn your memory back, to the point where Mrs. Bolton ran out of time. We were discussing alternatives with respect to peacekeeping operations and you were about to give us an example.

Mr. ADAIR. Would you give us that example?

Mr. Sisco. I think I was saying, Mr. Adair, that as far as the 

United States is concerned, as you look ahead to the future peacekeeping operations, we want to retain as many options, as many different ways to finance future peacekeeping operations as possible.

Then I went on to say wherever we can do it on the basis of a broad collective financial responsibility principle, let's do it simply because of the fact this will share the burden in the broadest possible way. 

Then I said let us look at the four Security Council resolutions that were adopted on Kashmir quite recently-a cease-fire, withdrawal of forces. You have had a small United Nations observor group in 

Kashmir. This observer group happens to be one example, as small as it is, which is paid from the regular budget. 

In other words, each one of the countries has a responsibility to pay for it on the basis of a legal obligation and an every-member canvass as such.

Wherever you have got this kind of even a temporary parallelism of interest, and the Russians by the way are paying for this 

Mr. ADAIR. And the French. 

Mr. Sisco. Yes.

Where you have this kind of parallelism, let's do it because it will cost us less and it will get the maximum number of countries to pay for it.

Another example is wherever an interested government that is prepared to support a peacekeeping operation can do it, let them do it. 

The example I have in mind is West New Guinea. In that particular instance the Dutch wanted to release West New Guinea and in that particular instance a thousand Pakistani troops were sent under U.N. auspices to supervise the transition from Dutch rule to essentially Indonesian rule. In that particular case the interested governments paid for that, it didn't cost the U.N. anything. 

Where we can do that, let's do that.

Mr. SISCO. Not that I can recall as it relates to the U.N., Mr. Adair. 

Mr. ADAIR. That was the arrangement worked out by Ambassador Bunker? 

Mr. SISCO. Yes.

of apportionment among them. So, again, this is a burden-sharing operation as such.

Over the past 4 years the Executive has programed $40 million more for Indus than was actually spent. The surplus for 1966 was over $12 million. Is there anything we can do to get better estimates out of the World Bank?

Mr. Sisco. I think the record is generally as you have indicated, Mr. Congressman. I think if one looks over the last 3 or 4 years, as you say, the estimates in most instances have tended to be larger than what was actually expended. I think this is something that we might very well take up with the Bank. 

There are apparently so many variables and imponderables on this one that the Bank has done what we consider a conscientious job in its estimate, but I think it is worth taking up with them again. 

Mr. FASCELL. One thing I think we ought to spread on the record here, and that is the difference in the U.S. share of UNEF cost for 

1966 and what is estimated for 1967. For 1966, chapter 3 funds are shown as $1.4 million, but the cost was more. 

Would you explain the difference between the 2 years and where the money came from last year, and why we are making a change this year?

Mr. SISCO. Mr. Fraser, one of the things that we have felt for a long time is that the staff within the Secretariat itself at the U.N. on the military side should be strengthened. The Secretary General has a limited number of military people available to him to render advice. It is not as strong as we would like. I think the reason for it is basically that, first, any substantial expansion would be costly; secondly, very candidly there has been a reluctance on the part of the U.N. Secretary General to expand it too broadly in view of the fact that there has been this fundamental difference between ourselves and the Soviet Union about what the role of the United Nations ought to be in the peacekeeping field. 

That is on the staff side. Secondly, we have done a good deal to try to stimulate a number of other countries to earmark forces that would be available pursuant to a United Nations decision or a recommendation.

Mr. FRASER. On that point, what specifically have we done? I know 

Lester Pearson took some initiative in this field, but what have we done to encourage not only the earmarking, but the specialized training that would be appropriate for earmarking? 

Mr. SISCO. On the specialized training in the last 2 or 3 years we have done relatively nothing. The reason for it, Mr. Fraser, is that this is really reflective of the differences of view over peacekeeping and we have not felt that it was politically feasible to press the U.N. to undertake any substantial training program of units. 

For this reason we have really concentrated on two areas; namely,. strengthening the staff and encouraging other countries to earmark forces for U.N. peacekeeping operations. The Scandinavians—the 

Danes and Swedes and Norwegians-have earmarked a group of over a thousand. We have tried to get countries to earmark these forces within their own armed forces.

Mr. Sisco. From time to time we have made diplomatic efforts, but these have been infrequent and low key for this reason. We have felt the best way to stimulate a number of these countries to do this is for such initatives to really come from what might be considered a much more impartial source, namely the U.N. itself. 

From time to time we have talked this matter over with the top officials of the Secretariat with a view to getting them to take steps. I have to say our own efforts, plus those of the U.N. have been circumscribed in this area because of the fundamental difference between the Soviet Union and the United States on peacekeeping operations.

EFFECTS OF MERGER OF THE EXPANDED PROGRAM FOR TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE AND THE SPECIAL FUND 

The creation of the U.N. development program has resulted in improved efficiency through the merger of the staffs of the expanded program of technical assistance (EPTA) and of the U.N. Special Fund, and the reduction of duplicating or overlapping positions. While previously there had been two governing bodies the Technical Assistance Committee for EPTA and the Governing Council for the Special Fund-there is now only one governing body composed of representatives of governments, the Governing Council of the U.N. development program, with a consequent reduction in costs of meetings. 

In recent years the volume of resources contributed to programs and supervised by the staff of the U.N. development program has been rising rapidly. For example, projects approved for implementation by the two constituent parts of the development program in 1964 amounted to $132 million. In 1965 the comparable figure was $162 million, an increase of 22 percent. During the early part of 1966 alone, projects costing $154 million were approved. The increased level of program activity is expected to overtake the internal savings resulting from the merger. It has already proved necessary to add more positions as the level of assistance provided by the development program increases. It is, however, clear that increases in administrative costs will be less in the merged program than would have been true if the two parts were separately administered.

As a result of these 22 projects costing $28 million he has been able to stimulate $1 billion worth of capital investment in a number of these countries.

Mr. SISCO. It will not exceed that 40-percent relationship.

 IAEA INSPECTION OF U.S. PEACEFUL USES FACILITIES 

The Atomic Energy Commission has made a preliminary estimate of the costs that would be incurred by the International Atomic Energy Agency in applying safeguards to essentially all of the U.S. peaceful nuclear facilities. For this estimate it was assumed that Agency safeguards would be applied to power and research reactors and to fuel fabrication facilities, reprocessing facilities, and nuclear research laboratories. The facilities included in this cost estimate are those that will be in operation within approximately 1 year. 

It was also assumed that safeguards would be implemented by Agency inspectors stationed in the United States.

To safeguard these facilities our preliminary estimate indicates that the Agency would require approximately 70 additional inspectors and that the cost to the Agency would be in the neighborhood of $3 million per year. The present staff of the Agency devoted to safeguards operations includes 13 inspectors. 

It should be noted that many administrative and policy matters would require resolution before any decision could be taken to place all U.S. peaceful nuclear facilities under Agency safeguards. These matters have not been considered in preparing the above estimate, nor has the IAEA itself been consulted. 

At present four U.S. facilities are under IAEA inspection. Mr. MORSE. the quid pro quo aspect of this for two reasons, really. It is absolutely true as you say that no one country can control the action of these international organizations. We are the major contributor. 

We feel that the more active a role the United States plays in developing the content of these programs as well as achieving reasonable budget levels, rather than excessive growth in the budgets, to that extent we think we are quite frankly not only playing the major role but the major influential role in these organizations. 

What we have done informally, we have put together a so-called Geneva group which is a group of the major contributors of the United Nations system. We meet regularly with these people with a view to trying to get them to act in concert with us in influencing the Directors General not only in the development of what we consider to be reasonable and sensible programs, but likewise to convince the Directors General that we are willing to support reasonable increase, but unwilling to support unreasonable increases. 

This is a way, frankly, that we have developed to try to keep the growth pattern within bounds because every one of these organizations has now become much larger with preponderant majorities made up of Africans and Asians. We feel the major contributors must play a decisive and active part in the actual decisionmaking process both as they relate to the program as well as the budgets.

 PROPOSED AMENDMENTS RELATING TO CONTRIBUTIONS TO INDUS BASIN DEVELOPMENT FUND 

H.R. 12449, the bill to amend further the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, includes the following provisions:

Section 108 (a) amends section 301 (a) of the act to authorize funds appropriated for international organizations and programs to be used for dollar-

1 repayable loans in connection with the Indus Basin development fund administered by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (the World Bank). These loans would be subject to the restrictions on development loan terms contained in section 201(d) of the act. 

Section 301 (a) now authorizes contributions from funds appropriated for international organizations and programs to be made only on a grant basis. 

This authority is now used to make grants for Indus Basin development. 

In 1964 the U.S. Government made a commitment in the form of an executive agreement, subject to appropriation of the necessary funds, to loan to Pakistan $51,220,000 for Indus Basin development, to be administered by the World Bank. 

Although this loan could be funded under the authority of section 201 of the act, by funding it under international organizations and programs, both grants and loans for Indus Basin development would be consolidated in one chapter. 

Section 108 (c) amends section 302 of the act, which relates to the authorization for international organizations and programs, by creating separate subsections for the existing grant authorization and for the new Indus Basin loan authorization.

First, a new subsection (a) substitutes for the obsolete fiscal year 1966 grant authorization a grant authorization of such amounts as may be necessary for each of the 5 fiscal years 1967 through 1971. 

Second, a new subsection (b) adds a new authorization for the appropriation of funds, in addition to other funds available for Indus Basin development, for dollar-repayable loans for the Indus Basin program. The funds are authorized for use beginning in the fiscal year 1968, when it is expected that the World Bank will request that the United States meet its 1964 commitment.

STATEMENT OF HON. WILLIAM S. GAUD, DEPUTY ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. GAUD. Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, I am pleased to appear before the committee today to discuss with you the President's authorization requests for the contingency fund, American-sponsored schools and hospitals abroad, and AID's administrative expenses. 

CONTINGENCY FUND 

The contingency fund is maintained to meet urgent assistance needs that are either unforeseen or cannot be meaningfully identified in advance. The fund serves the important purpose of permitting a prompt response to emergency needs.

We use the contingency fund as sparingly as circumstances permit. 

With the exception of the current fiscal year, there has been a considerable reduction in both the amount of the worldwide contingency fund and its use.

The President is requesting an authorization ceeiling of $150 million for the contingency fund for each of the next 5 years, and for fiscal year 1967 an appropriation of $70 million. With estimated recoveries of $5 million, $75 million would be available in fiscal year 1967. This is clearly a minimum request, but we believe it is adequate. If additional requirements should develop, we would request an additional appropriation.

We do not regard fiscal year 1966 demands on our contingency funds as normal. All of the $89 million special contingency fund for 617

southeast Asia has been programed. Similarly, the original worldwide contingency fund for fiscal year 1966 (consisting of $50 million in new appropriations and availabilities of nearly $6 million) was quickly programed. The amount of $37 million was required for use in the Dominican Republic alone to support the efforts of the provisional government to establish and maintain a stable environment prior to the coming elections in June.

These funds provided budgetary support to sustain essential government operations, pay the salaries of government workers, and assist public works activities which helped stem unemployment. The 

U.S. assistance was vital to the effort to avoid chaos in the Dominican Republic.

Another important use of fiscal year 1966 contingency funds was a $7.5 million commodity loan to Ceylon. Prior to the election of a new government in Ceylon and the subsequent settlement of the longstanding oil dispute with American oil companies, Ceylon was not eligible for U.S. assistance. The commodity loan was provided to help relieve Ceylon of its serious shortage of foreign exchange and assist the new government's efforts to achieve economic stabilization. 

Thus far we have used none of the $100 million supplemental contingency funds recently authorized and appropriated by Congress. 

We will use no more of these funds than is absolutely necessary. 

A breakdown of fiscal year 1966 uses of the contingency fund is shown in annex A.

AMERICAN SCHOOLS AND HOSPITALS ABROAD 

Sections 214 (a) and (b) of the Foreign Assistance Act authorize assistance to certain schools and hospitals abroad which are founded or sponsored by U.S. citizens. The United States has provided assistance under this program since 1959. 

The purpose of this assistance is to help a few selected institutions contribute to the economic and social development of the areas where they are located. As the Foreign Assistance Act states, these institutions serve "as study and demonstration centers for ideas and practices of the United States."

Each of these institutions is accepted by the government where it is located as a valuable contributor to the nation's efforts to develop men and women who will rise to the ranks of political and cultural leadership in their countries. In areas of professional scarcity they are trained to be doctors, nurses, teachers, public administrators, businessmen, agriculturalists, and specialists in other areas of importance to a growing society. 

Our support for these institutions must be limited. We can help them to improve and function effectively on a self-supporting basis. 

But we all recognize the need to see these schools and hospitals carry on independently in the coming years.

The President has requested an authorization for these programs for the 5-year period from fiscal year 1967 through fiscal year 1971 of such funds as may be necessary. An appropriation for fiscal year 1967 of $11 million is requested, $4 million more than was appropriated last year. This figure compares with programs of $19.8 million and $17.6 million in fiscal years 1964 and 1965, respectively.

Almost 95 percent of the $11 million is now planned for five institutions: the University of the Americas; the American University of 

Beirut; Robert College, Istanbul; the American University in Cairo; 

and Project HOPE. 

Of the proposed $4 million increase, $2 million would be used to assist the University of the Americas in Mexico City to construct a new campus complex. We expect that private sources will contribute an additional $1.4 million for this project. The amount of $3 million is now planned for the American University of Beirut, an increase of $1 million over assistance provided this year [security deletion]. 

A breakdown of the actual program for fiscal year 1965 and fiscal year 1966—and of the tentative fiscal year 1967 program is set forth in annex B.

ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSES 

Funds authorized and appropriated for administrative expenses meet the costs of directing and supervising the AID program in Washington and overseas. This includes establishing program policies and standards, planning, supervising, and reviewing the actual implementation of these policies, evaluating programs and projects, and providing such key management services as accounting, inspection, auditing, personnel administration, management analysis, and administrative support. Because administrative funds cover the costs of directing and supervising the AID program, it is of the highest importance that we have sufficient funds for the effective management of our assistance programs. 

The President has requested an authorization for "Administrative expenses" for the 5-year period from fiscal year 1967 through 1971 of "such funds as may be necessary." This language is consistent with that used in the past for Department of State administrative expenses authorized under section 637 (b).

We believe this type of request to be particularly appropriate for administrative expenses. Numerous factors-over some of which we have no control-affect the amount of administrative expenses required in a given year and result in increased costs, the amount of which cannot be accurately predicted in advance.

For example, our fiscal year 1967 appropriation request for administrative expenses is $57,387,000. This, together with $750,000 estimated to be reappropriated from prior year unobligated balances, will make available in fiscal year 1967 a total of $58,137,000. 

This is $1,333,000 more than this year's requirements. Most of this difference is due to increased costs over which the Agency has no control. These include rises in oversea wages and price levels, periodic within-grade pay increases and the Federal pay raise enacted last year. 

A small increase of $350,000 is being requested to support increased initiatives in agriculture, health, and education. However, this increase is partially offset by anticipated economies estimated at $150,000. 

The annual levels of our administrative expenses have been rising for the same reasons that account for the fiscal year 1967 increase inflation abroad, Federal personnel procedures, and Federal pay raises. 

We have no reason to believe that they will not continue to rise in the coming years. We therefore consider it essential to request an authorization for the next 5 years for "such funds as may be necessary.' 99

One further point on this subject: Our request for fiscal year 1967 ninistrative expenses includes funds to support our operations in tnam on a level equal to that of our original fiscal year 1966 prom. We will manifestly need additional administrative funds for 

Vietnamese program in fiscal year 1967. For this reason, the sident is requesting authority to use for administrative costs, if it omes necessary to do so, supporting assistance funds available for in Vietnam. A determination by the President under section (a) of the Foreign Assistance Act would be required before such ansfer could be made.

The Congress granted similar authority to the President in the fiscal r 1966 Supplemental Authorization Act. 

I will be glad to answer your questions on these or any other matters ating to the AID program. 

Mr. Chairman, I would like to add one thing more to my statement, may, before turning to your questions. would like to emphasize again for the committee, as Mr. Bell and ers have before me this year when testifying here, the importance ich we attribute to the administration request for a 5-year authortion for the AID program. 

I have just come back a couple of weeks ago from a trip to the Far st. I went to Laos, to Thailand, and Vietnam. I talked to as many our people overseas as I could, individually and in groups, out ere we had our AID officials. In talking to them I found that they re interested primarily in two things when we talked about the situon on the Hill :

One was the personnel legislation-the Hays bill-which was passed the House last year and on which the Senate is now holding rings. 

The other was the request for multiyear authorization. 

Mr. Bell and the other witnesses have testified about why we want multiyear authorization. I was very much interested in the reasons ich these men overseas gave me when I pressed them on it. Their mary feeling was that the AID program has gone on from year year; each year it goes through a struggle here on the Hill and in newspapers; each year the AID bill is treated as though it were ething that was going to expire at the end of the year. 

We are asked all the time the question of why is it that the AID ogram has so little acceptance throughout the country and in the blic mind. My feeling is that one of the main reasons for that is t we treat it as if it has no acceptance, we look at it each year as if were something new and debatable.

My own feeling-and this feeling was buttressed and supported by ny of these men that I talked to overseas-is that if you are in favor the AID program, if you believe it is something we should conue, the biggest boost you can give it from a morale standpoint is to t it on a multiyear basis. 

In terms of morale of our employees, in terms of its acceptance, its ognition by the other nations whom we are trying to encourage give more aid, in terms of our ability to use this to achieve better f-help performance, this single factor-the multiyear authorizan—in my judgment will do more than anything else. BREAKDOWN OF TOTAL REQUEST BY AID 

The $57,387,000 requested for administrative expenses includes $38,289,300 for salaries. The $2.4 billion in program funds requested includes $68,056,700 for salaries. The total estimates for salaries is $106,346,000. Supporting costs for these personnel are $9,342,600 for administrative expenses and $31,318,400 for program expenses. The program expense figures include direct-hire technicians but do not cover costs incurred by technical assistance contractors. 

Chairman MORGAN. How do you decide which expenses are to be charged to administrative funds and which are charged to program funds?

Mr. HALL. This is a decision that was made some time ago before 

I came with the program, Mr. Chairman. The line that we have tried to follow has been that things which can be tied to a specific project or a specific country program we charge against program funds. 

Things that are of a general character, for example, the Controller's office, all of our senior people, all of our mission directors, deputy mis sion directors, the AID Administrator, the Deputy AID Administra tor, the Assistant Administrators in Washington, people who are overhead are charged against administrative expenses.

Our personnel office is charged against administrative expenses. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Hall, we have always put a limit on administrative funds. Is there any possibility that by using program funds you can get around the limitation that we put on administrative funds? 

Mr. HALL. No, sir; we watch this very carefully. I personally approve any major move from administrative to program. We would also bring it to this committee.

We did bring last year or the year before a shift to correct certain funding situations; we moved some people from administrative to program and from program to administrative. 

That is the last change we have made. It is a close question when you get in the fields as to whether you will charge an automobile, for example, to a project or to administrative expenses. We have our people who approve these items and do watch this closely, and when there is a close question, they bring it to me. It is in final analysis a

subjective decision, but I try to watch this carefully and avoid any unjustified shift from administrative expenses to program expenses.

 PRESIDENTIAL DETERMINATION ON TRANSFER OF VIETNAM SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE FUNDS TO ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSES ACCOUNT 

The proposed amendment to section 402 providing for transfer of Vietnam supporting assistance funds to the administrative expense account would not exempt such a transfer from the requirements of section 610 (a) of the Foreign 

Assistance Act. 

The amendment, since it would be inconsistent with and a later enactment than section 610(b), would exempt such a transfer from the provision of section 610(b) which prohibits transfers to the administrative expense account. 

The amendment is not inconsistent with section 610(a) and thus the transfer provided for in the amendment would be subject to the provision of section 610(a) requiring a Presidential determination that a transfer is necessary for the purposes of the act.

This Agency has been in existence for 5 years. For 5 years we have come up here with a request for administrative expenses which the committee generally has considered to be reasonable. We have actually established a relationship with the committee, we have established a precedent, a practice, and it doesn't seem to me, sir, given the choice that you have here of trying to estimate in detail what our administrative expenses will be 5 years from now and going ahead on this basis, this doesn't, to me, seem to be an unreasonable choice, but the committee has to decide for itself.

You have suggested that there is some psychological problem in the field if we don't change the system we now have. Yet what is to be gained in any specific way by simply allowing you to make the decision with respect to the amount that you plan to spend in any one period. If this program, like many other programs were accepted by the Congress as something that would continue from year to year, as necessary if that acceptance were given the program, I think it would do a great deal to change the attitude of the people in this country toward foreign aid, and it would put the whole thing on an entirely different footing.

Beyond that there are other arguments. Mr. George Woods, for example, the president of the World Bank, feels very strongly-he has told me that a multiyear authorization would make it easier for the United States to deal with these countries to which we are giving a considerable amount of aid and encourage self-help and performance and the like.

I feel myself that in the European nations which we are trying to get to give out more aid each year, people who are against foreign aid use over and over again, and use effectively in their countries the fact that the United States goes through this agony every year of whether they will or will not have an aid program, and that it deters our effectiveness with these other countries. 

I can't quantify that. That is not a specific thing. You believe it or you don't. I believe these things deeply. I believe these are sound reasons for putting this on a multiyear program.

Vietnam. As far as the Agency as a whole is concerned, Mr. Fountain, if you will exclude Vietnam, the number of our direct-hire personnel has been decreasing. They are increasing very substantially in Vietnam.

For example, on June 30, 1965, the total of our direct-hire personnel in Vietnam, both U.S. nationals and foreign nationals, was 

1,629. As of June 30, 1966, we estimate they will total 2,365. By 

June 30, 1967, we estimate they will total 3,221.

Mr. GAUD. They are all full time. But they don't get any tenure. 

We are going to be faced with quite a problem as people come back from Vietnam, having served a tour out there, or as the requirement for personnel in Vietnam decreases, because we are going to have a lot of people who have spent some time with us, many of whom will want to stay with the Agency and the odds are that we will not be able to place them in the Agency because there are so many people working in Vietnam.

Mr. MONAGAN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Gaud, I notice in your statement that there is a reference to the proposed increase of $4 million in funds for educational institutions. 

Mr. MONAGAN. Included in the institutions mentioned are the 

American University of Beirut and Robert College in Istanbul, with

which we are familiar. These are old, established institutions and they are also located in relatively underdeveloped countries. 

However, I see here the proposal to provide $2 million to assist the University of the Americas in Mexico City to construct a new campus complex.

I am concerned about this for several reasons. First of all we have been hearing so much about Mexico in recent years as an example of a country that has come a long way, made tremendous progress economically speaking, there is a boom on there, so that I raise a question about the economic necessity of it. 

Second, about the character of the aid itself which is the construction of buildings there. It seems to me to be something that the country itself should be concerned with. And third, the need, if it is not an economic need, I don't see any political necessity for doing anything, but if there were a desire to do something of this sort in the hemisphere, there are many countries that are much more needy from this point of view than Mexico. 

Mr. GAUD. Those are good questions, Mr. Monagan. I would like to go into it in a little detail; the main answer lies in the nature of the authority that is contained in section 214 of the act. We have here a program which is quite different from any of the rest of our programs. Most of our programs, as you say, relate to giving aid to developing countries.

Section 214 directly and specifically and expressly authorizes us to give aid to American institutions located abroad. The University of the Americas is a school that was founded in Mexico- Mr. MONAGAN. Those have had reference more to primary schools- Mr. GAUD. No, sir. Some are hospitals, some are colleges and some are secondary schools, such as the International College in Beirut and Athens College in Athens, which, even though they are called colleges, are really secondary schools. This University of the 

Americas was founded by Americans in 1940. They came to us 2 years ago to ask us to help them build some new buildings. 

We appointed a committee consisting of the president of the University of Wisconsin, the president of the University of Houston, the vice president of the University of California and the vice chancellor of the University of Hawaii who went down and studied this institution and came back and recommended to us that we help them on two conditions: one was that the university would prepare long-range plans, financial academic, physical plans, acceptable to AID; and second, that it would demonstrate its ability to raise its share of the cost of constructing these buildings. 

They have come up with a plan that we think makes sense. They are in the midst of a fund-raising campaign. They have raised $700,000. Their target is $1.4 million, which they hope to reach by this summer. If they reach that target, we propose to make a grant of $2 million. We have gone into their plans for the future. We believe this institution will be self-supporting. We have no intention of getting involved with any budget support for it. It is only a question of helping them build their plant.

 U.S. ROLE IN SOUTH VIETNAM ELECTIONS 

In the view of the Department of State, an important political process has been undertaken in South Vietnam. Hopefully, this process will lay the groundwork for creating lasting political institutions which provide for orderly political change and which are responsive to the will of the Vietnamese people. This is a Vietnamese process in which the United States has no intention or desire to interfere. The United States supports this process and will respect its outcome. 

In the interim, until a new government emerges, the United States will continue to support the present government as the legitimate government of the Republic of Vietnam.

 ASSISTANCE TO THE AMERICAN UNIVERSITY OF BEIRUT AND THE POLISH CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL 

Relatively large amounts have been granted to the American University, Beirut, since fiscal year 1959 ($33 million) because it is a principal center for higher education in the Middle East. Approximately half the grants have been made to assist in the construction of a new medical center. AUB has provided important educational and training services for AID financed participants over many years. For these reasons, the U.S. Government has devoted important assistance to this institution.

U.S. support to the Polish Childrens' Hospital has totaled $10,475,000 from fiscal year 1961 through fiscal year 1966. The construction of the hospital has been completed and it was dedicated in December 1965. The $175,000 grant in fiscal year 1966 is to finance a feasibility study of a proposed research laboratory building, a nursing school, and residential facilities. It is not anticipated that the feasibility study will be completed in time to warrant an estimate for any fiscal year 1967 funds.

CONTINGENCY FUND CARRYOVER 

It is impossible at this time to estimate the amount of unobligated contingency funds, if any, remaining at the end of the current fiscal year. It is possible that situations will arise throughout the world which will necessitate the use or transfer of a large part or all of currently available contingency funds. We hope, of course, to use these available funds to the minimum extent consistent with U.S. interests. Whatever contingency funds remain unobligated at the end of fiscal year 1966 will be carried over into fiscal year 1967.

Mr. GAUD. Let me say a few words, if I may, about both of the propositions that you have been discussing. 

First, are we adequately set up in AID to deal with the broad question of development, including political development? 

We do not have in AID, as you know, any office-I will take that back-in our Program Office we have a group that is working on this subject. We do not have in our Agency a central group comparable to the engineers, the lawyers, the agriculturalists, who deal with this problem. We are doing a good deal more thinking about it, and are a good deal more conscious of it now than a year or 2 or 3 ago. 

On this recent trip I made out to southeast Asia I discovered that the man in our Thai mission who is in charge of rural development in Thailand will finish his second term out there and will be coming back to the United States this summer. 

I mentioned to him the importance, as I saw it, of his coming back and working in Washington and occupying such a job, at a central place in the Agency, where he would work on these rural development questions-political development, social development, economic development on an agencywide basis, and try to pull together the experience we have had in these various countries and at the same time disseminate that experience to the other parts of the Agency. 

I agree with you. I think it would be useful. 

To move to your second question as to whether Washington, the executive branch as a whole is set up adequately to deal with the question of Thailand or whatever it may be: To put one man in chargelet me just give you my personal views-to take one man and say "You are in charge of Thailand across the board, State Department, Department of Defense, AID, USIA, CIA, Agriculture Department, so forth and so on," this has real problems.

Look at it from our standpoint, for example. We have so many dollars to program for the entire world. We have to keep the programing authority in AID. We can't give it to 50, 60, 70 country directors or individuals who are in charge of particular countries. 

Each one of them will want more when you put them all together than the pie will sustain.

You have to keep some programing functions, some central control, in AID. I think that the same thing is true of most other agencies around town. Nevertheless, the President has taken a step in the direction in which you want to go, as I understand you. He has recently issued a directive to the executive branch setting up in the State Department a senior interdepartmental group, SIG, we call it, which will be chaired by the Secretary of State and have on it representatives of all of the agencies doing business in the foreign field. To this group under the leadership of the Secretary of State is given a great degree of control, a greater degree than any single agency has had in the past in this area.
