WEDNESDAY, APRIL 27, 1966 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, pursuant to adjournment, at 10:20 a.m., in room 

2172, Rayburn House Office Building, Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman) presiding.

The committee meets this morning for a continuation of the hearings on the Foreign Aid bills, H.R. 12449 and H.R. 12450.

Our first witness this morning is the Honorable Gilbert Rohde, president of the Wisconsin Farmers' Union, for the National Farmers

Union. 

Mr. Rohde you have a prepared statement. You may proceed, sir.

STATEMENT OF GILBERT ROHDE, PRESIDENT OF THE WISCONSIN FARMERS' UNION, FOR THE NATIONAL FARMERS UNION 

Mr. ROHDE. 

With me also this morning is Mr. Reuben Johnson, who is director of legislative services here in Washington, D.C., for the National 

Farmers Union. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Rohde, I believe that most members of the committee are well acquainted with Mr. Johnson. 

Mr. ROHDE. Thank you, sir.

We have prepared a statement which I should like to read and at various times I would like to depart from the statement to inject some pertinent information that I think the committee might be interested in. 

The members of National Farmers Union are interested in the wellbeing of farm people all over the world. This interest is practical economics as well as humanitarian. 

We believe that no nation can continue to be rich and secure simply by isolating itself from the poverty and hunger of surrounding nations and that our Nation's agriculture cannot hope to prosper and achieve more for the producers so long as most of the world's farmers can hardly feed themselves.

As a practical matter, we believe that the soundest kind of a food program is one in which all nations share the benefits as well as the responsibilities. We feel strongly that only when there is a worldplanned food program can there be a sound foundation for developing a world peace. And whatever encourages other farmers to produce more, and in the process to improve their own well-being, contributes to world peace. 657

That is why we give strong support to the efforts of the Agency for International Development to assist the people in the new and developing nations throughout the world. While we reserve the right to criticize some of its operations in an effort to improve the kind of assistance we are providing, we at the same time recognize and praise the far-reaching achievements of AID to date. 

Our members, too, identify food for freedom and AID as performing much the same kind of assistance, that of helping people in other ands. They do not differentiate, for the most part, where the assistance of the USDA leaves off and that of AID begins. And in this concept of measuring the total impact of our assistance there is considerable merit. Certainly hungry people are not concerned about the compartmentalized nature of our foreign assistance, but only the total mpact.

The food-for-peace program, as Congressman Alex Olson said- Enables us to substitute a partnership concept (for one of food dumping), so hat our farmers cooperate with those of other countries to meet the growing needs of the world. Our farmers will be able to furnish from their abundance che immediate assistance that people in other countries need to win the war gainst hunger. Our farmers will be able to do their part within the broad framework of a global self-help program that will assist farmers in other countries to gradually increase the productivity of their land. 

In this connection, the Farmers Union is encouraged by the importance that AID is now placing on agriculture and cooperatives in ts assistance planning.

We note that for fiscal year 1967, AID proposes to invest about $152 million in programs to speed agricultural growth in developing councries. That is one-third more than is being spent currently and onehalf again as much as was spent in fiscal year 1965. We commend this as a good start. But more needs to be done more money, additional personnel and more effort. In this effort, we are trying to reach 80 percent of the people with about 20 percent of the money available for 

Foreign assistance. Even so, we would like to point out that it is not only the amount of money, but how it is to be used, which will determine how effectively we are in fact reaching and helping the people in other countries. 

In this connection we have just examined the report on AID's cooperative assistance that was recently printed as a staff report to the 

Banking and Currency Committee's Subcommittee on International

Finance. The accomplishments for the past fiscal year are encouragng, and the participating cooperatives should be commended for their part. Certainly, we in the Farmers Union take considerable pride in he contribution we have made in manpower, membership participaion, and in other forms of assistance. 

Reference is made to section 601 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 961, better known as the Humphrey amendment, to encourage cooperative developments. We take special pride in that amendment, because the Farmers Union and its affiliated cooperatives pressed for such measure for a long time, and finally prevailed on the Vice President o give it the necessary active support to make it a law. 

First, we would like to know in what ways the Farmers Union might assist AID in expanding the cooperative assistance, recognizing that cooperative development is part of the overall country assistance and varies from nation to nation.

Secondly, we would like to know in what specific ways AID intends to utilize what the law says it should to speed the development of agriculture around the world. Are there any efforts made by AID to recruit cooperative assistance from U.S. sources; any plans for explaining because most of the people still are woefully lacking in basic information about our foreign assistance-what the needs are; any effort to encourage a better understanding and an appreciation of what cooperatives are uniquely fitted to do?

In making our own assistance available, we wish also to add that people and organizations in the other so-called advanced countries also are providing assistance. The AID cooperative report suggests that.

In our own case, Farmers Union for many years has worked very closely with farm and cooperative organizations of more than 25 foreign countries, who are members of the International Federation of Agricultural Producers. For many years we exchanged information, and at one time there were serious thoughts of creating an international pool of highly skilled and technical people in agricultural and cooperative subjects. We still think that such an idea would be extremely valuable to establish a people-to-people relationship, rather than government to government. 

Our members have supported, and in some instances have pioneered, ideas-ranging from a world food bank and world food reserve to plans for land reform and resettlement-that bit by bit are being accepted into the orthodox thinking of even some of the more conservative countries.

We have made these efforts, as we said earlier, because we believe that they make good sense, for our own farmers as well as those in other countries. And we say this without in any way detracting from the strong humanitarian sense, the spirit of the golden rule, that prevails among our members and farm people generally. 

We refer to this because in addition to the people our organization has contributed to help AID carry out its agricultural programs in South America, Africa, the Far East, and in the Near East and India, our own members have made a fine contribution to better understanding between peoples.

Nearly 300 of our Farmers Union families have opened their homes to foreign agricultural trainees brought to this country by AID, under an arrangement with our Farmers Union. They have been hosts, taken these young farm leaders in as members of the family. They have been guests, and these families have not charged a cent for board or room or any kind of services. They have gone out of their way to show them what American farm life is like, how democracy works, the politics of the community and county, the operations of cooperatives and how they fit into the life of the farmer and the business community. 

We are proud of the contribution-over and above the dollar equivalent of board and room-that these families have made to AID's program. This is the kind of people-to-people relations that I think 

AID should encourage.

Mr. Chairman, if I might depart from our prepared statement for a minute to relate and share with you some of our own personal experiences as we have known them to be in Wisconsin. For the past

eral years our organization has participated and cooperated with rnational organization in bringing Latin Americans to Wisconsin m homes. We first determine what families would like to have them their homes for a period of 6 weeks. We then assign these young ople, these Latin Americans, to these homes. 

They have a very limited knowledge of the English language, and it surprising how easily and rapidly they are able to communicate th each other. Our Latin Americans are considered not as hired men but as guests, ests of the family, but they do participate in all of the activities at the family engages in with respect to their social affairs, their work bits, and so on.

We feel that this has had a tremendous impact on these people. e Latins help in fixing the machinery, doing all the chores around e farm. We have found in many instances that the thing that presses them most is how hard our farmers work. 

We think in many instances when they get back home and are able adapt more readily to the work habits they have gained a considerle amount from that. Last year we held a special experimentation. Our organization has nping facilities of considerable size in Wisconsin, and we had some all of the Latin Americans that the Farmers Union sponsored, at r camp for 1 week. We held a special Latin American night in r home city of Chippewa Falls in cooperation with the chamber of mmerce of that city, where we asked the city folks to invite one of ese Latin Americans into their home to be a guest for one evening. 

The impact of this was considerable in our small town of 18,000. It ve our city friends an opportunity to learn firsthand of some of the essing problems that our Latin Americans have in developing their onomy. Our people in our hometown are looking forward to such event this year, when we will have nine Latin Americans participatin our program in 1966. To continue on with our testimony, we do not care to dwell on the ed to bring assistance directly to the people in the rural areas, rather un let a few drops trickle down from the top. There is general agreeent, we believe, that this was the weakness in Vietnam; we reached o few, with too little, too late. Certainly there is no need to repeat s in other countries.

In this broad sweep, we believe there is general agreement on what ould be done, and we are certain that there are recommendations and oposals and suggestions by the hundreds among the files of posi- -n papers in AID. Therefore, there is no need to add to the already ountainous accumulation.

The potential of cooperative development, which is still greatly in ed of emphasis, will have its greatest opportunity to prove itself en the functional experiences of operating cooperative personnel is erited to work within the overall framework of country developnt. 

The gestures to stimulate greater agricultural production will be eaningless until the man with a hoe, who raises the food, is reached, d believes that what is offered to him is a good thing. Cooperatives, ong with education and training, can speed the process of acceptance.

Farmers Union-and our affiliated agricultural cooperatives-stand ready to assist in whatever ways we can to make agricultural assistance a genuine success.

We appreciate very much the opportunity to present our views.

The National Farmers Union agreement with AID is to assist in securing competent personnel for rural cooperative projects abroad, develop cooperative leadership and to provide teachers and training facilities for cooperative classes. 

The contract is held in behalf of the U.S. members of the International Federation of Agriculture Producers which has membership in 32 countries. The U.S. members are the National Council of Farmer Cooperatives, representing most of the commodity cooperatives in the United States, the National Grange, oldest of the U.S. general farm organizations, and the National Farmers Union, with extensive cooperative affiliates in the Great Plains region. 

The projects are carried out under Latin American region and worldwide agreements. The U.S. organizations and the foreign farm organizations are prepared to furnish technicians and cousultants upon the request of AID. The advisory committee to the National Farmers Union, composed of representatives of IFAP, Food and Agriculture Organization, and International Labor Organiza tion of the United Nations, meets annually. 

Regional and country projects have been established to train people for cooperative positions and agricultural leadership in Africa, Latin America, and the Far East. The Farmers Union has asigned agricultural and cooperative specialists to Kenya, Uganda, Dahomey, Tunisia, and India. It has held hundreds of local cooperative meetings and conducted leadership seminars in Uganda, Kenya, and Tunisia. It has made evaluation studies to determine the feasibility of livestock and grain marketing cooperatives in Ecuador. U.S. training teams have helped to coordinate cooperative rural work in Latin America. 

A third group of 83 Latin American farm people was invited from Bolivia, Colombia, Peru, Chile, and Venezula to live with farm people in the United States. This group spent 3 months on U.S. farms, learning about agriculture, community life, and cooperatives, and 2 months in classes at Jamestown College in North Dakota and the International Cooperative Training Center at the University of Wisconsin. This project's main purpose is to develop community leadership for campesinos organizations, particularly as land reform and resettlement go into effect.

The Farmers Union furnished a technical cooperative specialist to the Afro- 

Asian Rural Reconstruction Organization. This Organization with a member ship of more than a score of Asian and African countries is concerned with the development of independent cooperative organizations and farm organizations. 

Currently the Farmers Union is sending cooperative and credit specialists, organizers and teachers, to Uganda, Kenya, the Philippines and is reviewing with AID opportunities for giving assistance in Korea, Vietnam, Tunisia. Ethiopia, Liberia, and Nigeria.

STATEMENT OF JOHN O. TEETER, VICE PRESIDENT OF PFIZER INTERNATIONAL, ON BEHALF OF THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES 

Mr. TEETER. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. I hope we can once again be helpful to you and the committee.

This morning I am here to present the views of the Chamber of Commerce of the United States on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1966. 

I am chairman of the chamber's foreign operations review subcommittee and also serve on the national chamber's international commit-

tee and its joint subcommittee on foreign aid, composed of representatives from six chamber policy committees. I am accompanied this morning by Jay H. Cerf, manager of the chamber's international group, and by John C. L. Donaldson and Jack Gilbert of the staff.

In presenting the national chamber's position on foreign aid, I will emphasize that the chamber:

Recommends a balanced program of foreign assistance geared to long-range development. 

Encourages increased emphasis on private resources in furthering foreign assistance objectives, and on reduction of Government programs after these programs have served their catalytic purposes. 

Supports selective aid to those countries determined to help themselves.

I will also present to the committee proposed amendments to the Foreign Assistance Act to implement these positions of our national federation.

Foreign aid in review: As you know, the concept of foreign assistance has been broken down into four major categories military, economic, social, and political or institutional assistance. Since 1945 the 

United States has directed its efforts toward various aspects of foreign assistance according to the demands of the time. Last year your committee and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee discussed at length various approaches for establishing effectively administered aid programs designed to achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives. Two foreign aid bills, H.R. 12449 and H.R. 12450, have been introduced by your chairman to implement the discussions carried over from the last session of Congress.

In addition to these two bills, various bills directly related to foreign assistance have been introduced in the fields of agriculture, international health, and international education. These bills underscore the current emphasis being given by the administration to human needs in establishing criteria for foreign assistance programs. 

Our federation commends, in general, these newly emphasized elements of foreign assistance. We urge, however, that these programs not be viewed as a substitute for long-range economic development. 

We are concerned, also, that this year's legislation not seem to relegate proper emphasis on private sector participation in foreign assistance to a minor rule. This concern causes our federation to urge that you give appropriate consideration to a balanced foreign assistance program that takes into account economic as well as social and political measures to help developing countries to help themselves. 

In consonance with the administration's emphasis on the improvement of activities and programs that influence human attitudes, we cannot stress too strongly the fact that self-help efforts through private initiative are the driving force that motivates emerging countries to develop, on their own terms, their resources-human and material-to solve their problems. 

Funds for development: Support for the principle of foreign aid does not necessarily imply approval of all the various programs known as "foreign aid" nor of every budget authorization request. Foreign aid administraion must be continually improved to yield budgetary savings.

The national chamber recommends a reduction of at least. $187 million in the funds requested for economic assistance in this budget. This means that not more than $2.28 billion should be authorized for fiscal year 1967 economic assistance.

Included in this $2.28 billion figure is $500 million requested for supporting assistance to Vietnam. The national chamber supports assistance to Vietnam in view of the fact that our Government and Congress, who have access to documentation on operational costs, have deemed necessary military assistance to Vietnam, for the purpose of resisting Communist aggression and domination in the national interest of the 

United States.

The necessity for providing funds covering increased military operations in Vietnam, the uncertainty of future military requirements and the acknowledged inflationary pressures, generated in part by the increase in spending for Great Society programs, other than in Vietnam, should be held at not more than the level of fiscal year 1966 appropriations. 

Private enterprise and foreign assistance: Government-to-government programs are needed initially to build the infrastructure for participation by U.S and foreign private sectors in developing foreign economies. These Government programs should be phased out after they have served their catalytic purposes. 

To establish free and viable economies in countries that want to develop rapidly but often lack the human and material resources to support this development, the national chamber recommends that the Foreign Assistance Act of 1966 be amended to provide that: 

Foreign participation in private enterprise projects should be encouraged, when feasible, as a means of meeting nationalistic concerns in negotiating such agreements. Business efforts to conclude equitable agreements should be fully supported by the U.S. Government.

I cannot emphasize too strongly that private enterprise and Government cooperation in efforts to locate opportunities for development of free and viable economies is a necessary prerequisite to improvement of local conditions. A stable and growing economy is a thing which in a developing country can provide markets for U.S. goods and services. 

A mechanism is needed to bring the business communities of the United States and the aid-recipient countries into workable agreements that serve as tools for balanced economic development. To meet this need, the national chamber recommends that the Foreign Assistance Act of 1966 be amended to provide that: 

A small, permanent advisory board of U.S. businessmen, with responsibility for mobilizing private resources for oversea economic development, should be established.

Although President Johnson referred in his foreign aid message to the importance of increased reliance on private sector participation in the development of emerging nations, we feel that more needs to be done to implement such pronouncements. 

Highest priority should be given to the recommendations of the so-called Watson report and to the International Cooperation Year

Conference recommendations for involving the private sector more in foreign assistance. We are aware that some action, although limited,

has been taken on the Watson report recommendations. These activities have been reported to you by various AID officials. 

At all U.S. Government levels, coordination of foreign economic policy and programs is long overdue. The expansion of the foreign assistance program this year to increase responsibility for various and new food, health, and education programs in various Government agencies emphasizes the immediate need to coordinate these programs if we are to implement effectively our foreign policies. 

The chamber recommends that this committee encourage the establishment of a coordinating mechanism at no lower than the Assistant Secretary level that should (1) have full presidentially delegated authority and support, and (2) provide adequate and specific opportunities for U.S. business views to be registered and applied in the development and execution of foreign economic policy and programs of our Government.

The role of foreign investment in economic development: Last year, I testified before this committee that direct foreign investment is one of the most effective means of gaining and preserving access to oversea markets that would otherwise be lost to the United States. 

My company, Pfizer International, has found this to be particularly true. We are heartened to see that other companies in the past year have expressed a similar view.

I want to emphasize again that investment in such developed countries as those of Western Europe and Japan often provides the wherewithal for U.S. companies to invest in the developing countries and to assist these emerging nations along the road of self-improvement to the point where they have the opportunity to enjoy the fruits of free and viable economies.

In dividends it earns abroad and in U.S. exports it generates, direct overseas private investment is one of the most important sources of payments received in the U.S. international accounts. 

Restriction of the free movement of private goods and capital is not the solution to balance-of-payment problems. Remedial measures should be oriented to expansion, rather than restriction of world trade and investment.

The national chamber urges Congress and the U.S. Government to take these facts fully into account so that business will not be asked or required to conduct its operations for a protracted period in ways that do not maintain it fully competitive with international business. 

To encourage more U.S. companies to develop and expand their foreign markets, the national chamber recommends that the investment survey provisions of the Foreign Assistance Act be amended to provide:

That the making of such survey shall be approved by the President. The U.S. 

Government shall make a 100-percent advance for local currency expenditures from U.S.-owned local currencies, wherever feasible. If the project goes forward, the person conducting the survey will make a 50-percent reimbursement in dollar equivalents to the U.S. Government. 

The investment survey section of the act should also be amended to provide that if the project does not go forward, the person conducting an investment survey will:

Repay 25 percent of the total survey cost in dollar equivalents.

This amendment would have the beneficial effects of improving our balance of payments and rewarding the investor who goes ahead with a project.

National chamber positions on 1966 AID recommendations: 

Special emphasis has been placed by the administration this year on five categories of foreign assistance that have received individual attention in past years. These categories include: (1) Self-help measures to encourage emerging nations to solve their own problems; (2) Separation of economic assistance from military assistance; (3) Multiyear authorization of aid funds; (4) Agricultural improvement to meet food needs and to deal with population increases; (5) Multilateral and regional assistance. 

Self-help: The chamber has long emphasized the importance of giving people, through the self-help measures, a sense of their own responsibility in the community of free nations. The attached chamber policy statement on foreign assistance points out that self-help criteria should be rigorously applied to the point of conditioning additional assistance on the quarterly fulfillment of written progress agreements.

To establish a procedure in foreign aid negotiations and to emphasize the importance of putting recipient countries in the position of solving their own problems, the national chamber recommends that the Foreign Assistance Act of 1966 be amended to provide that: 

Before allocating, reserving, earmarking, committing, or otherwise setting aside funds for use in any country under this title, the President shall require that recipient government representatives, after consultation with private sector representatives, submit a quarterly progress report with respect to the selfhelp and reform measures planned and achieved by the recipient country. 

Separation of military and economic assistance: The national cham ber has long advocated that the cost of military assistance should be allocated as a part of the Department of Defense budget. Present commitments on the Sino-Soviet periphery must be honored. We also urge that other industrial nations should bear more of the cost for military assistance programs.

Some students of foreign aid have said that military assistance must be included in the same package with economic assistance in order to "sell" economic assistance. This thesis was perhaps valid several years ago. However, the time has come for economic assistance to stand on its own merits. Long-range economic development of emerging countries must be presented in its true colors and not disguised in the gaudy wrappings of short-term palliatives.

Multiyear authorizations: Long-range economic planning and development must be emphasized in foreign assistance programs. To accomplish this goal, a 4-year authorization of foreign aid funds, subject to annual appropriations and review by appropriate congressional committees, is desirable.

Such a long-term authorization would provide the continuity that is needed to establish effective aid programs. Authorizations should

be extended to 4 years, instead of 5 years as recommended by the administration, to allow each administration 2 years to evaluate and revise, as necessary, foreign assistance programs in the national interest of the United States.

Agricultural improvement: Our federation welcomes, in general, the new emphasis placed by the administration this year on food requirements and the need to improve agricultural techniques to meet these requirements.

Relief provided by Public Law 480 programs is a temporary measure. A condition of this type of assistance should be the demonstrated improvement of agricultural techniques and productivity that can alleviate the pressing problem of population increase. 

This major new direction of foreign economic assistance must make it perfectly clear to recipient countries that such assistance is temporary and designed only to meet their basic nutritional needs while they correct the situations that cause food shortages. 

Another major emphasis of foreign economic assistance should be to provide funds for birth control programs, when such funds are requested by less developed countries. 

Multilateral and regional assistance: Multilateral development financing and technical assistance should be emphasized as an essential instrument for U.S. foreign policy. The private sector can serve a useful role in this field, particularly in regard to technical assistance programs.

International institutions, including regional development banks, in collaboration with other industrialized free world nations can play an increasingly important role in achieving foreign economic development objectives.

U.S. bilateral aid programs also serve a useful purpose. The national chamber recognizes a continuing need for a substantial U.S. bilateral program until acceptable multilateral programs are developed.

Conclusion: In summary, to provide necessary assistance to the developing countries and to further U.S. national interests, the national chamber urges this committee to consider favorably the proposed amendments to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1966 contained in this testimony. These amendments will insure continued refinement of a foreign aid program to- Provide effective coordinating mechanisms to represent and present U.S. business and Government views on foreign economic policy and programs.

Increase reliance on private sector assistance, and reduce Government programs accordingly.

Base loan commitments or demonstrated self-help and reform measures.

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I request that the attachments to this statement be made a part of the official record of your hearings. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection it is so ordered.

I. BASIC CHAMBER POSITION ON FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

(a) Foreign aid as a means toward foreign economic and social development continues to be a proper element of U.S. foreign policy. Its objectives and principles have long been endorsed by the chamber. (b) Refinement of the program must provide an effective base for the exercise of private enterprise and initiative in foreign economic and social development. Progress should follow the effective guidelines established by the AID Administrator. (c) Program objectives should be continually clarified as they relate to U.S. foreign policy and to U.S. and foreign private enterprise. The U.S. public demands clear justification of its foreign aid investment. 

II. CHAMBER PROGRAM PROPOSALS 

(a) Long-range economic planning and development must be emphasized. 

To accomplish this goal, a 4-year authorization of foreign aid funds, subject to annual appropriations and review by appropriate congressional committees, is desirable. Although long-term aid investment seldom has dramatic impact, in general it can yield far higher returns than short-term "gimmicks." Economic planning need not mean a government "planned economy" in underdeveloped countries. 

Recent efforts at country development planning have shown the need for private foreign investment. Foreign economic development programs must place increased reliance on private resources, and reduce government programs after these programs have served their catalytic purpose. 

Private enterprise and government should cooperate in their efforts to locate opportunities for the development of free and viable economies that can improve local conditions and provide markets for U.S. goods and services. In particular, foreign participation should be encouraged when feasible as a means of meeting nationalistic concerns. In negotiating such arrangements, business efforts to conclude equitable agreements should be fully supported by the U.S. Government.

A small, permanent advisory board of U.S. businessmen with responsibility for mobilizing private resources for overseas economic development should be established. (b) Government incentives to U.S. private foreign investment serve a useful purpose. But a more positive approach is imperative, centering around the

need to build an economic and political framework in which the profit motive can operate at full potential. Priority must be given to removal of disincentives that discourage private investment. Certain provisions in the Revenue 

Act of 1962 on taxation of foreign income are punitive and self-defeating. International antitrust standards and an international patent system should also be developed.

The United States should suspend foreign assistance to any nation that takes discriminatory or confiscatory action against U.S. private investment in such nation without taking appropriate steps to discharge its obligations under international law including prompt and full compensation or relief. Courts in the United States should determine and apply principles of international law in appropriate cases to encourage the development of an international legal system that will contribute to the improvement of the investment climate, and the protection of private property abroad. (c) Development loans should receive priority. The trend toward government lending to, and for the express development of, private institutions and organizations should be accelerated. Terms of development loans should take into consideration the overall debt management position of recipient countries. (d) A limited program of military assistance to selected allies is essential to total short-range free world security. Military assistance should be held to a minimum, particularly in Western Europe and Latin America. The cost to the 

United States of such assistance should be accountable to the Department of Defense. (e) Multilateral development financing and technical assistance should be emphasized as an essential instrument of U.S. foreign policy. In many instances, this approach is more practical and effective than the bilateral approach. Private international consortia should be utilized to the fullest extent possible. Congress and the administration should propose new means to achieve U.S. foreign economic development objectives through international institutions, including regional development banks, in collaboration with other industrialized free world nations provided the United States has voting rights commensurate to its contributions. Such programs must assign a major role to the private sectors of both donor and recipient nations, and the administrative cost of such programs must be equitably shared by the respective national governments. The chamber recognizes a continuing need for a substantial 

U.S. bilateral program until acceptable multilateral programs are developed. (f) Aid should be selective. The administration should apply great selectivity in choosing which nations and projects are to be aided from among ever-increasing requests for assistance. Assistance should be based on results. 

Self-help criteria should be rigorously applied, to the point of conditioning additional assistance on the quarterly fulfillment of written progress agreements.

Emphasis must be placed on technical assistance programs that can put aid recipients in the position of solving their own problems. (g) The food-for-peace program under Public Law 480, title II, serves in general the best interests of U.S. foreign policy. Relief provided by Public Law 

480 programs is a temporary measure. A condition of this type of assistance, and a major new direction of foreign economic assistance should be demonstrated improvement of agricultural techniques and productivity that can alleviate the pressing problem of population increase. Another major aid emhpasis should be to provide funds for birth-control programs when such funds are requested by less-developed countries. U.S.-owned local currencies should be used where available to finance investment surveys and the development of vocational training facilities. (h) The Alliance for Progress must be moved forward along the sound lines recommended by its Inter-American Committee (CIAP). A broader concept of the Alliance should be developed by encouraging other member countries to contribute appropriate financial and technical assistance for Latin 

American development.

The objectives of the Alliance must be realistically determined with emphasis on regional market integration and the availability of external resources. 

The Alliance must be coordinated througl, other institutions and programs. 

Alliance programs must create a stable atmosphere in which private investment and initiative, local and foreign, can operate beneficially.

(i) The aid task must be justly shared. The United States should continue to enlist greater cooperation from other industrialized nations in assisting less developed countries. The Development Assistance Committee of the OECD has an important duty as an instrument to serve this purpose. (j) Effective foreign assistance programs can only be implemented by competent personnel. Private enterprise urges, and is willing to cooperate with 

AID in, the maintenance of such standards. The administrators of the program must have the legislative authority to improve the quality and reduce the number of AID personnel, both domestic and overseas. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you for your statement.

Mr. Teeter, I noticed on page 3 of your statement you recommend a cut of $187 million in funds requested for economic assistance. I don't see any place where you break this down. 

Where specifically do you recommend cuts?

Mr. TEETER. We have not specifically broken it down. In the following paragraph you will note that we went along with the request so far as Vietnam is concerned. 

The cut actually would apply to countries other than Vietnam. 

This would be countries in the Near East, southeast Asia, and Latin America. This we feel is not a substantial cut, but it was our feeling that we would like to see appropriations kept to the level of the previous year.

The $187 million cut therefore comes in these areas, rather than Vietnam itself where we feel, as we stated here, it is impossible for us to really get into the depth of the problems because we do not have access to information about the military situation. We would go along with the administration's request in this regard. 

Chairman MORGAN. Your recommendation then is that we should stay within the limitation of last year's appropriation figure? 

Mr. TEETER. Yes.

Chairman MORGAN. This cut of $187 million should be spread by the Executive over those countries where you feel there are no acute problems.

Mr. TEETER. We felt it was not as important to increase fund levels for these countries as to keep funds at last year's level. Our policy statement reflects this position. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Teeter, on page 7, your last paragraph, "National chamber positions on 1966 aid recommendations": No. 1 refers to self-help measures to encourage emerging nations to solve their own problems.

When you come to No. 2 you recommend separation of economic assistance from military assistance. Is this any change in the chamber's position, or has this been your annual recommendation? 

Mr. TEETER. This has been our annual recommendation, Mr. Chairman, as you may recall from previous testimony. We have felt that military assistance is one thing, and economic assistance is something different. They do come together to a certain degree when you have situations such as in Vietnam at the moment.

We felt economic assistance should be put in its own budget category and should stand on its own two feet for this reason. We know your committee reviews these matters every year, and of course_reviews the military matters as well, but from the standpoint of budget categories, this has been the national chamber's recommendation, and

this is consistent, to specifically answer your question, with respect to our previous policy. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Teeter, this committee over a period of years has had strong feeling that both economic assistance and military assistance should be in a single package. Mr. TEETER. I don't. It is the feeling of the chamber, and my own personal feeling as well, there wouldn't be any danger of serious cuts.

If this takes place, I think the economic assistance program can pretty well stand on its own merit without having to be tagged onto the coattails of military assistance. I know we have discussed this problem before.

I really feel, and this is the feeling of the chamber, that economic and military assistance should each stand alone.

Mr. TEETER. May I explain, Mr. Adair. We had discussed this at length. Let's use the phrase "joint ventures." There has been a great deal of emphasis on the value of joint ventures abroad. 

I think joint ventures do have a great deal of value, although there is a particular problem that those of us in business do run into sometimes in trying to find an appropriate partner to establish a joint venture within a particular country. 

This is particularly true in the developing nations. In the more developed countries it is essential that you do have a joint venture- France and Japan are specific examples of this. I don't think there should be any discrimination against a firm wishing to do business in a particular country.

In other words, what I am trying to say is, there should be no method of forcing him to really take a local partner, because sometimes they are just unavailable. Maybe an example would serve the point. In Nigeria we established a pharmaceutical operation, a plant on a small scale. There was really no one there that we could go into local partnership with.

When it came to agricultural products, the manufacture of feeds, there was a local man who had experience and background. This did become a joint venture which was established in Nigeria. There has been an undertone we have felt, and this has been felt by the members of our chamber committee at its meeting, this was rather deeply discussed in January, that sometimes pressure is brought to bear on business that it must really go into a joint venture.

Mr. FRASER. The basic rationale for foreign aid is that we hope this will encourage countries to follow or move into the path of democratic practices to develop strength in democratic institutions.

Mr. TEETER. It should not bear the entire burden. We are bearing a great share of it. Consistently the chamber has recommended over

the years a reduction in foreign aid so that it could be quite realistic. 

I am not unmindful of what Mr. Fraser said a few moments ago. I think again, to just go back to that point, that development assistance is a world responsibility insofar as aid is concerned. I think that the entire developed world must assume the responsibility of aid to the underdeveloped nations so they can achieve a degree of development to make them important nations of the world and so they can improve their education, health conditions, sanitation, and so forth. 

I think this is quite important. Again, we have been consistent in our cutting of foreign aid funds. To be very realistic, the foreign aid bill, when I first testified on it, was up in the range of $4.8 billion. 

This was shortly before the Clay Committee was appointed. 

It was cut back to $42 billion. I had a very definite feeling at that time as did other members of the chamber, that this figure was entirely unrealistic. When the bill was cut below that, the fact of the matter was borne out the figure was unrealistic. Consistently we have been trying to pare this thing down and get it more oriented toward economic development through the business community.

[Western Union Telegram] Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, Chairman, Foreign Affairs Committee, House of Representatives, Washington, D.C.: 

DENVER, COLO., May 2, 1966.

The League of Women Voters of the United States continues it vigorous support of economic aid to the developing countries. We believe the request for a 

5-year authorization which is consistent with the long-term prices of economic

development, would enable your committee to concentrate more deeply on programs and policies.

As your committee well knows, league support has focused on development assistance both capital and technical. Separate consideration by Congress of economic assistance would in our view clarify for the public the rationale for development aid. We welcome the President's new initiatives in agriculture, education, and health, and greater emphasis by AID in these fields. We believe these initiatives can revitalize our assistance programs. But renewed emphasis on technical assistance should not be made at the expense of needed capital assistance. We're increasingly concerned with "barebones" requests for economic aid. There is mounting evidence that greater amounts of assistance could be absorbed in many of the developing countries. The need for economic growth in the developing world is so great and the moral obligation of the "haves" to help the "havenots" is so pressing that we believe that the time has come for an enlargement of U.S. efforts, along with those of other prosperous countries. 

We should now set an example for the world toward stepping up development assistance.

In view of the minimum nature of the request, we urge your committee to authorize the full amounts requested for development loans, technical cooperation, the Alliance for Progress, and contributions to international organizations. 

We regret that this wire must substitute for our testifying before your committee. Our entire board is in Denver for our national convention. 

Mrs. ROBERT J. STUART, President, League of Women Voters of the United States.

The committee meets this morning in open session for a continuation of the hearings on the foreign aid bills, H.R. 12449 and H.R. 12450. 

Our first witness this morning is Mrs. A. G. Patterson, national chairman of the Committee on Foreign Relief of the National Council of Catholic Women. 

STATEMENT OF MRS. A. G. PATTERSON, NATIONAL CHAIRMAN OF THE COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN RELIEF OF THE NATIONAL COUN- CIL OF CATHOLIC WOMEN Mrs. PATTERSON.  

I am Mrs. A. G. Patterson, of Austin, Minn., national chairman of the Committee on Foreign Relief of the National Council of Catholic Women.

It is a privilege for me to come before this committee to speak in support of H.R. 12449, the proposed legislation amending the Foreign 

Assistance Act of 1961, because of my organization's interest and participation in the international programs. 

At our 32d national convention, held here in the Nation's Capital in 

November 1964, we adopted the following resolution:

We see in the foreign relief program of the National Council of Catholic Women an opportunity to implement this hope of the late Pope John XXIII. 

Therefore, we will continue and extend our efforts to collect funds and clothing for the relief of the sufferings of the poor in new and old nations of the world, the needs of refugees from civil strife and communism, and the vast throngs of responsible men and women who look to us to help them to help themselves. 

This is a quotation of Pope John XXIII, allocution, January 16, 1961: 

We would like to hope-and in our prayers we ask this favor from God-that once the legitimate aspirations of people for liberty and independence have been satisfied, the richer will aid the poorer, the stronger support the weaker, the more advanced hold out a helping hand to the less developed, and in the end that all will feel themselves brothers, for all are sons of the same loving Father who is in Heaven.

The National Council of Catholic Women is a federation of 14,000 organizations of Catholic women throughout the United States and 693

American military installations abroad, with a total membership of about 10 million women. Our programs are carried on by a small staff in Washington and thousands of volunteers across this country. 

The foreign relief program was formulated in the years immediately following World War II to assist the victims of war in Europe. Funds and clothing collected by our women were allocated and distributed by War Relief Services, NCWC, now Catholic Relief Services, NCWC, the agency of American Catholics formed to bring relief to all in need, regardless of race, color, or creed.

In his message of February 1, 1966, to the Congress of the United States, President Johnson refers to our economic assistance programs in this manner:

They are the proof of our devotion to the works of peace. 

Pope Paul VI, in his historic address to the United Nations on 

October 4, 1965, pointed out thatpeace *** is built with the spirit, with ideas, with works of peace. 

There is no word in the English language or any language for that matter-so precious to a woman as the word "peace." 

We also have been fully aware and justly proud of the fact that our Government's economic assistance programs since 1945 have been a major factor in the preservation of peace in many areas of the world, and they must continue.

President Johnson has said, in his message already referred to: 

In this spirit of cooperation, I propose that the United States offer to join in new attacks upon the root causes of world poverty. 

The incessant cycle of hunger, ignorance, and disease is the common blight of the developing world. This vicious pattern can be broken. It must be broken if democracy is to survive. 

At the present time our efforts to aid the poor in the developing nations include medical care and training in child care and nutrition, provided for poor mothers at maternity clinics in about 80 countries, local food packages for poor families, support of orphans and children in poor families in Korea, training for young girls of refugee families in Hong Kong, scholarships for young girls in secondary schools in Africa, one of many self-help programs throughout the world, and, of course, constant collection of new and used clothing for children. 

This is the kind of cooperation between voluntary groups, our Government's vast resources, and the multilateral programs of the United Nations which is needed to overcome the problems of mankind in this technological age. But we feel that the goals for which all of us are striving can be achieved only through well developed programs, which in many instances will require a long-term commitment. Therefore, we fully support the President's request for a 5-year authorization of our economic assistance programs at a figure no less than he has requested. 

In closing, let me say that the foreign aid program of the United States is the conscience of the American people, our response to the amazing generosity of a loving Father who sees us as the custodians of His great gifts with which we may feed His poor, clothe His naked ones, heal His sick, house His homeless, educate His illiterate, so that the glorious world He has created for all His creatures may survive in peace. es

For the calendar year 1965, contributions to the Madonna plan totaled $33,578.47.

During international cooperation year, the Madonna plan and the help-afamily program were expanded to put emphasis on self-help; scholarships in secondary education in Africa are provided for girls in Africa, and training in home economics, secretarial skills and tailoring are given to teenage girls, daughters of refugees in Hong Kong.

The help-a-child program provided support for orphans and children in poor families in Korea to the extent of $105,694.33. These funds are the total of monthly contributions of $10 a month from American sponsors for these children. 

A total of $2,158.04 in cash was contributed for the purchase of new garments for infants and children under a project known as the Holy Father's collection

for children. Many of the garments are dispatched to needy children from a storeroom in Vatican City.

Operation Hong Kong provided $976 for women refugees in Hong Kong who make items which we have sold for them-dolls, bags, wool stoles. 

Cash contributions to designated individuals overseas, frequently priests and sisters working with the poor in the developing nations, totaled $406.95. 

The total cash contributions received by NCCW from January 1 to December 

31, 1965, was $162,020.31.

ANNUAL REPORT: FOREIGN RELIEF COMMITTEE, NATIONAL COUNCIL OF CATHOLIC WOMEN 

(Fiscal year 1964-65) 

1. MADONNA PLAN 

During the past year, the names of three leaders of the National Council of Catholic Women began to be known by women in farflung areas of the world. 

In Meru, Kenya, Gartner Hall was under construction as a Catholic action center. The funds for its construction came from madonna plan contributions of the Winona Council of Catholic Women, in honor of Mrs. Ludwig Gartner, past president of the Winona Council of Catholic Women, and second vice president of the National Council of Catholic Women National Board When Mrs. Gartner died, it was decided to memorialize her contribution to Catholic action by aiding women's Catholic Action in Africa.

In nearby Tanzania, the number of Mary Hannan Mahoney Memorial Clinics came to seven. These clinics were begun with a Madonna plan grant made by the National Council of Catholic Women affiliates after Mrs. Robert Hugh 

Mahoney, national president, died. It was under Mrs. Mahoney's presidency that the Madonna plan was inaugurated in 1958. 

In San Salvador, capital of El Salvador, Central America, the Elizabeth Ann Zepf Madonna shelter is carrying on its services from a new site after the building was hit in the May 1965 earthquake. The Madonna shelter honors a woman who is still living and who is still making a great contribution to Catholic action, after having served as foreign relief chairman and as president of the 

National Council of Catholic Women.

The funds for the running of the shelter are raised by the Toledo Council of 

Catholic Women.

These three overseas centers are proof of the personalized charity of the National Council of Catholic Women offiliates exercised through the Madonna plan. The Madonna plan is one of the six specific projects within the overall program of the National Council of Catholic Women's Foreign Relief Committee. These projects are conducted in cooperation with Catholic Relief 

Services-NCWC. A foreign relief secretary, Mrs. Margaret Zemo, in the National Council of Catholic Women headquarters, and a consultant, Miss Eileen Egan in the Catholic Relief Services-NCWC headquarters, work out the details of preparing and promoting the various projects. Cooperating with them are a foreign relief chairman, Mrs. A. G. Patterson of the diocese of Winona, and 

Mrs. Anthony Mazzarelli of the diocese of Grand Rapids. Both are volunteers. 

Among the directly sponsored projects of the Madonna plan during the past year were: The St. Columban Clinic at the 38th parallel in Korea was granted $200 monthly for the fifth consecutive year by the women of the St. Paul Archdiocesan Council of Catholic Women through their vanishing luncheon project (the St. Paul Archdiocesan Council of Catholic Women also helped for the fifth consecutive year our Fatima Clinic in Trivandrum, South India); the supply of

Dryco milk formula for the St. Martha's Clinic in Vatican City (serving mothers in the slums of Rome) was shipped for the seventh consecutive year. 

Other grants made from the general madonna plan collection were made to the following countries through the office of Catholic Relief Services-NCWC: 

Brazil.-Eight grants for a variety of programs including the purchase of sewing machines for homecraft and other courses, the provision of medicaments for mother and child clinics, the provision of salaries for doctors and nurses for slum areas and the supplying of necessary kits for two radio schools helping illiterates.

Colombia. A grant was made to Radio Sutatenza, otherwise known as Popular 

Cultural Action, to cover the costs of literacy kits, including transistor radios, blackboards, and other supplies, so that 40 more small villages in the Andes Mountains may be included in the radio school system. 

Chile. A grant went to the Nazareth Medical Center for the purchase of a refrigerator for medical supplies, and an electric stove. 

Guatemala. Four grants went to mother and child clinics in four areas: La 

Caridad, Peten; San Juan Ostuncalco; San Amtonia; and Jocotan.

Haiti. Two grants to the Salesian Fathers and one grant to the Salesian 

Sisters to provide extra nutrition, and training for mothers and children. 

India. Seven grants to mother and child medical and training programs conducted in Bombay, Calcutta, Kaipuzha, Kerala, Madras, Kashmir, and Lucknow.

Korea.-Two grants for rehabilitation and vocational courses for Korean girls and women in rehabilitation centers in Taegu and Nazareth Vocational Training 

Schools in Seoul.

Mexico. A grant for medicines and food supplement for mothers and children in Mexico City.

Pakistan.-Four grants for medical aid and training programs under the direction of various religious orders in Muzzafagarh, Bahawalpur, and Sargodha (West Pakistan), and to the St. Mary's Maternity Hospital, Mymensingh (East Pakistan).

Philippines.-A grant to the Heart of Mary Villa in Rizal, Manila, to help renovate quarters for poor mothers. 

St. Vincent, B.W.I.-A grant to St. Benedict's Day Nursery conducted by 

Rev. Roland Roberts.

Taiwan. A grant went to Our Lady of Maryknoll Clinic to help with the antihookworm program among needy Taiwanese. 

Ceylon. On special recommendation of Msgr. Joseph J. Harnett, Far East director of Catholic Relief Services-NCWC, five Madonna plan grants were made to five projects despite the fact that Catholic Relief Services-NCWC has no program in those areas. The grants went to the Blessed Martin's Home in 

Peredaniya; St. Bernard's Home, Fatima Canteen, St. Vincent's Home and 

Prithipura Homes (all in Colombo), to aid in the various welfare and training programs.

Contributions to Madonna plan during the past year, $35,218. 

2. HELP A FAMILY 

Help-a-family grants met a great variety of need among families around the world. During the past year, efforts were made to stress the freedom-fromhunger campaign sponsored by the United Nations. One freedom-from-hunger grant was made to Thailand in order to help the Thabom Rice Bank Cooperative. conducted by Rev. Harry Thiel, Redemptorist missionary, concerned with the social betterment of his area. A rice bank was constructed which will allow the villagers to store rice against the lean preharvest season when rice prices are high and poor families often go into debt. Another grant to Thailand went to a family aid and rehabilitation program under Rev. Anthony Terkowitsch of the 

Holy Redemption Church.

A grant went to the Young Christian Workers training program in Seoul, Korea. Rev. Francis Park, moderator of the Young Christian Workers has instituted a broad marriage training and family counseling program so that young Koreans (very often recent converts) can learn the deeper meaning of 

Christian marriage. Help-a-family grants were used by local agencies to meet particular problems of the area. The rehabilitation of families through the Suicide Prevention 

Center of Seoul, Korea, was helped with a continued grant. 

Other grants went to Brazil. Haiti, India, Pakistan, Peru, and Tanzania. 

Contributions to help-a-family during the past year, $22,047.

3. HELP A CHILD 

The help-a-child program by which American families sponsor individual Korean children was featured in the Christmas column of Katherine Burton in 

Sign magazine. As a result of Mrs. Burton's column, entitled "A Christmas

Challenge for the Coming Year” several hundred additional children were sponsored at the rate of $10 monthly. 

The new emphasis of the help-a-child program is in help to children in the poorest of poor families. The monthly contribution allows the family to pay its rent and also to send one or two of the children to primary school. The cost of the primary school is often $2 monthly. Many hundreds of the most deprived children of Korea are able to learn the tools of the intellect through sponsorships in the help-a-child program. A paragraph from Katherine Burton's column gives a good picture of the program: "For many people, $10 a month for a year is a considerable sum, but if it is divided among a group, it will cost each one no more than the Madonna dollar for which my readers collected so generously for Africa and Brazil. The givers of this help-a-child work will receive a report every 3 months from the one distributing the funds and also a picture of the child and letters from him and from them. A religious who operates an orphanage there wrote, "The two boys read your letters again and again and proudly show them everywhere.' A Korean sister writes: 'All the time the mother exerts herself for her children to make a living without hunger and sends deep thanks to you.' And Father

Pak wrote to the members of St. Anne's Society in the States that their adopted girl, Bernadette, had a sad and pessimistic nature (she is 12) but that she 'became happy with frequent smiles since she had adoptive parents in America.'' 

Contributions to help-a-child during the past year, $83,137. 

4. OPERATION HONG KONG 

Rehabilitation efforts on behalf of Hong Kong refugees included a grant to the Casa Ricci on Macau for the rehabilitation of mothers and children who had recently escaped from the China mainland. The stoles made by the Pius Handicraft Center were sold at the National Council of Catholic Women National Convention in Washington and at various conventions throughout the country. 

In response to an urgent plea, Madonna plan grant was made for the Hong Kong Catholic Marriage Counseling Service. This new welfare service has been made very necessary by the fact that there are large numbers of new Catholics in Hong Kong and also by the fact that so many other refugees are living in abnormal circumstances. 

5. CHILDREN IN NEED 

For 20 years the National Council of Catholic Women affiliates throughout the country have sent wearable garments to the Catholic Relief Services-NCWC warehouse in Brooklyn throughout the year, as well as during the Thanksgiving clothing campaign. Women's groups all over the country have been constant in their fidelity to the children-in-need collection. 

During the past year, 46,321 pounds of good clothing was sent to the warehouse. 

The value of the overall donation was $69,481.50. 

6. PAPAL COLLECTION FOR CHILDREN 

During the past year, the donation of layettes and new garments in the papal collection for children reached a total of 59,499 pounds. First communion outfits for boys and girls came to 1,978 pounds. Half of these donations were shipped directly to the Holy Father's storerooms in Vatican City. They were then distributed to needy institutions in Italy and in Europe on the basis of requests to the Vatican. The remaining half of the donations was sent around the world in the name of His Holiness. The garments were distributed through welfare centers, hospitals, dispensaries, and especially through institutions aided by the 

National Council of Catholic Women Madonna plan. 

Shipments of new garments were made to the following countries: Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, Chile, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Peru, Paraguay, and Venezuela.

In earlier years all first communion outfits were sent to Latin America to be used in connection with the welfare work of parishes in slum areas. During the past year, 500 first communion outfits were sent to Cebu City, Philippines,

on the basis of a special request from the bishop of Cebu City. The outfits were needed in connection with a great religious celebration commemorating the implanting of catholicism by Spanish missionaries in the Philippine Islands. 

Value of new garments and first communion outfits, $184,431. 

7. ARCHDIOCESAN COUNCIL OF FOREIGN RELIEF OF PHILADELPHIA 

The Committee for Foreign Relief, under the chairmanship of Mrs. Mary T. 

Lowery is an affiliate of the National Council of Catholic Women. 

For many years, the committee has specialized in helping Cloistered Orders of Sisters around the world. The committee has also sponsored a needy diocese in Taiwan. 

All donated items are packed for export by the committee in a center maintained by the committee in Philadelphia. During the past year, 524 cases of relief items weighing 17,350 pounds were shipped through the facilities of Catholic Relief Services-NCWC to destinations in Europe, Asia, and Latin America. In response to specific requests, 1,000 pounds of host flour and 220 Carmelite habits were donated. The sum of $9,497.17 was donated for the purchase of crates and other shipping supplies. 

Estimated value of overall donations, $234,700. 

8. CATHOLIC DAUGHTERS OF AMERICA 

The Catholic Daughters of America, one of the largest national affiliates of the National Council of Catholic Women, sponsors several relief projects in cooperation with Catholic Relief Services-NCWC. The overseas relief effort of the 

Catholic Daughters of America is called Relief for Peace and is directed by Mrs. Manila Caprine, supreme secretary of the organization, and chairman on 

Relief for Peace. Mrs. Caprine works closely with Miss Margaret Buckley, supreme regent of the organization.

During the past year, the special program of the Catholic Daughters of America on behalf of children born to leper parents in South Korea was organized to meet changing needs. The institution maintained for untainted children of leper parents by Archbishop Harold Henry of Kwangju has been taken over by the Korean Government authorities. Some of the children have been placed in other Catholic orphanages or in private families. The various courts of the 

Catholic Daughters of America had been sponsoring individual children in the institution. The board of directors of the Catholic Daughters of America decided to continue their aid to needy children under the care of Archbishop Harold Henry, whether these children were in orphanages or in private families. Other projects of the Catholic Daughters of America include help to individual families in Korea and grants-in-aid to needy priests in Vietnam. Special grants were made at the biennial convention of the Catholic Daughters of America in Florida in July 1964. These grants were made under the Catholic Daughters of 

America mother and child fund to such projects as the Catholic Maternity Institute in Santa Fe; Mrs. Dang Sy, whose husband, a Catholic army man, was sentenced to life imprisonment in Vietnam, and to the Multipurpose Social Center in Akhimim, Upper Egypt.

In addition to their cash grants to overseas aid projects, the Catholic Daughters of America makes generous donations of new and used garments and first communion outfits. 

Total cash donations to all programs, $30,500. 

The Junior Catholic Daughters of America contributed 1,592 pounds of sweaters for orphans overseas. The juniors also collected funds to buy Christmas gifts for orphans overseas. Both of these combined donations were sent to Archbishop Harold Henry for the needy children of the Kwangju Archdiocese. 

The value of the junior contribution, $5,177.

SUMMARY 

This report covers the fiscal year of the National Council of Catholic Women from July 1, 1964, to June 30, 1965. The overall 12-month total, including cash gifts and gifts-in-kind, amounted to $664,693.

STATEMENT OF J. ORRIN SHIPE, MANAGING DIRECTOR, CUNA INTERNATIONAL, INC. 

Mr. SHIPE.  

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, CUNA International, an association representing more than 18,000 credit unions throughout the world, is grateful for this opportunity to report to you on our credit union organizational efforts in underdeveloped lands. 

For well over a decade now, CUNA has been engaged in the challenging missionary work of bringing the thrift and lending services of credit unions to people in foreign nations. Since 1962, we have been materially assisted in this enormous undertaking by the Agency for International Development, which has contracted with us to augment our overseas efforts.

For that reason, we believe it is only proper that we should furnish the American public through the vehicle of this committee with a reckoning of how we have made use of the Government's assistance. 

Approximately $1.6 million has been expended under the CUNA- 

AID program during the past 4 years, averaging about $400,000 annually. At the same time, CUÑA has provided, from its own dues income, $400,000 to extend credit unions overseas. In fact, our

organization is presently expending some 12 percent of its dues income for credit union organization work among the poor of this country or in underdeveloped lands.

It was in the decade following the end of World War II that deprived people from all over the world and particularly Latin America began turning to CUNA for know-how and advice in estabishing credit unions. Clearly they saw in the credit union a simple lemocratic tool with which they could rid themselves of the bondage of usury and provide themselves with the capital to build a better life. 

When formally established in 1954, CUNA's world extension program concentrated its early efforts in Central and South America. It s in this area today where, with the financial support of AID, we are experiencing truly impressive credit union gains. 

You may have read in Time magazine only last week of the work undertaken in Peru by the Maryknoll missionary, Father Dan Mc- Clellan. His success in forming credit unions and savings and loan associations among the Indians in the Peruvian Andes, according o Time, is having a startling impact on the economic and social life of that people.

Since the CUNA-AID program was launched in 1962, the number of credit unions in Central and South America has spiraled from 430 o 2,000. Today, nearly half a million Latin Americans have accumuated $31 million in their credit unions and are currently lending to one another some $29 million.

But more important than the dollar statistics is the total impact of the credit union on the lives of the people. It has engendered new hope and confidence and has demonstrated that it is now indeed possible for them to make decisions and to do things for themselves that vill materially alter their environment and enhance their standard of living.

In whole villages there is broken centuries-old attitudes bred of despair and grinding poverty. They are supplanted by the cooperaive ideals of hard work, democratic participation and integrity in personal dealings.

The impressive credit union development in Latin America was made possible in such a relatively brief period because of the participation of AID in CUNA's world extension efforts. Without AID's packing, we estimate that it would have taken CUNA at least a decade o accomplish what was done in 4 years.

Following this statement, you will find an appendix which contains country-by-country breakdown of the CUNA-AID program. 

Three East African nations-Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda-are ncluded in the list. The programs there have only recently been aunched, but it is evident that our Latin American experience will be repeated. Our member credit union leagues in Michigan and Saskatchewan in the early 1960's took it upon themselves to finance the ending of a credit union technician to Tanzania. This mission showed clearly that the credit union idea is fully adaptable to East Africa. 

Since then, a CUNA-AID contract has been executed which will broaden and accelerate our African extension work. I might add there is included in the appendix a second chart conaining data on credit unions throughout the world.

​A key aspect of CUNA's credit union overseas program which must be emphasized is its self-liquidating or terminal nature. It is always our goal to impart credit union skills to indigenous people, to set up native institutions necessary to perpetuate the program, and then to depart. 

Thus, along with organizing credit unions, we strive to form a credit union league in each country. The league, like the credit union itself, is a voluntary, nonprofit democratic organization. Its job is to organize more credit unions, train leaders, represent the movement with the government, and promote the credit union idea generally. Where a strong and active league is present, it is possible as in Peru, for CUNA to withdraw its assistance, leaving a viable program in the hands of native credit unionists. 

In closing, may I suggest that this committee might find informative a staff report compiled by the Subcommittee on International Finance of the House Banking and Currency Committee. This report thor oughly analyzes the joint AID programs of 14 cooperative organizations like CUNA International. It reveals that the total cost to AID for these programs through 1965 was less than $5 million. 

I think you will agree that compared with other governmental expenditures, this is small, indeed. I hope you will also agree that in terms of total impact in underdeveloped lands this expenditure has been a prudent and rewarding investment by our Government. 

This concludes my statement. I appreciate very much the committee's courtesy in granting me this opportunity. Should you have any questions, I will be glad to endeavor to answer them.
