Mr. LYNN. After a few remarks I am going to call on Mr. Burmeister to highlight some of our suggestions as to the budget for the foreign assistance program for fiscal year 1967. 

We have been coming before this committee for many years and making recommendations with regard to the foreign aid program, beginning back some 10 or 12 years ago when we first suggested Public Law 480 type programs, now known as Food for Peace. 

We are concerned, as I am sure the members of this committee are, with the continued vast Government expenditure both at home and abroad, and we will try to demonstrate a little later where we think some reductions can be made in this authorization and still fulfill the needs of those countries seeking our aid. We were very delighted, Mr. 

Chairman, with certain points made in the President's message having

to do with this program in that many of the things in this message have been advocated by Farm Bureau to this committee over a long period of time.

On page 2 of the statement we have quoted two paragraphs from the President's message dealing with this matter. We were delighted to see the word "work" inserted in the administration's presentation to the Congress with regard to foreign aid. 

We have reflected many times to this committee that we don't believe there is enough emphasis given to the matter of work by the aid recipients, if you please, or do more to try to help themselves. We are pleased with this part of the President's message, and feel that it will mean a great deal as we move forward. 

An idea we have presented for 3 consecutive years to the committee is outlined very briefly on page 3 of our statement in the middle of the page, where we say that we believe "the money should be fitted to the plan based on sound, well thought-out development programs, rather than the plans being fitted to the money." Let me just elaborate on that briefly because I think this is the most constructive suggestion we have to offer.

Too often after the Appropriations Committee has provided the money for foreign aid, and we have the feeling, and after some very close checking well, the administrators of this program are too inclined to go out and get a lot of plans to fit whatever money that happens to be appropriated.

What we are suggesting here, Congressman Fountain, is this: Let's take India, for example, and let me add that we were a little disappointed that the United States rushed out to assist India, before getting some commitments. I don't mean to say that we opposed the assistance to India; but we thought this was a good opportunity to get some things done in India that we could get done by the use of our food and aid.

Briefly, here is what we mean by fitting the money to the plan. Take 

India, for example. Let's decide what is in the best interests of the 

United States and our cooperation with India. Is it to supply them food, or is it to help develop their country so they can produce more food for themselves? Make this a 10-year plan or a 5-year plan, if this is what is required. Then each year the administrative agencies of Government would come before this committee and demonstrate to you what progress they are making on the plan that you and, let us say, the AID administrators develop for India. 

Then this committee would recommend that the Appropriations Committee, based on your expert knowledge, fit the money in 1967 to the progress that they have made in carrying out the plan. 

This is contrasted to the way things have been done. In many cases we continue to pour out aid to people who kick us in the pants daily. 

We don't think this is in the best interest of the United States. 

We have at least four good examples of countries that we have helped guide in their economies, and I guess they are the best friends we have. Japan, Germany, Formosa, and Spain, and, if you please, we have not hesitated to help direct the aid programs in these countries, and we believe it has paid off both for us and for them. 

In contrast with that take Indonesia, for example. We continue to aid Indonesia. We continue to aid Egypt, and many of these coun-

1 tries for which we would like to see a little harder rule laid down. We should at least know which side they are on. 

On page 3 of this statement the President, again in his message, said: 

It must be clear that the principle of our assistance is cooperation. Those who do not fulfill their commitments to help themselves cannot expect help from us. 

This is stated very well. We are in thorough accord with this statement. 

Mr. Chairman, with your permission, I would like to ask Mr. Burmeister to review briefly our specific recommendations as to the amounts of money, and then I will come back briefly on food for freedom.

Mr. FOUNTAIN. We are delighted to have you with us, Mr. Burmeister. You may proceed.

STATEMENT OF GUSTAVE BURMEISTER, ASSISTANT LEGISLATIVE DIRECTOR, AMERICAN FARM BUREAU FEDERATION 

Mr. BURMEISTER. Thank you, sir.

With regard to military assistance, certainly we are not experts in this field. We have watched the military assistance program over the years. Certainly we were for it when the idea was to help countries build up a military establishment, particularly on the periphery of the Communist-threatened nations.

I think we have done a magnificent job in building up the military program in Europe. We are a bit put out, though, when we see some of the results. For instance, I looked at the 1965 program, and I find that we are still assisting in Europe to the tune of nearly $50 million, in Greece, in Turkey, and in India and Pakistan, and even some in Japan.

As far as Europe is concerned, and Japan, we think those countries certainly can carry their own load. Their economies are developed now to where they certainly can carry most of their military programs. 

We don't feel that the United States should be putting any more dollars into that area.

For Greece, Turkey, India, and Pakistan, well, we have seen Greece and Turkey fighting each other over Cyprus, and Pakistan and India fighting each other. If that is the way they are going to use our military assistance, then I think we should start withdrawing. 

In this year's request the administration says that the military assistance for Vietnam, Thailand, and Laos, that particular area is carried by the Defense Department and is not in this program. That was $500 million in 1965.

The total program in 1965 was $1.3 billion. That would get us down to $800 million. Then if you took out Europe, Greece, Turkey, India and Pakistan, Japan, we would have another $300 million. This would get us down to $500 million.

We are recommending $700 million for military assistance for 1967. 

We think this would be ample to carry on whatever is necessary in the areas that need our assistance and help in developing a military program.

For development loans, here again India, Pakistan, and Turkey have been receiving a large share, plus Brazil, Mexico, Nicaragua, Thai-

land, Nigeria, Tunisia, those are the countries that have been receiving most of the assistance through development loans. I want to point out, on page 5 of our statement, we have a number of different loan programs through the AID process. And through the end of 1965 there was around $12 billion invested in these kinds of loans. It will be $13.5 billion by the end of 1966, and maybe $14.5 billion by the end of 

1967, fiscal years.

In addition, we have all these international loaning agencies which is outlined on page 5 of which the United States is a major contributor in the capital, with a total of some $25 billion for loans to underdeveloped countries.

In addition, the Public Law 480 generated currencies from sales under title I and title IV are available to loan back to the countries for economic development.

We note also that, although we have not provided the total amounts requested in recent years for this loan program, there is still a big unobligated balance to be available as of July 1, 1966, of $365 million. 

We are suggesting that the request of $665 million, be cut back to $465 million, which, with the big carryover of unobligated funds, would provide a sufficient amount for development loans in fiscal 1967. 

In the same sort of reasoning with respect to the Alliance for Progress, we suggest a cut from the requested amount. 

Moving on to economic grants for outside Latin America the amount requested is $1,260 million. We again recommend that the technical cooperation and development, the supporting assistance, contingency fund, and the assistance for American schools and hospitals be combined into one program, that the Peace Corps also be combined with this group, that a coordinated program be developed. We think we would get more for our money and we could save money in this operation. The details are given here in the statement. 

Likewise we suggest cuts in our contributions to international organizations. Many of the programs carried on here are duplications of the programs that we are carrying on under our bilateral operations. So we think this can be reduced some. Then, if this level of a program should be instituted, the money that is needed for administrative expenses could be cut back. 

Sir, on the last page there is a table which summarizes our proposals and shows that it will not cut back the proposed expenditures in any of these areas in fiscal 1967. We have to start reducing now if we are to get down to the level we suggest. 

One other thing-and I am sure Mr. Lynn is going to bring this out in more detail—we think our food program could be made a cardinal part of our aid program, that the currencies generated under title I and under title IV or whatever titles are provided in the new program could expand the aid program tremendously. 

Thank you, sir.

(The prepared statement of Mrs. Gray is as follows:) STATEMENT OF MRS. VIRGINIA M. GRAY, EXECUTIVE SECRETARY, CITIZENS COMMITTEE FOR UNICEF Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee, I am Mrs. Virginia M. Gray, Executive Secretary of the Citizens Committee for UNICEF. The Citizens Com mittee for UNICEF is an informal clearing house of legislative information serving a number of national organizations which support continued participation by the United States in the work of UNICEF, the United Nations Children's Fund. These organizations have authorized me to present the following joint statement in support of a contribution of $12 million by the United States for Fiscal 1967 (the amount proposed by the Executive Branch) and, in addition, to request a special contribution of $1 million in this next year for the reasons and in the manner indicated later in this statement. The names of the organizations authorizing this presentation are listed at the end of the text. 

UNICEF's 20th Anniversary 

On December 11 of this year, UNICEF will celebrate its 20th anniversary.

This date will mark a generation of service to children. The first babies and small children, who may owe their very lives to UNICEF's timely aid, have now reached maturity and are taking their places in their communities. These first beneficiaries of UNICEF aid received emergency assistance: food, clothing, medicine. Yet this simple humanitarian undertaking, born quietly in the aftermath of World War II, marked a new dimension in the development of civilization; it was a recognition of mankind's united responsibility for all children wherever they may happen to be born.

From a relatively small beginning in 1946-in which several members of this Committee, past and present, played a major role the program to aid the world's children has brought life-saving aid to millions of children and mothers. 

In 1965 UNICEF was assisting 543 projects in 118 countries. In its nearly 20 years of service UNICEF has treated 11 million cases of trachoma, over 1 million cases of leprosy, 37 million cases of yaws, and has given 162 million TB vaccinations. In addition to these specific treatments to individual cases, UNICEF has helped to establish and equip over 30,000 maternal and child health centers and subcenters, and has provided scholarship and training allowances to thousands of nurses, auxiliary health and social workers where the extent of the benefits to children are incalculable.

The Nobel Peace Prize Award 

In dramatic tribute to the accomplishments of the Children's Fund, the Nobel Committee of the Norwegian Parliament announced on October 25 that its 1965 award of the Nobel Peace Prize would go to UNICEF in recognition of its contribution to world peace. The selection of UNICEF to receive this distinguished award marks the 8th time in the long history of the Nobel awards that the honor has gone to an organization; it is the second time that the prize has gone to an agency of the United Nations. The news of the award met worldwide acclaim. It was received by officials of UNICEF itself as an indication that the policies that have guided its actions over the years are basically correct. More importantly, however, it was accepted by UNICEF officials as a challenge to strengthen their activities for the greater fulfillment of children's needs.

U.S. Government Contribution to UNICEF 

The unanimous acclaim with which the announcement of the award was greeted did not increase the United States contribution to UNICEF, however. 

This fiscal year will mark the 8th consecutive year that the Executive Branch is recommending a contribution of $12 million to UNICEF by the United States. 

The organizations listed below endorse this recommendation with a full understanding and sympathy for the State Department's position in this matter. The 

Department's expert knowledge of the pledges already made or anticipated from governments other than the United States has led them to accept the strong probability that UNICEF will find it difficult to raise the necessary sums to match $12 million from the United States at 40% during the present year. With a few spectacular exceptions, such as Sweden which has increased its contribution by 50%, there are few other countries in a strong enough position economically to follow such an outstanding lead. The general upward trend in support continues, however.

Our organizations request this Committee and the Congress to make, in this year of the Nobel Peace Prize Award, a special contribution of an additional $1 million as tangible recognition for the outstanding work that UNICEF is doing for world peace. This $1 million contribution would be in every sense a gift-with no strings attached. It would be exempt from the computations of the 40 (United States) to 60 (other countries) matching ratio. We respectfully urge your support of this proposal. 

Why an Increase is Justified

A considerable increase in the U.S. Government contribution to UNICEF above the $12 million level would seem well justified. The following reasons suggest an increase far beyond our request for a special $1 million, but at this time we can only relate the reasons to this request for a modest increase: 

1. Without doubt, the most compelling reason for giving aid is the enormous need of children. Many basic threats to child development have scarcely been recognized, let alone attacked. In addition to the present ongoing programs that we have discussed in past years, there is an area of child needs that is only beginning to be seen. This concerns the problems of the very young child, the child aged 1-6. It is estimated that there are 400 million children in the world, aged 1-6. Of these, 200 million live in the developing countries which are being assisted by UNICEF. These children, weaned from their mother's milk but too young to go to school, frequently suffer from grave malnutrition in these most formative years of their whole life. Recent research has developed evidence that many abilities, motor skills, even intelligence, may be affected by nutritional deficiencies during these early years, defects that no amount of future treatment can overcome. Here, then, is one area where much remains to be done. 

2. The United States, although the largest contributor to UNICEF in dollar totals is not at all the leading contributor on a per capita basis. We rank only fifth, after: Cents per capita

Sweden__.

Looked at in another way, to cite again the example of Sweden, its contribution to UNICEF represents 2.2% of its foreign aid budget of $65 million. The corresponding percentage for the United States is almost too small to report: 10 of 1%. 

3. There is an inevitable competition for limited resources among various programs. During these years when the United States contribution to UNICEF has remained at the same figure, our contributions to other international organizations have increased. This is not to suggest that we are opposed to the accomplishments under the other programs, nor to deny that they also-indirectly perhaps benefit children in the long run. It is merely to point out the stark fact that the world's most precious resource, its children, could use a larger share of the present investments. 

4. In his AID message, President Johnson has stressed his conviction of the importance of channeling more foreign aid through multilateral sources and his recommendation that the foreign aid programs help those nations that help themselves. UNICEF is an organization to which these objectives could appropriately be applied. Increased aid from the United States is directed to the international lending agencies such as IDA and the World Bank, but not to the Children's Fund. UNICEF aid, from its beginning, has required a country to match in goods and services the international aid it receives. 

One could say that UNICEF has been a pioneer in its emphasis on self-help, which the President so rightly approves.

In conclusion, we should like to refer again to the point made in our testimony last year: the fact that there is a vast amount of aid to children that cannot even be planned until the resources to carry out the programs appear to be within reach. The figure mentioned last year was $9 million. The need still exists for these additional resources. A top UNICEF official has said that UNICEF could usefully allocate at least $50 million per year instead of the approximately $35 million now going into its current work. One of the ironies of this situation is that while UNICEF helps millions of mothers and children each year, it does so by spending less in a whole year than the governments of the world spend on armaments in two hours of a single day. In a speech on the occasion of the awarding of the Nobel Peace Prize, the former Chairman of the UNICEF Board suggested "that each abortive disarmament conference set itself a penalty—a contribution to UNICEF of the equivalent cost of one submarine or a dozen fighter planes. Surely today's children are the central factor in the strategy for peace and survival.”

May I make a personal observation at this point in my testimony, Mr. Chairman? 

Since appearing before this committee before, I have had the privilege of visiting some of the UNICEF work—I might add at my own expense, and I have visited, I have seen the shanty towns on the edge of Istanbul, some huts leaning up against the ancient Great Wall of Istanbul, which is so famous in history, shanty towns where the huts are built of flattened out pieces of tin, where one wonders if the slightest tremor would knock the whole thing down.

Yet these are places where families with their children are coming into the city, attracted by the supposed lure of job opportunities, where there is hope for the parents to make a better life for their children. 

Yet these pitiful conditions are not a place where it is safe for the children to be. Water is not available. They are crowded beyond our imagination; even in the poorer sections of this country I have never seen anything like this.

Also I have seen the children and their mothers in the clinics in Tunisia where they are being taken for care. I have seen the hope and the fear in the eyes of the mothers and the children as the child is examined by a pediatrician that is provided by the cooperation of World Health, Government, UNICEF and the supporting organizations. 

This is something that can't be put into statistics, but one sees the hope of these people for their children as they bring their children to the clinic, often waiting for hours to have their turn to have their child examined by the doctor.

I have talked with the doctors, the pediatricians in these clinics who have made impassioned pleas, unfortunately to me, because I was a

private citizen and I had nothing I could give them in return, except my sympathy, but there were pleas for increased laboratory equipment, equipment with which they could expedite their tests of children, which were not available then, but which they hoped could be added.

There is so much that needs to be done. 

A second reason for our feeling that the United States could justifiably increase its contribution is the fact that the United States is not, contrary to much popular thought, the largest contributor to UNICEF in per capita figures, even though we are in the gross amount, as such. 

The United States ranks only fifth, per capita. We rank after 

Sweden, after Norway, New Zealand, and Switzerland.

If we look at it in another way, the United States percentage of the contribution to UNICEF as expressed as a part of the economic budget which this committee is considering for foreign aid is only four-tenths of 1 percent. Certainly that is a very small amount to give to children. 

Of course, there is an inevitable competition for limited resources among various programs.

During these years when the United States contribution to UNICEF has remained at the same figure, our contributions to other international organizations have increased. This is not to suggest that we are opposed to the accomplishments under the other programs, nor to deny that they also indirectly, perhaps benefit children in the long run. It is merely to point out the stark fact that the world's most precious resource, its children, could use a larger share of the present investments.

In conclusion, we should like to refer again to the point made in our testimony last year-the fact that there is a vast amount of aid to children that cannot even be planned until the resources to carry out the programs appear to be within reach. The figure mentioned last year was $9 million. The need still exists for these additional resources.

A top UNICEF official has said that UNICEF could usefully allocate at least $50 million per year instead of the approximately $35 million now going into its current work. One of the ironies of this situation is that while UNICEF helps millions of mothers and children each year, it does so by spending less in a whole year than the governments of the world spend on armaments in 2 hours of a single day. But your suggestion is not that we make a gift with strings attached? 

There would be no necessity for others to contribute in addition to what we contribute? As I understand it, you do not want to have a 

40-to-60 ratio, which would mean that we would only provide this additional aid if other countries came up with 60 percent more? 

Mrs. GRAY. That is correct, Mr. Frelinghuysen, for several reasons.

It is primarily a matter of accounting. Of course, other countries are increasing their aid, their contributions to the central account.

The 40 to 60 matching ratio applies to the central account of UNICEF. 

Therefore, contributions by national committees or other organizations within the country, voluntary private contributions, are not included at all. The best estimates which UNICEF has been able to prepare do not indicate that UNICEF can do better than match 12 million, possibly a little bit more, but not very much more, because of various problems.

Some countries are eager to increase their contributions but they have exchange difficulties which reduce the dollar value of the contribution. It just looked as though this would be one way in this particular year to make possible an increase in a gift to UNICEF that we hope would be an inspiration, an example of our leadership.

I believe that gifts should be gifts, and not have strings attached in any case. But we are not fighting that 60 to 40 matching ratio any more. We have accepted it and have agreed with the State 

Department's position that it has been a stimulant to other countries to increase their matching.

The problem is, I think, more in the area where there are so many demands on the country for funds for matching. Our bilateral aid program requires matching. Our other multilateral programs require matching. The country, no matter how eager it is to help itself, has very severe limitations on this. 

Loans of course that are repayable, loans that are investments for future building, that will yield revenue, we can see the way those can be repaid. But it is very difficult to compute in terms of a child exactly what an investment in a child is going to yield.

I know in our school aid programs we have had many citations of figures that people with a high school diploma will earn so many thousands of dollars more in their lifetime than one who drops out. 

You can't be precise about this investment in children. I think we all know that the investment in children is one of the most important investments that can be made, not only in humanitarian terms, but in financial returns as well, even if we can't measure it precisely. 

Another point that I think the committee might be interested in knowing is that the Norwegian people who are so enthusiastic about the announcement of the Nobel Prize award immediately started raising money to match what the Nobel Prize amount is estimated to be. It is approximately $54,500. The people of Norway have now matched that as another voluntary gift to UNICEF as a way of showing their approval and their support and interest. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. As a practical matter, of course, there is a very real problem with respect to the differences of view between the so-called have-not nations and the have nations in international agencies. There is an understandable reluctance on the part of some of the have countries to approve budgets that constantly increase, which impose a major burden on them and not on the have-not countries. 

The have-not countries, without an equivalent burden, feel the necessity to expand more rapidly than do the have countries. I would suppose that the only way really to develop a common responsibility is through the matching approach. I would guess that if vou utilize the voluntary route too much you would have a destruction of the feeling that everybody must at least participate to some extent.

I would suppose, generally speaking, if we use the multilateral approach to reach children or to help illiterates, that we ought to try to do it in such a way as to develop an awareness and responsibility on the part of the other countries. 

Mrs. GRAY. I agree with your views, Mr. Frelinghuysen. I do not consider this in any sense an attempt to establish a precedent, to break away from the general program of matching. It is just that matching more than $12 million this year looks impossible. It looked impossible last year. We did not ask for it last year, but this year our organizations in fact have been pressing me to express their view in this matter.

The following information, requested by Mr. Fulton at the Hearing on May 3, is taken from an official document of the United Nations Economic and Social 

Council (E/ICEF/542) dated 9 April 66 and entitled "General Progress Report of the Executive Director" of UNICEF.

CURRENT PROBLEMS NEEDING MORE UNICEF ASSISTANCE 

Although the full range of needs is far from known, countries are seeking more UNICEF co-operation at the present time in regard to the following problems affecting children and youth: a) Youth. In developing countries many children have to seek work before the normal age for completion of primary school. Much more extensive vocational and para-vocational training for industrial work is needed both in school and out of school, and more UNICEF and ILO help is required. 

Systems of rural primary education need to be established, in co-operation with UNESCO and FAO, with a curriculum that includes preparation for the transformation of traditional agriculture. The prevention of delinquency, and minor's courts would benefit from more assistance. b) School-age children. More assistance is needed, along with the technical advice of UNESCO, for teacher training; and for the adaptation of the curriculum to help integrate children into the economic development of their country, including such aspects as the use of one's hands, health and nutrition education, the education of girls, etc. Ways need to be found and demonstrated to help parents develop realistic expectations about the benefits of schooling; as the proportion of children going to school increases, parents have to understand that only a limited number of school leavers can find white-collar work. Countries need help in meeting the material needs of children in schools, for a water supply, school meals, school health services and reading glasses, and assistance with decent clothing for a proportion of pupils. The large numbers of children who are out of school, either never having attended, or having dropped out too early to retain literacy, will be a large problem for the next decades and need some literacy training, some vocational training working hours, and some chance for gifted children to rejoin the educational system. In general, not enough means are yet available to avoid losing the talents of gifted children. c) Infants and young children are the hardest to help. Their needs tend to be approached purely from a humanitarian view-in fact incorrectly so, because much of the basis for the child's subsequent development is laid during these years. Assistance is needed, along with the technical services of WHO, to develop the infrastructure of rural health services, especially at their growing point, MCH services. A rough estimation is that not more than 

5 percent of young children past infancy are reached by these services. Even to double this percentage would require a large effort. Wide-spread undernutrition and malnutrition require mothers to be better informed, and food supplies to be increased, especially of protein and protective foods, and manufactured weaning foods. The lack of simple pre-school services is one of the reasons for children not adapting to school, and dropping out. d) Children in shanty-towns. The needs of young children are particularly acute in shanty-towns where many working mothers lack the means of having their children cared for during the day, and where the housing, material and social conditions are the worst imaginable for the formation of a new generation of city workers. Assistance is required, along with the services of the Department of Economic and Social Affairs of the United Nations Secretariat, to mobilize public and community resources. e) The rural child. Countries are seeking means to provide better services for rural children, as one means of slowing down the excessive movement to cities in advance of employment opportunities, and of teachning the skills required for producing more food. f) Handicapped children. In countries where only a small proportion of children in the upper-income brackets have the possibility to develop "normally", the vast mass of underprivileged children get priority over the specially handicapped. Nevertheless, more UNICEF help could usefully be given to national centres for finding the most appropriate methods of work in this field and for training personnel. g) Development areas. At the other end of the scale from the shantytowns, there are "development areas" where it is possible and desirable to make a new start with relatively good services for children. They include areas where irrigation is being introduced, land-reform areas, areas of new settlement after malaria eradication, and new industrial towns. Their planning has in common an assumption that people will change their habits

of life, and that the work force will deliver a higher-than-average level of skill. Hence there is a particular interest to develop the capacities of the rising generation, and this may be facilitated where the area is administered by a single special authority. h) "Special assistance." The Executive Board has taken note of the situation of the number of newly independent countries which do not have the personnel and resources to mount the basic structure of the health and education services on which any children's programme depends. Special assistance could be given to these countries to set up and operate an infrastructure for services in a few demonstration districts, and would be maintained over a period of years with the country gradually taking over all the expenses. Co-operation in this field would be greatly helped if bilateral aid could be given to the support of such projects. 1125 Training

In all the above problems, one of UNICEF's greatest potential contributions is to assist with the costs of training of national personnel, not in the form of fellowships tenable abroad which are mostly furnished by other agencies, but through help to build up national and regional training facilities. It represents one of the greatest fields of need for additional funds.

STATEMENT OF MRS. THOMAS KOUZES, MEMBER, NATIONAL PTA LEGISLATIVE ACTION COMMITTEE, NATIONAL CONGRESS OF PARENTS & TEACHERS Mrs. KOUZES. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I am 

Mrs. Thomas Kouzes, member of the Legislative Action Committee of he National Congress of Parents & Teachers (National PTA). I have been authorized to reaffirm our established policy of support for UNICEF (United Nations Children's Fund), and particularly to offer support of the recommended appropriation of $12 million as the U.S. 

Government's contribution to the UNICEF program for fiscal 1967, and the requested special contribution of $1 million additional. 

Since the inception of UNICEF in December 1946 to provide emergency postwar relief to needy children, the National Congress of Parents & Teachers has consistently supported this program. 

Our organization comprises approximately 12 million memberships n 50 States, in the District of Columbia, and among schools for American dependents overseas. It has been dedicated since its beginning, in 1897, to health, education, and welfare of American chilren. It has always been in the forefront in encouraging the developnent of UNICEF into a permanent organization concerned with the health and welfare of all children in the world. 

From UNICEF's small beginnings in 1946, the organization has rought lifesaving aid to millions of children and mothers. Today he first babies helped by UNICEF are celebrating their 20th year, as s UNICEF. This new generation of healthy young adults are steping into the adult world because mankind 20 years ago marked a new 701

dimension in the development of civilization, when it recognized man's united responsibility for all children, everywhere. 

In these years of service, UNICEF has treated 14 million cases of trachoma, more than 2 million cases of leprosy, and 40 million cases of yaws; and has given 193 million vaccinations for TB. UNICEF has further established and equipped more than 30,000 maternal and child health centers and subcenters, and has provided health scholarships and training allotments to thousands of nurses and auxiliary health and social workers. The consequence of this care is incalculable. 

These children are the potential leaders of tomorrow's world, who will work alongside our children as adults in an increasingly interdependent world.

The work of UNICEF is indeed spectacular within the limitations of its budget; a dramatic tribute to these accomplishments was the award of the Nobel Peace Prize in 1965. This is but the second time that this distinguished award has gone to a United Nations organization, and only the eighth time to any organization. The award was accepted by the officials of UNICEF as an indication that its guiding policies are basically correct, and that the award is a challenge to strengthen its activities for the fulfillment of all children's needs. 

The UNICEF program is achieveing notable success among the participating countries in the best traditions of self-help. In recent years the average contribution by each country aided was $2.70 in services, materials, and funds for every dollar of UNICEF money spent.

Because of insufficient funds, however, some $9 million worth of UNICEF projects could not be considered last year, and it would seem that a considerable increase in U.S. Government contributions would be justified, particularly because of the population explosion and the dramatic impact for good of UNICEF.

For the past 7 years, however, our Government has recommended that our contribution be $12 million on the basis of the State Department's expert knowledge that pledges already made or anticipated from other governments would indicate difficulty in raising the necessary sums to match more than $12 million at 40 percent. This also obtains for the present year. Despite the spectacular exception of 

Sweden, which has increased its contribution by 50 percent, few others have followed this lead. The general upward trend in support does continue, however.

The United States is the largest contributor in dollar total, but not at all the largest contributor per capita. We rank, in fact, fifth; with Sweden first, with 13 cents per capita, which will soon be 20 cents; Norway, 12 cents; New Zealand, 7.9 cents; Switzerland, 7.5 cents; United States, 6.2 cents, or four-tenths of 1 percent of our foreign aid budget.

President Johnson, in his AID message, stressed his conviction that more foreign aid should go through multilateral sources and to those who helped themselves. UNICEF could be described as a pioneer in its emphasis on self-help, which has always been a requirement for aid in this program. 

We would, therefore, strongly support the request of the Citizens Committee for UNICEF that this committee approve and that the

Congress authorize a special contribution of an additional $1 million n this year of the Nobel Peace Prize, as a tangible recognition of the outstanding work of this organization for peace. This $1 million should be in every sense a gift with no strings attached and no requirements for matching.

We would suggest that such a contribution will express our hope for a peaceful world when an organization like UNICEF helps milions of mothers and children each year with less money than the governments of the world spend on armaments in 2 hours of a single day.

We hope very much these messages may be taken to strengthen UNICEF as it extends its invaluable assistance to millions of children and youth to prepare them for useful lives in this rapidly changng world.

The prepared statement of Mr. Blackmon is as follows:) CMENT OF LARRY BLACKMON, PRESIDENT, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF HOME BUILDERS m Larry Blackmon, President of the National Association of Home Builders. 

a builder of homes and apartments in the Fort Worth, Texas area and in cities in the United States. th me here today are Dr. Nathaniel H. Rogg, executive vice president of the onal Association of Home Builders, and Edmund N. Wise, counsel for internal housing of the NAHB. e National Association of Home Builders is the trade association of the building industry, with more than 45,000 members organized in 396 local State affiliated associations in all 50 States, in Puerto Rico, the Virgin Is- , and the District of Columbia. ny of our members have participated in international housing programs, nany more are interested in participating in the future. It is our belief the wide experience and research that both our Association and our indusembers have developed over the years can be of considerable assistance in evelopment of more and improved housing in the less developed areas of -orld. previous years, we have submitted our views on legislation similar to that you are presently considering. Our interest in the bill presently pending e your Committee relates specifically to the continuation of the authorizafor investment guarantees for housing in Latin America under Section 224

and the use of the authorization under Section 221(b) (2) for housing guarantees in other less developed areas of the world. The specific sections of the bill to which my comments this morning are addressed are contained in Title III, Section 104 (a) (2) beginning on line 23, page 3 of the Committee Print, and Section 

104 (b) beginning on line 3, page 4.

The National Association of Home Builders has had an interest in this program from its inception in 1961 and believes that the program offers the best opportunity for American private business to participate in the development of private housing in Latin America and elsewhere. 

There has traditionally been considerable misunderstanding about the role of housing in economic development. In recent years it has become generally recognized that housing is an important means of raising the productivity of the labor force which, in turn, is an essential factor in the economic development of an underdeveloped country. No longer is private home ownership viewed as merely a reward resulting from the effective economic development of a country, but rather it is considered a basic ingredient in a successful economic development program. Further, it is well known that the private ownership of property is a significant stabilizing factor in less developed countries. As a consequence, meaningful programs to construct housing can do much to promote democratic change. This program, as conceived by the Congress, and developed over the past years has made rapid strides in this direction. 

I. USE OF HOUSING GUARANTEE AUTHORITY Section 221 (b) (2) of the Foreign Assistance Act provides for guarantees of housing projects throughout the less developed countries of the world. Section 

224 specifically provides for guarantee projects in Latin America. The program was initiated in Congress for Latin America in 1961, and later expanded to the other areas. Each year increasing authorization was approved for these deserving and worthwhile programs-and the programs expanded each year until 1965. 

Despite the directions of Congress to implement the programs during 1965, the Agency for International Development (AID) processed no projects beyond the amount developed during 1964. It is for this reason that we appear this year to request Congress to forcefully direct AID to carry out the housing guarantee programs in the manner and amount approved by the Congress in 1965 and ignored by AID this past year.

A. Section 224-Latin America 

The housing guarantee program in Latin America was initiated in Congress in 1961 to be patterned after the FHA program in the United States. Congress has committed increasing support to the program: increasing authorization from $10 million to $60 million in 1962; in 1963, from $60 million to $150 million; and in 1964, from $150 million to $250 million. While the program was slow getting started, the Congress has provided strong support for its effective growth and expansion.

At this time there are over $90 million of projects under contract for close to 17,000 housing units. Another $75 million has been committed for 12,000 units and $75 million more for 15,000 units is being reviewed. This total of $240 million is slightly under the $250 million authorized by Congress in 1964. 

Despite the fact that Congress increased the authorization in 1965 by $150 million AID did not use any of the new authority. In fact, its policy controlling processing projects under Section 224 (b) (1)—the private demonstration housing projects-is that any project not consummated will not be replaced by a new worthwhile project. The AID limit now is $240 million and could, conceivably, go lower, but never reach the $250 million Congress authorized. 

In the face of the purpose of Section 224 and the experience under the program, the administration in 1965 introduced a bill which would introduce four new types of programs and eliminate the private demonstration housing program. 

The Foreign Affairs Committee, while agreeing to introduce these new types of programs, also insisted on the continuance of the private demonstration housing program. The Committee made its position clear in its report in which it stated: "The principal purpose of these amendments to Section 224 of the Act is to assure that the focus of the guarantee program under that Section will not only continue to provide support for private housing projects demonstrating U.S. techniques for building, financing, and marketing privately developed housing,

but will also stimulate development in Latin America of institutions similar to those which in the United States have so successfully mobilized private capital for the financing of new homes and other types of institutions important to the success of the Alliance for Progress. WID "The administration requested an increase of $100 million in the ceiling of the face amount of guarantees that may be outstanding at any one time. No proposal was made to the committee by the executive branch to continue support for selfliquidating pilot demonstration housing projects beyond the $250 million guarantee issuing ceiling that was already provided in the Act. Despite the AID's testimony that it no longer intended or desired to continue the self-liquidating pilot or demonstration housing projects, the committee specifically provides continuing authority for supporting this program, which is now being carried on so successfully. The committee also provides an additional $200 million of guarantee issuing authority so as to assure the availability of adequate issuing authority to cover the pilot or demonstration housing projects." [Emphasis added.]

The Committee increased the guarantee authority for housing under Section 224 to $450 million, of which a portion was to have been used for the original purposes of the Act, for the demonstration housing projects. Although the Administration had requested an increase of $100 million, Congress increased this to $150 million to make the $450 million total. The Conference Committee agreed with the position of the Foreign Affairs Committee that the original housing guarantee program should be continued. The Conference report specifically stated that the other programs should not have priority over the private participation in the development of demonstration housing projects in Latin America. 

Despite specific Congressional mandate to continue the private project program of Section 224(b) (1), AID not only did not use any of the authority during 1965, but recently announced policies specifically excluding the private demonstration housing program contained in Section 224(b) (1): 

The AID housing guarantee program had been aimed at providing moderately priced housing for those individuals with some source of steady income who could afford monthly payments on a house. It is in this middle income area that the private American home builder can best participate. 

Whereas, it is right and proper for the U.S. Government to use that amount of loan funds it believes feasible for assisting low cost housing, the role of assisting the middle class in achieving home ownership can be met by the private sector; the existing program has assisted in this endeavor. It has not only permitted American home builders to assist in building demonstration housing projects in Latin America but has encouraged these same builders to continue on beyond the guarantee program to participate and contribute to the expansion and development of the private home building industry in Latin America.

This Committee in its report of 1962 summarized this position very well. 

The report stated: "Measures to raise housing standards of middle and lower-middle income families must be undertaken through the stimulation of private initiative and private investment. The plight of families comprising this segment of the population is as serious as that of low income families. To solve the problem of those whose income is adequate to warrant homeownership without government subsidy, it is essential that sources of mortgage credit be developed. 

Until such time as a reservoir of savings can be accumulated internally, longterm capital must be attracted from institutional investors in the United States * "The Committee believes the housing guarantee program can be utilized to accomplish the objectives of the Alliance for Progress. Instead of governmentto-government loans and grants, as are used for low-cost housing, private investment sources can be relied upon to assume that part of the responsibility which properly belongs in the private sector." 

Time and again, Latin American officials and other Latin Americans interested in this program have pointed out the great error in neglecting those in the growing middle income class and concentrating all efforts on only those in the low income level. The point has been stressed that the potential political and business leaders, those with education, ability and aspirations, emerge

from this growing middle class and if their needs cannot be met, a serious threat is posed to economic, political and social stability. 

In short, we need to provide effective assistance for the middle income group as well as the low income group, and private capital can, and should, be unleashed to help meet the staggering housing needs. 

The authority for the AID guarantee program is intended, in the language of the Act. "*** to facilitate and increase the participation of private enterprise in furthering the development of economic resources and productive capacities of less developed friendly countries and areas." 

The Latin American housing program was created "to stimulate private home ownership" in Latin America.

With the elimination of housing projects under Section 224(b)(1), the American home builders are effectively eliminated from the program. Other than the worthwhile labor unions projects, the only participation of the American private sector would be lending of funds. 

As AID has not used any of the authorization of last year, we are not requesting any increase in authorization. However, it is requested that of the $150 million, $100 million should be set aside for the continuation of the private housing program under section 224(b)(1) and that $50 million should be permitted to be utilized for experimental type programs. 

It is inconceivable that AID would ignore the specific directives of this Committee and the Congress, but this was the result of the AID policies con cerning Section 224. 

Recommendation 1

To assure the continuation of the private demonstration housing projects under Section 224(b)(1), the Act be amended in Section 224(c), to state, after the figure "$400,000,000" "Provided, that $350,000,000 be used for the purposes of Section 224(b) (1).”

B. Section 221(b) (2)—Other Areas of World 

Housing guarantees, similar to those in Latin America under Section 224, have in a few instances been granted in other areas of the world. From the very inception of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, such guarantees were permitted. Prior to the end of 1963 there had been no housing guarantee activity outside of Latin America. However, in 1963, AID agreed in principle to use authority under Section 221(b) (2) for housing guarantees in areas other than Latin America; and, this Committee in 1964, requested AID to expedite promptly applications for such guarantees in other areas. 

AID administratively set aside $50 million for this purpose in 1964. In 

1965 the Committee recommended that there be set aside in Section 221(b) (2) of the Act, $150 million for fiscal year 1966 for housing guarantees, and, after Conference, $125 million was set aside. This was an increase over the $50 million that AID had administratively set aside for housing guarantees under the Section. 

It was expected, since the authorization was for fiscal year 1966, that projects would be reviewed by AID for this amount. However, AID determined that it would utilize only the $50 million of the authority administratively set aside in 1964 and that this limit would be extended through fiscal year 1967. This would mean that through 1967 only $50 million of projects could be approved throughout the rest of the world other than Latin America, the same amount that had been set aside in 1964. As the Congress authorized up to $125 million for 

1966, it would appear reasonable that AID would, at the very least, permit the commitment for feasible projects for the amount of $125 million during 1967. 

To date, since the inception of the program outside of Latin America, only five projects for $23 million have been authorized in the African region, two projects for $10 million in the Far East and no projects have been authorized in the Near East-South Asia region. Considering the directions of the Committee last year, it is incredible how AID did not move forward at all. And in one area, Near East-South Asia, AID did not even accept application. 

Even as AID expresses concern over insufficient funds, a program using private funds not government funds-is being frustrated. The authority exists to guarantee private investment in new housing developments in the less developed countries.

Recommendation 2 

As a result of AID not expediting the use of the $250 million in the Latin American program prior to 1965, and the failure to use any of the authoriza tion added to Section 221 and Section 224 by the Congress in 1965, the Act should be amended, in section 221 (e), to state. "It is the sense of Congress that the authority provided in Section 224(b)(1) and Section 221 (b) (2) for housing projects be utilized as rapidly as is consistent with responsible administration."

II. INTEREST RATES 

The guarantee program has had constant problems due to the Treasury constantly establishing interest rates for the program below a figure that is marketable for U.S. long-term investors. It is an accepted fact that interest rates must be high enough to be attractive to private lenders. However, the long-term U.S. lenders in the guarantee program have become disillusioned because they cannot rely on any consistent criteria for determining interest rates. 

It should be noted that even with a marketable interest rate and other charges, the cost to Latin American homeowners under the housing guarantee program are much more favorable than are otherwise available to these people. In addition, the interest rate return to the U.S. long-term lender is comparable to the return received on mortgages financing new housing in the United States. 

AID must receive Treasury approval for each change in interest rates and long delays have taken place from the moment that funds are not available at existing rates until the time the Treasury approves an increase in the rate. 

Projects have been delayed for as long as six months due to this fact. 

The rate of return for an investment in an AID housing guarantee project must be predicated on the then current money market and the interest rate for such guarantee must be based upon an acceptable standard. 

Recommendation 8

The constant time delays in setting new interest rates for housing guarantee projects can be eliminated by amending the Act at the end of Section 

221 (c), to state, "Provided that any loan investment for housing projects under Sections 221 (b) (2) and 224 shall be eligible for guarantee if the interest rate on the investment shall not exceed the then maximum permissible interest rate plus 2 of 1% on commitments issued by the Federal Housing Administra tion for insurance of mortgages on single family dwellings." 

III. SALES PRICE CEILING 

Considering the purpose for which the program is designed and the fact that arbitrary limitations are not workable in dealing with individual Latin American countries, AID should revise its policy of placing the same arbitrary price limitation on housing units to be constructed for all countries of Latin America under the four new type experimental programs.

This policy is neither realistic nor feasible. An examination of housing prices in Latin America will readily show that comparable housing, for instance, in Caracas, Venezuela, is not the same as that, say, in Lima, Peru or 

Tegucigalpa, Honduras. 

Recommendation 4

Other than in Section 224(b) (1), AID be permitted to establish housing sales price limits in Latin America, but with limits dependent upon the particu lar conditions of each country. 

IV. BUILDER QUALIFICATIONS 

AID has had certain difficulties during the first years of the program, such as many applicants were not experienced builders despite the fact that the program was designed to capture the experience and ability of the American home builder. For this reason, the NAHB believes that AID would be assisted by a requirement that U.S. participants in the guarantee program be individuals or groups that have been qualified to do business before the FHA or have comparable qualifications. This would also apply to any foreign builders that may participate in the program. In this manner AID would be assisted in receiv-

3 3 ing applications from those able to contribute the best of the American home building industry to Latin American countries. 

Recommendation 5

U.S. or foreign participants in the housing guarantee program shall be qualified to do business before the FHA or shall have comparable qualifications. 

V. ADMINISTRATION OF PROGRAM 

Increased efficiency in the program could result with more effective division of the authority between the operations of AID and the operations of FHA. 

With the steady increase in the size of the program, the FHA should be required to increase its efficiency as well as the AID. Duplication could be avoided by vesting in AID all foreign policy aspects concerning the program, such as determining eligible countries and establishing the limits on the amounts of guarantees permitted for each country. In addition, the U.S. 

Embassy in the particular country should approve each project. 

With this limitation in mind, FHA should be vested with the technical approval authority for all individual projects without the involvement of the many committees and other offices in AID, as well as the interdepartmental committees, such as the Development Loan Committee and the National Advisory Council. The specific risk guarantee program of AID has operated extremely well over the years without the requirement of individual project approval by various agency and interagency committees. It is suggested that 

AID could streamline procedures within strict policy limitations, and with the agreement on the method of establishing an interest rate, projects could be administered by the FHA. The director of the responsible office in FHA could grant the project commitment in the same manner as a district office director of an FHA office in the United States and coordinate with only the Housing and Urban Development Division in Latin America and comparable offices in the other geographical regions. 

Recommendation 6

AID should furnish policies for the operation of the program to the FHA and once policies are determined, all technical aspects of the project should be considered by FHA, and that project approval, barring a foreign policy reason, should be approved by the director of the FHA project examination office.

VI. BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

One of the stated reasons of the Administration regarding the change in the type of housing guarantee program was the balance-of-payments problem. The home building industry is very mindful of the balance-of-payments problem and credit problems in the United States. In fact, there is no industry that is affected more by the present fiscal problems in the United States than the home building industry.

However, as it is shown in the accompanying exhibit, the housing guarantee program under Section 224 (b) (I) contributes very little to this balance-ofpayments problem. At the end of the first three years of a housing project, a maximum of 12% of funds invested is a deficit, as is shown in the exhibit. 

This is the maximum point. In fact, after six years, there is a plus factor in the U.S. balance of payments rather than a deficit. 

From the beginning of the sixth year, the program is an enormous positive contributor to the U.S. balance-of-payments situation. Thus, in ten years it would have made a net contribution of almost $250 million to the U.S. balanceof-payments gap. At the time all the loans would have been repaid, the program would have contributed perhaps as much as $850 million, and certainly not less than $500 million to the credit side of the U.S. balance-of-payments ledger. 

The accompanying exhibit shows that the house guarantee program is the most positive factor of foreign assistance in contributing favorably to the U.S. balanceof-payments problem.

The exhibit also shows a comparison between the housing guarantee program and AID program loans. It is shown that the program loans after a five-year period create over 15 times the balance-of-payments drain as housing guarantees. 

And after five years, the housing guarantees show a favorable balance-AID program lending takes 15 years.

AID states it needs more funds for the foreign aid program. The housing guarantee program requires no appropriations, creates a more favorable impact on the balance of payments than AID loans, and at the same time permits the participation of U.S. private enterprise in building such needed housing in the less developed countries. 

We firmly support the suggestion made in the recent address in Mexico City on April 27 by the Secretary of Treasury, Mr. Henry Fowler, speaking to the annual meeting of the Inter-American Development Bank, in which he stressed the point that in Latin America there is a unique opportunity to make use of the U.S. Government's private investment guarantee program. The NAHB is offering the assistance of its member builders in carrying out this suggestion; this offer is supported by the fact that the guarantee program has a much more favorable effect on the balance of payments than other types of direct U.S. 

Government loans.

It is inconceivable that when private enterprise tries to participate in a worthwhile foreign aid program that it receive such short-shrift. And it is more inconceivable when considering the fact that Congress last year specifically directed AID to include the private home building section in its housing guarantee program. AID has eliminated from its program those most professionally qualified, those who in 1965 built close to 70% of the housing units in the United States. It is for these reasons that we request that the Committee include specific legislative provisions thereby requiring AID to comply with the will of the Congress.

For these reasons and mindful of the fact that Congress last year authorized AID $150 million more in Section 224 and $125 million in Section 221, and that Congress directed specifically that AID continue the private housing guarantee program under Section 224 (b) (1), we request the Congress to put into the Foreign Assistance Act language to implement its directions to AID which were ignored in 1965. (Exhibit to statement of National Association of Homebuilders on Foreign 

Assistance Act of 1966) THE HOUSING GUARANTEE PROGRAM AND THE UNITED STATES BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

The Agency for International Development (AID) decision to use only a very limited portion of its housing guarantee authority is the direct result of the Treasury Department's concern over the impact of this program on the U.S. balance of payments. Prior to the intercession of the Treasury Department, AID contemplated a continuous and expanding Latin American housing guarantee program. Thus, for 1964, AID requested $100 million of additional authorization and a further request for the same amount was made in 1965. The 

Congress, in fact, authorized $150 million in 1965 for Latin America and set aside $125 million of authority for the rest of the world. Moreover, it was originally the executive branch position that this authorization be used as rapidly as projects could be processed. The present constriction and slowdown in the program results from the Treasury Department's misgivings about the program's effect on the U.S. balance-of-payments situation. 

The members of the National Association of Home Builders are also vitally concerned about U.S. balance-of-payments problems. They are prepared to cooperate in every way to improve this situation. It is submitted, however, that the impact of the housing guarantee program on the U.S. balance of payments has been grossly misunderstood and reflects a fundamental misconception on the part of the executive branch. 

We believe it can be demonstrated that the housing guarantee program creates favorable balance of payments effect of the entire foreign aid program of the United States. We further suggest that on balance-of-payments grounds the program should be enlarged-not cut back and slowed down. 

The AID housing guarantee program guarantees the long term financing furnished by U.S. investors for housing in the less developed countries. It is analogous to the U.S. Federal Housing Administration program for housing in this country. For the purpose of analyzing the balance-of-payments effect of the program, the following assumptions are made, as a basis for the graphical presentation on page 7.* The basis for each assumption is indicated: *The analysis is based upon the Latin American program, but is also true to a lesser extent for housing guarantees in the rest of the world.

(1) A program of $100 million per year in Latin America is the minimum desirable operating level. We understand that this level of operation coincided with the AID long-range planning prior to the determination to cut-back the program. (2) The guaranteed loans would be for terms averaging 20 years and would not include grace periods. The interest rate is calculated at a 

52% return to the U.S. investor. These assumptions are based on current 

AID commitments. It is understood that the interest soon will increase to 

54% and, on this basis, the positive effect is increased accordingly. The debt service factor is the most positive component in the favorable balance of payments effect created by the housing guarantee program. (3) The $100 million per year would be disbursed equally over a fiveyear period starting in 1967. While this is somewhat of an oversimplification of the timing of disbursements, it does not distort the conclusions. (4) The funds disbursed by the U.S. lenders will be used to reimburse builders for the direct and indirect costs of construction, land acquisition, urbanization, and builder's profits. AID's own estimate is that in the aggregate not less than 20% of the total amount disbursed would be retained by U.S. builders as reimbursement for U.S. placement fees and profit. Stated in an alternative fashion, 20% of the total amount disbursed would represent U.S. dollar costs and would not represent any adverse effect on the balance of payments. (5) The annual guarantee fee paid to AID in dollars would average 12% of the principal amount of the outstanding loans. This assumption is based on AID's experience to date and, while some minor shift in fees may take place, the change would not significantly alter the conclusions. (6) Reserve fund payments by home owners would average 1% of the principal amount of loans outstanding and would be transferred in dollars to banks in the United States. This is based on AID experience to date and is a conservative figure, since in some countries the charge has been as high as 32%. (7) The countries involved in AID housing guarantee projects buy a substantial portion of their total imports in the United States, and return almost immediately to the United States over 60% of all dollars received for purchases of U.S. goods and services. These assumptions are based on discussions with AID officials and were used by AID itself in analyzing the balance-of-payments impact from AID program loans as well as housing guaranties. This 60% does not represent a balance-of-payments drain. The remaining 40%, of course, does.

This analysis of the effect on the balance-of-payment problem, as it relates to the housing guarantee program, is shown in the graphical presentation on page 7 and produces the following conclusions: 

1. The maximum adverse balance of payments occurs in the third year of the program and the maximum balance-of-payment deficit is $36 million. 

2. Beginning in the sixth year the program will create a substantial positive effect for U.S. balance-of-payments. In ten years a net contribution of $250 million will be made to the U.S. balance-of-payments. At the end of twenty years the U.S. balance of payments will show the contribution to the 

U.S. of $850 million by the housing guarantee program. 

3. This tremendous contribution to U.S. balance-of-payments position would be accomplished at no cost to the U.S. taxpayer under a soundly administered program. Fees collected for guarantees, as in the FHA program, would provide income to the U.S. Government during the five-year period of construction in the hypothetical analysis and over 150,000 housing units would be constructed in Latin America. 

It is worthwhile to compare balance-of-payments results from the housing guarantee program and those of AID's "program" loans. These loans provide dollars to the recipient country, which dollars may be spent for such purposes as the recipient desires. While AID frequently requires the borrower collect normal commercial import documentation to demonstrate that the dollars have been "spent" in the United States, this is, in AID's own terminology, a "cosmetic" device. It is designed to permit AID to state that program loans give rise to U.S. procurement.

What occurs, in fact, is that normal commercial documentation for goods which would have been imported in any event, are collected and the loan proceeds

attributed by AID to these imports. AID then considers that the loan was used for U.S. procurement. In fact, such loans give rise to no more (nor less) U.S. procurement than would an equivalent number of free dollars under the housing guarantee program. 

It is acknowledged that "tied" procurement used with program loans in Latin America has no meaningful economic impact and that the dollars are freely available for such purposes as the recipient desires. AID Administrator Bell, in his presentation before the Senate Banking and Currency Committee on 

March 9, 1965, in discussing "tied" procurement, stated that: "The true net economic effect of foreign assistance on our balance of payments cannot be measured so simply * * * under a tied loan *** the country may use the tied dollars to buy goods that it would have otherwise bought with dollars it already owns. This is the so-called 'substitution' effect, * * * aid financed imports are substituted for imports that would have been bought with free dollars. To this extent, the effect of tied aid on the U.S. balance of payments is understated."

Program lending to Latin America is now at an annual level in excess of $250 million per year. However, for the sake of comparing the balance-of-payments effect of program lending with the projected housing guarantee program, we assume a figure of $100 million per year for five years. Program loans are normally made for a term of 40 years with a ten year grace period. The interest during the grace period is 1%, and is 2% thereafter. 

The assumption by AID on the use of program loàn dollars by Latin American countries is the one that was used in the analysis of the housing guarantee program (i.e. 60% is normally returned to the United States for goods and services). 

At the end of five years the net adverse balance-of-payments impact from the assumed level of program lending is in the order of $190 million. For the comparable housing guarantee program the net loss at the end of five years is only $10 million-less than 6% of the adverse impact of the program loans! In slightly over five years, repayments under the housing guarantee program exceed the balance-of-payments drain. To achieve this equilibrium point with program lending it takes about 16 years. At the time program lending reaches the point where its net impact is just beginning to be favorable, the housing guarantee program has already returned over $600 million in net balance-of-payments gain to the United States!

Based on the foregoing analysis, it is submitted that the balance-of-payments objections to the housing guarantee program are completely without foundation. 

Indeed, the housing guarantee program has highly desirable U.S. balance-ofpayments effects. In fact, as seen, it creates a much better effect than AID program loans.

The executive branch has authority available-without need of appropriations to operate this program. If the executive branch is really concerned about foreign aid and its impact on the balance of payments, and is forthright in its support of developing housing overseas through private enterprise. it will operate the housing guarantee program as directed by Congress in order to use the authorization legislated by Congress.
