STATEMENT OF JOHN H. EBERLY, THE GENERAL BROTHERHOOD BOARD, CHURCH OF THE BRETHREN 

Mr. EBERLY. Yes; with your permission I would like to read it. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. If you will proceed, sir.

Mr. EBERLY. I do represent a church, and the statement I am reading is what I believe is appropriate for a church to present. Though 

I would not want you to think that we are limited only to religious

916

platitudes, and I would like to take this opportunity to compliment the two previous speakers for we ourselves have had some experience in agricultural exchanges and we place a very high estimate on what the agricultural colleges are doing. 

I am John H. Eberly, Washington representative for the Church of the Brethren, speaking in behalf of the Brethren Service Commission of the general brotherhood board of our denomination. 

The Church of the Brethren has, in the past, and continues in the present, to give emphasis to the belief that the Christian is one who demonstrates his faith primarily through service and through labors of good will and helpfulness. This position is taken from the Scripture which says that one cannot love God whom he has not seen without loving his brother whom he has seen.

The Church of the Brethren since World War II has participated in many programs expressing this Christian concern for the needy people of the world. Among these programs have been material aid, volunteer service workers, both among youth and adults, and several forms of exchange programs. These are the high school exchange, college exchange, and particularly one which we designate the Polish 

Agricultural Exchange.

This latter program, at the present time, has in the United States 18 Polish agriculturalists and one from Bulgaria-men and women with graduate degrees, who are serving in practical research within our land-grant colleges or in actual work projects in agriculturally related businesses.

We have found the agricultural exchange a very excellent kind of technical sharing with the people of other nations and have been gratified to find it well supported by those in our own country whose assistance is needed to carry on the program. 

Many Brethren have had the opportunity of working directly in some assistance program abroad. We have had young people, and older specialists, serving in Europe, in the Middle and Far East, and in Africa. We have also had Brethren missionaries active in agricultural missions and in other aspects of village improvement carried on in our mission fields of India and Africa. From this background of experience and from the opportunity of observing the work of our own Government and others in aid, we wish to speak in strong support of the principle of economic assistance. 

We are glad to see that the AID program now before the Congress has separated economic from military aid. While we have had difficulty in feeling that military aid qualifies to be aid, it is not our purpose primarily to speak against that, but rather to urge a greater emphasis on economic assistance to the needy people in the world. 

Material and physical need is on the increase in the world. This situation is compounded by the acceleration of population. We are awar of the threatened famine in India. Poverty, hunger, ignorance, and ill health can be found in every nation in the world and in some it dominates the social order. These are ills that can be cured and we would hope that the United States will see its role of leadership in the world increasingly in respect to these ills. 

The record that our international aid has made from the days of the Marshall plan until now contributes some of the thrilling stories

¡ of history. We are not unaware of many of the justifiable criticisms that have been heaped on the AID program, but we believe in the greater validity of the success stories which are well known. 

Certainly we want to decrease the failures and the weaknesses of the program and increase the efficiency and the success of our foreign aid. 

The Brethren would like to join in all that the Government does to relieve the present suffering of the needy people of the world and in making long-range plans to help people to become self-sufficient and free from handouts. We are reminded of a statement in the Bible that should apply to the United States at this time in history which was spoken of an individual who had come "into the Kingdom for such a time as this."

We do not doubt the sensitivity of our Government for the role that the United States should take in a troubled world. We believe that the political and social instability which we would control primarily by military power, needs to be seen in the light of economic need. 

The policy of increasing our leadership in agricultural and industrial development for the needy countries of the world and at the same time decreasing our dependence on huge military reserves, needs to be more urgently considered and followed. There may have been a time when man engaged in political and military activity for its own. sake, but these have now become subordinate to man's need for economic security.

We, therefore, urge that the Congress take steps to vigorously increase our understanding and our efforts to build up the institutions that will assure the nations of the world of better and more food, lodging. education, and medical care. 

We wish to commend the Agency for International Development in its new initiatives in agriculture, education, and health. This begins to look like planned and controlled assistance as against a simple dole. 

It also indicates a kind of partnership between people who "have" with those who "have not.' ""

The important thing in aid is the manner in which it is given and administered. Aid that is needed can never be wrong except in the way it is given. We urge our Congress and the administration to pay special attention to the necessity to be moral in giving. Aid must be given to the people who need help for the purpose of helping them. 

Any other reason will encourage misuse and corruption in an aid program. It could well be that the instances in which foreign aid has been corrupted can be blamed on a faulty method and motive in its giving. 

For this reason the United States needs to give serious attention to aid given unilaterally for the purpose of supporting its foreign policy. This runs the risk of moral violation and is self-defeating. 

You cannot "win friends and influence people" by exploiting need. 

Assistance given for this purpose will fail, but given for the purpose of helping people, it will return manifold blessings to the giver. 

We should, therefore, consider channeling more of our assistance through such programs as the World Bank, U.N. agencies and private organizations. Our reluctance to do so is evidence of our insistence to make AID do something else. It is not the position of this paper that unilateral aid is of itself wrong. It is only that the temptation and risk of unilateral aid is more nearly avoided in multilateral programs.

In conclusion, we should remember that the real strength of a nation lies in its productive capacity. If this productive capacity is used to save lives and contribute to the welfare of mankind, it is a blessing, and history will record it with praise. If the productive capacity of a nation is used primarily for any other purpose except that which builds cities and institutions necessary for man's well-being, then history will record another failure in civilizations. We support the foreign aid program as aid to people in need and urge that it be expanded and as carefully administered as it possibly can be. 

We thank the committee for this opportunity to present testimony.

Mr. W. B. Hicks, Jr., executive secretary of the Liberty Lobby.

STATEMENT OF W. B. HICKS, JR., EXECUTIVE SECRETARY, LIBERTY LOBBY 

Mr. HICKS. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I am

W. B. Hicks, Jr., executive secretary of Liberty Lobby. I appear on behalf of the 185,000 subscribers to our legislative report, "Liberty Letter." 60-929 -66-pt. 6- -3

Liberty Lobby is well aware of the tremendous demands that are made on the time and attention of this committee. As the role of the 

United States in world affairs has expanded, the role of this committee has grown in direct ratio. Liberty Lobby is just one of the many citizen's groups and economic interests that come before you every year to present their view of the foreign aid program, although we are one of the few groups who do so with no thought of monetary gain for ourselves. Nevertheless, we recognize that your annual consideration of foreign aid is a trying task, and largely a thankless one. 

Under these conditions it is understandable that you might consider a bill such as H.R. 12449, which provides a 5-year authorization by which you can turn over your responsibilities in the troublesome area of foreign aid to the administration for a period of 5 years 5 years, during which you can turn your attentions to other questions of wars and international organizations without concerning yourselves with foreign aid.

But Liberty Lobby asks: Why must this important issue of foreign aid be turned over to the nameless, nonelected officials of the administration? Are there no elected representatives of the people who are willing and have the time to take the responsibility for full and fair consideration of an expenditure of the American people's money that regularly exceeds $3,000 million every year? 

And what of the traditional congressional practice of voting publicly on the authorization of such expenditures? Are the people to be denied the right to measure the performance of their elected represenatives by the way they vote on this important issue?

A vote on annual appropriations alone is no substitute for a full and fair hearing and a full debate on the foreign aid policies of the Nation.

There are many questionable aspects of our foreign aid policy. 

Does foreign aid lead us into wars? This question should be answered.

There is evidence that it leads the recipient nations into wars, such as 

Pakistan and India.

Has our military aid program been successful? Responsible experts such as those who form the Citizens' Foreign Aid Committee have concluded that our efforts to build a military deterrent have increased the danger of war, as in Turkey and Greece, while leaving our own strategic striking force as the only real deterrent to Soviet ambitions.

Has our economic aid helped to advance civilizations? The terribly slow progress of the backward areas seems to indicate otherwise. 

Indeed, our economic aid to such nations appears to be only a narcotic to which they become addicted, so that even a one-time exporting, food-rich nation like Indonesia cannot survive without it, once addicted.

Have we authorized too much money for foreign aid? The fact that over $5 billion of funds appropriated in the past still remain unspent seems to indicate that past authorizations have been excessive. Two years ago, Liberty Lobby called for a study of these unspent funds before this committee, and we still think that such a study is needed. Until that study is made, there should be no new authorizations for foreign aid.

Should foreign aid be administered by international lending organizations, who will be neither responsive nor responsible to the American people? Liberty Lobby thinks not, for what we think is a very good reason, which applies to the entire concept of H.R. 12449. 

Foreign aid-who gets it, and how much-is the people's business. 

The people pay for it. There are many questionable aspects to our foreign aid program, but there is no question at all about this undeniable fact: Congress is responsible for foreign aid, and if the Congress in its wisdom decides to put an end to foreign aid, it should do so; but the Congress should not and cannot solve the problem of foreign aid simply by concealing it for 5 years. 

In summary, Liberty Lobby recommends- (1) No new authorization for foreign aid until all previous appropriations are accounted for, (2) That this committee continue to authorize foreign aid only on an annual basis, and (3) That in the event this committee feels that it can no longer devote itself to a full and fair annual consideration of foreign aid, it should recommend to the House that a new committee be formed for that purpose. 

Thank you.

 WEDNESDAY, MAY 11, 1966 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, pursuant to adjournment, at 10:20 a.m., in room 

The committee meets this morning in open session on a continuation of the hearings on the Foreign Aid bills for the fiscal year 1967, H.R. 

12449 and H.R. 12450.

Our first witness this morning is the Honorable Charles E. Bennett, Member of Congress from the State of Florida. 

Charley, it is a real pleasure and honor to welcome you here. You have a prepared statement. You may proceed.

STATEMENT OF HON. CHARLES E. BENNETT, A REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF FLORIDA 

Mr. BENNETT. I do, sir. Thank you very much.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate this opportunity to appear on H.R. 

12449, H.R. 12450, and H.R. 53.

I am pleased to note that the economic and military assistance programs have been separated into two bills, a policy which I have supported for many years. I hope that this division of the two phases of our foreign aid program will lead to greater economy and efficiency in the operation of our assistance programs, bringing closer harmony between our Government and the governments and the peoples of the countries we help with our aid. 

Over the last decade or more I have advocated that the military portion of the aid program be placed in the Department of Defense's annual request to Congress and that this request be worked upon by the appropriate authorization and appropriations committees in the defense field in the House and the Senate. 

It is my belief that all items in the two bills should be listed as line items, allowing a closer look at what the taxpayer's money is going for. 

I would also hope that there would be an expiration date placed on all authorized projects, just as there is in the military construction legislation which annually comes before the defense committees and the Congress for consideration. The best possible staff and committee specialists should evaluate each military item with the same critical scrutiny given such line items for our own armed services. 927

Mr. Chairman, I would like to recommend for consideration my bill, H.R. 53, either by amendment to the bill before you or otherwise, which provides that U.S. payments to the United Nations shall not be used for programs contrary to the policies of the United States. 

In the present year, and for the last several years, the United States has contributed over 40 percent of the cost of maintaining the United 

Nations Special Fund, now under the U.N. Development Program title. 

This program, as you know, is to help economic and social development in the less developed countries. 

The essence of my bill would be to cut off our aid to those nations who are hoping and planning to bury us. In January of this year, the United Nations Special Fund approved a project at the University of Havana to train engineers and other technical persons, costing $2,096,500. Castro's Communist teachers, many of whom are Russians, were handed this money to carry out a program certain to undermine our efforts to keep the Western Hemisphere free from Castro and Russian totalitarianism. Our representatives at the United Nations objected to this, and voted against it, but it did no good. Just 2 years ago, the U.N. Special Fund also approved a grant to help Castro's ailing economy, which cost U.S. taxpayers $500,000. 

In the last 4 years, Cambodia has received almost $3 million from the U.N. Special Fund for various projects, which cost U.S. taxpayers $1.2 million. The most recent grant was for $611,900 in January 

1965. This is the same country which is led by Prince Sihanouk, who said on March 23, 1966, in announcing that Cambodia had given the 

Vietcong a shipment of rice- *** we have given this aid to them by closing our eyes because we and the Vietcong have a common enemy, which is U.S. imperialism. 

Foreign relations expert and columnist C. L. Sulzberger of the 

New York Times reported only last week that Cambodia isa sanctuary and supply source for the Vietcong on such a scale that the Pnompenh Government must know it. From the extreme south to Laos in the north, Cambodia is violating its proclaimed neutrality. 

I am hopeful the committee will seriously consider my bill as an amendment to the foreign aid authorization legislation. These are good examples of how our money is being used-to perpetuate our enemies.

Mr. Chairman, I am hopeful the committee will act favorably on my suggestions. The foreign aid program in many respects has been good, but today, I see where there has been waste and misdirected funds to those countries who are plainly not our friends. We need to do everything we can to present a clear and concise foreign aid program to keep the peace and preserve freedom around the world. 

Thank you for the opportunity to appear before the committee.

In the 1965 publication by the Expanded Program of Technical Assistance, 15 Years and 150,000 Skills, Poland was given as an example of a relatively small country program of EPTA ($116,300 for 1965) and as the recipient of the kind of assistance which EPTA extends to a country in a relatively well advanced stage of development. The bulk of the Program in Poland is in fellowships; for example, in specialized aspects of metal, chemical, mineral and engineering industries, labor statistics, agriculture, health, telecommunications, meteorology, internal and international postal services, and the use of atomic energy in industry. Only three experts were provided, for very brief consultant missions in tuberculosis control, language teaching, and health statistics.* 

In addition to aid from EPTA and the Special Fund, funds from the regular budgets of the United Nations and the Specialized Agencies are channeled into some Communist countries. (See the enclosed memorandum on U.N. aid to Cuba by Russell J. Leng of the Foreign Affairs Division.) 

A cooperative effort by the Special Fund, the International Labor Organization, and the Polish Government led to the completion in late 1965 of a management program in Poland.5 (See the enclosed clipping for more details on the 

Polish project.)

STATEMENT OF REX G. BAKER, JR., VICE PRESIDENT, NATIONAL LEAGUE OF INSURED SAVINGS ASSOCIATIONS Mr. BAKER.  

My name is Rex G. Baker, Jr., and I am vice president of the National League of Insured Savings Associations, a nationwide trade association whose member institutions are insured by the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation. I am also president of the 

Southwestern Savings Association of Houston, Tex.

I am a part-time consultant to the Agency for International Development, dealing with the problem of home financing in the establishment and organization of savings and loan industries in part of Latin America, and I have just recently been reelected to a third term as first vice president of the Inter-American Savings and Loan Union, and as vice chairman of the Texas Partners in the Alliance with Peru. 

With me is William J. Kerwin, assistant executive director of the national league.

Mr. Chairman, we appreciate the opportunity to appear before this committee to discuss the growing role of thrift institutions in the economic, social, and political development of friendly nations in Latin America, Africa, and Asia. The national league in conjunction with the State Department's Agency for International Development for the past 10 years has made a special effort to promote the development of private thrift and homeownership in these areas and we are pleased to report to you this morning that these efforts are now beginning to return substantial dividends to the nations overseas and to the United States.

As you know, the development of thrift institutions under the Foreign Assistance Act was made a statutory objective with the adoption of the so-called Humphrey amendment in the Foreign Aid Act of 1961. You will recall that this provision stated that- 

The Congress of the United States recognizes the vital role of free enterprise in achieving rising levels of production and standards of living essential to economic progress and development. Accordingly it is declared to be the policy of the United States to encourage the efforts of other countries to increase the flow of international trade, to foster private initiative and competition, to encourage the development and use of cooperatives, credit unions and savings and loan associations * *

Enactment of the Humphrey amendment represented a milestone in the oversea thrift program because it reinforced the conviction of many savings and loan industry executives that establishment of private housing and home financing programs was an essential ingredient to economic development. Moreover, these men believed that U.S. investment of relatively small "seed" capital loans in these countries would expedite the development of thrift institutions and thereby assist private homebuilding. 

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to report to you this morning that there are now 94 savings and loan associations operating in 9 nations of Latin America and in Ethiopia and eastern Nigeria in Africa. 

These associations represent 390,000 savers who have amassed $122 million in savings in a period of less than 5 years. Taken together with AID assistance, the total financial resources of these institu-

tions have been applied to the financing of almost 50,000 homes involving total mortgages of $226 million. 

We submit that this achievement provides convincing evidence that private thrift institutions are, in fact, the key to raising housing standards on a broad front in the underdeveloped part of the world. 

I might say, Mr. Chairman, that a dollar invested in a thrift institution such as a savings and loan association is a dollar that is constantly turned over time and again in the housing economy of a particular nation because as soon as the dollar is repaid, the money is reinvested in new housing. On the other hand, a dollar invested directly from government into a specific housing project is locked into that project or if repaid not necessarily available in the same manner for further home financing purposes.

At the present time the national league is actively working with AID to extend the free savings and loan concept to such countries as Jordan, Thailand, Argentina, Nicaragua, and Brazil and already a savings and loan cooperative association has been established in Pakistan as a result of guidance provided by AID and the national league.

This year the Foreign Assistance Act lays stress on agriculture, education, and public health, all sectors which properly require assistance. Think of the frustration of the young educated emerging middle-income professionals who can find no long-term home financing. We wish to point out that the well-being of an individual is conditioned by all factors affecting his environment, including decent housing.

Unless his shelter is undergoing improvement along with agriculture, health, and education, total development of the nation will be more difficult to achieve. In fact, as the people of the underdeveloped countries achieve better standards of health and education, there will be increasing dissatisfaction with their lack of adequate shelter.

Another factor which adds weight to the argument for greater emphasis on housing is the tremendous urban migration which is accelerating all over the world. It has been estimated that between 

1960 and 1970, 200 million people will move into the cities of Africa, Asia, and Latin America. This, in addition to the normal rates of population increases, will inundate the cities of the world in our generation.

For too long, housing construction for the masses has been left up to government in the underdeveloped countries and, unfortunately, these countries do not have the capital and resources to supply this need. But the U.S. Government through the foreign assistance program has shown a number of countries how to marshal local capital for long-term financing of housing. We members of the national league feel that efforts under the foreign assistance program to develop credit institutions have had a threefold result: 

1. The Government and private sector working together as a team has proven to be an effective vehicle to provide long-term credit at reasonable rates of interest for housing. 

2. The American Government through AID has laid the foundation for a sound, strong, credit system which has provided homes 60-929-66-pt. 6-

for nearly 250,000 people, and will provide homes for millions of people in the future. 

3. The economic impact of a given amount of housing construction is not limited to the expenditure that directly results from this activity. The income that is received by individuals as a result of such expenditures, appears again and again in the economy in the form of income to others as each set of recipients pays it out in consumption expenditures or taxes. Income that is saved also reappears as capital investment expenditures. It is estimated that the building industry of the United States has an impact of approximately 12 percent on the gross national product and it is conceivable that a housing construction industry financed through savings and loan associations sponsored under the foreign assistance program could have a greater impact on the gross national product of underdeveloped countries than the construction industry has in this country. The proposed legislation provides for an extension of foreign aid authorization for a 5-year period. By providing a longer authorization period, the executive branch of the Government can more carefully and effectively program its resources while, in our view, the Congress retains its eminent right of review and authority through annual appropriations. We feel this will be helpful in planning the development of sound private home financing and housing programs in these areas. 

Last year, Mr. Chairman, Congress enacted the Smathers amendment to the Housing Act to permit insured savings associations to invest up to 1 percent of their assets in Latin American housing projects guaranteed by AID. We note that out of $400 million available for loan guarantees in Latin America, $100 million has been set aside for low-cost housing projects including the development of thrift institutions. Even so, this is a relatively small amount in relation to the estimated need for 16 million dwellings in Latin America alone. 

For a number of years, the national league has sponsored legislation to establish an international home loan bank which would channel funds up to $14 million from savings associations in the United States to new thrift institutions in underdeveloped areas of the world. 

It would take a number of years to reach this optimum, if ever, but this is the private enterprise potential which could replace Government financing,

This legislation has been pending for several years before the congressional banking committees. The most recent proposal introduced is H.R. 11764 by Chairman Patman of the House Banking Committee. 

Last month I received a letter from Assistant Secretary of State Lincoln Gordon who expressed the Department's continuing interest in the international bank because he said the development of thrift institutions "comprises one of the more important accomplishments of the Alliance for Progress."

It is our belief that the international bank holds the greatest promise of rapid development of housing and home ownership programs under the foreign aid program and we would hope that this committee would continue to emphasize ways in which private enterprise and investment can make more contributions to the success of our efforts overseas.

937 The development of a savings and loan system in any country means more than the financing of a large number of houses; it is the development of a financial system that will exist long after AID and other agencies cease to exist. It is this development of thrift institutions which will mobilize heretofore untapped capital resources that will someday allow these underdeveloped countries to become independent of the need for foreign assistance.

Mr. Baker, since the incorporation of the Humphrey amendment in the Foreign Assistance Act in 1961 has the organization you represent here today, the National League of Insured Savings Associations, cooperated with the AID Agency in the operation of the Humphrey amendment? 

Mr. BAKER. Yes, Mr. Chairman, we have. 

Chairman MORGAN. Do most members of your organization endorse this approach to getting the underdeveloped countries off the back of the taxpayers?

Mr. BAKER. Yes, Mr. Chairman. Many of the national league executives contribute their time and effort by going to these foreign countries to advise government officials on the aspects of establishing savings and loan systems. They have actually established systems in a number of these countries which are operating today as we indicated. 

Chairman MORGAN. You say in your report that 94 savings and loan associations are operating in the nations of Latin America, Ethiopia, and eastern Nigeria. Are there any other countries other than Ethiopia and Nigeria in Africa where there is any hope that we can establish such institutions?

Mr. BAKER. Yes; there are. We have experts from our industry who have gone over to Libya, Sierra Leone, Turkey, Iran, and Pakistan. We had a mission recently report back from Thailand. 

Mr. KERWIN. Mr. Chairman, I call your attention to this little pamphlet, which I believe you have a copy of, that describes some of the developments in this program over the last several years. We have been in Africa quite extensively I would say for the last 4 years.

Loan Foundation, made an extensive survey in 14 African countries several years ago in an effort to elicit support and interest in the development of private thrift institutions. 

The league is very much interested and aggressively attempting to promote this program overseas and we feel quite confident that we have the full support of the members of the league in this endeavor. 

Chairman MORGAN. I notice on the last page of this pamphlet in the list of industry executives who have contributed time and energy to this program that you are listed as president of the Southwestern Savings Association and have been in Nicaragua. What has been your success in that country?

Mr. BAKER. In that country they have two associations at this time that have total resources in excess of $8 million. We are advising the country and prepared a model statute to the free savings system for them to adopt which I understand is before their congress right now,

Mr. Chairman, and which the savings and loan industry and the Minister of Finance has endorsed.

Chairman MORGAN. In some of the Latin American countries labor unions have established savings and loan institutions. Do you work closely with this type of organization?

Mr. BAKER. We have worked closely with the American labor union group which has been working in Latin America. There is one country, Peru, that I believe has this particular type of institution.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Yes, thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Baker, I don't know if the thought has ever occurred to your organization. You know, we have counterpart funds, excess counterpart funds in a lot of these countries in which you are setting up these savings and loan institutions. You put in seed money; I presume it is American money. Has it ever occurred to you that you might take your American money and exchange it for counterpart funds and use that and we could use up some of that money we have got, and then also you could increase the capital in these various countries by using some of these counterpart funds? Has that ever occurred to your organization?

Mr. BAKER. We have thought of that. Some of our reports have requested that. Thus far most of the counterpart funds that we have requested were already designated for other uses. For instance, in 

Peru there was a request for counterpart funds existing there, but they had other plans for those funds at that particular time. To this date we have not used counterpart funds as a resource. We know they exist. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Have you ever gone to AID and asked them to use a little pressure on any of these countries where counterpart funds exist so that they can be utilized?

Mr. BAKER. We did in one case, but they were spoken for. I think this deserves some attention, Mr. Farbstein. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. I know various of these countries do not want any of this counterpart fund used. They want it to remain there for time immemorial, so to speak. So whatever we sell to generate these funds will be considered as grants.

It seems to me that we should try to utilize that money, because it belongs to us. STATEMENT OF MRS. MORTIMER JACOBSON, NATIONAL PRESIDENT OF HADASSAH FOR THE HADASSAH MEDICAL RELIEF ASSOCIA- 

TION, INC. 

Mrs. JACOBSON. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

May I thank the members of the committee for the privilege of being here this morning. While I would like to feel every Member of the 

House and the Senate is familiar with the work of our organization, I know it is good from time to time to have the opportunity to review the record and the history of our organization. 

I am here specifically today to enlist the assistance, cooperation, support, and friendship of this committee to have Hadassah included in section 214 of the Foreign Assistance Act to enable Hadassah to receive a grant of $1 million in Israel currency, or I£3 million for the enhancement and the development of our medical program in Israel.

First, may I state for the record that we are an organization of over 300,000 women and that we have chapters in every one of the 50 States, and Puerto Rico. When I say the 50 States, I really mean we are organized in the large and the small cities. Our organization is in existence for some 54 years. We started as a medical organization, and we still are a medical organization. 

We were created in 1912 by an American woman, Henrietta Szold of Baltimore. She started our organization with 12 women and today we have grown to, I think, one of the largest voluntary women's organizations in the United States.

With our growth has come an additional acceptance of responsibility to the development of medical programs. Mr. Chairman, I have distributed to the committee additional documentation which gives a background of the program of our organization. I do want to briefly review for you that we have built and do maintain in Jerusalem, in Israel, a medical center comprising of a 600-bed hospital, a separate mother-child maternity building, a nursing school, dental school, medical school, postgraduate school, an Asian-African Institute for the training of doctors overseas from the Asian and African countries. 

We have an outpatient department to which 1,000 people come for treatment every single day. Arabs, as well as Jews, have a warm feeling toward our organization and its services, and medical work has by now become a part and parcel of the land. 

Why is it that we come to this committee for assistance? I think you will agree that we live today in a period where medicine is in one of its most dynamic stages of development. Every modern medical institution must keep up with the developments of today, with the new techniques for heart surgery, kidney transplant, child psychiatry, for the enhancement of nurses programs so that you can keep good people in the nursing profession. It is essential to give doctors today the opportunities to perform the kind of medical practice that their abilities enable them to produce.

Hadassah has brought to the United States during these past years some 200 of our doctors who have been trained in specialties in this country and who have gone back to be heads or key members of their department. Because of their special talents, we have been able to develop in Israel the kind of American institution which we think brings great credit to the American people as well as benefit to the people of Israel. 

Therefore, when the American Government has a program for helping American institutions which are operating overseas, we would like to think of ourselves as one of the organizations worthy of being encouraged to continue the kind of work we do and which merits help in our development. 

We face many special challenges in the future. We know that we have to enlarge the program in our nurses training school and also provide a residency for nurses. We regret that our magnificent facilities have not as yet been able to provide any residency for our nurses or for our doctors.

There is great pressure for facilities for child psychiatry in our institution; unfortunately, this is one of the great problems in Israel today. There is great need for research space. We have many, many urgent needs that we must fulfill if we are to keep pace with the high standards that our organization has achieved up to now. 

Mr. Chairman, we are a responsible organization. I think our record will show that whatever program we undertake we carry through, we maintain, we develop, and bring to it the very special quality and standards that are uniquely American. Last year we had made an application to receive a grant under section 214, but unfortunately we were too late in our application. 

So we come before you today to ask the cooperation and help of this committee to see to it that this year Hadassah is included for the 3 million pounds that we are requesting. 

Thank you.

STATEMENT OF MRS. MORTIMER JACOBSON, NATIONAL PRESIDENT OF HADASSAH 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is indeed a privilege to be given the opportunity to testify on behalf of Hadassah, the organization of which I am privileged to be National President. I welcome this opportunity to set before this important Committee the record of development and achievements of Hadassah for I truly believe the accomplishments of our organization reveal one of the greatest sagas of voluntary efforts on the part of women. 

First, let me state briefly that Hadassah is an organization of over 300,000 American women organized in all of the 50 States of the Union and in Puerto Rico. This means we have functioning chapters in the smallest, as well as the largest communities. Our organization was founded in 1912 by Henrietta Szold of Baltimore, a social worker, educator and humanitarian. She succeeded in convincing 12 Jewish women that it was urgent to send a medical mission to Palestine, then a land plagued by poverty and disease. 

These 12 women accepted the challenge and in 1913 sent two American trained nurses to do pioneering work. This, then, was the beginning of our organization. Since that time we have labored in war and in peace to develop modern 

American standards of medicine, and if Israel today is a country that is aware of the necessity to provide all its citizens with proper healing, teaching and research facilities, Hadassah can claim a large share of the credit. 

Indeed, if many developing nations of the world have become conscious of the primary need to provide good standards of health in order to develop responsible citizenship. it is because Israel has demonstrated that healthy bodies are essential to produce healthy minds and attitudes. 

I have distributed to the Committee data giving information on the program and services presently being performed by the Hadassah Medical Organization

in Israel. I think you will agree that it is a pretty impressive report. Our aims have remained the same throughout our long and distinguished history-to bring American standards and know-how to a nation struggling to absorb people who come from more than 60 lands, half of whom come from primitive backgrounds. 

Our goal is to provide the best possible care for the sick, both in-patient and outpatient; to sponsor undergraduate and post-graduate teaching and to encourage research in all fields. 

Because medicine knows no frontiers and every achievement benefits all mankind, Hadassah has played a noteworthy role in helping the medical programs of the developing countries in Asia and Africa. This is accomplished by Hadassah doctors being sent to these countries to help them start clinics for both treatment and preventive medicine. Last year, at our National Convention, Hadassah was privileged to receive a citation from the Government of Liberia for the brilliant work done by our doctors in that country. Two of our doctors established 

Liberia's first 22-bed Eye Hospital. Between 5 and 6 of the doctors from our 

Ophthalmology Department rotate service in African countries. 

At our Nurses Training School, 13 girls from Malawi (Nyasaland) and 2 from Liberia are studying. Their studies are conducted in English and they learn sufficient Hebrew to communicate with the patients. 

MEDICAL SCHOOL 

Since its inception over 800 physicians have completed their training at the Medical School. 73 students from developing countries in Asia, Africa and South 

America are presently studying in the School. These students will eventually become leaders in the field of health in their respective countries. 

Last year, 105 medical students came from their respective medical schools to take summer courses with us. · Our out-patient departments are located on 4 floors serving 1,000 patients a day. A visit to these clinics will show a tremendous variety of ethnic groups waiting for attention. Services are given to all who apply regardless of race, color or creed. One sees Arabs, Christian and Moslem, people from countless lands-all feel at home at Hadassah. Here one can really marvel at the role medicine plays in helping to mold a nation. 

I would also like to stress the unique volunteer aspects of Hadassah. The National Board controls the budget and the policy of our organization. Department by department; item by item, we analyze, approve, or reject the program that is submitted for consideration. Our medical program is an American program. It is based on U.S. methods. We have an Advisory Board of distinguished American doctors who assist us in making decisions. Our Israel doctors come to the United 

States on fellowship programs and there is a continuous flow of people and knowledge between Israel and the United States. 

To give a specific example of how Hadassah brought a uniquely American technique to Israel, let me briefly tell you about the voluntary service program we pioneered in that country. Over 500 Israel women have been taught how to make bandages, feed patients, bind books, read to children and assist the nurses and doctors in the countless services that can be done by such a group. This type of voluntary work was completely unknown in Israel and we are now teaching other hospitals to develop a similar program. Thus, we were able to transfer to 

Israel the American concept of women doing volunteer work in hospitals. 

Our great challenge today comes from the magnificent developments that are taking place in modern medicine. We live today in an era of great change in treatment; we live today in a period where science and research are providing new techniques almost daily. No medical institution can stand still. It must keep pace with modern developments or become second rate. This is especially true of a teaching hospital which has the responsibility of providing students with the opportunity to study new methods of treatment and diagnosis. Medical equipment is expensive and complex and becomes obsolete all too quickly. Healing is certainly a rewarding art, but it is also an expensive one. 

With all this, the medical and nursing professions all over the world are having difficulty in attracting the best students who today are seemingly more attracted to other sciences. In order to bring the best minds to medicine, it is essential to have facilities to enable gifted men to contribute the best they are capable of producing.

The special dimensions of Hadassah's work have established our Medical Center as a place of international renown which attracts a continuous stream of

professional and lay visitors. Many Members of Congress and other representatives of the United States Government have visited our institutions and all have been enthusiastic about our program of work and generous in their praise of our accomplishments.

There is no doubt that. Hadassah's pioneering medical work in Israel has been decisive for the health of the country and its citizens. It established patterns of health care, preventive and curative, and its staff combines professional excellence with dedication. It is these contributions and these qualities which assure Hadassah its unique place in the history of medicine. While we have made an enormous expenditure in money and effort, our Medical Center has not reached its final stage. The great progress in medical science demands increases in expenditure, changes in equipment and new methods of treatment, and if we wish to survive as a great Medical Center we shall have to expand our physical facilities to meet the changing needs. 

It is to help reach these new horizons that Hadassah asks for financial assistance and we are confident that this Committee will recognize Hadassah's contribution in the field of health to the individual, to Israel, to newly emerging nations, and, indeed, to mankind. We therefore urge that we be included in 

Section 214 of the Foreign Assistance Act for one million dollars in Israel currency or (3 million Israel pounds). 

DESCRIPTION OF THE MEDICAL PROGRAM OF HADASSAH MEDICAL RELIEF ASSOCIA- TION, INC., 65 EAST 52D STREET, NEW YORK, N.Y. 

INTRODUCTION 

Hadassah Medical Relief Association, Inc. is a New York membership corporation carrying on a charitable program as a voluntary, nonprofit organization. 

Hadassah is registered with the President's Advisory Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid and enjoys tax exempt status under the United States Internal Revenue Code. Attached is a copy of the United States Treasury Department letter granting Hadassah tax exempt status. (See Exhibit "A") 

MEMBERSHIP AND PROGRAM 

Hadassah was organized in 1912 by Miss Henrietta Szold, who was born in Baltimore, Maryland, and was a social worker and educator. Hadassah has grown from its original 12 members in the United States to over 300,000 women members, organized in chapters in 50 states of the Union and in Puerto Rico. 

The membership of Hadassah participates in its program as volunteers. These programs are supported primarily by voluntary contributions from members and from the general American public. 

Hadassah's medical and educational facilities in Israel and in America are nongovernmental, non-profit and are not church connected. 

Hadassah now has an internationally recognized program of healing, teaching and research in Israel, and also vocational education, child rehabilitation and land reclamation. In the United States it has a program of education, youth activities and American civic affairs.

HADASSAH MEDICAL ORGANIZATION 

Through HADASSAH MEDICAL ORGANIZATION, Hadassah carries on in 

Israel a comprehensive program of medical education; preventive, diagnostic and curative medicine; and an extensive program of medical and scientific research.

The The major portion of Hadassah's medical work is centered in and fans out of the Hadassah-Hebrew University Medical Center, Jerusalem, Israel. 

Medical Center complex includes the following:

Henrietta Szold School of Nursing. 

Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School. 

Afro-Asian Institute.

Hebrew University-Hadassah School of Dentistry (founded of Alpha Omega). 

School of Occupational Therapy. 

Department of Social Medicine and Public Health. 

Institute of Post-Graduate Medical Training. 

wan

Medical and scientific research laboratories. 

Exchange fellowship program.

Teaching hospital (containing about 600 beds). 

Mother and child pavilion. 

Outpatient clinics.

Hospital pharmacy (used by the students of the above-mentioned Medical School).

John F. Kennedy Memorial Building. 

Community health services for preventive medicine (at Kiryat Yovel, a village adjacent to the Medical Center).

HADASSAH POLICIES MADE BY UNITED STATES CITIZENS 

All of Hadassah's medical and teaching institutions in Israel were established by United States citizens. The National Board of Hadassah, consisting of representatives from all parts of the United States, is the sole authority making all policy decisions. Policy decisions relating to its Israel program are implemented by counterpart bodies in Israel. These counterpart bodies under the direction and control of the National Board of Hadassah are set up for the sole purpose of carrying out policies. American citizens as well as Israel nationals serve on these counterpart bodies.

STAFF INCLUDES UNITED STATES CITIZENS 

The Director-General of Hadassah Medical Organization and the principals of the various schools operated by Hadassah are Israelis. However, the teaching staffs and medical personnel include many United States citizens. Many of the Israelis working for Hadassah are American trained, and bring to their positions American standards and expert knowledge.

ADVISORY COMMITTEES COMPOSED OF UNITED STATES CITIZENS 

While Hadassah alone operates, manages, and controls its work in Israel, it has the advantage of volunteer technical advisory committees composed of well known, respected and highly qualified United States citizens serving as counsellors. The advisory committees help develop the standards used for Hadassah's program in Israel, which are based completely on practices and procedures used by similar facilities in the United States. Attached are listings of the members of the Medical Advisory Board and the Youth Reference Board. (See Exhibits 

"B" and "C.")

STUDENTS PRIMARILY ISRAEL NATIONALS 

The majority of students at Hadassah's schools are Israel nationals.

In con- sonance with the United States program of international cooperation, a number of students are from developing nations in Africa and Asia. 

COURSES OFFERED 

The Hadassah schools offer technical training in the various disciplines of medicine. Courses in language, literature, geography and history of Israel are requirements for matriculation. A knowledge of the English language is necessary since some of the courses are given in English and many of the textbooks are in this language.

Since the 13 years of the Medical Residency Training Program 37 doctors formerly with Hadassah have become heads of Departments in other institutions and key hospitals in Israel.

HENRIETTA SZOLD-HADASSAH SCHOOL OF NURSING 

The Henrietta Szold-Hadassah School of Nursing, established in 1918, was the first nurses training school in what was then Palestine. The school has housing and teaching facilities for 150 student nurses. The standards set by this school have been followed and adopted by the Government of Israel as the minimum requirements for other nurses training schools in that country. Hadassah's school still ranks as the leader in the field of nursing and sets the standards for other similar institutions in Israel. 

Under consideration for implementation is Hadassah's plan to add to the nursing curriculum which may entail additional plant facilities.

950

The additional period of training is in response to a pressing need in Israel for teachers, supervisors, and researchers in the nursing field. The expanded curriculum, producing more highly trained nurses, will add greatly to the economic development of Israel. The additional curriculum of training will enable the graduates of the school to receive a University Bachelor's Degree in nursing in addition to the RN.

Hadassah has the exclusive jurisdiction, control and responsibility for curriculum, teaching, administration and financing of the Henrietta Szold-Hadassah 

School of Nursing. 

HEBREW UNIVERSITY-HADASSAH MEDICAL SCHOOL 

The Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School was the first medical school established in Israel. It was opened in 1949 with a student body of 50. Its outstanding faculty has helped produce a corps of expertly trained physicians in Israel. Of the 747 student body in its present enrollment, 520 are in the medical department, 72 in the pharmaceutical department and 128 in the micro-biology department. There are also 15 students enrolled for graduate courses in medical science and 12 in post-graduate work in public health. 

Hadassah has full and exclusive jurisdiction, control and responsibility for maintenance and administering of the clinical (bedside teaching) sections of the Medical School. The pre-clinical sections of the Medical School are under the joint control of Hadassah and the Hebrew University. 

AFRO-ASIAN INSTITUTE 

In 1961 the Afro-Asian Institute was established to train medical students from countries in Africa and Asia who later return to their native lands to practice and to teach medicine. 

Students came from Liberia, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Ghana, British Guinea, Cyprus, Kenya, Mauritius, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda, and so forth. The Afro-Asian

Institute was established to assist the developing countries of Africa and Asia whose own educational facilities are very limited or non-existent. These students, on graduation, have the requisite training to educate a generation of young doctors in their own countries. 

HEBREW UNIVERSITY-HADASSAH SCHOOL OF DENTISTRY (FOUNDED BY ALPHA OMEGA) 

The Dental School grew out of the small number of American dentists sent by Hadassah to Palestine in 1918. Since that time, the school has developed into a modern School of Dentistry with a network of dental services. It is the only 

Dental School in Israel. 

The present student body of the Dental School is made up of 120 students. 

Hadassah has full and exclusive jurisdiction, control and responsibility for the maintenance and administration of the clinical (chair teaching) section of this school. 

INSTITUTE OF POSTGRADUATE MEDICAL TRAINING 

The Institute for Postgraduate Studies was founded in 1962. It provided for refresher courses for Israel physicians, courses for newly arrived general practitioners, and courses in specialized branches of surgery and medicine. These courses are given in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv, Beersheva and Afula so that local forces for teaching purposes can be utilized. 

Postgraduate training is given to foreign physicians, some of whom have come from widely divergent areas such as Burma, Thailand, the African continent, England and Australia. Training is given in ophthalmology, dermatology, haematology, etc.

MEDICAL AND SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH 

Research work done by Hadassah doctors and scientists has attracted international attention; papers are published in outstanding scientific and medical journals; grants have been received from world famous institutes, funds and foundations, including the U.S. Government's National Institutes of Health. 

Ford Foundation, Rockefeller Foundation, Royal Society of London, and others.

Over 54% of the bio-medical research papers and 90% of the medical research papers published in Israel are by Hadassah doctors and scientists. The work

of these researchers is making a significant contribution to the world's store of medical knowledge. The attached list includes some significant published papers of Hadassah doctors and scientists (See Exhibit "D"). In order to meet Israel's requirements for more medical and scientific research, Hadassah has increased its laboratory facilities and has provided the necessary facilities for kidney transplant and open heart surgery.

EXCHANGE FELLOWSHIP PROGRAM 

Hadassah participates in the United States Exchange Fellowship Program under DSP-66 P 111-1411. Since 1946, through this comprehensive fellowship program, Hadassah has sent over 200 physicians, nurses and hospital administrators to receive additional specialized training in universities and hospitals in the United States and Europe. This specialized training has helped these fellows to set American standards in Israel. 

FACILITIES AT THE HADASSAH-HEBREW UNIVERSITY MEDICAL CENTER 

Hospital: This 600 bed patient hospital has 28 Departments and 31 Institutes and Laboratories. Approximately 17,000 in-patients are treated annually. 

Mother and Child Pavilion: This facility has 50 obstetrical beds and 64 bassinets providing facilities for care of mother and new born infant. (These figures are included in the 600 mentioned above).

Out-patient Clinics: There are 32 out-patient clinics treating well over 200,000 patients annually, thus providing a direct link between the community and the hospital. Within the out-patient clinics there are sub-clinics manned by highly specialized personnel. The names of some of the clinics are: Ophthalmology, Internal Medicine, Pediatrics, Ear, Nose and Throat, Obstetrics, etc. 

Pharmacy Department: This department, serving the in-patient and out-patient clinics, fills approximately 500,000 prescriptions a year. This pharmacy is used as a teaching facility for the Department of Pharmacy which is part of the 

Medical School. 

New Nurses' Residence: A new residence for graduate, unmarried nurses is being constructed by Hadassah in close proximity to the hospital at the Medical Center. This facility is necessary to give nurses living quarters near the hospital as an inducement to their continuing in hospital service and to add to the efficiency of their work.

New Medical Residence: Hadassah is now in the process of planning a residence for its interns, residents and other medical personnel, such as visiting doctors from abroad who serve the hospital for a stated length of time. This residence is sorely needed, since the hospital has only minimum living accommodations. This new residence will increase the effectiveness of interns and residents who are always on call.

COMMUNITY HEALTH SERVICES-PREVENTIVE MEDICINE 

The Community Health Center at Kiryat Yovel, a village adjacent to the Medical Center, is a pilot plant which has attracted considerable attention from the international community. The Health Center serves a population of 20,000 families, mostly new residents in Israel, who originate from over 50 different countries.

The fundamental principle of operation of the Health Center is that the health of the individual is involved with that of his family and is influenced by emotional, social and economic conditions. Thus the whole family is treated by a team of physicians, nurses, psychologists and social workers. 

An average of 15,000 patients are seen annually by physicians and nurses. In addition, 45,000 prescriptions are filled and 12,000 laboratory examinations are made. 

The Health Center also serves as a teaching and research facility for students at the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School. As a pilot project it has been emulated by other agencies in Israel. Other nations, as well as the World 

Health Organizations of the United Nations, have sponsored the initiation of similar projects.

INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION 

In consonance with the United States program of international cooperation. 

Hadassah has made available some of its doctors and nurses, part of a corps sent to several Asian and African countries to set up health facilities and iusti- 60-929-66-pt. 6- -5

952

tutes for medical teaching in those countries where such facilities are sorely needed. Hadassah doctors and nurses were involved in the eye clinics established in Ethiopia and Liberia and other African countries. 

IMPROVEMENT OF MEDICAL TECHNIQUES AND RAISING OF STANDARDS 

Many United States medical authorities are invited to present to Hadassah's medical personnel papers on new developments in medicine and new surgical techniques. This exchange, in addition to the Exchange Fellowship Program, makes it possible to enhance the skills of many more of the medical personnel than are able to leave Israel under the Exchange Fellowship Program. In this way United States standards and techniques are available for inclusion into Hadassah's program. 

SUMMARY 

Hadassah's overall training program for all levels of medical education has influenced 1,357 graduates. In the 46 years of the existence of the Henrietta 

Szold-Hadassah School of Nursing well over 1,000 nurses have been graduated to serve the Israel community in hospitals, out-patient departments and in-patient medical service.

In the 18 years existence of the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School, over 800 physicians have been graduated to serve in all parts of Israel, in border settlements, in public health stations, in hospitals and in private medical service. 

In the 12 years since the establishment of the Department of Pharmacy, over 60 students have completed their courses of training and are serving in hospitals and out-patient and private work. 

Over the past 19 years since the Fellowship Program was initiated, more than 200 physicians have been outside of Israel for refresher courses (mostly in the United States) and observation to take back to Israel the latest scientific developments in their respective fields. 

In total, Hadassah has given to the State of Israel 2,231 highly trained personnel without which no modern state can carry on its vital functions. Medicine has no boundaries; Health has no frontiers. 

Respectfully submitted.

TREASURY DEPARTMENT, OFFICE OF COMMISSIONER OF INTERNAL REVENUE, 

Washington, December 2, 1941.

HADASSAH MEDICAL RELIEF ASSOCIATION, INC., 

New York, N.Y.

SIRS: It is the opinion of this office, based upon the evidence presented, that you are exempt from Federal income tax under the provisions of section 101 (6) of the Internal Revenue Code and corresponding provisions of prior revenue acts. Accordingly, you will not be required to file returns of income unless you change the character of your organization, the purposes for which you were organized or your method of operation. Any such changes should be reported immediately to the collector of internal revenue for your district in order that their effect upon your exempt status may be determined. 

Since any organization which is exempt from Federal income tax under the provisions of section 101 of the Internal Revenue Code also is exempt from the capital stock tax pursuant to the express provisions of section 1201 (a) (1) of the Internal Revenue Code, you will not be required to file capital stock tax returns for future years so long as the exemption from income tax is effective. 

Furthermore, under substantially identical authority contained in sections 1426 and 1607 of the Code and/or corresponding provisions of the Social Security Act, the employment taxes imposed by such statutes are not applicable to remuneration for services performed in your employ so long as you meet the conditions prescribed above for retention of an exempt status for income tax purposes.

Contributions made to you are deductible by the donors in arriving at their taxable net income in the manner and to the extent provided by section 23 (0)

of the Internal Revenue Code and corresponding provisions of prior revenue acts. 

Requests, legacies, devises or transfers, to or for your use are deductible in arriving at the value of the net estate of a decedent for estate tax purposes in the manner and to the extent provided by sections 812(d) and 861(a)(3) of the Code and/or corresponding provisions of prior revenue acts. Gifts of property to you are deductible in computing net gifts for gift tax purposes in the manner and to the extent provided in sections 1004(a) (2) (B) and 1004 (b) (2) and (3) of the Code and/or corresponding provisions of prior revenue acts. 

The collector of internal revenue for your district is being advised of this action.

By direction of the Commissioner: 

Respectfully, T. MOONEY, Deputy Commissioner.
