Chairman MORGAN. Our next witness is the Honorable Lester Wolff, 

Member of Congress from the State of New York. Congressman, it is a real honor and privilege to welcome you before this committee today. 

You have a prepared statement and you may proceed, sir.

STATEMENT OF HON. LESTER L. WOLFF, A REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF NEW YORK 

Mr. WOLFF. I appreciate the opportunity to appear before you here. 

I cannot let the opportunity pass, however, before reading my prepared statement to comment on the previous witness. I should like to lend my support to the request that is being made by the Hadassah organization for their hospital in Israel. 

Mr. Chairman, once again this distinguished committee is being asked to authorize moneys for foreign assistance. Such aid has been a major feature of American foreign policy since, under the brilliant leadership of President Truman and Secretary of State Marshall, we helped raise the war-ravaged nations of Western Europe back to the affluence and prosperity they enjoy today.

Foreign aid has generally been a successful instrument of American foreign policy in building the economies of devastated nations and preserving them from the pressures of communism that feeds on such devastation.

I am in favor of judiciously administered foreign aid to those nations who appreciate it and who evidence that appreciation by not following courses opposed to our national interest. I have spoken out more than once on this subject in opposition to further aid to those nations who seek our help on the one hand, but vilify us and burn our libraries on the other. But today I would like to speak on another aspect of our foreign aid policies. 

I believe that in many cases the effectiveness of the assistance we give other nations has been severely limited because of poorly conceived, poorly administered, even capricious projects that have helped no one. I am speaking about those programs we have all heard about which have turned out to be fiascoes and have even made the great United States a laughing stock in certain foreign capitals. 

I hesitate to consider an authorization for foreign aid or for any other expenditure of public funds unless I am satisfied that such assistance achieves the maximum return for the nation involved and for the vital interest of the United States. 

I have grave doubts that many of our commercial assistance or investments abroad have always been based on commonsense business principles upon which this Nation has achieved its great preeminence. 

I suspect that many instances where projects have failed have come about because the expertise of our private sector has not even been consulted.

For this reason, Mr. Chairman, I should like to offer an amendment today to this foreign aid authorization bill to establish a business advisory council, composed of American business specialists, to pass judgment, in the field, on each and every commercial loan or grant contemplated for a foreign nation under the AID program. 

I am not without experience in this field. I have seen AID missions in operation in dozens of countries especially in critical areas. 

I observed our programs in Vietnam last November, along with my colleague from New York State, Mr. Halpern.

It is my observation that the AID program has not attracted personnel from the private sector who have achievement in the practical survival school of experience that every successful businessman must graduate from if he is to survive. It is a school I attended for 25 years before coming to Congress.

Mr. Chairman, I believe our foreign aid program has been characterized by too many bureaucratic generalists. What the program needs is a few hard-working sergeants who have come up through the ranks of American business and whose experience is invaluable, even indispensable to our Nation's interest.

I am asking this distinguished committee to amend the legislation now before it to include the setting up within the AID program of a review system whereby a loan, say to establish a fertilizer plant in Vietnam, should be studied and reviewed by a panel of American businessmen with long experience in the fertilizer field, before such a loan is made. And such review should be conducted in the field to gain a maximum appreciation of all factors involved. 

I believe American industry and business, which has brought this Nation to the position where it is rich enough to consider such vast expenditures of our national wealth, will rise to this challenge and

provide the cadre of business leaders necessary to provide the judgment and experience required to make good, sound loans and grants when it is in our national interest. 

Mr. Chairman, my amendment would substitute expertise for innocence. It's a tough world, and we are involved in a tough scrap in 

Vietnam. And there will probably be others.

Let's apply the tough judgment of proven businessmen to our programs of assistance to friendly nations.

Should a nation grown strong because of the hard work of businessmen do less?

Foreign assistance should be a temporary program to assist nations establish a firm independent economic foundation so that a strong democratic nation can flourish and that the ultimate goal of establishing trading partners in the world community can become a reality. 

Trade is a two-way street. Our balance-of-payments problem and many political problems can easily be solved if these nations to which we render aid can ultimately stand on their own feet and buy and sell to us with their own money. I have never known anyone to kick a good customer in the teeth.

Our handling of AID financing under present circumstances and procedures, I am sorry to say, is so full of dirt it must constantly be swept under the rug.

Inept bureaucrats seeking to perpetrate their jobs act as judge and jury of the programs placed before them for implementation. Waste, gross waste, undermines what could become the salvation of the free world as we know it today.

The free enterprise private sector which has been generally critical of AID, I am certain, would step forward to assist the implementation of an effectual program if the "Ivory Tower" boys would for a moment accept ideas that were generated outside of AID or the State Department. In an attempt to protect this private domain, total disregard to experience prevails and this permeates loan and grant procedures in AID. I would substitute a reserve of business leaders expert in their fields who would serve 1 month a year to act as panels in all nations where aid is distributed as a review board to act upon the merits of projects up for consideration.

The Department of Commerce has a roster of hundreds of successful men who have agreed to serve without compensation on trade missions. Thousands of "business expert" not pseudo experts now employed as overall generalists, could be found who would serve our nation for a limited time without compensation and render to the overall problems the greatest assist we have ever achieved in making AID commercial loans and grants a working reality instead of a frightful fiasco.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Congressman Wolff. 

Congressman, will you expand a little bit more on your suggested amendment? Would you establish a different business council for each project or each country, or how would this amendment work? 

Mr. WOLFF. A council would be set up that would draw upon all varieties of industry within the United States. Then when specific loans were requested, people from this particular industry would be requested to serve on a review board in a particular area.

It would be a reserve force, a pool of qualified personnel that could be drawn upon as needed. For example, as I quoted in my statement, if a request came in for a particular loan in a particular country, you would draw upon this reserve for people in that industry or someone who had some connection with the industry involved. 

Chairman MORGAN. Congressman, you know we have one organization now functioning in the foreign aid field headed by Frank Pace. 

It is headed as a committee of business people, and AID is cooperating. 

They have been in operation about a year, I believe. Part of their funds are from business groups in this country and AID finances part of the operation. The volunteers are mostly retired business people or people who take leave from their business. They get per diem while overseas but no salaries.

AID testified here during these hearings that the per diem for sending these businessmen overseas, ranges anywhere from $800 to $1,000 a month. AID has been picking up part of this. Does this work in with the suggestion that you have? 

Mr. WOLFF. It could with the exception, Mr. Chairman, that this would be more than having an advisory group in limbo. They would utilize the services of a group such as this to provide reserve cadre to pass upon the loans, similar to the way some banks operate. Banks use advisory groups to sit in judgment upon loans, giving them outside assistance in coming to a decision.

I have known a number of loans that have been made or not made by AID, based upon the judgment of an individual who sits either as a desk officer or as a project officer in a foreign land who has had no prior experience whatsoever with the type of industry or the field that he is supposed to pass judgment upon. 

I think this group under Mr. Pace and perhaps it can be added to could provide a group of people who could sit with the project officer and advise and recommend on these particular loans. 

Chairman MORGAN. Are you familiar with the so-called Javits amendment that has been in the foreign aid bill? 

Mr. WOLFF. No, I am not, sir.

Chairman MORGAN. He has had ideas along this line for a good many years for increasing the participation of the business community foreign aid operations. This committee has been very sympathetic to views of this kind. We have over a period of years included language in the act to bring private enterprise and the business community into the foreign assistance program. 

As you know, there have been several committees. Are you familiar with the Watson committee? 

Mr. WOLFF. Yes. 

Chairman MORGAN. Is that committee's work along the line of your suggestions? $

Mr. WOLFF. It is. The only point I am trying to make is the fact that I think we should utilize these people in addition to acting in the broad advisory sense, as well in the operational area, actually within the framework of the AID program, in the field and to assist with reconsiderations on the passing of individual loans and in the implementation of the programs after they have been passed. 

I am fairly familiar with the AID programs in southeast Asia, having served on two trade missions to southeast Asia. I was requested 1 b

to go into an area while on a trade mission to look over the idea of setting up a department store in Bangkok. After looking over the area, I decided this was an impossible task to set up a department store on the basis outlined. 

Yet our local people in Bangkok, having no knowledge of retailing whatsoever, were promoting this project and were very disturbed over the fact that I felt there was no real raison d'etre for a department store in that area.

What I am getting at is the fact that I did come out of the private sector at that time and I was in the field on the site and as a result of which I think I was instrumental in stopping an investment on AID in something that could not possibly be successful. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Would the gentleman yield?

Chairman MORGAN. I yield. 

Mrs. BOLTON. What kind of an organization? What could have been done there?

Mr. WOLFF. I think there could have been some small stores set up. Actually the problem, Mrs. Bolton, was the fact that we were attempting to set up a showcase project, and the project itself really did not have merit because of the additional ramifications. They wanted people to invest in the physical building of a department store and then only wanted to give them a 10-year lease. Our economic officers at that time were strongly pursuing this idea and trying to get the private sector to come in on that basis, which was really a fallacious one. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mrs. Bolton. 

Mrs. BOLTON. I think you are perhaps unconsciously working with us in the idea that we are quite unable to get facts such as you bring us now as we are set up. If we had some way of sending out, say, two of our number and a staff member to really see these plans, and see them before they take place, and also afterward, we would have a more fitting and more accurate determination from it. We could really know what we are doing. It is very difficult to sit in Washington and know what is going on over in Mali or somewhere else. I think your opinion here is going to be very valuable to us. 

Thank you very much.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Farbstein. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. I want to compliment you, Mr. Wolff, on what I think is an excellent idea, an excellent thought. I think it is one that is worthy of our very sincere and mature consideration.

We have in the AID program what is known as an Executive Service Corps. These people are called upon to give advice in particular instances, but we do not have a permanent business advisory council attached to either the AID program or any other organization that has to do with foreign aid. 

The Watson committee is occasionally called in-it is now the Watson committee, tomorrow it is another committee-but we do not have I repeat, any permanent organization of business people that are connected with the AID organization. 

I think this would be very salutary so that not alone should they review as I envision it, I don't know if I am adding to your idea-

Mr. WOLFF. I would welcome it, sir. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Not only review possible loans or grants, but perhaps aid in particular instances in obtaining aid or grants. The 

AID agency working simultaneously with a business advisory council can aid each other. If one goes to the AID organization and seeks aid and is turned down, they can go to the business advisory council and have them ask why.

Conversely if it is granted, the business advisory council can advise, as you said, about Bangkok, whether the project should go forward. 

If you can work out a definitive plan, I would be glad to handle it, because I think it is an excellent one, and thank you for coming. 

Mr. WOLFF. Thank you, Mr. Farbstein.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Whalley. 

Mr. WHALLEY.  

Congressman Wolff, I think your idea is an excellent one. I have heard it suggested several times before in different ways. There always has to be a start.

Of course Government people are limited to a certain extent. 

Sometimes people in business do not realize that. I was in business myself before. I do think your plan should be given every consideration to see what could be done to at least get started along this line. 

Thank you very much. 

Mr. WOLFF. Thank you very much, Mr. Whalley.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Roybal. 

Mr. ROYBAL. I yield.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Culver. 

Mr. CULVER. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Congressman Wolff, I would also like to join my colleagues in commending you on this. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Mike. 

Mr. CULVER. I say I also would like to join my colleagues, Congressman Wolff, in commending you on what I consider to be an extremely valuable suggestion. I share your belief that we could avail ourselves in a much more constructive way than we have to date with the expertise of the remarkable business community that this Nation enjoys. I am troubled in a specific way with your suggestion, and that is the idea that in 30 days an American businessman. can completely acclimate himself to all the factors which characterize business activity and conduct in various foreign lands. I would be interested in a possible elaboration by you as to how you feel this might be accomplished, or whether in fact you feel this would be adequate time to have a historical perspective and a general understanding of the unique environments that he would be called upon to lend his recommendations and suggestions to. 

Mr. WOLFF. Certainly I thank you for your comments, Mr. Culver.

I certainly don't believe that we can get all the answers within 30 days. However, I think with adequate briefing of the individuals—I want to comment at this point on the very excellent program that the Department of Commerce has in trade mission groups, whereby they take a 5-day or 3-day briefing, and with adequate source material they are able to provide the average businessman with a thorough

grounding in the local circumstances. By assimilating this material, and actually getting out into the field, I do believe that within a month's time, and this can be elastic, I do believe within a month's time a very serious and important contribution can be made by an individual or group to the judgment of a particular project. 

I think that in addition, these business people would be able to give some part-time assistance to this program, in addition to a month of full-time activity, and this would serve to fully answer the time limitations you so rightfully question. 

Mr. CULVER. Would you envision a geographic or area specialty within the business community itself so that the knowledge over an extended period of time might be developed to where there would be great familiarity with country problems? 

Mr. WOLFF. I think that would be an excellent contribution.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Roybal. 

Mr. ROYBAL. May I also thank you for bringing this proposal before this committee. Along the line of questioning that you just had, I would like to ask this question: Do you believe that the men passing judgment on a particular loan request should also have knowledge of the economics and of the people of the recipient country? 

Mr. WOLFF. Very definitely. We, through the Department of Commerce, today already conduct market studies in the particular area where the individual plant is to be located or the individual enterprise is to be set up. I do believe that the overall economic aspects of the picture are extremely important in assessing a particular project and I do believe the State Department can adequately provide the basic general economic data required.

I am sure too that a prudent businessman would very definitely require economic and market data in depth to fully assess any proposition.

Mr. ROYBAL. I ask that question because I have had the opportunity of visiting the Chile-California program. This is a situation where men from Chile and California get together to study the economics of Chile to make recommendations for joint ventures.

If a similar situation were to develop in other countries, I think it would be probably one of the best things that could happen. Your proposal, however, calls for a permanent committee composed of a number of people who would be experts, some in Latin America, some in Asia, some in Europe, who would then pass on the loans going to those particular areas of the world, is that correct? 

Mr. WOLFF. That is correct, except the fact that the committee itself would be fairly extensive and would actually be a reserve pool of people to be called upon. It would be a permanent body. I think you, Mr. Roybal, mentioned what I consider a magic word, and that is "joint venture." I have been exposed to a great number of joint ventures in foreign lands.

I think this is one of the most effective means that we have of establishing friendly relations with countries and also establishing them in a manner that gives the local national an opportunity of exercising his own judgment, his own abilities. We are pooling resources. 

I think this is the basis of foreign assistance, the idea of pooling re-

sources with other nations. I don't think that anyone likes to go around with a cup in his hand, especially the private sector. I think we cement our relations through this vehicle. 

Mr. ROYBAL. Thank you. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Wolff, I think your suggestion has a great deal of merit and I assure you that the committee will take it into consideration when we start the markup. Section 601 of the bill, as the act is now written, provides for encouragement of free enterprise and private business. 

It includes provision for an advisory committee that is supposed to meet once a month, composed of nine people, and had an authorization of $50,000. It was to report by June 30, 1965, and was then given an extension to 1966. Is it your suggestion to go deeper in the study specific projects, or do you suggest an overall group of advisers primarily business people? This advisory committee is now made up of business, labor, and professional people. They have made a report just recently.

This advisory committee was the result of action by the other body, which after some modifications we accepted in conference. I am not sure personally that this advisory committee has been very valuable. 

They issue an elaborate report, Members of Congress read it, but I am not sure how much impact it has.

The work of this overall advisory committee for private enterprise has never convinced me that I should vote for continuing its existence. 

You have come today in front of the committee with an interesting proposal, and as Mr. Farbstein suggested, if you could expand it a little further in the form of a specific amendment and furnish it to the staff of the committee before the markup, together with a little explanation of your amendment, I am sure the committee would give serious consideration to your suggestion. 

We all feel there is, as you pointed out, a great deal of delay on the part of the Government on these projects. I agree with you that there are cases where the people who make the final decision on specific projects on foreign aid don't know too much about the type of operation that they are making the decision on. 

I suppose we will never avoid criticisms of foreign aid operations. 

During my long tenure on this committee I have heard over the years people talk about foreign aid supplying striped trousers for Grecian undertakers, iceboxes for Eskimos, collapsible toothpaste tubes. 

Critics of foreign aid have been willing to go a long way to come up with minute details about the program. 

The extreme stories get the most attention from the press. Foreign aid over a period of years has been discussed in the book "The Ugly American," and other type publications. If there is any way that by following your suggestion we could stop waste in the foreign aid program, I would be glad to have your help. 

Mr. WOLFF.  I appreciate your comments. I want you to know that I am here not as a destructive critic of foreign aid but one who really appreciates this as a great weapon in the arsenal of democracy, and I am here for constructive criticism. 

Chairman MORGAN. We welcome you here. We know of your background in business before you came to this body. We consider the testimony of yours very valuable. 60-929-66-pt. 6- -6

You have already proved to me personally that you make a very excellent Congressman. 

Mr. WOLFF. Thank you, sir.

I am sorry I was unavoidably detained. I will read my colleague's testimony. I do know from our past conversations that his suggestions are constructive.

There are organizations such as the CIPM and other business groups that are from the free enterprise area assisting underdeveloped countries. I believe that your proposals are worthy of full consideration. I also want to commend you, sir, for coming before the committee and giving your views. 

Thank you very much. 

Mr. WOLFF. Thank you, Mr. Zablocki.

THURSDAY, MAY 12, 1966 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, pursuant to adjournment, at 10:40 a.m., in room  

The committee meets this morning in open session for a continuation of the hearings on the foreign aid bills for fiscal year 1967, H.R. 

12449 and H.R. 12450. 

Our first witness this morning is Hon. Birch Bayh, Member of the 

U.S. Senate from Indiana.

Senator, earlier this year during its consideration of the supplemental authorization, your amendment was adopted in the other body. 

It was eliminated in conference. I want to put in the record at this time the statement made by the House conferees. 

(The statement follows:) 

The managers on the part of the House pointed out that the amendment before the committee of conference dealt with matters which had not received consideration by the Committee on Foreign Affairs during its consideration of the bill nor had there been any discussion during debate in the House, but they recognized that this question deserved careful consideration. Because there has not been adequate opportunity to review in detail the full impact of the Senate provision, the managers on the part of the House were unwilling to accept the Senate language, but they agreed that the Committee on Foreign Affairs should look into the whole question during the consideration of the pending foreign aid bill. 

We will be glad to hear your views today. You have a prepared statement, and you may proceed.

STATEMENT OF HON. BIRCH BAYH, U.S. SENATOR FROM THE STATE OF INDIANA 

Senator BAYH. I do have a prepared statement. I am grateful to you as chairman, and members of the committee for granting me this opportunity. I know well the close study that you and your committee are making of this important legislation and thus am able to understand why you might be reluctant to consider at this late hour the amendment which was adopted by the Senate. 

With your permission I would like to read my prepared statement and then if you have any questions. I will be glad to answer them.

Senator BAYH. Mr. Chairman, I am grateful for your letting me have a chance to appear here today to discuss the 1967 Foreign Eco nomic Assistance Authorization Act and to present an amendment for your consideration. To put my criticism of this problem in proper perspective, I would like to point out that since coming to the Senate, I have consistently voted for foreign assistance authorizations and appropriations. I have opposed certain individual programs such as assistance to Indonesia and certain military assistance programs. 

Generally, I have supported our AID program, although our foreign assistance program is not the most popular Federal program in my home State.

I believe that our foreign assistance program meets our responsibility to assist in the development of emerging and less developed nations, and at the same time to make a positive contribution to the 

U.S. foreign policy objectives.

In past weeks, I have been critical of the procurement policy of the 

Agency for International Development in the purchase of galvanized iron and steel products for South Vietnam. I have done so although our AID program is critically important to our total effort in southeast Asia.

The amendment which I propose refers to the purchase of iron and steel products for Vietnam under AID financing and is similar to one which I introduced in the Senate during its consideration of the 1966 supplemental foreign aid authorization bill. The Senate adopted the amendment without dissent, but it was removed later in a House- 

Senate conference.

At that time, representatives of the appropriate House and Senate committees pledged to give the proposal full consideration at hearings of this year's general foreign aid authorization bill. 

Although I am certain that the members of this committee are familiar with the background of this amendment, having dealt with it earlier in conference with the Senate, I will, with your indulgence, Mr. Chairman, rehearse the development of this situation for the benefit of the committee's records.

In June 1963, the Agency for International Development adopted new regulations affecting the procurement of products under supporting assistance programs, "to lessen the adverse effects of the foreign economic assistance program on the U.S. balance of payments." The policy adopted at that time not only required that the item procured with AID financing come from an eligible source, but limited to 30 percent of the f.o.b. sales price the components of the item which could originate in advanced foreign countries. Under the regulation, Korea and Taiwan continued to import and galvanize Japanese black plate for sale to Vietnamese importers under AID financing.

The Korean and Taiwanese suppliers contended that less than 30 percent of the components by value, as measured against their final sales price, came from an ineligible source-Japan-particularly since the Japanese black sheet was made in large part from U.S. scrap. 

In January 1964, AID tightened the 70/30 componentry ratio to 

90/10 that is, no more than 10 percent of the f.o.b. sales price on each item could result from components originating in advanced foreign countries. Stated another way, 90 percent of the components

in each item had to originate either from the United States or from eligible developing nations, such as Taiwan or Korea. 

Korea continued to import and galvanize Japanese black plate for export to Vietnam, rationalizing its actions by importing U.S. scrap for delivery to bonded warehouses in Japan for the purpose of making black plate to be shipped to Korea for further processing. 

In its own words, Mr. Chairman, and I quote, "AID found it increasingly difficult to police and enforce the 90/10 componentry ratio in connection with these Korean exports of galvanized steel plate and sheets to Vietnam."

So AID suspended shipments of galvanized products under AID financing from Korea to Vietnam.

On January 31, 1966, AID issued a source ruling removing its 90-10 componentry ratio requirement. This ruling had the following effects: 

1. All black plate, which ultimately would be shipped as galvanized sheets to Vietnam and paid for with AID funds, was purchased by Korea, Taiwan, or other eligible source countries from Japan providing an indirect subsidy to the steel industry of a nation in vigorous competition with our own steel industry. 

I would like to introduce into the record an exhibit showing the phenomenal increase since 1958 of U.S. imports of selected steel mill products from Japan.

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered.

Present indications are that this rate will increase considerably during 1966. 

I can say without qualification, Mr. Chairman, that we are facing similar competition from the Japanese steel industry throughout the world. I have no basic objection to this, for I am a firm advocate of free enterprise system both for ourselves and for others. But I do submit, Mr. Chairman, that our AID program is dedicated to the fundamental principle that it will not affect adversely our balance-ofpayments problem. It seems clear to me that by indirectly supporting the Japanese steel industry, AID is doing injury to its own stated goals. 

2. The January 31 memorandum in no way affected the quality of the product which originated in Japan and was galvanized in Korea. 

I will submit, at the conclusion of my remarks, a report from an independent firm employed by AID which substantiates allegations I have

made that Japanese black plate is inferior and is galvanized in Korea with insufficient quantities of zinc. The result, as you will see in the report, is that these products purchased in the past must be replaced with greater frequency than higher quality products which adds to the final cost to the American Government. 

AID officials have assured me of their agreement with me on this point and are taking steps to assure better quality in the future. It is in their credit that they are cognizant that steps need to be taken to remedy the extremely inferior quality product that was being sold. 

This product not only wasted tax dollars, but also fanned inflation since more of it had to be purchased. (The report referred to is as follows:) 

REPORT OF INSPECTION, SAIGON, MARCH 15, 1966, UNITED STATES AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT TO VIETNAM (USAID)-SAIGON GALVANIZED FLAT AND CORRUGATED IRON SHEETS ORIGINATING FROM KOREA 

At your request and for your account, but being not provided with any specific name of ship, or Receiver, or particulars relating to any special consignment, we made inquiries in Saigon and Cholon vicinities, from 9th through 14th March 1966, with a view to ascertain the average quality of Korean Galvanized Iron Sheets, flat or corrugated, at the time of delivery after unloading from ships, and also their in-use durability.

According to information picked up on the market, we wish at first to point out that most of the Galvanized Iron sheets imported from Korea to Vietnam during the last twelve months or more are flat sheets. 

What is cost of corrugating

Once received here, they are corrugated locally by several Vietnamese enterprises equipped with machines able to corrugate heaps of ten sheets in one time. whatever their thickness may be. 

It is of common knowledge that Korean factories are using raw Iron originating from Japan, where same product is processed chiefly from salvaged scrap, and therefore gives a lower quality of milled products. 

We have had good opportunities, through previous inspections on some merchandise, to ascertain that Korean Galvanized Iron Sheets were showing two main defects: (1) Iron processed with a high percentage of scrap. (2) Defectuous coating which is quickly weather-worn. 

On the other hand, it must be pointed out that Vietnamese wholesalers (most of them being of Chinese origin) are mainly interested in importing Iron Sheets of small thicknesses, since retail prices on such commodity are based on the unit and not on the weight. U.S. gauges most often specified are ranging from 20 to 34, with a higher percentage of 24, 27, 28, 29, 30. As a matter of fact, the thinner the sheets are, the poorer the quality and in-use results. 

For the present inspection, we selected three of the corrugating enterprises located as follows: 

In Saigon : n° 60/62, Ky Con St. 

In Cholon: n° 33, Van Kien St.. n° 44. Mac Cuu St. and investigated among various consignments of Korean Galvanized Iron flat sheets during the course of their corrugation.

The names of Korean Suppliers were given by the marks of each consignment, i.e. 

1°) XXX-USO #34-1m x 2n supplied by KUY DONG STEEL CO., LTD., Pusan, Korea 

2°) XD-USO #34-1m x 2n coating 0.6 oz/n-Made in Korea supplied by

SHIN HWA SILUP CO., LTD., Seoul, Korea. 

3°) Crown-USO #33-1m x 2n coating 0.6 oz/Ft2 supplied by ILSSIN IN 

DUSTRIAL CO., LTD., Seoul, Korea. 

Our findings

The sizes of sheets were comformable to specifications 1 x 2 meters. 

The thickness was rather irregular from one sheet to another, but final average was corresponding to specified U.S. gauge, although individual weight per sheet appeared slightly lower.

As a general remark available on both consignments, galvanization was irregular. All Korean factories are known to use spray-processing for Iron galvanization and we ascertained that such processing was not actually satisfactory on the inspected Iron Sheeting. Certain sheets where galvanization is defectuous were showing brightless spots which surface is slightly rough and blistered, where rust will soon appear (see attached samples and pictures). 

However, still according to importers' opinion and since they are made to import same in a highest proportion, Korean Iron sheeting is considered one grade above iron sheeting from Taiwan, which is said to be of the lowest quality. 

Among various Korean Galvanized Iron sheetings, the importers' choice is mostly fixed on "DRAGON" brand.

There is little to say about local corrugation, which is not better but not worse than any other, excepted that all defects shown on a flat sheet are stressed out once same sheet is corrugated. 

Cost of the operation is of about 1 to 1.50 piasters per sheet. Sizes after corrugation are 0.9 x 2 meters.

Then we investigated among consumers here and there in Saigon/Cholon, and requested them to show us in-use Korean Galvanized corrugated Iron sheets, and to give us their opinion about each item after a few months use. 

Most of them were complaining about short life of the sheets they have bought. chiefly during the rainy season. Owing to a rather low quality of material and often defectuous coating, all sheets used as roofs or fences are quickly losing their brightness, thus affected by rust and must be replaced within a shorter period than with Iron sheets of Western origin.

We were not in a position to check how long a Korean Galvanized Iron Sheet in use resists as compared with same item of other origin (Taiwan excepted), but all consumers we approached were unanimous to agree upon the fact that the price they pay for Korean sheeting is less than ever justified by the latter's quality and durability. (See attached samples and pictures.) 

All our inspections are carried out to the best of our knowledge and ability, but without any responsibility neither for us nor for our organization. 

M. O'CONNELL, Manager. 

Senator BAYH. I would simply reiterate that for a long period of time, Korea violated previous policy with the rationale that the Japanese-made steel contained large quantities of U.S. scrap. The Japanese black plate had a large scrap content and was considerably thinner than the thinnest stock item manufactured in the United States. 

It was galvanized in Korea with less than half the amount of zinc that would meet minimum specifications of the U.S. Bureau of Standards. Thus, on three counts, the steel sheet sold to Vietnam under 

AID financing did not meet any reasonable test of quality. 

3. As the result of the impact of the memo, the prices paid by Vietnam with AID financing for inferior products were outrageously exorbitant. Although AID had sought to avert effects on our balance of payments, using tied letters of credit to make payment to eligible countries, profits were so high that they permitted the recipients of the tied letters of credit to subvert easily the intent of these letters to the detriment of the American economy. (The prices referred to are as follows:)

Prices paid by AID for 32 gauge corrugated steel sheets: 

1963-$179 plus $16.50 freight (Korea).

Senator BAYH. In 1963, the price of a galvanized ton of steel to 

Vietnam, f.o.b. Korea, was $170. In 1964, this price boomed to $270,

and in 1965 it was lowered to $260. The year that the price rocketed upward, the cost of Japanese black plate decreased. Some of the upward cost may be attributed to monetary changes in Korea, but surely the great increase demands investigation and, in my estimation, a change in policy.

While Korea was selling a galvanized ton of 32-gage steel sheet to Vietnam for $260 plus shipping and handling, it was buying black plate from Japan for $140 a ton. Thus, Korea was adding about $120 a ton for galvanizing and handling. Now, most American companies using twice the amount of zinc per square foot and paying their labor many times the amount Korean laborers are paid-charge approximately $60 to $70 a ton for galvanizing sheet steel. In point of fact, Mr. Chairman, a galvanized ton of sheet steel from the United States, shipped directly to Saigon would cost no more-and in some cases less than the Vietnamese were paying for Japanese steel poorly galvanized in Korea and shipped to Saigon under AID financing. 

The reason underlying this odd circumstance is ensconced in documents currently classified as secret. Suffice it to say, however, that a system of kickbacks, collusion, and corruption are at the root of the problem. I would not suggest that members of the AID staff, top or bottom, are involved in this particular type of activity. The procurement system that has been followed makes it almost impossible to avoid practices which none of us want to tolerate. 

Responsible AID officials, in whom I have the greatest confidence, are making every effort to contain this situation, but I see no way in which they can succeed short of imposing artificial price ceilings on these products. Such a method is not only contrived but also does not alleviate the problem of American aid dollars flowing out of the United 

States with no residual benefit. 

4. The problems and cost of effectively policing the quality and price of Japanese-made, Korean-galvanized sheet steel, plus the problems and cost of effectively policing proper use of the tied letters of credit are so enormous as to render them impractical-if not impossible. 

This point not only is relevant to past procedures but as a useful measurement of certain proposed formulas which have come or will come to the attention of this committee. I have already quoted an official AID report on the problems of effectively policing the 90/10 componentry ratio when the galvanizing is done outside the United States. However, it seems to me more realistic to expect effective policing of the 90/10 ratio than policing the quality of products, prices, and use of letters of credit by non-American firms.

As I have tried to demonstrate regarding inflated profits, we are not dealing with businessmen who play by the rules of Marquis de Queensbury. Letters of credit can be circumvented by those who seriously seek to do so.

The most obvious means is to buy eligible American products and resell them at less than cost. This can be done because the recipients of the letters of credit already have made a killing-profits at about 60 percent higher than normal-in selling steel sheet to Vietnam. 

Thus, to turn these letters of credit into cold, hard cash, they can afford to take a small loss on the products they buy with letters of

credit and still come out profitably in the deal. In the meantime, by offering these products at prices cheaper than those quoted by American companies, they can be assured of quick sales that, in turn, close off potential markets to American firms. In this way, letters of credit do not achieve their purpose of increasing potential American iron and steel sales abroad.

The idea of tying the use of American aid dollars for purchases of American steel by use of letters of credit is a good effort made by some of our top officials in AID. I admire and respect these persons for what they are trying to accomplish. However, it seems to me if policing the previous 90/10 ratio is futile then there is small chance of policing these letters of credit.

The letter of credit, as you know, is designed to insure that any dollars received for black plate or for galvanized products in turn be used to purchase perhaps more sophisticated steel products that are produced in the United States, so that the final business comes from the United States. I have yet to see how it is going to be possible to prevent purchases of these products by holders of these letters of credit for resale to other markets. For example, Korea could purchase a steel lathe, and after it is in Korea's possession, she could ship it practically anywhere in the world and sell it in a market that had existed for an American lathe.

Again, it seems to me, this whole problem could be prevented-but only by checking every invoice, every bill of lading, every transaction involving the use of the letter of credit. There simply is no other effective way of policing the prohibition against reexport of products purchased with the letters of credit.

The proposal I am offering, Mr. Chairman, would place the purchase of iron and steel products for Vietnam back on the 90/10 componentry ratio.

In effect, it would mean that black plate or finished galvanized products would be bought from American firms-thus being assured of good quality at prices free from corruption and kickbacks. Such a policy would in no way prevent the continuation of the practice of having black plate galvanized in Korea-providing that the Koreans met improved standards for galvanization and charged reasonable prices for their services.

It is important to recognize significant contributions being made by the Korean Government to our war effort in Vietnam. Thousands of Korean soldiers are fighting alongside American troops and Vietnamese soldiers. We must continue to support efforts of the Korean 

Government to improve the economy and welfare of its people. Reports of the fine conduct and high caliber of the Korean troops in the field are noteworthy.

It should be made clear that since 1949, the United States has provided economic assistance to Korea in excess of $2.5 billion. We should certainly continue to contribute generously to the welfare of the Korean people. In the present bill there is a significant amount contained for such purposes in the future. I don't need to go into detail as to the sacrifice made by American families to make it possible for the Koreans to enjoy freedom.

Mr. Chairman, I have supported our foreign aid program with only a few exceptions, primarily in the area of military aid to certain nations.

It has always been my belief that foreign aid, properly administered, is in the best interests of the people of the United States as well as the people who benefit directly.

In regard to Vietnam, I am doubly sympathetic with our aid program, for I agree with the President of the United States, that the Vietnam question will never be solved through military action alone, but with a determined effort to oppose all the forces and conditions suitable for communism-whether the form of Vietcong terrorists, North Vietnamese regulars, or hunger, poverty, and disease among the people of South Vietnam.

Let us not overlook the fact that the latter, traditional enemies of mankind, are equally a threat to peace and freedom as an armed aggressor.

The United States, in its supporting assistance program, seeks to bolster the free economy of South Vietnam. It does not seek to manage the economy nor does it seek to dictate economic goals or economic policy. Our commercial import program has not been geared to provide what Americans thought necessary for the economy of 

South Vietnam, but to provide what the Vietnamese market demands.

This philosophy must be maintained. It is important, however, that careful scrutiny be given to the type and quantity of commodities being licensed under the commercial import program. If we are not careful, products entering Vietnam with our support may reflect the desires of those Vietnamese motivated by quick, high profits rather than the needs of the people.

For example, when the Vietnamese were using very thin corrugated roofing which deteriorated very rapidly, it would have to be replaced at least twice as fast as thicker-grade roofing. In Vietnam they buy the product by the ton, fabricate the roofing and sell it by the sheet. 

The thinner the sheet the greater the profit per ton. Importers and others who sell this roofing have a vested interest in a thin product. 

I don't think the U.S. Government should contribute to such projects. 

Much more attention must be paid to the priorities given to goods flowing into Vietnam under the commercial import program to insure that the limited financial resources of Vietnam and its overtaxed transportation system will be devoted only to those goods which will be important to the welfare and progress of the Vietnamese people. 

As our military effort has increased in South Vietnam, so has our economic assistance increased. The bill now being considered by this committee would authorize economic assistance for Vietnam far greater than our efforts in any other part of the world. Supporting assistance for South Vietnam is requested in an amount even greater than fiscal year 1966.

The supporting assistance has grown from $216 million in fiscal 1965 to $532 million in fiscal 1966, and is now projected in excess of $550 million for fiscal 1967. As U.S. involvement has grown militarily, it is understandable that our economic involvement also would grow. 

We in Congress recognize the administrative problems that must inevitably result from this rapid increase in AID spending. The AID staff in Saigon has been taxed to its limits and has been unable to oversee properly the level of AID financing. Until recently, just one man staffed the commercial import program. Now fewer than 10-

I think the last report indicated only 6-are engaged in overseeing a commercial import program of $300 million. 

I have tried to demonstrate the problems which have resulted relating to a single commodity representing less than 10 percent of the commercial import program. There are other examples and other problems, Mr. Chairman, that the committee might care to look into at a later date.

Secretary Rusk disclosed recently that certain chemicals imported into Vietnam under AID financing were possibly falling into the hands of the Vietcong for use as explosives.

I learned recently that a Vietnamese businessman was using a highgrade tinplate imported under special priorities for specific use in canning food to manufacture footlockers and trunks for sale to American servicemen. Specifications for products for which licenses are requested under the commercial import program are required to be filed for review by the mission in Saigon prior to issuance of licenses, but it is virtually impossible to make any systematic, thorough review. 

Several men without proper data processing facilities cannot establish and maintain quality and price standards for $300 million worth of diverse commodities. We must recognize that our operation in 

Vietnam today is of such scope that the most sophisticated management techniques, procedures, and equipment are required to insure proper administration.

I know that the Agency is making a concerted effort to add staff to the Saigon mission, but today there are still less than 10 men attempting to control a $300 million program. I recommend that the committee provide authorization for whatever staff and equipment are necessary for the proper administration of our foreign assistance program in Vietnam. The manpower and equipment required to manage effectively the foreign assistance program must be provided. 

Mr. Chairman, as I have advocated an amendment to assure that 

American dollars expended for steel products in our AID program for Vietnam will flow back into the American economy, I have also advocated that steps be taken to spend slightly more money to insure that our huge assistance program is effectively supervised. This small investment will pay for itself many times over. 

I am old-fashioned enough to believe that there is little to be gained from being penny-wise, yet pound-foolish. Just as each of us believes that no expense should be spared so that our fighting men in Vietnam have the best possible equipment, we should see to it that our people there who are fighting the quiet war against want are adequately equipped. 

We must win our objectives on both fronts, Mr. Chairman, if we are to bring about a peace that will bring our boys home to us soon.

3. $280.44 to $310.44. 

4. $306.50 to $336.50. 

5. $300 to $330.00. 

6. $309 to $339.50.

COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C., March 22, 1966.

Hon. DAVID E. BELL, 

Administrator, Agency for International Development, Washington, D.C. 

DEAR MR. BELL: The discussion of the Bayh amendment to H.R. 12169, supplemental foreign assistance authorization for fiscal year 1966, and its consideration by the Committee of Conference indicate the desirability of a comprehensive review of the procurement of iron and steel products for Vietnam and of the supplying of such products to Vietnam by Korean manufacturers.

It is essential that the Committee on Foreign Affairs have a more complete report of the facts with respect to these matters, and I believe that the Agency for International Development is in a better position to collect this information in a short time than anyone else.

Would you undertake to submit to us everything you regard as significant, including analyses of the following issues: 

1. Could galvanized sheets of satisfactory quality financed by the United States be obtained more cheaply from any other source or under any other arrangement? 

2. Is the galvanizing industry a more effective vehicle for stimulating the 

Korean economy in terms of creating employment or developing manufacturing facilities, or for political impact, than other industries or operations to which the 

United States might give preferred treatment? 

3. Is the United States steel industry getting a significant volume of business from Korea as a result of the restricted letters of credit now being issued? 

4. What would be the impact on the United States steel industry in terms of production and of jobs if means could be found to arrange for procurement in the United States of the galvanized sheets required for Vietnam or of the steel for galvanizing in Korea or elsewhere in the Far East? 

5. Under the regulations now in effect, is competition with Korea for the Vietnamese market for galvanized sheets developing? Is it likely that such competition may have an adverse economic or political effect on Korea? If Korea loses its present "monopoly," will it be necessary for the United States to work out some other special arrangement to attain our political or economic objectives for Korea?

Your analysis and recommendations on this entire subject will be appreciated. 

Sincerely yours,

THOMAS E. MORGAN, Chairman. 

DEPARTMENT OF STATE, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT, OFFICE OF THE ADMINISTRATOR, 

Washington, D.C., May 12, 1966.

Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, Chairman, Committee on Foreign Affairs, 

House of Representatives, Washington, D.C.

DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: We have examined the matters raised in your letter of March 22, 1966 concerning the Bayh Amendment on procurement of galvanized iron products for Vietnam while working on a resolution of the problems in this element of our program. 

Historically, sources of galvanized iron products under the A.I.D. commercial import program for Vietnam have been in the Far East, because the suppliers are nearby and the cost of transportation is low. A.I.D. has, however, been progressively restricting sources for supply. At first, any free world country was eligible, then the industrial countries (such as Japan) were eliminated. 

Very recently the list was further restricted to only nine less-developed countrie's which have agreed to accept payment by tied letters of credit. Under this arrangement, all dollars earned by the supplier country must be spent in the United States. In addition to the above, A.I.D. also sought to enforce a requirement that 70 percent-later changed to 90 percent-of the value of an item sold by eligible countries must have originated therein or in the United States. 

It was this last requirement which posed a problem in the sale of galvanized sheets to Vietnamese importers by Korea and the Republic of China. The 

Koreans argued that they were complying with the purposes of the 90 percent rule by buying iron scrap in the United States to be used in making iron sheet in Japan, and additional U.S. scrap to pay much of the Japanese fabricating cost. 

The arrangement was not acceptable to A.I.D., however, because: (1) it was not clear that the additional scrap was additive to normal U.S. exports: (2) it was extremely difficult to police; and (3) Korea was the only eligible Far 

Eastern country to devise this means of claiming compliance with the 90 percent rule and had, therefore, no Far Eastern competition on galvanized products to keep its prices down.

We suspended further A.I.D. financing of Korean galvanized products in 

November 1965 until we could work out what we considered a more satisfactory arrangement. In January, we devised and issued a new procurement regulation on this commodity for Vietnam only. Under the new policy, we limited the sources for galvanized sheets sold to Vietnam under A.I.D. commercial

import financing to (1) the United States, which is always eligible; and (2) to those Far Eastern countries which accept letters of credit tied to purchase of iron and steel machine tools, metal-working machines and a limited amount of steel scrap from the United States.

Under the new A.I.D. procedure, Korea could purchase its iron sheet for galvanizing from Japan, but every A.I.D. dollar earned on sales to Vietnam of galvanized products must be spent by Korea in the United States for iron and steel products, including tools with high iron and steel content or a small amount of iron and steel scrap.

In devising the new procedure, which was on a trial basis, A.I.D. had in mind five principal considerations: (1) the need for nearby sources of roofing and other products at delivered prices that would not feed inflation in Vietnam; (2) the desire to permit Korea, which is making a major contribution to our military effort in Vietnam, to at least have a chance to continue sales to that country; (3) protection of the U.S. balance of payments; (4) promotion of U.S. steel exports; and (5) competitive, fair prices.

We considered and rejected the alternative of insisting that Korean or other Far East suppliers use only U.S. blackplate in the galvanized products, because (a) this would substantially raise galvanized product prices they could quoteprobably above the high U.S. prices on galvanized products-and, consequently, (b) might cause the Vietnamese Government to finance these imports with its own foreign exchange, with all this business going to the lowest price source, Japan. In either event, this would effectively deny Korea continued sales to 

Vietnam at a time it was considering doubling its 20,000 man troop commitment to Vietnam.

As a result of intensive investigations made by A.I.D. in the Far East, we have concluded that prior actions taken by this Agency needed to be supplemented by even more restrictive measures. We have recently instituted the following measures to complement and supplement the procedure established in January, 1966: (1) galvanized iron and steel products now must meet U.S. commercial standards of 1.25 oz. of zinc coating per sq. foot; (2) the items must be inspected by an independent testing and inspection agency in the source country; (3) the bidding and award system is to be so arranged to preclude collusion between suppliers or suppliers and importers; (4) fifty percent value must be from the 

United States; (5) price must be reasonable and honestly competitive: (6) Far

East suppliers must have an opportunity to make offers, but if successful will receive payment under A.I.D.'s restricted tide letter of credit procedure, with scrap, however, eliminated. A copy of our new procedure is enclosed. 

We believe the revised procedure is the best means of serving several United States interests in this matter. It will take some time before the tied letters of credit are translated into orders for U.S. iron and steel products. When these orders do start flowing, they will inevitably increase our iron and steel and tool exports to countries which have been only minor customers of these U.S. industries. Since it is estimated that A.I.D.-financed commercial imports of galvanized sheet by Vietnam will total $25 million, in calendar 1966. a substantial boost will be given U.S. iron and steel and tool exports when the tied A.I.D. payments to Far Eastern suppliers are spent in the United States. 

The following are answers to your specific questions: 

1. "Could galvanized sheets of satisfactory quality financed by the United

States be obtained more cheaply from any other source or under any other arrangement?"

No, unless we are willing to finance procurement from Japan. With respect to the 50 percent of the business allocated to the United States alone under our revised rules, we could obtain sheet more cheaply from Far Eastern sources, if they were permitted to use Japanese blackplate. 

2. "Is the galvanizing industry a more effective vehicle for stimulating the 

Korean economy in terms of creating employment or developing manufacturing facilities, or for political impact, than other industries or operations to which the United States might give preferred treatment?"

In connection with question 2, I invite your attention to the "Report of the 

Special Study Mission to the Far East, Southeast Asia, India, and Pakistan, No vember 7-December 12, 1965," under the Chairmanship of Congressman Clement

J. Zablocki. This report to the House Foreign Affairs Committee recommends 

(at page 13): "The United States should do everything possible to develop and expand Korea's export market, including items produced in Korea which might be valuable to the U.S. military and economic effort in Vietnam."

After listing illustrative items which might be furnished by Korea, the Report concludes, "Some [items] might successfully find commercial markets in Vietnam or be purchased through U.S. aid programs in Vietnam. Responsible U.S. officials should thoroughly explore these possibilities." 

A cessation of A.I.D.-financed purchases would deprive Korea of all exports of galvanized products. The Korean industry has no export possibilities except 

A.I.D.-financed purchases because the highly efficient Japanese industry can undersell any competitor in the Far East. The point which distinguishes the galvanizing trade from others in Korea is that it has had the Vietnam business; 

Korea would be deprived of a chance to continue to bid for its continuance in the absence of the new A.I.D. procedure. 

3. "Is the United States steel industry getting a significant volume of business from Korea as a result of the restricted letters of credit now being issued?" 

The U.S. steel industry will get the benefit of whatever galvanized products sales are made to Vietnam by Far East countries. All dollars these countries earn will return to the U.S. to buy U.S. iron and steel, machine tools and tools with a high steel component. No effect can be yet demonstrated because no transactions have been executed under this system. 

4. "What would be the impact of the United States steel industry in terms of production and of jobs if means could be found to arrange for procurement in the United States of the galvanized sheets required for Vietnam or of the steel for galvanizing in Korea or elsewhere in the Far East?" 

If all the procurement of either black sheet or the finished galvanized sheet for Vietnam were directed to the United States it would certainly require some additional man-hours of U.S. labor but we cannot quantify the number of additional jobs. U.S. sheet production (and galvanizing) is highly automated. It is our belief, however, that the manufactured iron and steel products and tools which must be purchased in the United States, with the dollar earnings of Far East suppliers of galvanized products to Vietnam, will involve considerably more labor and have greater impact in terms of production. 

5. "Under the regulation now in effect, is competition with Korea for the Vietnamese market for galvanized sheets developing? Is it likely that such competition may have an adverse economic or political effect on Korea? If Korea loses its present 'monopoly,' will it be necessary for the United States to work out some other special arrangement to attain our political or economic objectives for Korea?"

Korea had competition on tenders received in Saigon on March 31 and April 4, from Taiwan, Thailand, Singapore, and the United States. (No business has been awarded under these tenders, which will have to be rebid under the new procedure.)

Although Korea will lose its recent Far East monopoly advantage, we doubt seriously that it will lose a sufficient amount of the market to require the United States to work out a compensating special arrangement to attain our political or economic objectives in Korea. We have responded to Korea's requests to be an eligible source of supply, and have permitted it to bid for sales under its existing pattern of trade. rather than to requests for an exclusive position in the market. In fact, the new system is designed to provide Far Eastern competition for Korean galvanized products, in order to assure reasonable prices. 

Provision for Korean opportunities to bid under the circumstances described, even with U.S. and Far Eastern competition, will be a sufficient response to reasonable Korean export promotion ambitions as far as galvanized product sales to Vietnam are concerned. 

If you desire further information or clarification, please let me know. 

Sincerely yours,

DAVID E. BELL. 

GALVANIZED SHEET PROCEDURE 

The following procedure has been devised to meet the criteria for supply of galvanized iron and steel sheet: 

1. Quality must be acceptable to U.S. standards. 

2. Price must be reasonable and honestly competitive. 

3. Fifty percent of the dollar value must be from U.S. sources. 

4. Far East suppliers must have an opportunity to make offers but if successful will receive payment in letters of credit requiring all dollar earnings be spent in the U.S. for iron and steel products and machine tools.

It is proposed that: 

1. All Vietnam commercial import requirements of galvanized iron and steel sheet shall comply to ASTM Specification A-525-64T under coating class desig nated as 1.25 oz. commercial, subject to inspection at source by an independent inspection company. 

2. No sheet thinner than gauge 31 shall be eligible for A.I.D. financing. 

3. Procurement of galvanized iron and steel sheet shall be under formal bidding, the sealed bids to be opened in the presence of an A.I.D. observer, but otherwise privately. 

4. The Director of Commercial Aid will aggregate requests for quotations received from Vietnamese importers and divide them into two gauge groups as nearly as possible equal in dollar value. He will then issue two invitations for bid: (a) U.S. only for the thicker (lower numbered) gauges, and (b) U.S. and eligible Far East sources for the thinner group. All Far East suppliers would be paid on basis of Small Business Memo 64-4A-26, March 29, 1966, including the restricted tied letter of credit except that scrap would be eliminated as eligible commodity under the tied letter of credit and from the blacksheet requirement. 

5. Invitations for bids will require that each bidder forward: (a) One set of sealed bids to DCA. (b) One duplicate set of bids to A.I.D., Washington, D.C. 

6. The DCA will receive offers, open bids in private, but with USAID/Vietnam present, tabulate and evaluate prices and quantities. 

7. When the bids are received A.I.D. will furnish to DCA a confidential ceiling price established for each gauge on the date bids are due or thereafter. Any 

Far East bidder's price quotation in excess of this pre-established ceiling will be automatically rejected. 8. The DCA will quote prices by gauge and secure confirmation and earnest money from each Vietnamese importer of the total tonnage of each gauge he will accept. The DCA will not then disclose suppliers or source countries. 

9. On basis of these confirmed tonnages, the Director of Commercial Aid will: (a) Determine lowest cost offers. (b) Allocate not less than fifty percent of the dollar value of the total business to low bidder among the U.S. bidders. (c) Allocate balance to low bidders among the Far East suppliers. In the event that there are insufficient U.S. bids to total half the business, the DCA shall award to Far East bidders an amount not exceeding the amount awarded to the U.S. A second bid invitation, again split 50-50, maybe required. In order to balance U.S. and Far East awards, the DCA may split a gauge between sources. If so, he will average or blend the prices and split the sheet supplied each importer. (d) Open letters of credit in favor of successful bidders, including among provisions of the letters of credit: (1) Instructions to suppliers to consign shipments to DCA. (2) Requirement for an inspection certificate from an independent inspection company if merchandise originates in a non-U.S. source country. 

10. After contractual arrangements have been completed, including issuance of letters of credit to successful bidders, all participating bidders will be sent copies of notices of awards. Such notices will be publicly displayed by the DCA and will be furnished to USAID/Vietnam in sufficient copies for transmittal of one set to A.I.D., Washington, D.C.

11. When shipments have been made by the supplier, DCA will notify participating importers in a timely manner of the anticipated arrival of the merchandise, will arrange for deposit of balance of counterpart to the extent this deposit has not already been covered by payment of earnest money, and license assignment of the merchandise to the importers following clearance through customs. 

12. USAID/Vietnam would advise GVN and importers that if irregularities are found in this procedure, we reserve the right to insist on U.S. procurement authorities handling entire import of galvanized sheet.
