STATEMENT OF HON. WILLIAM S. GAUD, DEPUTY ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, I have, Mr. Chairman. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Will the gentleman yield, Mr. Chairman?

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mrs. Bolton? 

Mrs. BOLTON. I just want to say publicly that I regret very much that you have been scheduled a second time at the latter part of the morning. I would hope if we don't finish today, we give you a really better place to present things we do want from you and that we need very much. 

Mr. GAUD. Thank you, Mrs. Bolton. 

Mrs. BOLTON. You don't have to comment on that. 

Mr. GAUD. Shall I go ahead with my prepared statement, Mr. Chairman? 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. If you will, sir. 

Mr. GAUD. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, as you know, over 90 percent of all the commodities financed by the Agency for International Development are now bought in the United States. 

This is in sharp contrast to the situation which existed in 1960, when only 49 percent were bought here.

The problem which is now before you arises out of the less than 10 percent of our commodity purchases which are made overseas. More specifically, it arises from our commercial import program in Vietnam, which accounts for the bulk of our offshore procurement. 

The commercial import program provides Vietnam with dollars to finance the importation of essential goods required by the Vietnamese in excess of their own foreign exchange capabilities. These imports absorb the greatly expanded market demand resulting from the war effort which, if not met, would create dangerous inflation. The imported goods are paid for by Vietnamese businessmen, and then sold in local currency.

3 Galvanized sheets are one of the principal items financed by the Vietnam commercial import program-approximately $20 million is the estimate for fiscal year 1966.

If I may depart from my prepared statement for a moment, when Senator Bayh was testifying here last Thursday, he estimated the business in galvanized sheets in Vietnam at $50 million for this coming year. Frankly, we can't fit that figure into the facts. We see licenses for $20 million for fiscal year 1966, rising perhaps as high as $25 million for calendar year 1966, and neither in terms of past business nor what we see to be the future business do we think it will grow to anything like as much as $50 million this year. 

These sheets are used by the Vietnamese primarily for roofing. Beginning in 1963, Korean galvanizers developed a substantial market for these sheets in Vietnam, using Japanese blackplate as a basic component. In June 1963, for balance-of-payments reasons, AID adopted a "componentry rule" restricting to 30 percent the material in finished products which could come from a source other than the supplier country or the United States. In January 1964, again for balance-of-payments reasons, AID adopted a 90/10 componentry rule which restricted to 10 percent the material which could come from a source other than the supplier country or the United States. 

This ruled out the use of Japanese blackplate. A Korean galvanizer who attempted to use U.S. blackplate found he could only sell his galvanized sheets at a loss.

In May 1965, the Koreans worked out a new procedure which they asserted complied with the AID componentry rule. Under this procedure, they bought U.S. iron and steel scrap and in effect bartered it to Japan to pay for most of the cost of Japanese blackplate which they then galvanized and sold to Vietnam. After extended discussions, we told the Koreans that this did not meet the 90/10 rule. 

We therefore ordered suspension of procurement of galvanized sheet from Korea on November 1, 1965.

This suspension came just at the time that the Korean Government sent its Tiger Division to fight in Vietnam. In February 1966, the 

Vietnamese Government asked for a second Korean division, plus a combat brigade. Shortly thereafter the Korean Government agreed to send these additional troops to Vietnam.

The Koreans have for several years been mounting an intense export drive, which is reducing their need for U.S. aid. They are naturally eager to maintain and expand their sales to Vietnam. 

We believe and we acknowledged to the Korean Governmentthat it is reasonable for Korea, a developing country and an ally which will soon have 40,000 troops in Vietnam, to have an opportunity to compete for some of the U.S.-financed procurement supporting the war effort. Galvanized products represent at least threefourths of Korea's present total exports to Vietnam. This is business that Korea has had. Enforcement of AID's 90/10 componentry rule would have cut off this business at a most inopportune time. We therefore decided to adopt a new procedure for the procurement of galvanized sheets which would permit Korea to bid for the businessand if they got it-to be paid in dollars which could only be spent in the United States for iron and steel products or a limited amount of steel scrap. To assure competition, we offered the same opportunity to several other Far East countries as well as the U.S. industry.

When we announced this new procurement policy, Senator Bayh raised several objections. He cited information indicating that the quality of galvanized sheet from Far Eastern sources had been poor, and that prices paid were higher in some instances than appeared reasonable in the light of the suppliers' costs. He also urged us to reinstate the 90/10 componentry rule which would have prohibited the use of Japanese blackplate and instead to require the use of U.S. blackplate by Far Eastern galvanizers. 

We undertook investigations on these three issues and other aspects of the problem. During these investigations and up to the present time we have not financed any galvanized sheets under the procedure challenged by Senator Bayh. In other words, the matter has been in suspension since November 1, 1965. Our investigation confirmed that many of the sheets had been of poor quality. This resulted primarily from inadequate specifications provided by Vietnamese importers. We now intend to deal with this deficiency by eliminating thinner gage sheets and by requiring zinc coating meeting U.S. commercial standards as defined by the American Society for Testing Materials. We will also require that an independent testing agent certify compliance with these standards at the source prior to shipment to Vietnam.

At the last hearing on Thursday, a number of the members of this committee asked Senator Bayh if he thought that we had dealt satisfactorily with this question of quality. This is obviously an important question. We are grateful to Senator Bayh for having raised it. 

We feel that we have gone 100 percent of the way to meet his objections, and I would like to call the committee's attention to the exhibit annexed to my statement. It is headed "Galvanized Sheet Procedure," following page 7 of my statement. If you look about one-third of the way down the first page there, you will see our proposal on quality. 

And it provides that all Vietnam commercial import requirements of galvanized iron and steel sheet shall comply to ASTM specificationsthat is the American Society for Testing Materials Specifications- 

A-525-64-T, under coating class designated as 1.25 ounces commercial, subject to inspection at source by an independent inspection company. 

In other words, we have issued, we did this a month ago, a very specific requirement that any further galvanized sheets which are imported into Vietnam must meet this specific requirement of the American Society for Testing Materials and before anything may be shipped into Vietnam, it must be tested and inspected by an independent inspection company. I don't see how we could be more precise, more specific. I respectfully submit that there just isn't any question in the case from here out about quality. Whether this comes from Korea, whether it comes from the United States or whether it comes from anywhere else, it all has to meet this very specific requirement which is an American requirement. 

With respect to the prices we found indications of possible collusion and kickbacks by suppliers to Vietnamese buyers. Our new rules will guard against this in several ways. We will require that procurement invitations and awards be managed by a single Vietnamese authority with official U.S. participation, so as to prevent contact between supplier and buyer. We also will set reasonable price ceilings above which awards will not be made.

1013

With respect to source, we have considered three alternatives: requiring procurement only from the United States, or requiring the use of U.S. black plate, or requiring that procurement be split between 

United States and Far Eastern suppliers.

We concluded that a shift to total U.S. procurement would not only deny Korea the opportunity to bid but also would greatly increase the cost of galvanized sheets at a time when we are trying to check inflation in Vietnam. Our cost analysis indicated that if we insisted on the use of U.S. black plate, Korean suppliers could not deliver galvanized sheets to Saigon at prices competitive with U.S. galvanized sheets. Consequently, this alternative would exclude Korea from a chance to compete unless we barred U.S. galvanizers from competition. 

This we are not prepared to do. 

The third alternative was to require that some part of the business be directed exclusively to the United States. We have decided to adopt this alternative, requiring that at least half of the galvanized sheet by value be bought from the United States. To the extent that Far 

Eastern countries obtain the other half of the business, they will be paid in dollars which can be spent only in the United States and only for iron and steel products including machinery, but excluding scrap. 

Thus, although U.S. industry will not be guaranteed all of the Vietnamese market for galvanized sheet, it will get at least half directly and will get indirectly an amount of business equal to the remainder through sales of other iron and steel products to the countries earning these tied AID dollars.

Attached to this statement is a detailed outline of our new procedure. In summary, it will insure that— (1) All AID dollars spent on galvanized sheets for Vietnam will remain in the United States and be spent on U.S. iron and steel products. (2) U.S. galvanizers will obtain 50 percent of the galvanized sheet business and will be eligible to compete for 100 percent of it. 

U.S. iron and steel and machinery manufacturers will ultimately receive business on the balance through tied letters of credit. (3) Eligible Far Eastern countries such as Korea, Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, and Thailand will be able to compete for 50 percent of the business and use black plate from any free world source galvanized by them. These countries will be paid not in free dollars, but in a specially restricted tied letter of credit which can be used only for the purchase of U.S.-produced iron and steel products, including machine tools. (4) U.S. "commercial" grade quality standards will be required as a minimum from all sources, with independent inspection before shipment. (5) We will finance only U.S.-produced gages, up through 31. (6) We will insist on procurement on an aggregate basis, managed by a Vietnamese Government authority with U.S. Government participation in the award decisions. (7) AID will not finance purchases at prices above those it determines to be reasonable. (8) Existing offers made to Vietnamese importers will be rejected, and all new business will be conducted on the basis of our new procedure.

1014

We believe the revised procurement arrangements are fair and meet our various objectives. We will keep this matter under constant review, and will adjust our procedures as may be necessary to protect U.S. interests. We do not believe that a highly complicated and technical administrative matter such as this need be dealt with by legislation.

I will be glad to respond to your questions. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you, Mr. Gaud.

Your statement today reassures the committee that a new procurement formula covering galvanized sheets has been initiated because of the complaints and questions raised about past procedures. The question still remains, Why has not AID followed these procedures or plans or formulas in the first instance? Why should complaints have to be made before AID corrects its procedures?

Mr. GAUD. There are several points on that, Mr. Chairman. As far as the quality is concerned, we walked into a market where the Vietnamese were already buying galvanized sheet according to their own specifications from the Koreans and others, and we took the market as we found it. We did not feel that it was incumbent on usor that it was desirable to move in and insist upon American specifications. As time went on and when Senator Bayh called our attention to these questions of quality, we concluded that we had made a mistake and that we should change our standards.

As far as price is concerned, the same thing. When we looked further into this, we found that there was good basis for his complaint and we decided we should take action to rectify it. 

Now, as to why we didn't do this sooner, why we didn't discover it sooner, you raise a question there which is very pertinent and which applies to much of our Vietnamese program. It has increased, as this committee knows, enormously within the last 6 to 8 to 9 months. This is particularly true of the commercial import program. We have had a very difficult time recruiting people to go to Vietnam. We have increased our staff considerably in the last 6 months. We are still working on increasing it. We are spending a lot of time recruiting for it. And I am frank to say that we have not had in Vietnam in the past enough people to manage this program the way it ought to be managed. We are getting geared up and in the future, I think we will do a better job, I am confident we will do a better job on these things than we have done in the past. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. On page 2, you refer to the Koreans working out a procedure which we found was in violation of our 90/10 componentry rule. But what about the charge that the Koreans and the Chinese have violated the 70/30 and 90/10 import rule for several years?

Mr. GAUD. I don't think that that charge is substantiated by the facts, Mr. Chairman. We put the 70/30 componentry rule into effect in June 1963. Prior to that time, there was no such rule and the 

Koreans were selling the sheets to the Vietnamese perfectly legally and perfectly properly. Between July and December of 1963 for the first 6 months after the 70/30 rule was issued, no licenses were issued for AID-financed galvanized sheet from Korea or from Taiwan. In 

January 1964, we adopted the 90/10 rule and similarly, except for deliveries under prior contracts, issued before the componentry rule went into effect, no licenses were issued under the 70/30 rule. Later in 1964, the Koreans attempted to get back into the market by using

U.S. black plate. They couldn't they weren't competitive, they lost money. And there were no further Korean sales to Vietnam other than a few small deliveries using U.S. black plate until 1965. 

They then started under this procedure that I outlined in my statement, when the Koreans bought scrap from the United States, sent this to Japan, and in theory, it was used in making up the Japanese black plate which was then exported to Korea and made up into galvanized sheets for shipment to Vietnam. That procedure was followed for a number of months. We discovered it and we ruled that it did not meet the componentry rule. So the fact of the matter is that the violations of the componentry rule were over a limited period of time and did not extend over a period of several years. In the case of 

China, orders in violation of the 90/10 rule were placed, only from the fall of 1964 until March 1965, when we suspended them.

There is only one issue left in this case, and that is: Is all of the business to go to the U.S. industry or isn't it? Now, U.S. industry basically has only one factor to consider. They would like to have the business, and I don't blame them. And the same thing is true for the Steel Workers: they would like to have the business. 

We, on the other hand, have several things to keep in mind. One, we want at least some of it to go to U.S. business, no question about that. We also have to worry about the price of galvanized sheets in 

Vietnam, because of the inflationary situation there. If we give all the business to U.S. industry, those prices will go a good deal higher than they are now. Third, we have to consider the fact that the 60-929-66- -10

Koreans had this business and should we take away from them at this particular time when we are trying-and I am talking now of the AID program and U.S. policy-when we are trying to help Korea build an export trade. It doesn't seem to us that we should. 

Now, what is the solution? The answer, as we see it, and the answer that we have come up here with, is that we will award some of the business to U.S. industry. We will go ahead and encourage the 

Koreans to bid, give them an opportunity to bid-we are not going to award them any business out of hand; they will have an opportunity to bid for the balance. 

If, however, they are awarded contracts, we will require that the money, the dollars which they earn with those contracts are spent, not only in the United States, but for iron and steel products to be exported to Korea. Now, the significance of that is that in 1965, in the first 10 months of 1965, Korea bought 79 percent of her iron and steel products from Japan and 16 percent from Western Europe. She brought only $1.3 million worth of iron and steel products from the 

United States.

Now, if Korea should get 50 percent of this business, which I have estimated at something like $20 million for the year, if she should get $10 million worth of this business, she will be paid in special letters of credit which she must spend in the United States for iron and steel products. And that will mean that instead of Korea buying only $1.3 million of iron and steel products from the United States, she will buy $10 million worth of iron and steel products from the United States. 

So that we do give additional business to U.S. industry and we do at the same time enable Korea to stay in the business. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Well, this proposal, I presume, has been presented to the other side; has it not? 

Mr. GAUD. Well, we presented this proposal to Senator Bayh. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. And he wouldn't buy it?

Mr. GAUD. He would not buy it. We think it is a fair proposal. 

We don't see how we can go any further. This is it, as far as we are concerned. We don't see how we can fairly go any further and meet the various objectives that we have to consider. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Well now, the basis for his objection, evidently, doesn't appear tenable to you? 

Mr. GAUD. No, sir; they do not. His objection, I think I can say it accurately, is that he believes that the United States should get all the business.

 SHIPPING TO NORTH VIETNAM 

While free world shipping to North Vietnam has declined sharply since the fall of 1965, Communist-flag shipping has increased slowly from its already substantial level in the spring and summer of 1965. 

The monthly average number of free world arrivals for the last quarter of 1965 and the first quarter of 1966 was about 13. The average number of Communist-flag arrivals for the corresponding period (last quarter of 1965 and first quarter of 1966) was considerably higher.

Cargoes arriving at North Vietnamese ports on free world ships have been nonstrategic and small-primarily fertilizer, soft coal, some foodstuffs and consumer goods. Many of the free world ships going to North Vietnam in recent

months have arrived in ballast, their assignment being to pick up anthracite coal at the ports of Hong Gay or Cam Pha.

Communist-flag ships, on the other hand, have been carrying a wide range of items essential for North Vietnam's economy and the maintenance of its industry. its transport and communications systems. These cargoes have ranged from rice, sugar, and fertilizer to POL, motor vehicles, structural steel, machinery and spare parts, and pharmaceuticals. Deck cargoes of motor vehicles (primarily trucks) on Soviet ships have been photographed by the U.S. Navy and some pictures have been released to the U.S. press. (Further classified information also has been made available to the Committee.)

Mr. HAMILTON. Now, let me go to one other, because I know we have time pressure here. Is my understanding correct that you proposed these new procedures only after Senator Bayh made the criticisms that he did? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes. 

Mr. HAMILTON. You said a moment ago-I hope you will pardon me here for coming to the defense of my Senator-that his only interest was the United States get all of the steel business. 

It seems to me his interest extends a good bit beyond that. A major part of that interest is to see that these imports are adequately policed and carried out. Wouldn't you grant that? 

Mr. GAUD. That is right. I think, sir-forgive me, I meant to say, and I hope I said, that the only issue remaining today is whether the U.S. industry will get the whole business. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Yes, but doesn't that assume that the quality and the price that you have said are of the three issues, in fact, adequately policed?

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir; it does.

Mr. HAMILTON. The history is that this has not been adequately policed; right?

Mr. GAUD. We have had a lot of trouble; yes. But we haven't operated under this procedure before. If we can't enforce this procedure, we are going to run into trouble again; you are quite right. 

Mr. HAMILTON. May I express my own concern that you have taken on a tremendous burden of policing here, it seems to me, in looking over the points you set out on page 6 of your statement. How many men are you going to require to get that done? 

Mr. GAUD. Well, I don't agree that the burden is that great. As far as the quality is concerned, requiring conformance with the specifications that we refer to here, this is no different from any other requirement that American specifications be met.

As far as the other thing is concerned, the business of the letter of credit, I don't think Senator Bayh understands how this thing works, Mr. Hamilton, and I think that is why he is worried that we can't enforce it. What actually happens here is, if this procedure goes into effect, the Korean manufacturer ships his goods to Vietnam, and he is paid by his own government in won, in Korean currency. We then deposit dollars in a U.S. bank to the credit of the Korean Government and those dollars can only be spent for iron and steel products. 

Mr. GAUD. Well, there will be a checkup. There will be a checkup, Mr. Adair. To begin with, materials shipped under a special letter of credit are specially marked. In other words, the box is especially marked so that you know that those things are traveling under a special letter of credit and they are relatively easy to identify. When the stuff is shipped, the bank which has passed on the shipping documents and the like, will send a copy of the documents, if they are being shipped to Korea, to our people there, and there can be a check made fairly easily. We will also require the addition of a customs receipt to the regular shipping documents. But, here again, this is a point 

Senator Bayh raised: What is to prevent these people in Korea from buying the goods from the United States and then reshipping them elsewhere? Well, how can they, if they are going to have to pay two freight rates shipping them to Korea and then shipping them from 

Korea to somewhere else? How are they possibly going to do that on a competitive basis when the hypothetical purchaser to which they might be going can buy directly from the States and only pay one freight rate. It doesn't make any sense to me. 

Mr. ADAIR. Now, on another point: Is there any difference in your opinion and I recognize that neither you nor I are experts in steel except as we learn something about it here-is there any difference in the quality of Japanese blackplate and U.S. blackplate? 

Mr. GAUD. Well, I am told not.

Now, Korea has very substantial requirements for iron and steel products. When a person in Korea goes to the Government and asks for an import license, he is granted it and he is told, "Buy your goods from the United States against these dollars." This is precisely the same procedure we use today under all of our program lending. We are used to it, the banks in New York are used to it, the importing countries are used to it. Vietnam doesn't have a darned thing to do

with it. The individual exporter of galvanized sheet in Korea doesn't have a darned thing to do with it. We don't pay him with a letter of credit, which seems to be Senator Bayh's impression. That procedure, as I say, is well known to the banks, well known to these countries with which we are doing business. So I just can't accept the proposition that we are getting into some kind of a terrifically complicated Rube Goldberg procedure.

Mr. HAMILTON.  

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Adair. 

Mr. ADAIR. Just briefly, Mr. Gaud. Now, on this point that you were just discussing with Mr. Hamilton, suppose these items are purchased in the United States, will there be any checkup or any reason for checkup to be sure that they are, in fact, delivered to Korea; and second, that they are not reexported from Korea?

Mr. ADAIR. Now, who will, if anyone, check the quality of the blackplate, of the material going into Vietnam and who will check the galvanizing?

I mean who is going to be there looking at it or testing or whatever they do? 

Mr. GAUD. We would have to designate some company, make sure that some independent company makes the check on our behalf. 

Mr. ADAIR. Is that proposed to be done?

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir, in the source country; that is, before it is shipped from Korea, we will insist there be some contractor there who will test it.

Mr. ADAIR. My final question: In your opinion, are these galvanizing companies in Korea, Korean-owned or is there a substantial segment of Japanese ownership?

Mr. GAUD. As far as we know, the companies in Korea are Korean. 

Mr. ADAIR. I understand there are a considerable number of Japanese personnel present there and that has given rise to suspicion in some quarters that there was also a segment at least of Japanese ownership.

Mr. GAUD. There is a company called the Sincere Co. in Taiwan. in which some Japanese were interested.

Mr. ADAIR. I thought it was in Taiwan and also in Korea. 

Mr. GAUD. Well, it may be, but, as you know, the growth of the private sector in Korea over the last few years has been phenomenal. 

There are a great many purely Korean enterprises now which didn't exist a few years ago. It is our understanding that that is true of these particular outfits here. 

Mr. ADAIR. Thank you. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you, Mr. Gaud. This hearing has been of particular interest to me because the Far East study mission recommended that the United States should do everything possible to help develop and expand the Korean export market, including items produced in Korea which might be valuable to the U.S. military and economic effort in Vietnam. We were impressed to see the extent of current economic growth in Korea. I believe that those of us who desire to see Korean economic growth continue are nevertheless troubled by some of the charges made. Are you satisfied, Mr. Gaud, that the new procurement rules will provide satisfactory galvanized

sheets for Vietnam and correct the problems of quality shown in the 

Swiss report and the complaints made by Senator Bayh? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes; I am, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you very much, Mr. Gaud.

EFFECT OF COOPERATIVES IN FOREIGN DEVELOPMENT 

Question 1. What evidence has there been compiled within A.I.D. as regards the effectiveness of cooperatives as a basis of democratic development? 

Answer. Comprehensive surveys of the impact of cooperative institutional development on the generation of democratic participation of people in the vital decisions and affairs of their lives and communities are the A.I.D. annual reports to Congress covering cooperative growth in the A.I.D.-assisted countries for the years 1962, 1963, 1964, and the current one for 1965. copy was transmitted to Chairman Morgan on 10/25/65. A copy of our transmittal letter and the report are enclosed.) (A The report covering the 1965 progress of cooperative development to the A.I.D.-assisted countries describes in its eight introductory pages, the growth of cooperatives and mutual institutions and their significance in involving people in their own economic and social affairs. 

Examples from the 1965 report illustrating democratic participation are: a. In fiscal year 1965, more than 300,000 people attended rural cooperative meetings which were made possible through assistance originally provided by A.I.D. b. The National Agricultural Cooperative Federation of Korea which, through local cooperatives, serves 2.2 million families in more than 18,000 villages, is preparing to put cooperatives on an independent and self-supporting basis by 1973.

Question 2. On the basis of the Watson Committee report, much emphasis was given the development of private enterprise with cooperatives an important element. What implementation is being given to the encouragement of cooperative development? 

Answer. An important contribution of the Watson Committee report to cooperative enterprise implementation was to point up the significance of free enterprise as a tool of development. This report has stimulated requests for feasibility surveys for the development of cooperative institutions in several countries, for example: a. USAID/Panama has requested a full-time cooperative institution specialist. b. USAID/Honduras has requested two A.I.D. cooperative contractors to survey that country's need for cooperatives in agriculture, fishing, credit housing, etc. c. USAID/India has a request for assistance from cooperatives to make a comprehensive survey for the production and distribution of fertilizer and for processing oil seeds in India. A number of Indian officials believe that cooperatives can act as a yardstick in the market place for fertilizer and oil seeds.

Question 3. What emphasis is being placed in A.I.D. on reaching the campesinos with cooperatives and other democratic organizations? 

Answer. The fostering of cooperatives to help the campesinos is a slow process. There have been resettlement projects supported with U.S. surplus agricultural commodities in northeast Brazil, Chile and India. Surplus U.S. agricultural commodities have been furnished to members through their cooperatives. This has helped to develop working capital for the cooperative organizations to expand their members' services. Campesino cooperatives and credit unions are also in the preliminary stages of development in Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Honduras, as follows: a. Plans are being made to extend supervised agricultural credit to campesinos in Ecuador and Panama on a low-cost basis through rural credit unions. b. An experiment in the province of Veraguas, Western Panama, has been

provided a grant of $10,000 from the Special Project Fund to USAID/Panama. 

From this grant, loans are extended to campesinos and fishermen through pre-cooperative groups which will be federated into a regional, all-purpose cooperative. c. In Peru, a Nation-wide program of cooperatives in community development called Cooperacion Popular has carried out, through its 48 field centers, 6,000 projects, of which 2,000 are completed. There are 11,000 additional community projects which cannot be carried out because of lack of funds. 

Outstanding examples of how cooperatives have made use of modern agricultural methods to increase production and income can be noted in Taiwan and Korea where approximately 2.4 million farm families get fertilizer and credit help through cooperatives.

In Taiwan, the Farmers' Associations of Taiwan are organized on three levels: (1) On the provincial level, (2) on the county and municipal level, and (3) on the district and township level. At the base, they are composed of about 5,000 small agricultural units. Members of these Farmers' Associations are limited to those engaged in land cultivation with more than one-half of the total income earned from farming. More than one-third of the delegates to the Members' Representative Congress must be owner-farmers, tenants, farmers and farm hands. Of considerable significance is the expanded use being made by A.I.D. of non-government resources in the development of cooperatives. Under Section 

601 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, popularly referred to as the Humphrey Amendment, cooperatives and nonprofit organizations were encouraged to carry out cooperative development work overseas under agreements with A.I.D. Presently, seven national cooperative and mutual organizations, plus the International Cooperative Training Center at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, Wisconsin, are providing cooperative assistance under global agreements with A.I.D. Thus, the resources of U.S. cooperatives and the active support of large segments of the membership are made available to help A.I.D. in carrying out its self-help, person-to-person type of assistance.

BRIEF STATEMENT ON OUR SALES POSITION IN THE MIDDLE EAST (EXTRACT OF MR. KUSS' PRESENTATION ON APRIL 19, 1966) 

In the Middle East our actions are directed toward maintaining a reasonable stability through the provision of limited arms designed to promote internal security and legitimate self-defense. It should be noted that the introduction of nearly $2 billion in Soviet Bloc arms poured into the area has contributed toward altering its arms balance and stability. 

The U.S. wants to avoid contributing to an arms race in the Middle East and becoming a major supplier in the area. Accordingly, the U.S. reserves the right to consider limited sales of defensive equipment to friendly states in the Middle East, but the "case-by-case" principle must be maintained. Every effort will be exerted to prevent both nuclear proliferation and the introduction of other sophisticated weapons systems into the area that may jeopardize the delicate balance of power. CIVIC ACTION BY MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-RECIPIENT COUNTRIESCAT 

17 2007

The U.S. Military Assistance Program has supported and encouraged civic action programs in approximately 40 countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America over the past four years. MAP is providing equipment to many existing foreign military units to complete their materiel inventory. Small U.S. training teams also assist in developing their military, technical and administrative skills. The capabilities of the units to perform their basic military missions are thereby strengthened, and on-the-job performance of civic action has actually added to this overall competence. Civic action by other units has also increased as a result of this MAP support. 

At the four-year mark, approximately 50 foreign engineering battalions have received MAP support and assisted in the construction or repair of more than 10,000 miles of roads-feeder roads, farm-to-market roads and national highways, usually in the more remote areas of their countries. Of these units, 30 battalions are working full time on civic action. More than 1,000 schools have been built, ranging from small rural elementary schools to medium-level vocational training centers for recruits. In four years, hundreds of clinics and hospitals have been built, and several million civilians have received care. 

MAP-supported medical, dental and sanitation teams of foreign armies, navies and air forces operate in areas unserved by civilian medical personnel. Several air transport squadrons are devoted full time to civic action in areas of the less-developed countries unserved by civilian airlines, and naval craft perform coastal and river services important to the development of new lands. SUPER

FUNCTIONAL SUMMARY 

Results of civic action performed by foreign military units (details not available on some units):

TEALLY 

A. Construction 

1. Roads. Virtually every MAP-recipient country uses its armed forces at times in road construction, repair and maintenance, usually in the more remote areas. In Bolivia, 125 miles of roads were completed in 1965, 118 miles have been under construction since 1964, and 34 miles are being repaired and maintained. In Brazil, 32 miles are under construction with extensive new projects planned. In Chile, 75 miles have been under construction since 1964, and in Colombia, 231 miles of roads were begun in 1965, and 690 miles have been assigned to the Army for maintenance. 

In Ecuador, 100 miles have been assigned for construction by the Army since 1961 and 35 miles have been completed, with an additional 9 miles repaired in 1965. In El Salvador, 21 miles were assigned to the Army for repair and maintenance. In Ethiopia, of the 745 miles detailed to the Army in 1963, more than 186 miles have been completed. In Greece, 250 miles were completed in 1964. In Guatemala, 25 miles are under construction, and in Honduras, 44 miles are being built. In Liberia, 26 miles of roads were built from 

1962 to 1964. In Nicaragua, 17 miles are under construction, and in Pakistan, 250 miles have been built since 1961. In Panama, 12 miles are under construction, and in Paraguay, 760 miles have been or are under construction, and 550 miles are assigned to the Army for continuing maintenance. In Peru, 1,000 miles of roads have been built or are planned for construction by the Army. In the Philippines, 81 miles have been built since 1963. In Senegal, 52 miles were completed by 1965. In Thailand, 106 miles were built in the past three years, and in 1964, 108 miles were repaired. In Venezuela, 211 miles are under construction. In Vietnam, 500 miles of roads including bridges have been assigned to the Army annually for construction and repair. 

2. Schools. In most countries, construction, repair and site clearance are frequently performed by military units. For example, in Bolivia, 148 schools were built between 1963 and 1965, and in Chile, 29 schools are under construction. In Iran, 31 are being built, and in Thailand, the Army helped build or repair 44 schools in 1963 and 1964. In the Philippines, 283 pre-fabricated schoolhouses were built by the Army. 

3. Medical Facilities.-In Colombia, 15 dispensaries and a small hospital were built in 1964 and 1965, and in Vietnam numerous dispensaries and villages clinics have been built. 

4. Other Facilities.-The Argentine Army completed two highway bridges in 

1965, and in Bolivia, the Army has built a public library and rebuilt a public

plaza. Brazil leads all MAP-recipient countries in the construction of railroads by armed forces with 675 miles completed or under construction. In 

Ecuador, the Army completed eight miles of sewer systems, installed electrical transmission lines and completed nine village wells and a community center. 

In Jordan, the Army completed three water-conservation and four tourist projects. In Paraguay, the Army has completed seven village wells. In 

Thailand, in 1963 and 1964 the Army completed 17 village wells and 22 bridges, dredged 42 canals and in 1965 built or repaired 46 bridges. In Vietnam, the 

Army has built numerous market places and other local facilities. 

B. Services 

1. Health and Medical.-Units of the local armed forces in Bolivia treated approximately 1,000 civilians in 1964; in Chile, 16,000 in 1964; in Colombia, approximately 205,000 annually; in Paraguay, 11,000 annually; in Thailand, 100,000 in 1963 and 1964; in Venezuela, 48,000 in 1964; and Vietnam approximately 3 million annually. In addition, local units are staffing 12 mobile clinics in El Salvador; 6 mobile clinics in Korea; 2 hospitals and 11 dispensaries in Paraguay; 6 river boats and 4 C-47 flying clinics in Peru; a hospital in Thailand; and a coastal ship in Vietnam. 

2. Vocational.-Most countries provide vocational training for recruits through either formal or informal programs, thereby adding to civilian skills for use after discharge. For example, in Iran, approximately 7,200 receive training annually; in Peru, the 2,500 trained annually will increase to approximately 6,000 per year by 1971; in the Philippines, approximately 1,000 per year; and in 

Venezuela, 300 annually. 3. Literacy.-Most countries provide literacy training for recruits. In Chile, 400 are trained annually; in Colombia, more than 20,000; in Mexico, 34,000; and in Peru, 10,000. In El Salvador, the military operates 926 literacy centers and in Iran, more than 16,000 teachers have been trained for the Literacy Corps. 

4. Air Transport and Photography.-Civic action is performed by most air forces. For example, in Argentina, 3,500 tons of grain were airlifted to cattle in a drought area; in Chile, 21 tons of prefabricated buildings for schools and dispensaries were airlifted in 1965 to a remote area, return flights carrying 16 tons of wool; and in Paraguay, 950 patients were flown to medical centers in 

1964. In the Philippines, 519 people were emergency airlifted in 1965, along with 60,000 tons of relief goods; 1.7 million hectares were covered by aerial photography as part of a land-reform program. 

5. Agriculture.-In Mexico, approximately 1 million trees are planted annually by the Army; in the Philippines, 70,000; and in Venezuela, 50,000 trees. 

In Peru, roads have opened up or will provide access to 4.5 million acres of sparsely populated but rich lands. 

6. Donated Materials.-As a result of excess materials, gifts from military personnel themselves or other sources, large quantities of materials are donated by local armed forces each year. In Korea materials were donated for 281 classrooms, 40 rural clinics and 10 water supply systems in 1964. In Thailand, 20 tons of cement, 2 tons of fertilizer, 800 farm tools, 800 blankets and 21,000 notebooks were donated, and in Venezuela, 1,300 sets of books and notebooks and 27,000 trees were donated in 1964. 

7. Other Services.-In Paraguay, the Army provides the only communications for civilians in 41 outlying communities, and in Turkey, the armed services have adopted 650 "sister villages" where civic action is carried out by neighboring units. 

GEOGRAPHIC SUMMARY 

Illustrative projects in Iran, Colombia and Peru, as well as overall programs in other areas: Iran The MAP-sponsored civic action program in Iran is an excellent example of interdepartmental and international cooperation: 

1. Iranian Army units are very active in working with the rural people for the construction of roads essential to marketing crops, transportation of supplies to presently inaccessible rural villages and delivery of fodder to farmers. 

In villages, irrigation ditches have been constructed and wells drilled. During severe winter months, military units spend long hours on snow-removal projects, clearing roadways that would otherwise remain impassable until Spring.

2. Joint military and civilian teams of doctors visit the Persian Gulf and 

Gulf of Oman areas to administer medical treatment to thousands of villagers. 

3. The Gendarmerie performs tuberculosis detection and control in provincial centers, as well as operating a mobile dental clinic to treat villagers in remote areas. 

4. During severe winter weather, the Iranian Air Force conducts massive airlifts to drop food, clothing, medical supplies, corn and bran to starving people and livestock in isolated villages of the Azerbaijan and Gorgan areas. 

The Air Force provided flood relief to villages in the Dezful area a year ago, including medical supplies, food, clothing and transportation. 

5. The Iranian Navy has a continuing program to deliver drinking water and provide medical assistance to the islands and remote areas along the 

Persian Gulf. 

6. The armed forces are fighting illiteracy by teaching recruits to read and write. The Army's vocational training centers have been established with 

U.S. assistance and teach the recruit a basic skill before he returns to his village. From this has grown the countrywide programs of the Literacy 

Corps, Health and Sanitation Corps and the rural development program that have brought into action on a cooperative basis the Ministries of War, Health, Agriculture, Education and Economy. 

Latin America

In Latin America, 17 countries now have U.S.-supoprted civic action programs. Bolivia was the first to organize one with U.S. assistance. After the 1952 revolution, the Bolivian Army was reorganized, with one of its basic missions that of aiding the country's economic development. Two engineer battalions were assigned to build roads and bridges in remote areas and to help clear the land for farming. By early 1963, the Bolivian Army had helped build 42 rural schools as its share of a 100-school program supported by the Agency for International Development (AID) and had engaged in numerous other projects of road construction and colonization. U.S. surplus food has been used as "food for wages" in meeting some of the costs of local civilian labor on the projects. 

Colombia.-MAP support for civic action in Colombia was initiated in 1962. 

The program is designed to help combat rural violence, strengthen militarycivilian relations and, at the same time, improve economic, social and health conditions. At sites where civic action projects are underway, there has been a pronounced reduction of disturbances and hostilities. For example, the 8th 

Brigade with headquarters at Armenia, Caldas State, was created in 1962 with the specific mission of restoring public order in the coffee-rich Quindo area. 

People had been either openly antagonistic or apathetic toward the Government, the military and the police. The Army built roads and water systems and assisted in constructing, equipping and operating schools and health centers. The roads have served the dual purpose of moving goods to and from markets and facilitating the operations of military and police units. While violence has been brought under control, it has not yet been entirely eliminated. However, the people in this area have established a faith in the Government. Since initiation of the civic action program, there has been a reduction in the number of active insurgent and bandit groups. Military and civilian deaths at the hands of bandits and insurgents have dropped by approximately two thirds. The most successful types of civic action projects in 

Colombia have been: 

1. Health centers operating in conjunction with fixed, floating and flying dispensaries provide the only medical services to vast areas and are a result of close cooperation between the armed forces and the Ministry of Health. 

2. Road construction and maintenance opens new areas for colonization and provides a means of transportation and communications for rural people. 

3. Literacy training has raised the social and cultural level of individuals, provides close soldier-civilian relationships and facilitates the exchange of ideas. 

4. Air and water transportation service provides the only means of transportation in approximately 50 percent of the country, spreads medical services to isolated areas and demonstrates the support of the Government to inhabitants of remote regions.

Peru.-MAP and AID for support for civic action in Peru began in 1962. 

Today civic action is receiving extensive budgetary and other support from the Peruvian Government, and all military forces are participating. Civilian lead- 

60-929-66-pt. 7-2

ers, as well as the people at large, frequently turn to the military for assistance in the economic and social development of the country. In many remote mountain and jungle areas of Peru, there is little knowledge and understanding of governmental processes. It is not uncommon to find people who have had no contact with Peru's civilization or government and who have no concept of the nation of which they are a part. The military bring schools, medical and dental assistance and other forms of public service. 

By this means, the Government is beginning to integrate primitive people into the social, cultural and economic life of the country. 

The major civic action projects are the construction and maintenance of penetration highways; vocational and literacy training; medical and dental assistance; colonization; and water and air transportation to remote areas. 

Using the first for illustrative purposes, penetration roads are high-priority civic action projects since they will provide access to the low and high jungle on the eastern slopes of the Andes and into the Amazon River basin. These areas have a good climate, fertile soil and vast potential for development. 

With Peruvian Army participation and MAP assistance, the Northern Trans- Andean Highway System will consist of an access highway, three major penetration roads and numerous principal feeder roads. For example: 

1. The 134 km Chamaya-San Ignacio road is now providing access to 250,000 acres of excellent agricultural land; the road will also serve as the Ecuador- 

Peru link of the highway of the Selva (a joint Colombia-Ecuador-Peru-Bolivia- 

Alliance for Progress project). 

2. The 6th Engineer Battalion completed in FY 1965 the Ingenio-Rio Imaza road project. The assigned mission in FY 1966-FY 1971 is expected to be continuation of the western sector of the 262 km highway. This highway will provide access to the Department of San Martin containing 1,250,000 acres of good agricultural land. This is the highest priority development project in Peru. 

3. During the period 1964-1980, the Bagua-Nazareth-Rio Maranon Highway and its major feeder roads are opening up an estimated 2,000,000 acres of new agricultural land; in addition, a 500 km highway will upon completion in the mid-1970s provide the best route linking the Peruvian coast with the navigable waters of the Amazon River system. This is one of the two most important development projects in Peru. 

4. The 2nd Engineer Construction Battalion is being reorganized, equipped and trained. During the period FY 1967-FY 1971 this unit will be committed to construction of the 120 km Peruvian sector of the first international highway to link Peru and Brazil. 

5. The 3rd Engineer Construction Battalion is assigned the construction of new highways in La Convencion Province, Department of Cuzco. A 52 km highway will be completed in FY 1966, and a 100 km project in FY 1967. 

These two roads will provide access to the 85,000 people now living in the La Convencion and Lares valleys. In FY 1967-FY 1971 this battalion will be assigned additional construction projects to open up new colonization areas. 

6. The 100 km Atalaya-Itahuania-Manu road extends an existing highway into the Province of Nanu, the most promising area in Peru for immediate colonization. This highway with a system of feeder roads will provide access to an estimated 1,000,000 acres of new agricultural land. 

Other Latin American Programs: Widespread civic action programs are carried on by the armed forces of almost all Latin American countries and are assisted by approximately $10 million of MAP support annually. The principal type is the construction of roads, schools and water and sanitation systems. In addition, almost all of the countries have some form of medical civic action and provide literacy and, in many cases, vocational training to civilians and conscripts. Several of the countries are attempting remote-area colonization. Civic action in Latin America is a unique mixture of military and volunteer civilian labor. Africa

MAP encourages and supports civic action in several countries of Africa, for example: 

1. Ethiopia. A major civic action project is the construction by an Ethiopian engineer battalion of farm-to-market roads urgently needed to improve the economy. Projects at the local level are helping to improve education, sanitation and health. MAP has furnished construction equipment and is providing supplies for out-patient medical treatment.

2. Guinea. The U.S. is providing equipment, materials and training through 

MAP to help Guinean Army engineers build and repair feeder roads. 

3. Liberia.-A Liberian engineer battalion, supported and equipped by MAP, has rehabilitated schools and constructed feeder roads connecting villages to main roads. The battalion has also introduced modern sanitation methods to parts of the back country. These projects have enhanced the Government's program of rural and tribal intergration into national life. 

4. Senegal.-A Senegalese Army engineer battalion works on civic action projects using MAP equipment. The battalion has engaged in construction of all-weather, farm-to-market roads and is planning to build or improve airstrips for all-weather operations. 

Far East

In Southeast Asia, where the Communist threat is serious and the countries face difficult problems in making economic progress, MAP-supported military forces are being employed, where possible, on useful projects to help the people. 

In Thailand, the Royal Thai Army is cooperating with other Government agencies in civic action projects in villages, principally in the northeast area, where insurgency appears to be a growing threat. Units are engaged in welldigging, road and bridge construction, repair of schools and digging irrigation and drainage ditches. In Vietnam, in addition to medical civic action listed above, Vietnamese armed forces have 4 companies, 45 regional teams and 4 regional platoons which support rural reconstruction and carry out civic action in the hamlets and villages. As their military duties permit, twenty Vietnamese engineer battalions carry out construction projects of direct help to civilians, and the Vietnamese forces in general provide transport and other assistance. 

In Laos, the village cluster program is receiving support from the Laotian forces in both economic and security aspects.

Elsewhere in the Far East, Korean and Philippean units carry out construction and medical projects, and vocational and literacy training is provided military personnel.

Training Teams 

Since the beginning of the MAP civic action program, U.S. Mobile Training 

Teams (MTT) have been sent to countries in Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the Middle and Far East. The qualifications required for these teams include proficiency in such fields as engineering, public health, sanitation, agriculture, education and public relations. Normally consisting of one to 15 officers and men, each MTT is created according to the specialties and talents needed for the particular job. Language training is an important part of the final orientation of the team. 

Basic Principles

From past and current experience, certain basic principles underlying successful civic action have emerged: 

1. Civic action should essentially be a host-country program. The United 

States gives assistance, but the major effort has and should come from the country itself. 

2. In putting professional and military skills to use in helping people better their living conditions, the armed forces should work with the people, not just for them. 

3. By working side by side on civic action projects, the civilian and soldier develop a better understanding of each other's needs and proper roles, as well as each learning how he can contribute to economic and social development. 

STATEMENT OF DR. ALONA E. EVANS, AREA REPRESENTATIVE, WORLD PROBLEMS, AND DR. VICTORIA SCHUCK, CHAIRMAN, LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM COMMITTEE, OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITY WOMEN 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, on behalf of the American 

Association of University Women. I am pleased to submit this statement in support of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1966. As an organization fundamentally concerned with education, AAUW has maintained for some 80 years two fellowships programs which have enabled American women to study here and abroad and foreign scholars to study in the United States.

As a charter member of the International Federation of University Women, an organization of university women in 54 countries, many of them in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, this Association is particularly aware of the conditions under which emerging countries struggle to build viable social, political, and economic institutions within their own borders which, in turn, will contribute to the goal of "building a decent world order," as Secretary of State Rusk put it last year. Those countries, such as the United States, which have achieved a "decent order" within their own frontiers have the responsibility, on the basis of self-interest and humanitarian principles to provide guidance and support to peoples in the initial stages of this development.

The proposed Foreign Assistance Act of 1966 represents the latest phase in the evolution of the great humanitarian movement which has included such programs as UNRRA, the Marshall Plan, the Displaced Persons Act, the Refugee Relief Act, the Alliance for Progress, and the Peace Corps. 

During the past two decades this movement has evolved from programs of relief and rehabilitation, through assistance to socio-economic development, to the current emphasis upon self-development founded upon broadly-based assistance.

Two premises of the 1966 Act may be mentioned for comment. There is a sound emphasis upon sharing the cost of international aid. The financial cost today, as the level of development of emerging states rises and the nature of the programs becomes more complex, cannot be assumed by any one state; consequently, the emphasis upon encouraging other countries to join in developing or expanding their bilateral programs of assistance, as well as the expansion of programs sponsored by international agencies, such as the International Development Association or the World Bank, should lead to a healthy spread of financial responsibility. At the same time, the cost in expertise of these programs should be spread, so that emerging states may benefit by the broadest range of socio-economic experience of the developed countries. 

The principle of the multiyear authorization has two advantages. From the point of view of the grantor and the recipient states, it ensures continuity in planning programs and in the execution of these programs, particularly where long-range planning is necessary, as in education, public health, conservation, or industrial development. From the point of view of the economic use of legislative energies and expertise, an authorization of a minimum of three to a maximum of five years duration, will enable the Congress to direct its attention to the examination of the large issues of policy-making and of methods of execution of policy. The separation of the economic and military assistance programs should also contribute to this objective.

In view of the continuing urgency of the gap between population growth and food resources in many parts of the world, however, the American Association of University Women has been disappointed to note the seeming disparity between the enunciation of United States foreign policy goals of international economic and social development and the financial means which have been requested for the implementation of these objectives. We believe it regrettable that at a time when the United States is urging other donor states to increase their assistance and recipient states to greately increase their own self-help efforts this country has been steadily reducing the percentage of its own gross national product devoted to foreign assistance programs. The AAUW urges the enactment of an authorization bill in which the appropriation requested in H.R. 12449 will be treated as the minimum for the programs enumerated in the Administration's proposed Foreign Assistance Act of 1966. 

STATEMENT OF NORTH DAKOTA COUNCIL ON WORLD AFFAIRS, BY ROBERT MOSES, SECRETARY 

The North Dakota Council on World Affairs, Bismarck, N. Dak., is pleased to report on its participation in various U.S. Government international development programs in recent years and in support of the administration's fiscal year 1967 proposed foreign economic assistance programs.

1. COOPERATION ON TEACHER DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM 

For the past three years the North Dakota Council on World Affairs has cooperated with the U.S. Office of Education and the Agency for International 

Development in a teacher development program, conducted at Georgetown University and through visits to various parts of the United States, including 

North Dakota.

Each year since 1963 the Council has assisted AID and the Office of Education in providing several days of educational experience and personal contact programming in North Dakota for groups of English-language teachers from developing countries studying the latest English-language techniques in this country. This programming has consisted of numerous home visitations with many community leaders, tours of schools, visits to the offices of Gov. 

William L. Guy and other North Dakota officials, and many additional educational experiences. This activity has taken place in Bismarck, Mandan and other North Dakota communities.

North Dakota public officials, educators and private citizens have hailed the AID-Office of Education teacher development program for the gains it is making, both in broader knowledge of English-language techniques for foreign teachers and also in aiding increased international understanding. Once again in 1966 the North Dakota Council on World Affairs is looking forward to this August when we will again provide our completely voluntary services to another visiting delegation of English language teachers from various countries visiting our state, giving more of our citizens an opportunity to discuss international education in their homes, schools and offices with teachers of many lands-all made possible through this very effective AID-Office of Education program. 

2. NORTH DAKOTA CONFERENCE ON INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION 

The North Dakota Council on World Affairs is now undertaking a second program involving our country's foreign assistance program, a project we feel will be very successful for our state and of much value to our country and the world. 

Patterned after the White House Conference on International Cooperation, held November 28-December 1, 1965, in Washington, D.C., the North Dakota

Conference on International Cooperation will be held at North Dakota State University in Fargo, N. Dak., with cooperative participation from the University and many North Dakota groups.

To our knowledge this is the first such statewide Conference on International Cooperation to be held in any state since the highly successful White House 

Conference of last fall. In a recent letter to the North Dakota Conference on International Cooperation executive committee, Mr. Herbert J. Waters, As sistant Administrator for Material Resources of AID, wrote: 

"I was pleased to hear about what you are doing in North Dakota with the International Cooperation idea. It sounds like an idea that should be picked up in other states."

The North Dakota Council on World Affairs warmly supports the administration's requests to Congress to help conquer world hunger, ignorance and disease, through stepped-up programs of assistance in food and agriculture, education and health. Although we are a small state World Affairs 

Council in a sparsely populated state (and operating on a totally voluntary basis), we nevertheless wish to add our voice to those of others in support of these proposed programs. Of particular interest are those calling for enlargement of aid in the areas of food and agriculture, education and health.

Because North Dakota is the state most heavily dependent upon agriculture (and due to the overwhelming North Dakota support of the Food for Peace program), it is only natural that our council should schedule a food and agriculture committee panel as one of the six panels at our North 

Dakota Conference on International Cooperation this fall. We trust that many North Dakotans, eager to promote broader expansion of food and agriculture aid in our foreign policy, will make significant contributions to the total U.S. food and agriculture aid program, as this milestone North 

Dakota conference is concluded.

Of no less importance at this conference are its five other panels-on education and cultural exchange, health and population, commerce and travel, science and technology, and human rights. Committee reports from these panels will be presented to conference participants. North Dakota 

Lt. Gov. Charles Tighe is chairman of the North Dakota Conference on 

International Cooperation, serving in a role similar to that played last fall at the White House Conference by Vice President Hubert H. Humphrey, who has been invited to address the North Dakota conference on October 24.

Already, as of the date of this report (May 5, 1966) there has been considerable discussion and planning within our conference committee on education and cultural exchange, calling for an extension of the Administration's recently enacted U.S. Arts Foundation program. This proposal would lead to establishment of an International Training Center for the Arts in Developing Countries.

Drawing on North Dakota's success in recent years in planned programs of aid to the arts and native cultures of our own developing peoples, the American Indians (through numerous North Dakota-based national Indian arts exhibitions and cultural organizational efforts), this new North Dakota proposal also would call on expansion of aid to such Arts Festivals in developing countries as the April, 1966 festival held in Dakar, Senegal. The international arts proposal would utilize local currencies now held in developing countries through the P.L. 480 Program to develop national arts programs, strengthening the native arts in developing nations, and, in the process, strengthening the pride of the peoples of these nations. 

The North Dakota Council on World Affairs will present a summary of this conference to appropriate committees of Congress, to the executive branch of the Government, and to interested organizations. 

We have outlined just a few of the many programs of international development in which North Dakotans are and have been participating and which will have an increasingly good effect on our State. Other North 

Dakota groups and individuals have participated in a broad variety of programs in support of international development-the type of programs which have produced widespread favorable response in our state and which have helped play a small part in the important work of our country with the developing nations.

We conclude that good foreign aid, like good government, is good for people anywhere in the developing countries as well as in North Dakota. That which will help make developing peoples more self-sufficient cannot help but serve the best interests of the citizens of North Dakota and the United States.

STATEMENT OF THE NATIONAL RURAL ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATION 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, my name is Robert D.

Part ridge. I am the Legislative Representative for the National Rural Electric 

Cooperative Association. NRECA is the national service organization of nearly 1,000 rural electric systems operating in 46 states. These rural electric systems operate on a non-profit basis, providing electric service to farm and other rural consumers in 2,700 of the nation's 3,200 counties. NRECA is a non-profit cooperative, providing its members with legislative, management, information and insurance services. Membership in NRECA is entirely voluntary. Nearly two-thirds of our activities are self-supporting through sales of services to our members.

America's rural electric systems for more than 20 years have had an effective organization to develop an aggressive program for the expansion of rural electrification in the United States through the cooperative system. We have seen the impact on rural area development and the increasing production in the rural areas of the United States brought about by electrification through the cooperative REA pattern. It has long been our feeling that this pattern can be effective in all of the developing countries of the world and that the need is urgent to get the job started in all these countries as an instrument of economic, social and political development of each country. 

NRECA was one of the organizations that urged the inclusion of cooperatives and similar organization as a part of our foreign assistance program. 

This was formally implemented by the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 which includes a declaration of policy placed in the Act by the then senior 

Senator from Minnesota, Hubert Humphrey, which reads as follows: "It is declared to be the policy of the United States to encourage the development and use of cooperatives, credit unions, and savings and loan associations."

Our General Manager, Clyde Ellis, has made trips to all of the regions of the world where we have AID Missions in company with other members of our staff and all of our people that have participated are convinced that more must be done to provide assistance in rural areas of the developing countries. I should like to quote from Mr. Ellis' recent book, A Giant Step, statements that he made following a comprehensive survey of the Latin 

American countries in 1961: "It is no wonder, I thought, that these people revolt-that the siren song of the communists sounds good to them. It was easy to see how they could be duped into believing the line from the Communist Manifesto which says, 'You have nothing to lose but your chains.' "It was obvious everywhere that the people were not passively accepting the grinding poverty into which they had been born. They mean to have something better, and to have it in a hurry. They are desperate, and revolution of some kind is in the air everywhere. "This revolution is coming. The only question is what form will it take? It will be peaceful or it will be bloody. It will leave people on the side of the United States, and freedom, or on the side of Russia and China, and communism. From a standpoint of either human compassion or our national interest, the responsibility of the United States to help the Latin people lift themselves up is clear. We must demonstrate with action programs that their hope for the future lies in democracy and not communism."
