Villagers in South Vietnam have been intensely interested in the early development of these cooperatives. Recently more than 1,200 petitioned AID urging haste in bringing electricity to their villages and I would like to quote from that petition to give you the poignancy of their appeal: "Rural electrification is a program which will give us the opportunity to have the light of civilization. It will help us improve our rural life, mechanize our agriculture and give us better results from our labors. "Where there is light, darkness steps back; and where there is no poverty, communism is not possible."

A second cooperative has been organized in Ecuador in the Daule community and they have made real progress to date with the help of their own government and with contributions from the rural electric systems in Kentucky. An AID loan is being prepared to give them assistance and the people are making real progress on a self-help basis. 

CONCLUSIONS 

NRECA has had a wide range of experience around the world under its AID contracts and all of these experiences convince us that rural electric cooperatives can be successful in all countries where we have a foreign aid program. The 60 people who have represented us are unanimous in their endorsement of the program; most have recommended the program to their 

Congressmen by contact or by letter. When they explain the program publicly our people support the program. Typical is this statement in a letter from one of our top managers to his congressman: "Jim, I know the response and enthusiasm of the people in groups I have talked with since my assignment in 1963 has been most enthusiastic when they understood actually what we were striving to accomplish. I have talked to more than fifty groups since my return, these groups ranging from a dozen to several hundred. Without exception the response was the same."

One of our statewide managers who has been overseas says: "I hold strong convictions that whenever the members of any electric cooperative are given a full explanation of the significance of these overseas AID assignments for managers or key personnel or attorneys, they will support the decision of their board of directors in granting a leave-of-absence and take pride in the opportunity their cooperative is given to be of service to our government."

The membership of NRECA has endorsed this program at its regional meetings and its annual meetings for the last 5 years. Attached is copy of 60-929-66-pt. 7—3

the resolution of our membership at the annual meeting in Las Vegas, February, 1966, attended by nearly 9,000 delegates.

A recently completed research study shows rural electric cooperatives being developed in Latin America should increase farm income in these areas by 11% and investments in rural electrification should return $4.4 to the national economy for each $1 of input. Rural electric cooperatives will have widespread impact on the economic, social and political development of these rural communities. 

We appreciate the opportunity to present our views to your Committee. 

ELECTRIFICATION IN INCREASING FARM PRODUCTION AT HOME AND ABROAD 

Whereas a world-wide War on Hunger will do more to encourage peaceful progress in the emerging nations of the world and strengthen them against Communist insurgency than any other course of action; and 

Whereas the United States of America has successfully pursued such a policy on a limited scale through the Food for Peace and Agency for International Development programs, which attack the problem of world hunger both through food shipments and through technical assistance to help the people of the less developed countries help themselves; and 

Whereas the farmers of our nation have the agricultural productive capacity and the technical know-how to wage an expanded and more effective War on Hunger in the emerging countries of the free world; and 

Whereas an adequate supply of dependable electric power is essential for the effective development of a nation's agricultural potential; and 

Whereas the REA pattern has proved to be so effective in the electrification of rural America: Now, therefore, be it 

Resolved, That we support the concept of using America's agricultural abundance to fight hunger and the poverty of economic and social opportunities in the less developed nations of the world; and be it further 

Resolved, That we recommend the use of foreign currencies generated by the sale of U.S. agricultural products abroad for the development of cooperative rural electrification in those countries, and that U.S. assistance for rural electrification in less developed countries follow the REA pattern insofar as possible.

STATEMENT OF UNITED STATES SAVINGS AND LOAN LEAGUE 

The United States Savings and Loan League' favors the objectives of section 224 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, and urges that the language and programs set forth under this section be retained in their present form.

Last year, during the 88th Congress, section 224 was considerably broadened and expanded by the addition of four new programs. These new programs joined the existing self-liquidating pilot housing project program which had been the mainstay of section 224 since it was first drawn in 1961. With these additional objectives, the scope and direction of section 224 was considerably altered and its new aims were mainly in the direction of encouraging lowcost housing projects in Latin America as well as providing for direct placement of seed capital in "credit institutions in Latin America engaged directly or indirectly in the financing of home mortgages such as savings and loan institutions. ... Besides expanding programs under section 224, 1965 amendments also increased the total face amount of guarantees that could be outstanding at any one time to $400 million with this authority continuing to June 30, 1967. This represented an increase of $150 million over the previous authority. 99 At the same time the Congress was enlarging the scope and direction of section 224, the Housing Act of 1965 was being amended to permit Federal 1 The United States Savings and Loan League is a nationwide trade organization with 5,100 members, including Federally chartered and state chartered, insured and uninsured associations. Its principal officers are C. A. Duncan, Jr., President, Nevada, Missouri; 

Otto L. Preisler, Vice President, Chicago, Illinois; Norman Strunk, Executive Vice Presi dent, Chicago, Illinois; C. R. Mitchell, Legislative Chairman, Kansas City, Missouri: and

Stephen Slipher, Legislative Director, Washington, D.C. The League's Washington Office is at 812 Pennsylvania Building, Washington, D.C., 20004; Telephone: 638-6334.

savings and loan associations in the United States to invest up to 1% of their assets in U.S. Government guaranteed loans made under section 224 of the 

Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. Taken together, this meant that Federal associations in the U.S. could, for the first time, engage in mortgage lending operations in Latin American countries as well as provide direct seed capital loans for counterpart institutions in Latin America.

Although section 224 contains the basic statutory authority for the loan guarantee program and investment of U.S. capital abroad, it must be remembered that the basic concept and principle of aid and assistance to Latin American countries is enunciated under section 601 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 whereby the United States commits itself, in part, to a policy of encouraging other countries to develop and use cooperatives, credit unions and savings and loan associations. The success of both programs over the years is underscored by the fact that since 1961, when the Foreign Assistance Act was first drafted and put into effect, $250 million worth of section 224 self-liquidating pilot housing projects have either been insured or committed to be insured under the loan guarantee program. This figure, incidentally, represented the total guarantee authority available under the act until last year's amendment. Moreover, there are now 105 savings and loan associations in Latin America which have provided financing for 35,000 homes. 

H.R. 12449, in part, would amend section 224 of the Foreign Assistance 

Act of 1961 by extending the permissible dollar amount of guarantees outstanding under this section to June 30, 1971, rather than the present June 30, 1967. This means that the additional $150 million guarantee authority granted by the Congress in 1965 for loans made under this section would have to be stretched over an additional four-year period. The U.S. Savings and Loan League is opposed to this proposition because any stretch-out of guarantee authority at this time would tend to act as a brake on the overall objectives of section 224.

First of all, there are now five programs operating under section 224 all of which will be vying for the recently added guarantee authority. The additional authority made available by the 1965 amendment to the act amounted to $150 million over the next two years, terminating in 1967. To extend that $150 million insuring authority another four years and ask at the same time that it be spread over five programs could be a crippling blow by denying the new programs adequate guarantee authority needed to properly launch them and get them underway. In practice, it could tend to choke off investor incentive because the additional $150 million authority would be used up long before June 30, 1971, thus denying many investors the opportunity to use the loan guarantee program. Investor interest could fall off because of lack of opportunity to participate. Capital that was once willing to flow into Latin American investments would then seek other outlets.

Secondly, the loan guarantee program has been able to generate sufficient investor interest up until this time so that it now has a certain amount of momentum. This momentum was recharged when the Congress voted the program an additional $150 million of insuring authority in 1965. 

On top of this, Federal savings and loan associations, as noted before, were granted new authority to invest in loans made under section 224 which meant that a new source of long-term capital was made available for Latin American investments under the program. This new source of capital should be encouraged and stimulated to use the program. However, if the amendment currently pending before the Committee in H.R. 12449 is allowed to stand, it would most probably stifle this new source. 

The U.S. Savings and Loan League has an avowed interest in the success of the loan guarantee program. The League firmly supported the 1% amendment to the Housing Act of 1965 that ultimately gave Federal savings and loan associations the authority to invest in guaranteed loans made under section 224. As a follow-up to this piece of legislation, the U.S. 

League entered into an informal agreement with the Agency for International Development late in 1965 whereby the League agreed to work with and through AID in fostering the establishment of mutual thrift institutions in developing countries, thus making the entire professional staff of the League, plus its 5,100 member organization, available for this effort. Prior to this time, a subsidiary organization of the U.S. League, the American 

Savings and Loan Institute, had already signed a formal contral with AID

whereby the Institute undertook to translate its library of savings and loan textbooks into Spanish for consumption by savings and loan associations in Latin America, an effort, incidentally, that is well underway. Because of this, the League is vitally interested in the success of the program set forth under section 224 and believes that this amendment would be detrimental to the success of those programs. 

We respectfully urge the Committee to reject the amendment to section 

224 contained in H.R. 12449.

STATEMENT OF REPRESENTATIVE SEYMOUR HALPERN (REPUBLICAN, NEW YORK) THE HADASSAH EFFORT DEMANDS SUPPORT 

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate this opportunity to submit my views to your distinguished committee.

I would like to concentrate on one particular issue which recently developed. 

This concerns the decision of the Agency for International Development to deny funds to the enormously fruitful Hadassah medical organization in Israel. 

I urge the committee, before proceeding further, to consider this matter closely and incorporate the necessary provisions in the pending foreign aid bill. 

It is my feeling that this abrupt and wholly unjustified denial on the part of our government contradicts the essence and guiding principles of our overall economic assistance programs. 

For this reason, I appeal to the committee to approve funds toward Hadassah's hospital, nursing facilities, and other medical services in Jerusalem, Israel. I wholeheartedly concur in the testimony presented to your committee by Hadassah's distinguished President, Mrs. Mortimer Jacobson, who appeared before you on May 11.

I must confess that I can see no logic in the arguments made by AID in rejecting Hadassah's request. The Agency insists that it does not wish to enlist new beneficiaries in the program, although, paradoxically, it is seeking for fiscal year 1967 a substantial increase in the funds allotted to this institutional program. In fact, I understand that the Agency has requested an appropriation of $11.3 million, while it requested only $7 million last year under Section 214.

I am familiar with the operations of the Hadassah services in Israel, and I can testify to their tremendous import. I want to comment briefly on this, but it is mandatory that the Hadassah hospital be included among the other American universities and hospitals receiving assistance. 

The American University at Beirut, Lebanon, has received $33 million of American aid since 1959. It is true that Israel no longer receives grant aid, but neither does Lebanon. Moreover, such requests should not be handled indiscriminately; nor should artificial and wholly irrelevant qualifications be attached. The AID contention that no additional recipients should be added to the list is spurious and illogical. Each application must be examined on its merits, and the Hadassah organization urgently needs funds to carry on its impressive work.

It is for this reason that Hadassah has appealed to the committee, requesting funds to make up the deficit in the operation of its educational, hospital and nursing facilities. They would like I£3,000,000 Israeli (the equivalent of 

US$1,000,000) counterpart funds in Israel. I urge the committee to authorize provisioning of these funds.

There is good reason to grant their request; the project has more to recommend itself than most. Hadassah is a voluntary non-profit American group with a long history of health assistance in Palestine and now Israel. Its medical school is the best in the country, affiliated with the Hebrew University. 

The institution is administered directly by Americans, and they are assisted by a committee of superb American physicians. Besides the qualifications of its sponsors, the school has a great deal to recommend itself. It maintains a nursing school with a student body of 150; a medical school with 747 students; the only dental school in Israel; schools of social medicine and public health, occupational therapy, and pharmacy; and an Afro-Asian Institute to train people from developing nations. It provides ongoing post-graduate medical education for practicing physicians; an exchange fellowship program with the 

United States and several European countries; extensive research facilities; and a six-hundred bed teaching hospital and outpatient clinic. And finally,

it operates an experimental preventive medicine health service at an adjacent village. This is a pilot plant, where medical teams provide total physical and mental care for entire families. 

The medical school and its satellite institutions provide important training. The largest portion of the student body are Israelis; its graduates go on to important positions in other hospitals. Also, in keeping with American feeling about helping developing countries, Africans and people from other parts of Asia are trained there and can return to their homes equipped to establish teaching facilities of their own. In addition, the hospital has sent teams to Asian and African countries to set up clinics, especially for treatment of eye disease.

Why should we help this group to continue its work? In the first place, the notion that their project should be disqualified because it is not new is absurd. It is clear that this particular center is expanding its services in response to internal Israeli problems (such as the experimental total medicine approach in the village), and also to help others with experience similar to its own.

From a more positive point of view, this medical school is largely responsible for the good health care in Israel. Minimal public health standards are something no developing country can do without, and with our continued support this project can be a very effective model for people from other new nations. 

Another aspect of the hospital's importance is its support and management. 

It is based upon cooperation of public and private sources, with management by the private agency. Our government is spared the trouble and expense of operating and/or approving operations, and at the same time, the school is assured of American support without any tincture of propaganda, and with some flexibility which is often missing from government operations. The project can be a model for other developing countries as an example of efficient and "free" but definitely American aid.

And finally, the location and disposition of Israel makes our continued support of the hospital a great potential source of expanding good will. The hospital is beginning to expand into a training center for other nationalities, and with our encouragement and support will be able to develop itself much more quickly. This can become an experiment wherein American money helps another country to give its own foreign aid, quite distinct from the dollars necessary to start and help maintain it. Our dollars can help to develop a kind of Medical School of the East, providing the basis for vast expansion of health services in very backward areas, in a way that would be impossible for us even to begin to do alone. Besides the obvious accomplishments of training health personnel and keeping a lot more people healthy, such a center could have great innovative impact on our foreign aid policy. The example of close cooperation with Americans, on a private and public basis shows the clear and positive gains that are possible from such an affiliation. 

The school services all aspects of health needs in its country, and continues to expand and develop and create new ways of doing it better. 

It is the pacesetter for health standards in the country. And it is actively beginning to help other new nations to solve their public health problems by training personnel and establishing clinics. Finally, the new aspect of our helping others to give foreign aid is an important first step toward sharing our responsibilities. 

When an institution asks to take the initiative, in this way; when it acts effectively to deal with a country's problems; when it continues to develop and innovate; when it starts to share problems; then our foreign aid program must find room to accommodate such effectiveness. 

I strongly urge that the Committee take the necessary action on this urgent appeal of the Hadassah organization. 

STATEMENT OF JACK E. CORBETT, REPRESENTING THE DIVISION OF PEACE AND WORLD ORDER, GENERAL BOARD OF CHRISTIAN SOCIAL CONCERNS OF THE METHODIST CHURCH 

Honorable Chairman and distinguished members of the Foreign Affairs Com mittee. I am Jack E. Corbett, Director of the Washington Study Program of the General Board of Christian Social Concerns of the Methodist Church.

I am presenting this testimony for that organization and wish to express on their

behalf my sincere gratitude for this opportunity to support the foreign economic aid proposals now under consideration. 

THE POSITION OF THE METHODIST CHURCH 

The last meeting of the General Conference of the Methodist Church, which was composed of 1,400 lay and ministerial representatives of the more than ten million Methodists of the United States, met in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania in 1964 and approved the following statement: "The desperate unmet needs of people in this world are of grave concern to Christians. The economic gap between the rich nations and the poor nations is widening as time elapses. The population explosion further jeopardizes the stability and progress of many lands. "We believe that economic assistance, which seeks to make the benefits of scientific advance and industrial progress available for the improvement of underdeveloped areas, is an example of both Christian love and practical international brotherhood. "All programs of technical assistance and economic aid should be designed primarily to benefit the people of underdeveloped countries and their economies rather than to serve political or military purposes. For maximum effectiveness, it is important that these programs be on a long-range basis. "We endorse the principle of multilateral assistance, especially through the U.N., and urge upon the nations wholehearted and generous participation in 

U.N. development programs. The Bible and the history of mankind contain ample warning to affluent peoples who will not share their abundance." 

This declaration represents the official position of The Methodist Church as taken by the General Conference, the church's highest authoritative body. The 

General Conference includes men and women from all walks of life-businessmen, farmers, lawyers, teachers, scientists, housewives, and clergymen. 

At this point I would like to lift up certain portions of our official policy statement on "World Economic Development" for interpretation and personal comment.

LONG-RANGE PROGRAMS 

General Conference delegates declared: "For maximum effectiveness. it is important that these programs be on a long-range basis." We recognize that may be ideal and impossible at this juncture of history. Yet we should not sweep our minds clear of this worthy objective for the future. If our nation is to engage seriously in committing ourselves at the point of helping nations to build the kind of infrastructure-such as dams, roadways, and power systemsnecessary for the economies of newly developing nations to thrive. then we must be prepared to engage in long-term agreements. Here, our credibility-a matter of substantial importance to Christians-is at stake. For the question is: Can nations involved in long-range projects risk placing their confidence in a United 

States which can make commitments only a year at a time? Or again: Does one-year authorization lend itself to making credible a consistently expressed aim of the United States-that recipient nations submit long-range goals and plans for their achievement. 

SEPARATION OF THE ECONOMIC FROM THE MILITARY 

"9 

Methodist leadership meeting at Pittsburgh in 1964 stated: "All programs of technical assistance and economic aid should be designed primarily to benefit the people of underdeveloped countries and their economies rather than to serve political or military purposes.' Coupling military assistance and economic aid in the same program has often served to confuse ultimate U.S. objectives. While economic aid has largely been used to help people in need, military assistance has often served, unintentionally, to either entrench dictators in power or to stir bitter enemies to combat against one another, both using U.S. furnished weaponsas in the recent India-Pakistan clash over Kashmir. Although it is recognized that complete separation of the economic from the military may not be possible, one step in this direction could be to separate these through two independent authorization bills as proposed by the Administration this year. Methodist leadership has felt that the economic development program would best stand on its own, untarnished by some of the negative aspects resulting from the use of U.S. military aid.

INCREASED

MULTILATERAL ASSISTANCE 

The official position of Methodist leaders has affirmed: "We endorse the principle of multilateral assistance, especially through the U.N., and urge upon the nations wholehearted and generous particiaption in U.N. development programs." 

Undoubtedly there is a place for bilateral programs where certain specific U.S. foreign policy interests are of paramount concern. However, it appears that both Christian compassion and the overall objectives of the United States are best served through channeling a substantial portion of U.S. funds through 

United Nations organizatons such as the World Bank, the Internatonal Develop ment Association, the Special Fund, and the Expanded Technical Assistance 

Program. Multilateral assistance seems more desirable since, when a newlydeveloping nation applies for aid from a U.N. agency, it must sell this proposal to the committee on its own merits quite aside from any political considerations. 

Also, U.S. development dollars tend to go further when given through international agencies contributed to by many nations of the world. Methodist leaders have viewed multilateral assistance, not only as a means of preserving the dignity of the recipient, but also as a step toward the kind of international cooperation that makes for peace.

GREATER FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Methodist General Conference delegates declared: "The Bible and the history of mankind contain ample warning to affluent peoples who will not share their abundance." The serious threat of starvation in India this summer is one evidence of the disturbing need that continues to plague our consciences. A few years ago the United Nations established one percent of a country's Gross National Product as a guide for the developed nations in determining their giving to international development programs. It appears that the United States provides about one-half of one percent of its GNP if one adds to our foreign aid bill appropriations our contributions in support of the Peace Corps, Food for Peace, the International Development Association, World Bank, Asian Bank, etc. Therefore, it is questionable as to whether or not the United States, as the richest nation in the world, is doing enough. France, for instance, gives over one percent of its GNP to development projects. And the President of the World 

Bank has recently stated that the underdeveloped world could usefully absorb about $3 or $4 billion more in development funds if these were available. 

Thus, Methodist leadership has called for a more "generous" program in sharing our abundance-a program which represents, not just political considerations, but a continuing compassion for those afflicted by poverty, illiteracy, and disease. 

This would require that the United States and other developed nations allocate substantial resources over many years if serious efforts are to be undertaken to implement our worldwide commitment.

We appreciate the opportunity to present this testimony and urge a strengthened economic aid program that the day forecast by the ancient prophet may come to pass-when the builders will outstrip the destroyers.
